1. Whoever raised that desire of your holiness, may he himself satisfy it. Although we do not presume that what we are going to say is our harvest, but that of God, nevertheless, with more reason we repeat what the Apostle humbly said: We have this treasure in clay vessels so that the excellence of the power may be God's and not ours. We have no doubt that you remember our promise. We did it in the presence of him for whom we now fulfill it. Well, at the time of doing it we asked him to be able to fulfill it; and if now it is a reality, we have received it from him. Your charity will remember that on the morning of the Nativity of the Lord we postponed resolving the question that had been proposed, because there were many who celebrated with us the dignified solemnity of that day, even those for whom the word of God is usually heavy.' Now, however, I consider that no one has come who does not want to listen to it. SERMO

CAPUT I. — 1. Tractanda quaestio proposita in die natali Christi. Spvciaculorum dics.—Expectationem Caritatis vestrae ille impleat, qui cxcitavit. Etsi cnim quae dicen sunt vobis, non nostra sed Dei esse praesumimus; tamen multo magis nos dicimus, quod humiliter dicit Apostolus: Habcmus thcsaurum istum in vasis fictilibus, ut eminentia virtutis Dei sit, et non ex nobis (2 Cor 4,7). Non dubitamus itaque meminisse vos pollicitationis nostrae. In ipso [333] promissimus, per quem nunc reddimus. Nam et cum promitteremus, ab ipso petebamus: et cum reddimus, ab ipso accipimus. Meminit autem Caritas vestra nos morning Natalis Domini distulisse quam solvendam proposuimus quaestionem; This is not the only occasion in which Augustine speaks of deferring a question for another day for the simple fact of a massive and occasional attendance that would not withstand a long stay in the temple. In Treatise 8:13 to the Gospel of Saint John it says: «If it pleases your charity, we will defer until tomorrow what concerns the mystery of this miraculous fact, so as not to tire your weakness and mine too much. Today perhaps there are many here because of the solemnity of the day, not because of hearing the sermon. Tomorrow, those who come, let them come and listen. In this way the diligent will not be disappointed nor will we be a burden to others. See also sermon 68,1 ( = Mai 126).

Our word will not, therefore, be for deaf ears or dull spirits. That your expectation is a prayer for me. But there is something else. Being the day of the muñera1 drove many away from here. We urge you, brothers, to worry about their salvation as much as we do. Also pray to God intensely for those who have not yet given themselves over to the spectacles of the truth, because they are involved in those of the flesh. I know, and of this I am certain, that there are now some among you who despised them; but they break what they themselves sewed. Men change, for better and worse. Examples of this arise every day, which alternately produce joy and sadness in us. We rejoice with those who correct themselves and we are sad for those who go wrong. For this reason the Lord does not say that he who began will be saved, but rather: He who perseveres to the end will be saved. 2. He not only added to his flock the spectators of the frivolous games, but also some who are there on the scene: could he have done something more sublime? He hunted for salvation not only the partisans of the hunters, but the hunters themselves, by becoming a spectacle himself. Listen how. He said it himself; He himself predicted it before the show, and through the word of the prophet he predicted what was going to happen, already taking it for granted. Per feminam venenum, per feminam salus.—Hoc ergo ut faceret Dominus noster Iesus Christus, utique nascendo de femina, filius hominis factus est. At enim si non nasceretur de María virgine, quid esset minus? Dicit aliquis: Homo esse voluit: esset homo, non tamen de femina nasceretur: non enim et primum hominem quem fecit, ex femina fecit. Ad hoc vide quid responderatur. You say, ad nascendum utquid elegerit feminam? Respondetur tibi: Immo ad nascendum cur fugeret feminam? Puta me non posse ostende quid elegerit, ut de femina nasceretur: tu ostende quid fugere in femina debuit. Sed aliquando iam dicta sunt, quia utique si fugeret feminae uterum, velut significaret se ex illa contaminan potuisse. Quanto autem erat per substantiam suam immaculabilior, mucho non debuit formidare uterum carnis, quasi posset inde maculan: sed natus de femina, This is an idea constantly repeated by the Saint. What interests Augustine above all in the story of the Lord's temptations is to show Christ as the Christian's teacher; If he wanted to be tempted it was to give his future disciples a lesson on how to behave in temptation. In this regard, you can see Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 52,3; Ennarration to Psalm 30,11, s.1,10; 90,11, 7; Sermons 210.3; 313 E,4 ( = GUELF. 28). The human sex is made up of males and females. If, then, being a man (as it was appropriate for him to be) he had not been born of a woman, women would lose hope, remembering their first sin: the first man was seduced by a woman. They would think that there was absolutely no hope for them in Christ. Coming as a man, he chose the virile sex, and being born as a woman, he consoled the female sex, as if speaking and saying: “So that you may know that the creature of God is not evil, but that it was evil will that perverted it, when at the beginning I made man, I made him male and female. Therefore I do not condemn the creature that I created, but the sins that I did not commit. Both sexes recognize their dignity; one and the other confess their evil and both of them hope for salvation. The woman gave the poison to the man who was going to be deceived; May the woman also offer salvation to the man who is to be redeemed. Let the woman compensate for the sin of the man whom she seduced, by giving birth to Christ. For this reason, it was the women who before anyone else announced the resurrection of God to the Apostles. A woman announced her husband's death in paradise; Women also announced salvation to men in the Church. There are blind people who strive to make a problem of something that the entire world of the earth already believes, trying to blind others, without seeing what should be seen, at the same time they try to destroy what should be believed. They reply saying: “Do not burden us with the authority of the world of the earth 9, let us look at the Scripture. Do not act with demagoguery; the crowd, deceived, is on your side. To this I respond first: «Is the crowd, deceived, on my side? This crowd was once a small group. How did that crowd come to be that was announced so far in advance with such dimensions? I'm not saying: it was a small group, but: it was only one: Abraham. Observe, brothers; At that time, Abraham was the only one in the whole world, the only one among all the men scattered throughout the entire world, among all the peoples; the only one to whom God said: In your descendants all Apostoli erant gentibus nuntiaturi will be blessed: Apostolis feminae nuntiarunt. Nemo ergo calumnietur Christo nato ex femina, de quo sexu Liberator maculari non posset, et quem sexum Creator commendare debenet. CAPOT III.—4. Evangelii fides toto orbe recepta.—Sed, inquiunt, quomodo credituri sumus natum ex femina Christum? Respondeam: Ex Gospel quod praedicatum est et praedicatur universe orbi terrarum. Sed rei iam creditae per omnem terram quaestionem conantur ingerere caeci, excaecare alios affectantes, et non videntes quod videndum est, dum conveliere conantur quod credendum est. Respondent enim, et dicunt: Noli nos auctoritate orbis terrarum premere; ipsam Scripturam considermus. Noli populariter agere: multitudo tibi seducta favet. Primo hic responded: Multitudo seducta mihi favet? Haec multitudo, paucitas Fuit. Unde crevit haec multitudo quae in istis incrementis both ante nuntiata est? Non enim crescere visa est, quae non est praevisa. Non dico: Paucitas erat; unus erat Abraham. Consider yourself, fratres, unus erat Abraham per totum mundum illo tempore, per totum orbem terrarum inter omnes homines, Inter omnes gentes, cui homini dictum est: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes (Gen 22,18).

Quod credidit unus Auctoritas is one of the arguments that, according to the rhetors of antiquity, had to be resorted to to prove one's position (QUINTILIAN, Institutio oratoria V, 11,36-64). On the other hand, Augustine very frequently resorts to the auctoritas, which represents the entire globe of the earth already present in Christ to prove the truth of the Christian faith. In this regard, the following texts can be seen, among others: customs of the Church I, 12; The usefulness of believing 17.31; The true religion 47; Against Faust III, 2; XXIII, 9; XVIII, 4; Letters 118.32; 102.14; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 7,5; Sermon 116,3.

So, with an affectionate heart, without the slightest hesitation, we answer yes, that Matthew is an evangelist. "Do you believe him?" they reply. Who does not answer: "Yes, I give him credit"? CAPUT VI.—Quomodo autem natus sit, et inter homines apparuerit, narrari iam debent; et consequens est ipsa narratio, per quam credimus Dominum nostium lesum Christum non solum natum de Deo sempiterno, coaeternum ei qui genuit ante omnia tempora, ante omnem creaturam, per quem facta sunt omnia; sed etiam iam natum de Spiritu sancto ex virgine Maria, quod pariter confitemur. Reminiscimini enim et nostis (Catholicis quippe loquor fratribus meis) have this fidem nostram, hoc nos profiteri et confiten. Pro ista fide interfecta sunt millia martyrum, toto orbe terrarum.

Those who seek to abrogate faith in the Holy Books 12 also want to mock what follows, as if to show us that our faith is reckless: When Mary, her mother, was married to Joseph, before they began to live together, she found herself pregnant by the work of the Holy Spirit. José, her husband, as was fair, not wanting to betray her, decided to leave her secretly. Knowing that she was not in a state due to his work, with some logic he already considered her an adulteress. Being fair, as the Scripture says, and not wanting to give it away, that is, divulge it, since many codices also have this word u, he decided to abandon it in secret. He is certainly disturbed as a husband, but he is not angry as a just man. So much holiness is attributed to this man that he neither wanted to have an adulteress with him, nor did he dare to punish her by denouncing her. He decided to leave her secretly, he says, because he neither wanted to punish her nor reveal her. See, then, his sincere holiness. Wanting to have her with him was not the reason he wanted to forgive her. There are many who, out of carnal love, forgive their adulterous wives, and want to retain them even though they are adulteresses to satisfy carnal lust. This righteous man does not want to have her with him; Therefore his love is not carnal. And yet, he doesn't want to punish her; then his forgiveness comes from mercy. This is a great righteous one! Nor does he retain the adulteress, and the reason for forgiveness does not come from libidinous love; and yet neither does it. Conceptio Christi de Spiritu sancto. Number of generations. lili enim per calumnias suas ad The same idea in sermon 225,2: her husband was the witness of her virginity so that no one would think that she was pregnant due to adultery.

Saint Jerome is more lavish in listing reasons why Saint Joseph was associated with the work: to show Mary's lineage; so that she would not be stoned to death as an adulteress; so that he would have company in the exile to Egypt and to deceive the devil, who was unaware of the virginal conception (Commentary on Matthew I 72-79). The word salvator does not belong to classical Latin. Augustine reminds his listeners of this on some occasion: "The terms salvare and salvator were not Latin before the coming of the Savior" (Sermon 299,6). It is, therefore, a term forged by Christians in imitation of the Greek sotér. In the aforementioned sermon Augustine also mentions the objections that the grammarians put to his use, objections that were not strange to the Hippo preacher himself in his early Christian days. In fact, at first he only used more classical terms, even if they were pagan: in The Happy Life 36, for example, he used Uberator, and in Faith and the Symbol 6 he used reparator.

They invite us and lead us to talk about it. If we live religiously, if we believe in Christ, if we do not intend to fly the nest before our time, this is what they lead us to: the knowledge of the mysteries. Your holiness, observe the usefulness of heretics, usefulness from the point of view of God, who knows how to use evil people well. As for them, they are rewarded according to what they intended, not according to the good that God brings out of their actions. For example, how much good he did not get from Judas! By the passion of the Lord all peoples were saved. But, so that the Lord would suffer, it was Judas who handed him over. God, while redeeming the people with the passion of his Son, punishes Judas for his crime. No one would discuss the mysteries hidden in that number, everyone being content with the simplest faith, and therefore no one would find them, because no one would unravel them, if it were not for the fact that the challengers give the call. When heretics present their objections, those who are small are disturbed; When troubled, they search; and their search is like the blows of the head on the mother's breasts, so that they give as much as is just for the child. Troubled, they search; Those who, on the other hand, have learned and know the mysteries, because they have scrutinized them and God opened them to them in response to their call, these in turn reveal them to those who are disturbed. And so it happens that heretics, while with their objections they try to lead to error, are useful in finding the truth. If it did not have mendacious adversaries, the truth would be sought with less diligence. It is appropriate, says the Apostle, that there be heresies. And, as if we were asking him the reason, he added id nos inviting, et adducunt. Si pie vivamus, si Christum credamus, si non de nido ante tempus cupiamus volare, ad id nos adducunt, ut mysteria cognoscamus. Intendat itaque Sanctitas vestra utilitatem haereticorum; et utilitatem quidem secundum Deum, etiam malis bene utentem. Secundum ipsos vero hoc redditur, quod voluerunt; non hoc quod de ipsis Deus bene facit. Sicut de luda quantum boni fecit? Passione Domini salvae factae sunt gentes. Sed ut pateretur Dominus, ludas eum tradidit. Deus ergo et gentes liberat passo Filio, et Iudam punit pro scelere suo. Sacramenta enim quae illie latent, nemo discussret, simpliciore contentus fide; et ideo nemo inveniret, quia nemo discussret, nisi pulsantibus calumniatoribus.

Cum enim haeretici calumniantur, parvuli perturbantur: cum perturbantur, inquirunt: inquisitio eorum, quasi percussio est de capite in ubera matris, ut tantum manent, quantum parvulis sat est. lili turbati quaerunt; qui autem norunt et didicerunt, quia scrutati sunt, et aperuit illis pulsantibus Deus, aperiunt et ipsi turbatis. Et sic fit ut illi sint useful ad inveniendam veritatem, dum calumniantur ad seducendum in errorem. Neglegentius enim veritas quaereretur, si mendaces adversaries non haberet. Oportet enim, inquit, et haereses esse. Et quasi quae-

immediately: That those who enter may be manifested, you are of proven virtue. 12. What do they say then? The following: Matthew, after enumerating the generations, says that from Abraham to David there are fourteen, fourteen from David to the transmigration to Babylon and as many from the transmigration to Christ. Multiply fourteen by three, and it becomes forty-two. If, however, you count them one by one, it turns out that there are only forty-one. From here, they challenge the text and, mockingly, insult those who believe in it. What does it mean when it is said in the Gospel that it is fourteen times three, and yet, counting them all, it is found that they are not forty-two, but forty-one? Without a doubt, a great mystery is hidden there. We are happy, and for this we thank God, that, as an opportunity for us as challengers, we have found something that the more hidden it was for us to search for, the greater the delight it will cause once discovered 16. As we said previously, we are going to present a spectacle for your mind. From Abraham to David there are fourteen generations. At this point, we begin to count from Solomon: David, in fact, begat Solomon. Therefore, the series begins with Solomon and reaches Jeconiah, in whose life the transmigration to Babylon took place.

The number of generations of this group is also fourteen, counting Solomon as the head of the series and also counting Jeconiah, with whom the series itself closes; Only by counting like this does the number fourteen result. The third group, in turn, begins by telling Jeconiah again. 13. Pay attention to your holiness: it is something mysterious and sweet. I confess to you that this is how it is for my heart, and I think that once I have explained it and you have liked it, you will say the same. Pay attention, then. From Jeconiah, with whom the third series begins, to the Lord Jesus Christ, there are fourteen generations. Jeconiah, therefore, is counted twice: as the last of the other series and as the first of this one. Someone will ask: "Why is Jeconiah counted twice?" Nothing happened in ancient times among the people of Israel that was not a figure of what was going to happen in the future. Not without reason, then, Jeconiah is counted twice. If there is a dividing sign between two fields, be it a boundary stone or some type of fence, whoever is on the other side measures to the same fence, and whoever is on the other side also measures to the fence, so that it is counted twice as the starting point. We must now explain why the same was not done in the junction between the first and second series, since from Abraham to David we count fourteen generations, and then, starting with Solomon, that is, without repeating David, another fourteen. A great mystery is hidden here. Pay attention to your holiness.

The transmigration to Babylon took place when Jeconiah was made king upon the death of his father. Then the kingdom was taken from him and another was proclaimed king in his place. But it was during Jeconiah's life that the transmigration to the Gentiles took place. No guilt is indicated in Jeconiah to deprive him of the kingdom; On the contrary, the sins of those who succeeded him are abundantly proclaimed. The consequence is, therefore, captivity; The march towards Babylon begins. It's not just the bad ones who march; The saints also go with them. The prophet Ezekiel was in that captivity; Daniel was also there; There are also the three children who became famous in the midst of the flames. They all went, fulfilling the prophecy of the prophet Jeremiah. 14. Remember Jeconiah, who, rejected through no fault of his own, ceased to reign there and passed over to the Gentiles at the time of the transmigration to Babylon; see in it an anticipated image of what was going to happen with our Lord Jesus Christ. The Jews did not want our Lord Jesus Christ to reign over them, even though they found no fault in him. They rejected him in his own person and in that of his servants, and thus the passage to the Gentiles was effected, as in other times to Babylon. Jeremiah also proclaimed that it was the Lord who ordered the march to Babylon. And those who told the people not to do it, he called false prophets, even though they presented themselves as prophets. Those who read Scripture, remember it with us; Those who don't read it, believe us. To those who refused to go to Babilo-

nia, Jeremiah, in the name of God, threatened them; To those who went, however, he promised rest and a certain happiness, resulting from the planting of vineyards and orchards and the abundance of their fruits. In what way was what was previously a figure, namely, the passage of the Jewish people to the Gentiles, carried out in reality? Where did the Apostles come from? Did they not belong to the Jewish people? Where did Paul himself come from? For I also, he says, am an Israelite, of the race of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. There were many Jews who believed in the Lord. From among them the Apostles were chosen. From among them came more than five hundred brothers who deserved to see the Lord after the resurrection. Of the same people were the one hundred and twenty who were in a house when the Holy Spirit arrived. And once the Jews rejected the word of truth, what does the Apostle say to them according to the account of the Acts of the Apostles? We had been sent to you, he tells them; But since you have rejected the word of God, we are going to the Gentiles. There was, therefore, a transmigration to Babylon adapted to the economy typical of the time of the Lord's incarnation, an economy that was already announced in the time of Jeremiah. But what does Jeremiah say to the deportees in relation to these Babylons? In their peace will be your peace. Israel, in the person of Christ and the Apostles, passed to Babylon, that is, the Gospel reached the Gentiles. What does the Apostle say on such an occasion, repeating in a certain way the words spoken then by Jeremiah? I pray that above all requests, prayers, supplications, thanksgivings be made for

At that time, then, the transmigration to Babylon took place through Jeconiah, who was allowed to reign over the people of the Jews, thus becoming the image of Christ, whom the Jews did not want as their king either. Israel passed to the Gentiles, that is, the preachers of the Gospel passed to the Gentile peoples. Why then do you wonder that Jeconiah is counted twice? If he was a figure of Christ in his passage from the Jews to the Gentiles, pay attention to what Christ is between Gentiles and Jews. Is he not the cornerstone? Consider that the angle is both the end of one wall and the beginning of another. You measure one wall to the cornerstone, and from there you measure the other. The stone that joins both walls is counted twice. Jeconiah, therefore, being an image or figure of the Lord, represented him as the cornerstone. Just as Jeconiah was not allowed to reign over

the Jews and immediately afterward the transmigration to Babylon took place, so also Christ, the stone that the builders rejected, was constituted as the head of the corner, so that the Gospel could pass to the Gentiles. Do not hesitate, therefore, to count the head of the angle twice, and you will get exactly the number written; That is to say, in this way there are three groups of fourteen each, and yet, added together, they do not result in forty-two generations, but forty-one. For as in a series of stones placed in a straight line, they are all counted one by one, in the same way, when the series is twisted so as to form an angle, the stone that forms it is appropriately counted twice because it belongs both to the series that finds its end in it and to the one that takes its beginning. The same thing happens in the series of generations: while the people are limited, they remain with the number of fourteen, without making an angle; but when the series twists for the transmigration to Babylon, it can be said that the angle is formed with Jeconiah, so that it is convenient to count him twice as a figure of that other cornerstone worthy of veneration, Christ. 16. The classic form of adoption gave the adoptee the status of son (filiusfamilias) of the new family with all the relative duties and rights, especially with regard to inheritance; He received the name and rank of the adoptive father: a commoner adopted by a patrician became a patrician, and vice versa. There was also a later evolution in this. Roman law, in addition to authentic marriage (iustae nuptiae), admitted concubinage, a form of life in common between a man and a woman that was distinguished from marriage itself in that it was not celebrated either because it was not possible (for example, due to different social status), or because the people involved did not want it. In the latter case, only the will of the parties concerned meant that it was not an authentic marriage. Of course, this concubinage could not coexist with authentic marriage, nor with two women at the same time. The children of this union were called spurious or natural; They took the name and status of the mother, since the father did not have patria potestas in front of them. Matthew follows the descending line, to signify our Lord Jesus Christ who descended to bear our sins, so that all peoples would be blessed in the descendants of Abraham. Luke, on the other hand, follows the ascending line and begins to count the generations not from the moment of the Lord's birth, but from the narration of his baptism by John. Luke, however, who follows the ascending line of generations from the baptism of the Lord, enumerates seventy-seven, beginning with our Lord Jesus Christ, ascending through Joseph, and reaching God through Adam. 'Quomodo, inquit, explicaberis ab his angustiis?' This heresy flourished in the 2nd and 3rd centuries. Its best-known representatives were Noetus of Smyrna, Sabellius and Praxeas.

8. You like the proposed difficulty. God help us so that you also like it once it is resolved. Pay attention to what I say, so that it frees both me and you. In the name of Christ we remain in the same faith, under the same Lord we live in the same house, under one head we are members of the same body, and the same spirit animates us. So that the Lord can get us all out of the trouble of this very difficult problem, to me who speak to you and to you who listen to me, this is what I say: «It is the Son, not the Father, who was born of the Virgin Mary; but both the Father and the Son carried out that same birth which is of the Son and not of the Father. It was not the Father who suffered, but the Son; but both the Father and the Son worked such a passion. Not the Father was resurrected, but the Son; but the resurrection was the work of the Father and the Son. It seems we are now free from this difficulty, but perhaps only because of my words; Let's see if the divine ones also confirm it. It is up to me to demonstrate with testimonies from Holy Scripture that the birth of the Father was accomplished by the Father and the Son. The same is said about the passion and resurrection. Both the birth and the passion and resurrection are exclusive to the Son. These three things, however, belonging to the Son alone, have not been the work of the Father alone, nor of the Son alone, but of the Father and the Son. Let's try each of these 4 things; you act as judges; The cause has been exposed, the witnesses parade. Tell me your court what is usually said to those who handle cases: "Try what you propose." With the help [21] 8. Placet uobis quaestio proposita; deus adiuuet, ut placeat et soluta. Ecce quod dico, ut me et uos ab his angustiis dominus libetet. In one enim fide stamus in nomine Christi, and in one domo sub one domino uiuimus, and in one corpore membra sub one capite sumus, and one spiritu uegetamur. Vt ergo dominus ab his angustiis molestissimae quaestionis liberet, et me qui loquor, et uos qui auditis, hoc dico: 'Filius quidem, inquam, non pater, natus est de uirgine Maria; sed ipsam natíuitatem filii, non patris, de uirgine Maria et pater et filius operatus est. Non est quidem passus pater, sed filius; passionem tamen filii et pater et filius operatus est. Non resurrectexit pater, sed filius; resurrectionem tamen filii et pater et filius operatus est.' De quaestione ista uidemur iam expediti, sed forte uerbis meis: uideamus etiam utrum uerbis diuinis.

Pertinet ergo ad me sanctorum librorum testimoniis demonstrare, natiuitatem filii et patrem operatum et filium, ita passionem, ita resurrectionem: ut, cum filii tantum sit et natiuitas et passio et resurrectio, haec tamen tria, quae ad filium solum pertinent, nec a patre solo facta sint, nec a solo filio, sed a patre utique et filio. Probemus singular; iudices auditis, causa proposita est, testes proceedant, Dicat mihi iudicium uestrum quod solet causa agentibus dici: 'Twelve quod promittis'. Twelve plans,
Augustine transfers the procedures of the forum to the preaching and exposition of the divine Word: there is a cause, a judge, witnesses, a legal expert, etc.

of the Lord I am going to test it, and I plan to do it by reading the celestial code. You listened to me carefully when I proposed the cause; Listen to me more carefully even now, as you try it. 9. I must begin with the birth of Christ, proving how it was the work of the Father and the Son, although what they both did belongs only to the Son. I quote Paul, distinguished doctor of divine law 5, since there are lawyers who claim Paul's authority to rule on disputes, even among non-Christians. I refer to Paul, I say, as a judge of peace and not of strife. Let the holy Apostle show us how the birth of the Son is the work of the Father. When the fullness of time came, he said, God sent his Son born of a woman, made under the law to redeem those who were under the law. You have heard him and, since his testimony is plain and clear, you have understood him. Behold, it is the work of the Father that the Son was born of a virgin. When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, that is, the Father, Christ. How did you send it? Made of a woman, made under the law. The Father, therefore, made him a woman and subject to the law. 10. Or are you worried that I said of a virgin and Paul of a woman? Don't worry, and let's not waste time; I'm not talking to incompetents. The Scripture says one thing and another: about a virgin and about a woman. As a virgin, when? Behold, a virgin will conceive and give birth to a Son. As a woman, you already heard it. There is no contradiction. It is characteristically domino, et caelestis iuris recito (358) lectionem. Intend audistis proposentem, audite intentius iam probantem. [22] 9. De Christi natiuitate mihi primodocendum est, quomodo eam et pater fecerit et filius fecerit, quamuis nonnisi ad filium pertineat quod fecit pater et filius. Paulum recito idoneum iuris diuíni consultum—nam et causidici habent hodie Paulum dictantem íura litigatorum, non christianorum—recito, inquam, Paulum dictantem pacis iura, non litis. Ostendat nobis sanctus apostolus, quomodo natiuitatem filii pater operatus sit: Cum autem uenit, inquit, plenitudo temporis, misit deus filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum sub lege, ut eos qui sub lege erant redimeret (Gal 4,4-5). Audistis, et quia planum et apertum est, intellexistis. Ecce pater fecit filium nasci de uirgine. Cum enim uenisset plenitudo temporis, misit deus filium suum, utique pater Christum. Quomodo eum misit? Factum ex muliere, factum sub lege (ib.). Fecit ergo eum pater ex muliere sub lege. 10.

An forte hoc mouet, quia 'de uirgine' dixi, et Paulus dicit ex muliere? Non moueat; non immoremur: ñeque enim rudibus loquor. Vtrumque de scriptura dicitur: et 'ex uirgine', et 'ex muliere'. 'Ex uirgine' quomodo? Ecce uirgo accipiet in ulero, et pariet filium (Is 7,14). 'Ex muliere' autem, sicut audistis. Non est contrarium. Proprietas enim locu5 The jurist was the interpreter of civil law, whose response, in typical law, had the force of law.

ristic of the Hebrew language to call all females women, and not just those who have lost their virginity 6. You have it evident in the book of Genesis, already when Eve was made: And he formed her into a woman. In another place the Scripture also says that God commanded to separate women who did not know a man's bed. This must be already known to you; Let us not stop at that, so that, with the help of the Lord, we can explain other things that will rightly require more time. 11. We have proven, then, that the birth of the Son was the work of the Father; Let us also prove that it was the Son's. What do we affirm when we say that the Son was born of the Virgin Mary? Who assumed the condition of a servant. What else does it mean for the Son to be born, but to receive the condition of a servant in the womb of the Virgin? This too is the work of the Son. Listen to him: Who, existing in the condition of God, did not consider being equal to God an object of plunder; but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son born of a woman, born of the seed of David according to the flesh. We see, then, that the birth of the Son is the work of the Father; but since the Son himself emptied himself by taking the condition of a servant, we see that it is also the work of the Son. Having proven this, let's move on. Receive carefully what follows in order. 12. Let us prove that the passion of the Son is also the work of both the Father and the Son. Is it the work of the Father? which

He did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all. Is it also the work of the Son? Who loved me and gave himself for me. The Father gave the Son and the Son gave himself. Only one suffered this passion, but it was the work of both. Like the birth, the passion of Christ was not the work of the Father without the Son, nor of the Son without the Father, the Father gave the Son and the Son gave to himself. What is typical of Judas, except sin? Let us leave this and come now to the resurrection.

tionis hebreae 'mulleres' non corruptas uirginitate sed feminas appellat. Habes euidentem scripturam Geneseos: quando ipsa primo [23] Eua facta est, formauit eam in mulierem (cf. Gen 2:22). Dicit etiam alio loco scriptura, iubere deum separan mulieres, quae non cognouerunt cubile uiri (cf Num 31,17-18; lud 21,11). Hoc ergo iam notum esse debent; nec teneat nos, ut allia, quae merit tenebunt, domino adiuuante explicare possimus. 11. Probauímus ergo natiuitatem filii a patre factam, probemus et a filio factam. Quid est natiuitas filii de uirgine Maria? Certe assumptio formae serui. Numquidnam est aliud nasci filio, nisi accipere formam serui in uirginis uterus? Audi quia hoc et filius fecit: Qui cum in forma dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est esse aequalis deo; sed semetipsum exinaniuit, formam serui accipiens (Phil 2,6-7). Cum uenit plenitudo temporis, misit deus filium suum ftctum ex muliere (Gal 4,4), qui factus est ei ex semine Dauid secundum carnem (Rom 1,3). Videmus ergo natiuitatem a patre factam; sed quia ipse filius semetipsum exinaniuit, formam serui accipiens, uidemus natiuitatem filii et ab ipso filio factam. Probatura est hoc. Transeamus hint. Intenti aliud accipite, quod ex ordine sequitur. 12. Probemus et passionem filii et a patre factam, et a filio factam. Faciat pater passionem filii: Qui proprio filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis
See note to sermon 49 A,

13. Let us see, in fact, that it is the Son who is resurrected, not the Father; but the resurrection of the Son is the work of the Father and the Son. Work of the Father: For this reason he exalted him and gave him a name above all names. Therefore, the Father resurrected the Son, exalting him and raising him from the dead. And did the Son resurrect himself? Yes, indeed. Alluding to his body, he said of the temple: Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up again. Finally, since the giving of life is included in the passion, so also in the resurrection the taking it back; Let us see, then, if the Son actually gave his life and the Father returned it to him, but not he to himself. That the Father returned it to him is evident. Referring to this, the psalm says: Raise me and I will give them what they deserve. Why do you expect me to say that the Son also came back to life? Let him say it himself: I have the power to give my life. I still haven't said what I promised. I only said: to give and you already acclaimed, poromnibus tradidit eum (Rom 8:32). Faciat et filius passionem suam: Qui me dilexit [24] et tradidit se ipsum pro me (Gal 2,20). (359) Tradidit pater filium, tradidit filius se ipsum. Passio haec uni facta est, sed ab utroque facta est. Sicut ergo natiuitatem, ita passionem Christi nec pater fecit sine filio, nec filius sine patre. Tradidit pater filium, tradidit filius se ipsum. Quid hic fecit ludas, nisi peccatum? Transeamus ethinc. Veniamus ad resurrectionem. 13. Videamus filium quidem, non patrem, resurgentem, sed resurrectionem filii et patrem et filium facientem. Operetur pater resurrectionem filii: Propter hoc enim exaltauit eum a mortuis, et donauit ei nomen, quod est super omne nomen (Phil 2,9). Resuscitauit ergo pater filium exaltando eum et excitando eum a mortuis. Numquid et filius resuscitat semetipsum? Resuscitat plane. In figuram sui corporis of the temple he said: Soluite templum hoc, et in triduo resuscitabo illud (lo 2,19). Postremo, sicut ad passionem pertinet animam seguiré, sic ad resurrectionem animam iterum sumere, uideamus si filius quidem animam suam posuit, et ei animam suam pater reddidit, non ipse sibi. Pater enim quia reddidit, manifestum est: inde enim psalmus dicit: ~Et suscita me, et reddam illis (Ps 40,11). Sed quia et filius animam suam sibi reddidit, quid a nobis exspectatis? Ipse dicat: Potestatem drool ponendi animam meam (lo 10,18). Nondum dixi quod promisi, ponendi dixi; thirst iam clamastis,

that you have anticipated. Having been instructed in the school of the celestial teacher, as those who attentively follow his lessons and piously give them, you are not ignorant of what follows: I have power, he said, to give my life and I have the power to take it back. 'No one takes it from me, but I give it and take it again. 14. We have kept our promise; We have proven, I believe, our statements with the very solid evidence of the testimonies of Scripture 8. Hold fast to what you have heard. I summarize it briefly, and I recommend that, as something extremely useful, in my opinion, you keep it in your minds. The Father was not born of the Virgin; However, this Virgin Birth was the work of the Father and the Son. The Father did not suffer on the cross; However, the passion of the Son is the work of the Father and the Son. The Father did not rise from the dead; However, the resurrection of the Son is the work of the Father and the Son. There you see the distinction of people and the inseparability of operations. Let us not say, then, that the Father does something without the Son, or the Son does something without the Father. Do the miracles that Jesus did worry us as if he had done something that the Father did not do? Where do you leave that: But the Father who abides in me, he does the works? What we have said were simple things; you just had to say them. It is not tiring to understand them, but you have to worry about remembering them. quia praeuolatis. Erudíti quippe in schola magistri caelestis, tamquam lectiones attempt [25] audientes, pie reddentes, quid sequatur non ignoratis: Potestatem, inquit, habeo ponendi animam meam, et potestatem babeo iterum sumendi eam. Nemo tollit eam a me, sed ego pono eam a me, et iterum sumo eam (lo 10,18). 14. Exsoluimus quae promisimus: propositiones nostras firmissimís, ut arbitror, ​​testimonyrum documentis probauimus. Have yourself quod audistis. Breuiter replied, et rem utilissimam, quantum existimo, mentibus uestris collocandam commendo. Pater non est natus de uirgine: natiuitatem tamen istam filii et pater et filius est operatus ex uirgine. Pater non est passus in intersection: passionem tamen filii et pater et filius operatus est. Non resurrection pater a mortuis: resurrectionem tamen filii et pater et filius operatus est. Habetis personarum distinctionem, et operationis inseparabilitatem. Non ergo dicamus, aliquid patrem operari sine filio, aliquid filium sine patre. An forte miracula, quae fecit Iesus, mouent uos, ne forte aliqua ipse fecerit quae non fecit pater?

Et ubi est: Pater autem in me manens facit opera sua? (14:10). Haec quae diximus plana erant, tantum digan erant: non laborandum ut intellegerentur, sed curandum ut commemorarentur. ' See the note to the sermon 19,4. Note the language from classical rhetoric: provere, propositiones, firmissima documenta, testimonia. Augustine never gave up on the well-learned rhetoric he had taught for several years.

15. I still want to add something, for which I require from you a truly more lively attention and devotion to God. Only bodies are subject to space and occupy place. Divinity is beyond corporeal places. Nobody looks for it as if it resides in space. It is everywhere, invisibly and inseparably: not here more and there less, but everywhere in its entirety and nowhere divided. Who sees this? Who understands it? Let's stop a little; We will remember who we are talking about and what we are talking about. This or that, whatever God is, let it be piously believed, holyly meditated upon, and to the extent that it is granted to us, to the extent that it is possible, let it be understood even if it is not possible to express it. Cease words, hold your tongue; wake up and lift your heart there. It is not something that has to rise to the heart of man, but something to which the heart of man has to rise. Let us pay attention to the creature: Since the creation of the world, the invisible of it is known by the mind through what has been made. Perhaps in the things that God made, with which we have a certain familiarity through custom, we can find some similarity that will serve to prove that there is a set of three things, which appear to us separately and act inseparably. 16. Hey, brothers; pay the utmost attention. See first of all what I intend: since the Creator is far above us, perhaps he can find such a similarity in the creature. Perhaps some of us, whose mind has been touched by the radiance of truth with a kind of 15. Aliquid adhuc uolo dicere, ubi uere et acriorem intentionem uestram requiro et deuotionem apud deum. Etenim locis corporalibus non tenentur nec (360) occupantur nisi corpora. Vltra corporal locos are diuínitas. Nemo eam tamquam spatio requirat. Vbique inuisibilis et inseparabilis adest: non in parte maior, in parte minor; sed ubique tota, nusquam diuisa. Quis uidet hoc? quis capit hoc? Compescamus nos: [26] meminerimus qui, unde loquamur. Illud, illud, quidquid est quod deus est, pie credatur, sanete cogitetur; et quantum datur, quantum potest, ineffabiliter intellegatur. Quiescant uerba, cesset lingua; cor excitetur, cor illuc leuetur. Non enim est illud tale, quod in cor bominis ascendat, sed quo cor hominis ascendat.

Adtendamus creaturam—inuisibilia enim eius a creature mundi per ea, quae jacta sunt, intellecta conspictunlur (Rom 1:20)—ne forte in his, quae fecit deus, in quibus habemus quamdam consuetudinis familiaritatem, inueniamus aliquam similarityinem, unde probemus esse aliqua tria, quae tria separabiliter proferantur, inseparabiliter operentur. 16. Heia, fratres, adestote toto animo. Videte prius quid promittam, ne forte in creatura inueniam quia creator a nobis excelsus est. Et forte uerba quisquam nostrum, cui fulgor ueritatis aliqua mentem quasi corus-

lightning, can appropriate those words: I said in my rapture. What did you say? I have been cast out from the presence of your ophos. It seems to me that whoever said this lifted up his soul to God and poured it out above himself; Upon hearing that he was told every day, Where is your God?, he came with a certain spiritual contact to that immutable light, a light that he could not endure due to the weakness of his gaze. Then he fell back into his illness and weakness, compared himself to it and experienced that the view of his mind could not yet adapt to the light of the Wisdom of God. And as this had happened to him in a state of rapture, abstracted from the bodily senses and absorbed in God, when in a certain way he was revoked by God to his condition of man, he exclaimed: I said in my rapture. In ecstasy I saw something that I could not endure for long; and returned to the mortal limbs and the many thoughts of mortals coming from the body that aggravates the soul, I said. What thing? I have been cast out from the presence of your eyes. You are very elevated; I am very low. What can we say, brothers, about God? If you have understood what you want to say, it is not God; If you could understand it, you understood something else instead of God. If you were able to understand something, your imagination has deceived you. If you could understand it, it is not God; If it is really about God, you did not understand it. How then do you want to talk about what you could not understand? 17. Let us see, therefore, if we can find something in the creatures with which we can prove that some set of three catione perstringit, potest dicere uerba illa: Ego dixi in éctasi mea. In ecstasi tua quid dixisti? Proiectus sum a facie oculorum tuorum (Ps 30,23). Etenim uidetur mihi iste, qui hoc dixit, leuasse ad deum animam suam, diffudisse super se animam suam, cum ei diceretur quotidie: Vbi est deus tuus? (cf. Ps 41,4) peruenisse spiritali quodam contactu ad illam [27] incommutabilem luzem, eamque infirmitate conspectus ferré non ualuisse, et in suam quasi aegritudinem atque langorem iterum recidisse, et comparasse se illi, et sensisse adhuc contemperan non posse aciem mentis suae luci sapientiae dei. Et quia hoc in éxtasi fecerat, abreptus a sensibus corporís et surreptus in deum, at ubi quodammodo a deo ad hominem reuocatus est, ait: 'Ego dixi in éxtasi mea (Ps 30,23).

Vidi enim nescio quid in ecstasi, quod diu ferré non potui; et, redditus mortalibus membris et multis mortalium cogitationibus a corpore quod aggrauat animam, say: quid? Proiectus sum a jacte oculorum tuorum (ib.). Longe sursum es, longe deorsum sum'. Quid ergo dicamus, fratres, de deo? Si enim quod uis dicere, si cepisti, non est deus. Si comprehendere potuisti, aliud pro deo comprehendisti. Si quasi comprehendere potuisti, cogitatione tua te decepisti. Hoc ergo non est, si comprehendisti; si autem hoc est, non comprehendisti. Quid ergo uis loqui, quod comprehendere non potuisti? 17. Videamus ergo, ne forte in creatura inueniamus aliquid, ubi

things, which manifest themselves separately from each other, act inseparably. Where are we headed? To heaven to dispute about the sun, the moon and the stars? Or, perhaps, to the earth to perhaps talk about the fruit trees, the other trees and the animals that fill it? Or are we to speak of heaven itself, or of the earth, which contain everything that is in heaven and earth? Oh man, how long will you be hanging around creation? Turn to yourself, contemplate yourself, probe yourself, examine yourself 9. If you look for in the creature some set of three things that manifest separately and that act inseparably, if you look for it in the creature, I repeat, look for it first in yourself. Are you not also a creature? You look for a similarity. Are you going to look for it in a beast? You were talking about God, when the idea came to you to look for a similarity. You spoke of the Trinity, of the ineffable Majesty; and because you failed in divine things, you confessed your weakness with due humility, and you turned to man. Examine it. Do you direct your search to the beast, the sun or a star? Which of these has been made in the image of God? You better look for such a thing in yourself, since you are better known. Indeed, God made man in his image and likeness. Search yourself; Possibly the image of the Trinity has left some vestige of the Trinity itself. What image? A created image that is far from the model; a resemblance and an image that is far from the original. It is not an image like the Son, which is what misprobemus aliqua tria et separabiliter demonstrari et inseparabiliter operate. What ibimus? Ad caelum, ut de solé et luna et sideribus disputemus? Ad terram, ut forte de frutectis, de arboribus, de animalibus terram implen tibus? An de ipso cáelo, an de ipsa terra, quae (361) continent 1281 omnia quae sunt in cáelo et in terra? Quamdiu, homo, circumis creaturam? Ad te redi: uide you, inspice you, discusses you. In creature quaeris aliqua tria et separatim demonstranda et inseparabiliter operantia. Si in creatura quaeris, in te prius quaere: non enim tu non es creatura? Similitudinem quaeris. Quaesiturus is in pecore? De deo enim loquebaris, cum quaereres quamdam similarityinem, de trinitate ineffabilis maiestatís loquebaris; et quia defecisti in diuinis, tuamque infirmitatem debita humilitate confessus es, ad humano uenisti. Ibi argues. Quaeris in pecore? quaeris in sole? in stella? Quid enim horum factum est ad imaginem et similarityinem dei?

Prorsus familiarius et melius aliquid horum quaeris ín te. Hominem enim deus fecit ad imaginem et simililudinem suam (cf. Gen 1:26). In te quaere, ne forte imago trinitatis habeat aliquod uestigium trinitatis. Et quae imago? Facta longe distans. Similarity tamen et imago longe distans. Non quomodo imago filius, hoc quod pater. Aliter enim imago in filio, aliter in speculo. Multum distance The return to one's own interiority is one of the pillars of Ogustinian spirituality. See Supplementary Note 38: Augustinian interiority vol. VII p.757.

more than the Father. One thing is the image that is reproduced in a mirror and another is the image that is reproduced in a child. One is very far from the other. In your child, you yourself are your image. Your child is the same as you in terms of nature. He is of the same substance as you, although he is a different person. Man is not, therefore, an image as is the only begotten Son, but was made in a certain image and in a certain likeness. Search within yourself for something, in case you can find a set of three things that are pronounced separately and act inseparably. I will search; search with me. Not I in you or you in me, but you within yourselves, and I within me. Let us jointly seek and jointly explore our common nature and substance. 18. Look, oh man, and see if what I am about to say is not true. Do you have a body? Do you have meat? I have it, you say. How else do I occupy a place and move from here to there? How do I hear the words of the speaker except through the ears of the flesh? How do I see the mouth of the speaker except with the eyes of the flesh? You have it, I know. There is no reason to tire for a long time over a manifest thing. Take your look further; observe what works through the flesh. You certainly hear with the ear, but it is not the ear that hears I0. There is someone inside who hears through the ear. You see through the eye; look at him. Did you know the house and despise him who lives in it? Does the eye see for itself? Is it not someone else who sees through him? I do not say: "The eye of a dead man does not see, from whose body he who inhabited it has gone"; What I am saying is that the eye of someone who is thinking about something else does not see the face of In filio, imago tua tu ipse es. Hoc est enim filius, quod tu natura. Substantia hoc quod tu, persona alius quam tu. Non ergo homo imago tamquam unigenitus filius, sed ad imaginem quamdam et ad quamdam similarityinem factus. Quaerat in se aliquid, si possit inuenire, et tria quaedam, quae separabiliter pronuntientur, inseparabiliter operentur. [29] Quaeram, quaerite mecum: non ego in uobis et uos in me, sed uos in uobis et ego in me: quaeramus communiter, et communem naturam atque substantiam communiter pertractemus. 18. Vide, homo, aduerte si uerum est quod dico. Habesne Corpus? do you have carnem? 'Habeo, inquis. Nam unde est unde in loco sum, unde loco in locum moueor? unde uerba loquentis audio, nisi per aurem carnis? unde os loquentis uideo, nisi per oculos carnis?' Habes, constat, nec diu satagendum est de re manifesta.

Vide aliquid aliud: uide quod operatur per carnem. Audis enim aure, sed non ab aure audis: alius est intus, qui audit per aurem. Vines per oculum; ipsum intuerc. An domum agnouisti, habitatorem neglexisti? Numquidnam uidet oculus per se ipsum? nonne alius est, qui uidet per oculum? Non dico: 'Non uidet oculus mortui, de quo constat corpore habitatorem abscessisse', sed ocu10
The same idea, regarding the eye in sermons 126,3 and 241,2.

who is present to him. So, look back at your inner man. It is there above all where we must look for the similarity of three things that manifest themselves separately and that act inseparably. CAPUT V.—5. Misericordes.—Attende quod sequitur: Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsorum miserebitur Deus. Fac, et fiet: fac cum altero, ut fiat tecum. Quia abundas et eges: abundas temporalibus, eges aeternis. Mendicum hominem audis, mendicus ipse Dei es. Petitur a te, et petis. Quod egeris cum petitore tuo, hoc aget Deus cum suo. Et plenus et inanis is: imple inanem de plenitudine tua, ut dei plenitudine impleatur ¡nanitas tua. CAPUT VI.—6. Mundicordes.—Attende quod sequitur: Beati mundl cordesi hoc est, qui mundi corde sunt; quoniam ipsi 'Deum videbunt, Hic est finis amoris nostri; finís quo perficiamur, non quo consumamur. Finitur cibus, finitur vestís: cíbus, quia consumitur edendo; you dress, quia perficitur texendo. Et illud finitur, et illud: sed finis iste pertinet ad consumptionem, ille ad perfectionem.

Quidquid agimus, quidquid berjg agimus, quidquid nitimur, quidquid laudabiliter aestuamus, quidquid inculpabiliter desideramus, ad Dei visionem cum venerit, plus non requj. remus. Quid enim quaerat, cui adest Deus? aut quid sufficiat ei, cui non sufficit Deus? Videre Deum volumus, videre Deum quaerimus, videre This thought is very common; see also sermons 61,4; 83.2; 123.5, etc. For him, he who does not possess God is a beggar, even if he abounds in all other kinds of goods (^.narrative to Psalm 144:22). Under different formulations the same idea is repeated in the sermons 53 A,*)

see him and we burn to achieve it. Who doesn't? But look what was said: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Prepare your heart to see. Speaking carnally, how is it that you desire the sunrise, having diseased eyes? If the eyes are healthy, that light will produce joy; If they are not, it will be torment. You will not be allowed to see with an impure heart what is not seen except with a pure heart. You will be rejected, pushed away; you won't see it. For blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. How many times have you repeated the word blessed? What are the causes that produce this happiness? What are the works, the duties, the merits, the awards? Until now, nowhere has it been said why they will see God. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who cry, because they will be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy. Nowhere has it been said why they will see God. We have come to the pure in heart; They were promised the vision of God. And not without reason, because there are the eyes with which God is seen. Speaking of these eyes, the apostle Paul says: Let the eyes of your heart be enlightened. At present, because of their weakness, these eyes are illuminated by faith; Then, once vigorous, they will be illuminated by reality itself. For while we live in the body, we are pilgrims far from the Lord. Indeed, we walk in faith and not in vision. What is said about us as we walk in the light of faith?

Deum inardescimus. Quis non? Sed vide quid dictum est: Beati mundicordes, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Hoc para, unde videos. Ut enim secundum carnem loquar, quid desideras ortum solís cum oculis lippis? Sani sint oculi, et erit lux illa gaudium: non sint oculi sani, erit lux illa lormentum. Non enim corde non mundo videre permitteris, quod non vkletur nisi corde mundo. Repelleris, aufereris, non videbis. Beati enim mundicordes, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Quoties blessed iam numeruvit? quas beatitudeinis causa, quae opera, quae doll, quae menta, quae praemia? Nusquam dictum est, Ipsi Deum videbunt. Beati pauperes *:iritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum. Beati mites: ipsi hereditale possidebunt terram. Beati lugentes: ipsi consolebuntur. Beati esurientes et sitíenles iustitiam: ipsi saturabuntur.. Beati misericordes: ipsi niiscricordiam consequentur. Nusquam dictum est, Ipsi Deum videbunt. Wntum est ad mundicordes, ibi visio Dei promissa est. Non sine causa, nisi quia ibi sunt oculi, unde videtur Deus. De his oculis Paulus aposlolus loquens ait: Illuminatos oculos cordis vestri (Eph 1,18). Modo ergo (indi isti pro sua infirmitate illuminantur fide: postea pro sua firmitate llluminabuntur specie. Quamdiu enim sumus in corpore, peregrinatnur a Domino. Per fidem enim ambulamus, non per speciem (2 Cor 5, 6 et 7).

Now we see darkly as in a mirror, then we will see face to face. 7. In this regard, do not think of a bodily face. For if, inflamed with the desire to see God, you prepare your bodily face to see him, you will also wish that God had the same. If, on the other hand, you have at least the idea that God is spiritual, so that you no longer think that he is something corporeal - which we talked about in more detail yesterday 6, although I do not know with what fruit; if we have already broken in your heart, as in the temple of God, the simulacrum of human form; If the passage in which the Apostle rebukes those who, believing themselves wise, became fools and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of a corruptible man, comes easily to your mind and possesses your interior; if you already detest and avoid this evil; if you purified the temple of the Creator; If you want him to come and make his home in you, then think worthy of the Lord with kindness and seek him with simplicity of heart. Consider to whom you say, if you say it, if you say it sincerely: To you my heart said: Your face I will seek. Let your heart also say it, and add: Your face, Lord, I must seek. You look for him well if you look for him with your heart. They talk about the face of God, the arm of God, the feet of God, the throne of God, the footstool of his feet, but do not think about human members. If you want to be a temple of truth, break the idol of Quamdiu autem in hac fide sumus, quid de nobis dicitur? Videmus nunc per speculum in aenigmate; tune autem facie ad faciem (1 Cor 13:12). 7. Dei facies et manus el pedes quid.-—Non hic corT367]porea facies cogitetur. Nam si accensus desidetio videndi Deum, faciem tuam praeparaveris corporalem ad videndum; talem faciem desiderabis et Dei. Si autem iam saltem spiritualiter de Deo sapis, ut Deum non cogites esse corporeum (unde diutius herí egimus, si tamen aliquid peregimus); si in corde vestro, tanquam in Templo Dei, formae humanoe fregimus simulacrum; si iam vobis bene venit inmentem, et viscera vestra interiora possedit, ubi detestatur Apostolus eos qui dicentes se esse sapientes, stulti facti sunt; et immutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei et similarityinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis (Rom 1,22.23). CAPUT VIL—Si iam tale malum detestamini, si adversamini, si Creatori mundatis templum suum, si vultis ut veniat et mansionem apud vos faciat: Sentite de Domino in bonitote, et in simplicitate corás quaerite illum (Wis 1,1).

Videte cui dicatis, si tamen dicitis, si I will see dicitis: Tibi dixit cor meum, Qt/aeram faciem tuam. Dicat et cor tuum, et adde, Vultum tuum, Domine, requiram (Ps 26,8). Bene enim requiris, quia corde requiris. Dicitur Dei vultus, dicitur Dei brachium, dicitur Dei manus, dicuntur Dei pedes, dicitur Dei sedes, dicitur scabellum pedum eius: sed noli membra humano cogitare. Si vis esse templum veritatis, frange idolum falsitatis. Manus Dei, potentia Dei. Facies Dei, notitia Dei. Pedes
This is probably referring to Sermon 23, which talks about the vision of God.

the falsehood. The hand of God is his power; his face, his knowledge; his feet, his presence; His throne, if you want, is you. Or will you dare to deny that Christ is God? "I don't deny it," you say. "Do you also grant that Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God?" “I grant it,” you say. Listen: The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom. Where does God have his throne but where he dwells? Where does he live but in his temple? Holy is the temple of God, which is you. See, then, how you conceive of God. God is spirit; It is advisable to worship him in spirit and in truth. Enter the ark of the covenant into your heart, if it pleases you, and let Dagon roll on the ground. Now, therefore, listen, and learn how you should desire God and how to prepare yourself to see Him. Blessed, he said, are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Why do you prepare the eyes of the body? If he could be seen with them, he would occupy a local space. He who is everywhere in his entirety does not occupy any space. Clean the eye with which you can see him. 8. Listen and understand me, if with your help I can explain myself. May He help us to understand the duties and rewards of which we have spoken and to see how they correspond to each other. What award, in fact, was mentioned that does not agree, that is not related to the respective obligation? Because the humble give the impression of being excluded from royalty, says the Lord: Blessed are the humble," for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Because meek men are easily excluded from their land, he said: Blessed are the meek, Dei, praesentia Dei. Sedes Dei, si vis, tu es. An forte deniale audebis Deum esse Christum? Non, inquis. Concedis et hoc, Christum Dei virlutem et Dei sapientiam? (1 Cor 1,24). Deum. Spiritus est Deus; in spiritu et veritate oportet adorare Deum (lo 4,24). videbunt. CAPUT VIII.—Quid praeparas oculos corporis? Si sic videbitur, in loco erit quod videbitur. Non est in loco qui ubique totus est.

Pracmia operibus congrua in sentcntiis beatitudinum.—Audi, et intellegc, si ipso iuvante potero explicare: adiuvet nos ad intellegendum omnia supradicta opera et muñera, quemadmodum congruentibus apposita sint. Ubi enim dictum est de praemio, quod non congrueret operi, quod non consonaret? Quia humiles quasi a regno videntur alieni: Beati, inquit, pauperes spiritu, quia ipsorum est regnum caelorum. Quia mites Ilumines facile excluduntur de terra sua: Beati, inquit, mites, quoniam ipsi

because they will inherit the land. The other beatitudes are manifest and clear, and are known spontaneously; They don't need anyone to explain them; only those who remember them. Blessed are those who cry. Who, if Hora, does not desire consolation? They, he said, will be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice. Who, if hungry and thirsty, does not seek satiety? They too, he said, will be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful. Who is merciful but he who desires that, because of the work he did, God behaves in the same way with him, that is, that he does to him what he does to the poor? Blessed, he said, are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy from God. See how, one by one, they all have the appropriate complement and nothing is promised as a reward that does not conform to the precept. The precept is that you be poor in spirit; The prize consists of the possession of the kingdom of heaven. The precept is that you be meek; The prize consists of possession of the land; The precept commands you to cry; The prize is to be consoled. The precept is that you hunger and thirst for righteousness; the prize, being satisfied. The precept is that you be merciful; the prize, getting mercy. In the same way, the precept is that you cleanse the heart; the prize, the vision of God. 9. Regarding these precepts and these rewards you must think correctly. When you hear: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God, do not think that the poor in spirit or the meek will not see him, nor those who cry, nor those who hunger and thirst for justice or the mercifulhereditate possidebunt terram. Iam cetera aperta sunt, clear, sua sponte cognoscuntur: disputatore non egent, commemoratore opus habent. Beati qui lugent. Quis lugens [368] non consolationem desiderat? Ipsi, inquit, consolebuntur. Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt iustitiam. Quis esuriens et sitiens non satietatem requirit? Et ipsi, inquit, saturabuntur. Beati mercies. Quis misericors, nisi qui optat ex ipso opere reddi sibi a Deo vicem, ut circa se fiat, quod circa pauperem facit? Beati, inquit, misericordes, quoniam ipsorum miserebitur Deus. Quomodo per ipsa singula singulis propria apposita sunt, et nihil adhibitum est in praemio, quod non congrueret praecepto? praeceptum est enim ut sis pauper spiritu: praemium est ut habeas regnum caelorum. Praeceptum est ut sis mitis: praemium est ut possideas terram. Praeceptum est ut sis lugens: praenium, ut consoleris.

Praeceptum est ut esurias et sites iustitiam: praemium, ut satureris. Praeceptum est ut sis misericors: praemium, ut misericordis consequaris. Sic praeceptum est ut mundes cor: praemium, ut videas Deum. CAPUT IX.—9. Visio Dei quomodo mundicordibus speciatim promissa.—Non ergo ita sapias in his praeceptis et praemiis, ut cum audis, Beati mundicordes, quoniam ipsi Deum vídebunt, putes pauperes spiritu non visuros, aut non visuros mites, non visuros lugentes, non visuros esurientes et sitientes iustitiam, non merciful visuros. Non arbitreris

you are Do not think as if only the pure of heart should see him, excluding the rest. Everyone is all of these things at once. They will certainly see Him, but not because they are poor in spirit, or merciful, or because they cry, or hunger and thirst for justice, or because they are merciful, but because they are pure in heart. It would be the same as if the bodily works were matched with the members of the body, and someone said, for example, “blessed are those who have feet, for they will walk; Blessed are those who have hands, for they will work; Blessed are those who have a voice, for they will cry out; Blessed are those who have mouth and tongue, because they will speak; blessed are those who have eyes, for they will see. In a similar way, pretending in a certain way spiritual members, he taught what corresponds to each. Humility is adequate to achieve the kingdom of heaven; meekness is to possess the land; crying is suitable for consolation, hunger and thirst for justice is suitable for society, mercy is suitable for obtaining mercy and a clean heart is suitable for seeing God. 10. If then we desire to see God, with what shall we cleanse this eye? Who will not worry, who will not look for something to clean the eye with which he can see the one he desires with all his heart? It is expressed in this divine testimony: Purifying their hearts with faith. Faith in God cleanses the heart, and the clean heart sees God. There are men who, deceiving themselves, sometimes conceive faith as if it were enough to just believe; and some, by the fact of believing, even if they live badly, promise themselves the vision of God eos tantum quasi visuros qui mundo sunt corde, illis a visione separatis. Omnia enim haec iidem ipsi sunt. Ipsi videbunt, et non ideo videbunt, quia pauperes spiritu sunt, quia mites sunt, quia lugentes, quia esurientes sitientesque iustitiam, quia misericordes: sed quia mundi sunt corde. Quemadmodum si corporalia opera membris corporalibus coaptarentur, ac diceret, verbi gratia, quisquam: Beati qui pedes habent, quia^ ipsi ambulabunt: beati qui manus habent, quia ipsi operabuntur: beati qui vocem habent, quoniam ipsi clamabunt: beati qui os et linguam habent, quoniam ipsi loquentur: beati qui oculos habent, ipsi enim videbunt. Sic tanquam spiritualia membracomponens, docuit quid ad quid pertineat.

Apta est humilitas ad habendum regnum caelorum; apta mansuetudo ad possidendam terram; aptus luctus ad consolationem; apta fames et sitis iustitiae ad saturitatem; apt mercy ad impetrandam misericordam; aptum mundum cor ad videndum Deum. CAPUT X.—10. Fide cor mundatur ad videndum ~Deum.—Si ergo desideramus videre Deum, oculus iste unde mundabitur? Quis enim non curet, quis non quaerat unde mundet, que videre possit quem toto affectu desiderat? Expressit hoc divina testatio: Fide, inquit, mundans corda eorum (Act 15,9). Mundat cor fides Dei, mundum cor videt Deum. Sed quia ipsa fides aliquando ab hominibus, qui se ipsos fallunt, talis determinatur, quasi sufficiat tantummodo credere (promittunt enim sibi

and the kingdom of heaven. Enraged and somewhat indignant against them for their spiritual charity, the apostle James tells them in his Letter: You believe that God is unique. You applaud your faith; You see that many wicked people consider that there are numerous gods, and you enjoy believing that God is only one. You do well. The demons also believe, and tremble. Will they also see God? Those who are pure in heart will see Him. Who will call unclean spirits pure in heart? Yet they believe and tremble. 11. We must distinguish our faith from that of demons. Our faith cleanses the heart; theirs makes them prisoners. In fact, they do evil and, consequently, they say to the Lord: What is between us and you? Hearing them talk like that, do you think they don't recognize him? We know, they say, who you are. You are the Son of God. Peter says this, and is praised; The devil says it, and is condemned 7. How so but because, although the voice is the same, the heart is different? Let us distinguish, then, what our faith is. Let's not settle for believing. There is no faith that cleanses the heart. Purifying, he says, their hearts with faith. But with what faith, with what kind of faith but with that expressed by the apostle Paul when he said: The faith that works through love? This faith is distinguished from that of demons; is distinguished from evil and quidam etiam conspectum Dei regnumque caelorum credentes et male vivos); contra hos succensus et spirituali caritate quodammodo stomachans Iacobus apostolus in Epistola sua dicit: Tu creais quoniam unus est Deus. Plaudis tibi de fide: attendis enim multos imp[369]pios aestimare multos esse déos, et tu tibi gaudes credendo quia unus est Deus. Bene facis. Et daemones credunt, et contremiscunt (Iac 2,19). Numquid et ii Deum videbunt? Videbunt qui mundo sunt corde. Quis autem mundicordes dicat spiritus immundos? Et tamen credunt, et contremiscunt. 11. Fides Christianorum discernenda a fide daemonum. Fidei committees spes et caritas.—Discernenda est fides nostra a fide daemonum. Fides enim nostra mundat cor: fides autem illorum reos facit. Male quippe operantur, et ideo Domino dicunt: Quid nobis et tibi est? Cum audis hoc daemones dicere, putas eos non agnoscere? Scimus, inquiunt, qui sis. You are Filius Dei (Luke 4:34). Dicit hoc Petrus, et laudatur (Mt 16,16.17): dicit hoc daemon, et damnatur. Unde hoc, nisi quia vox par, et cor odd? Discernamus ergo fidem nostram, nec credere sufficiat. Non est talis fides quae mundat cor. Fide, inquit, mundans corda eorum.

Sed qua fide, quali fide, nisi quam defini t Paulus apostolus, ubi ait: Fides quae per dilectionem operatur? (Gal 5,6). Ista fides discernit a fide ' Augustine very frequently stops to reflect on the fact that two identical actions in one person find praise and in another condemnation. The answer to this question is always found by going to the intention, to the heart. The most typical case is found in the surrender of Jesus to death by the Father and by Judas, in addition to his own self-surrender. See Supplementary Note 29: The fact and the intention vol. VII p.754.

lost customs of men. Faith, he says. What kind of faith? The one who works for love and waits for what God promises. Nothing more exact, nothing more perfect than this definition. There are, then, three things. It is necessary that he in whom there is faith that works through love, wait for what God promises. Companion of faith is, therefore, hope. Hope, therefore, is necessary as long as we do not see what we believe, lest by not seeing it we faint from despair. It saddens us not to see, but it comforts us to hope to see. Therefore, hope exists and it is a companion of faith. And then charity, love, for which we desire, for which we try to reach the goal, for which we are inflamed and for which we feel hunger and thirst. This is also added and faith, hope and love are given. How can there not be love there, not being something different from dilection? Faith itself was defined this way: that which works out of love. Eliminate faith: believing disappears; suppresses love: acting disappears. The fruit of faith is that you believe; fruit of charity, may you work. If, then, you believe and do not love, you do not feel impelled to do good actions; and if you sit, you are like a slave, not like a son: for fear of punishment, not for love of justice. Faith, then, that works out of love is what cleanses the heart. 12. And what is now the work of faith? With so many testimonies of the Scriptures, with so many readings, with so varied and abundant exhortations, what does faith do, but that we now see, although darkly, as in a mirror, and then face to face? But don't ever think about a face like yours again. Think of the face of the heart. Obliga daemonum, discernit ab hominum flagitiosis ac perditis moribus. Fides, restless. Quae fides? Quae per dilectionem operatur, sperat quod Deus pollicetur. Nihil ista definitione perpensius, nihil perfectius. Ergo tria sunt illa. Necesse est ut in quo est fides, quae per dilectionem operatur, speret quod Deus pollicetur. Comes est ergo fidei spes. Necessaria quippe spes est, quamdiu non videmus quod credimus; ne forte non videndo et desperando deficiamus. Contristat nos, quia non videmus: sed consolatur nos, quia visuros nos speramus. Adest ergo spes, et est come fidei. Deinde et caritas, qua desideramus, qua pertingere conamur, qua inardescimus, qua esurimus et sitimus. Adhibetur ergo et haec: et erit fides, spes et caritas. Quomodo enim non erit ibi caritas, cum nihil sit aliud caritas quam dilectio?

Ipsa autem fides definita est, quae per dilectionem operatur. Tolle fidem, perit quod credis; tolle caritatem, perit quod agis. Fidei enim pertinet ut credas; caritati, ut agas. Si enim credis, et non amas, non te moves ad bonum opus: et si moves, ut servus moves, non ut filius: timendo poenam, non amando iustitiam. Illa ergo, inquam, fides mundat cor, quae per dilectionem operatur. CAPUT XI.—12. Deus non cogitandus ut corpus.—Et moda ipsa fides quid agit? Tantis testimoniis Scripturarum, tam multiplici lectione, tam varia copiosaque exhortatione quid agit, nisi ut videomus nunc per speculum in aenigmate, postea facie ad faciera? Sed non iterum you redeas
The Beatitudes

to your heart to think the divine; force him, urge him. Reject anything that comes to mind similar to the corporeal. You cannot yet say "This is it"; say at least "It's not this." When will you be able to say “This is God”? Not even when you see it, because what you will see will be ineffable. The Apostle claims to have been caught up to the third heaven and to have heard ineffable words. If the words are already ineffable, how will the person who pronounces them be? When you think of God, perhaps a human form of admirable and vast breadth appears to your imagination. You put it before the gaze of your mind as something great, very broad, sublime, of enormous corpulence. Still, you had to set a limit. If that's what you had to do, it's not God. If you didn't set limits, where is the face? You think of enormous stature; but to distinguish the members you have to establish limits. There is no other way to distinguish some members from others if it is not by giving a limit to the mass. Foolish and carnal thought, what are you doing? You have built a great mass for yourself; and all the greater because you believed that in this way you honored God more. But another can come and add a cubit to it, and it will make it bigger.

Heaven is my throne, that is, my seat; Throne is a Greek term that means, in Latin, seat 8. The earth is my footstool. Didn't you also read that other thing: Who measured the sky with the palm of the hand? I think you read it; You know the text and you confess to believing it. We read both things there, giving them faith. Now start thinking and teach me. I make you a doctor and I become a toddler. Teach me, I beg you. Who is there that sits in the palm of your hand? 14. Behold, you attributed to God forms and contours in the likeness of the members of the human body. Perhaps the thinking that we were made in the image of God according to the body 9 influenced this. For now I accept it as a topic to consider, discuss, search for and clarify through dispute. If it is to your liking, listen to me, because I also listened to what pleased you. God sits in the sky, a sky that is measured with the palm of the hand. Does the sky itself become wide when God sits in it and narrow when it is measured? Or is God, when seated, as big as the palm of your hand? If this is so, God did not make us in his likeness; the palm of our hand, in fact, is much narrower than the part of the body on which we sit 10. If, on the other hand,

13. "I've read it," you say. What did you read, if you understood nothing? Still, say what you read. Let's not reject the child who plays with his heart. Tell us what you read. Heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool. I'm telling you, I've read it too; but maybe you consider yourself superior because you read it and believed it. I also believe what you said. We create both. What do I say? Let's look for both. Look, consider what you read and believed: ad istam faciem tuam. Faciem cordis cogita. Coge cor tuum cogitare divina, compelle, urge. Quidquid simile corporis cogitanti occurrerit, abice. Nondum potes dicere, Hoc est: saltem dic, Non est hoc. When you say, Hoc est Deus? Nec cum videbis: quia ineffabile est quod videbis. Raptum se dicit Apostolus in tertium [370] caelum, et audisse ineffabilia verba (2 Cor 12,2 et 4). Si sunt ineffabilia verba, quid est cuius sunt verba? Cogitanti ergo tibi de Deo, occurrit aliqua fortasse in humano specie mira et amplissima magnitudeo: constituisti eam in conspectu cogitationis tuae, tanquam magmim aliquid, amplissimum, grande, ingentissima mole diffusum. Finisti alicubi. If finisti, Deus non est. Si non finisti, facies ubi est? Cogitas molem, et ut membra distinguas, definis molem. Aliter enim membra distinguishe non potes, nisi moli dederis finem. Quid agis, stulta et carnalis cogitatio? Grandem molem fecisti; et both grandiorem, quanto te putasti Deum amplius honorare. Addit alius unum cubitum, et facit maiorem. CAPUT XII.—13. Locus Isaiae in speciemcontraras.—Sed legi, inquis. Quid legisti, qui nihil intellexisti? Et tamen dic, quid legisti? Non repellamus parvulum cotde ludentem. What is the law? Caelum mihi throneus est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum (Is 66:6). Aio: Legi et ego: sed tu forte potiorem te putas, quia legisti et credidisti. Credo et ego quod dixisti. Simul credamus. it has quod legisti, et credidisti: Caelum mihi throneus est, id est, headquarters; throneus enim graece, latin sedes est: terra autem scabellum pedum meorum.
