Do you fear falling into the list of your enemy and do you not fear God's judgment? Where is the faith? Fear while there is time to fear. The day of judgment is certainly far away, but the last day of each individual man cannot be very far away, since life is short. And since brevity itself is uncertain, you do not know when your last day will come. Correct yourself today, thinking about tomorrow. Be of benefit, even for now, the correction that you receive in secret. I speak in public, but I censure in secret. I appeal to the ears of all, but I call to judgment the consciences of some. If I said: "You adulterer, correct yourself," perhaps I would begin speaking without knowing the facts; perhaps in secret arguimus. Ubi contigit malum, ibi moriatur malum. Non tamen vulnus illud neglegimus; ante omnia ostendentes homini in tali peccato constituto sauciamque gerenti conscientiam, illud vulnus esse mortiferum: quod aliquando qui committunt, nescio qua perversitate contemnunt; et nescio unde sibi testimonia nulla et vana conquirunt, dicentes: "Peccata carnis Deus non curat." Ubi est quod hodie audivimus: Formcatores et adúlteros iudicat Deus? Ecce attende, quisquís tali morbo laboras. Quod dicit Deus audi: non quod tibi dicit favens peccatis tuis animus tuus, aut eadem tecum iniquitatis catena ligatus amicus tuus, vel potius inimicus tuus et suus. Audi ergo quod dicit Apostolus: Honorabiles, inquit, nuptiae in ómnibus, et torus immaculatus. Fornicatores autem et adultereros iudicat Deus (Hebr 13:4). CAPUT IX.—12. Vita cita emendanda.—Age ergo, frater, esto correctus. Times ne te inscribat inimicus; et non times ne te iudícet Deus? Ubi are you fi[512]des?

Time cum is when timeas. Longe est quidem dies iudicii: sed uniuscuiusque hominis dies ultimus longe esse non potest; quia bievis est vita. Et quia ipsa brevitas sempet incerta, quando sit dies tuus ultimus, nescis. Correct you hodie, propter eras. Prosit tibi et moda in secreto correptio. Palam ením loquor, et in secreto arguo. Aures omnium pulse: sed conscientias quommdam covenant. If we say: "You adulterer, correct yourself"; primo forte dicerem quod nescirem; strong
has fraternal correction

It was a suspicion, something recklessly believed. I do not say: "You adulterer, correct yourself," but: "Whoever in this town is an adulterer, correct himself." The correction is public, but the amendment is secret. I am sure that whoever feels fear will correct themselves. 13. Do not say in your heart: "God does not care about the sins of the flesh." Do you not know, says the Apostle, that you are temples of the Holy Spirit and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Whoever violates his temple, God will destroy him. Let no one be deceived. But perhaps someone will say: "My soul is the temple of God, not my body, for he also added this testimony: All flesh is hay and all the splendor of the flesh is like the flower of hay." Wretched interpretation! Thought worthy of punishment! Meat is compared to hay because it dies; But beware of resurrecting, stained with crimes, what dies in time! Do you want to see that sentence explained right there? Do you not know, says the same Apostle, that your bodies are in you a temple of the Holy Spirit which you receive from God? You despised bodily sin; Do you despise the sin against the temple? Your own body is the temple of the Holy Spirit in you. Now see what you have to do with the temple of God. If you chose to commit adultery in the church, within these walls 6, who would be more criminal than you? Now you yourself are the temple of God. When you enter, when you leave, cuanquod fear audieram, suspicarer. I do not say: «You, adulterer, correct yourself»; sed: "quisquis in hoc populo adulter es, correct you." Publish this correctio, sed secret correctio. Scio quia ille qui timuerit, corrigit se. CAPUT X.—13. Peccata carnis non contemnenda.—Non dicat in corde suo: “Peccata carnis non curat Deus.” Nescitis, inquit Apostolus, quia lemplum Dei estis, et Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis? Quisquís templutn Dei violaverit, disperdet illum Deus (1 Cor 3:16-17). Nemo fails. Be strong ait aliquis: «Templutn Dei animus meus est, non corpus meum»; adiecit etiam testimonium: Omnis caro [enurn, et omnis claritas carnis ut flos feni (1 Petr 1,24). Infelix interpretatio! punienda cogitatio! Fenum dicta est caro, quia moritur: sed quod ad tempus moritur, non resurgat cum crimine. Vis nosse apertam etiam inde sententiam? Nescitis, inquit idem apostolus, quia corpora vestra templum in vobis est Spiritus sancti, quem habetis a Deo? (Iam non contemnatis corporalia peccata: ecce quia et corpora vestra templum in vobis sunt Spiritus sancti, quam habetis a Deo).

Contemnebas corporale peccatum, contemnis quod peccas in templum? Ipsum corpus tuum templum in te est Spiritus Dei. Iam vide the crux of the temple Dei. If you choose in ecclesia faceré adulterium intra istos parietes, quid te esset sceleratius? Modo autem tu ipse es tern6 These words remind us of those other autobiographical ones from the Confessions: "I also had the audacity to ardently desire and negotiate a way to procure for myself fruits of death in the celebration of one of your solemnities and within the walls of your church" (III, 3,5).

When you are at home, when you get up, you are a temple. Look what you do; Take care not to offend him who dwells in it, lest he abandon you and you become ruins. Do you not know, he said, that your bodies—and he spoke of fornication, so that you would not despise bodily sins—are in you the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you receive from God, and which does not belong to you? You have been bought at a great price. If you despise your body, consider your price. 14. I know, and every man who has considered it with a little more attention knows it with me, that, among those who fear God, only those who think that they must live longer still do not correct themselves under the weight of their words. That is what kills many; while they say: "Tomorrow, tomorrow" their mouth suddenly closes. He remained outside with the voice of a crow, because he did not have the moan of the dove. «Cras, eras» (tomorrow, tomorrow), is the voice of the crow 7. It moans like a dove and beats your chest; wounded with those blows, correct yourself, so as not to give the impression that you do not hurt your conscience, but that with your fists you pave your bad conscience and make it more solid, not more correct. He moans, but not with a vain moan. Perhaps you say to yourself: “God has promised me forgiveness when he corrects me; I am calm; I read in the divine Scripture: On the day when he turns from all his wickedness and acts justly, I will forget all the wickedness of the wicked. I am calm; When I correct myself, God will forgive me all my wrongs. plum Dei. Templum intras, templum exis, templum in domo tua manes, templum surgís. Vide quid agas, vide ne offendas templi habitatorem, ne deserat te, et in ruinam vertaris. Nescitis, inquit, quia corpora vestra (et hoc de fornicatione loquebatur Apostolus, ne contemnerent corpotalia peccata) templum in vobis est Spiritus saneti, quem habetis a Deo, et non estis vestri? Empti enim estis pretio magno (1 Cor 6,19.20). Si contemnis corpus tuum, consider pretium tuum. CAPUT XI.—14. Correctio non procrastinanda. Vox croaker. Homines bona volunt habere omnia praeter vitam.—Scio ego, et mecum omnis homo qui paulo attentius consideraverit, neminem Deum timentem sub verbis eius non se corrigere, nisi qui putat, quia plus habet vivere. Ipsa res est quae multos occidit, cum dicunt: «Cras, cras»; et súbito ostium clauditur. Remansit foris cum voce corvina, quia non habuit gemitum columbinum. "Cras, cras"; corvi vox.

Geme ut columbus, et tunde pectus: sed pestas tibi [513] giving in pectus, caesus correctus this; ne non videaris conscientiam caedere, sed malam conscientiam pugnis pavimentare, solidiorem reddere, non correctiorem. Geme non inani gemitu. Forte enim dicis tibi: «Promisit mihi Deus indulgentiam, quando me correxero; securus sum; lego divinam Scripturam: Iniquus in qua die conversus fuerit ab iniquitatibus suis, et fecerit iustitiam, omnes iniquitates eius obliviscar (Ezech 18,21 et 22). Securus sum; when I ran7 The same thought is repeated in sermon 224,4 and in the enarración to psalm 102,16.

What can I say? Should I complain against God? Am I going to say to him: "Don't forgive him"? Can I say that this is not written, that God did not promise forgiveness? If I said this, I would say a falsehood. You speak well, you speak the truth; God promised forgiveness to your correction; I can't deny it. But tell me, I beg you; I agree with you, I grant you; I recognize that God promised you forgiveness, but who has promised you tomorrow? In the text in which you read that you must receive forgiveness if you correct yourself, read to me how long you will live. "I don't read it," you say. You do not know, therefore, how long you have to live. Correct yourself and always be prepared. Do not fear the last day as a thief who, while you sleep, opens a hole in your wall; On the contrary, stay awake and correct yourself today. Why do you postpone it until tomorrow? Suppose life is long; be good, although long. No one defers a long and good meal, and do you want to have a long and bad life? Certainly, if it is long, it had better be good; If it is brief, it has been a good thing to make it good. This is what happens with men; They neglect their lives and only want to have a bad life. If you buy a villa, you want it good; If you want to take a wife, you choose a good one; If you want children to be born to you, you want them to be good; If you borrow a caliga, you don't want it bad; and you love a bad life! 8 How has your life offended you so that you want only it to be bad, so that among all your goods only you are bad? 15. Therefore, my brothers, if I would like to correct alrexero, dat mihi Deus indulgentiam de malis meis. Et quid ego dicturus sum? Contra Deum reclamaturus? Dicturus sum Deo: Noli illi will I give indulgentiam? Dicturus sum hoc scriptum non esse, hoc Deum non promisisse? If ista dixero, omnia false dico. Bene dicis, verum dicis: indulgentiam correctioni tuae promisit Deus, deniale non possum; thirsty said mihi, I beg you; ecce ego consentio et concedo et cognosco quia indulgentiam Deus promisit tibi; crastinum enim diem quis tibi promisit? Ubi mihi legis indulgentiam te accepturum, si te correxeris; lege ibi mihi quantum victurus sis. "Non layman," he inquired. Nescis ergo quantum victurus sis. This correctus et semper patatús. Noli timere diem ultimum, tanquam furem qui te dormiente effodiat parietem: be vigilant, et correcte te hodie. Quid differs in crastinum? Longa vita erit. Ipsa longa, bona sit. Prandium bonum longum nemo differt, et vitam malam longam vis habere?

Utique si longa erit, melius bona erit: si brevis erit, bene factum est, ut bona produceretur. Sic autem homines neglegunt vitam suam, ut nolint habere malam, nisi ipsam. Villam emis, bonam quaeris; uxorem vis ducere, bonam eligis; filios tibi vis nasci, bonds optas; crazy caligas, et non vis malas: et vitam amas malam! Quid te offendit vita tua, quam solam vis malam, ut inter omnia bona tua tu solus sis malus? CAPUT XII.—15. Pastoris onus non abiciendum.—Ergo, fiatres mei,
See the note to the sermon 56,14,

someone separately, perhaps he would listen to me; I correct many of you in public; everyone praises me; Someone pay attention to me! I do not love him who praises me with his mouth and despises me in his heart. If you praise Me and do not correct yourself, you become a witness against yourself. If you are bad and you like what I say, displease yourself, because if being bad you are displeased with yourself, once corrected you will please yourself, which is what I said, if I am not mistaken, the day before yesterday 9. In all my words I present a mirror. And they are not mine, but I speak at the command of the Lord, for whose fear I do not remain silent. Well, who would not choose to remain silent and not give an account of you? But we already accept the burden that we neither can nor should shake off our shoulders 10. You heard, brothers, when the letter to the Hebrews was read: Obey your superiors and study submissively, because they watch over your souls, as those who must give an account of you, so that they do so with joy and not with sadness, since it is not convenient for you. When do we do this with joy? When we see men progress along the path of the word of God. When does the farmer work with joy in his field? When you look at the tree and see the fruit; when he looks at the harvest and sees the abundance of fruit on the threshing floor. His work was not in vain, he did not bend his kidneys in vain, it was not useless that his hands were stuck; The cold and heat endured were not useless. This is what it says: It is important that you do it with joy and not with sadness, because it is not convenient for you. Did he perhaps say: "It is not convenient for them"? No, if aliquem vestrum vellem in parte corripere, forte audiret me: muí tos vestrum publice corripio; omnes me laudant; audit me aliquis. Non amo in voce laudatorem, et in corde contemptorem. Cum enim laudas, et non te corrigis, contra te testis es. Si malus es, et quod dico placet tibi, displice tíbi: quia si malus displicueris tibi, correctus placebis tibi, quod nudiustertius, nisi fallor, dixi. In omnibus verbis meis speculum proposes Nec mea ista sunt verba: sed Domino iubente loquor, quo terrente non taceo. Nam quis non electaret tacere, et rationem de vobis non reddere? Sed iam suscepimus onus, quod ab humeris nostris excutere non possumus, nec debenmus. Audistis, fratres mei, cum Epístola ad Hebracos legeretur: Oboedite praepositis vestris, et subditi estote; quia ipsi vigilant pro animabus vestris, tanquam rationem reddituri pro vobis: ut cum gaudio hoc faciant, et non cum tristitia; non enim expedit vobis (Hebr 13:17).

When facimus ista cum gaudio? Quando vide[514]mus homines proficere in verbis Dei. When laborat cum gaudio operanius in agro? When attendit arborem, et fructum videt; quando attendit segetem, et frugum inarea prospicit ubertatem: non sine causa laboravit, non sine causa dorsum curvavit, non sine causa manus attrivit, non sine causa frigus et aestum toleravit. Hoc est quod ait: Ut cum gaudio
What is it referring to? Maybe to sermon 81.3? It seems not. It alludes, without a doubt, to his episcopal consecration.

but he said, It is not expedient for you. For it is convenient for superiors to be sad because of your evils; the same sadness is beneficial to them; but it is not convenient for you. We don't want anything that suits us if it doesn't suit you too. Therefore, brothers, let us do good at the same time in the field of the Lord, so that we may enjoy the reward together.
Topic: Forgiveness of offenses (Mt 18:21-35). Location: Probably in Milevi. Date: Around the year 409.

1. Yesterday the Lord warned us 1 not to neglect the sins of our brothers: If your brother sins against you, correct him alone. If he listens to you, you have won your brother; If, however, he despises you, take two or three with you, so that with the testimony of two or three witnesses every word may acquire firmness. If you also despise them, tell the Church. And if he despises the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and publican. The following chapter we have hoc faciant, et non cum tristitia; non enim expedit vobis. Numquid said: "Non illis expedit." Non; sed dixít: Non expedit vobis. Nam illi praepositi quando contristantur de malis vestris, expedit illis; ipsa tristitia prodest illis: sed non expedit vobis. Nihil autem nobis volumus expediré, quod non expedit vobis. Simul ergo in Dominico agro, fratres, bonum operemur; ut simul of mercedes gaudeamus.
DE VERBIS EVANGELII MATTHAEI, CAP. 18,21.22: «QUOTIES PECCABIT IN ME FRATER MEUS», ETC.

CAPUT I. — 1. De remittendis iniuriis.—Hesterna die sanctum Evangelium admonuit nos non neglegere peccata fratrum nostrorum: Sed si peccaverit, inquit, in te frater tuus, curripé eum inter te et ipsum solum. Si te auditerit, lucratus es fratrem tuum. Si autem contempserit, adhibe tecum duos vel tres: ut in ore duorum vel trium testium stet omne verbum. Si autem et ipsos contempserit, dic Ecclesiae. Quod si Ecclesiam contempserit, sit tibi sicut ethnicus et publicanus (Mt 18,15-17).
See sermon 82,4.
Forgiveness of offenses

heard when it was read today deals with the same topic. Having said this to Peter, the Lord immediately asked the Master how many times he should forgive the brother who had sinned against him; and he wanted to know if seven times was enough. The Lord answered him: Not only seven times, but seventy-seven. He then gave him an extremely terrible parable: The kingdom of heaven is like a father of a family who began to ask his servants to account, among whom he found one who owed him ten thousand talents. And having ordered all his property to be sold and even he and his family, falling on their knees in the presence of their lord, asked him for a period of time, and obtained the remission of everything. As we have heard, his lord took pity and forgave him the debt in full. But he, free from debt, but a servant of wickedness, after he left the presence of his master, also found a debtor of his, who owed him, not ten thousand talents—this was his own debt—but one hundred denarii; He began to drag him, half drowning him, and tell him: Repay what you owe me. He prayed to his fellow servant, just as he had prayed to his master, but he did not find his fellow servant as he had found his master. Not only did he not want to forgive the debt; He didn't even give him the time limit. Now free from the debt to his master, he squeezed him to pay him. This displeased his fellow servants, who told their master what had happened. The master ordered the servant to be presented and said to him: Wicked servant, although you owed me so much, I took pity on you and forgave you.

I donated everything; Was it not fitting, therefore, that you also should have pity on your fellow servant as I did on you? And he ordered that everything that had been forgiven be demanded from him. 2. He therefore proposed this parable for our instruction and wanted that with his warning we would not perish. Thus, he said, your heavenly Father will do to you if each of you does not forgive his brother from the heart. See, brothers, that the thing is clear and that the warning is useful. Therefore, truly salutary obedience is due to fulfill what is commanded. In fact, every man, at the same time that he is a debtor before God, has his brother as a debtor. Who is there who is not indebted to God, except he in whom no sin can be found? Who does not owe his brother as a debtor, except the one against whom no one has sinned? Do you think there can be found in the human race someone who is not chained to his brother for some sin? Every man, therefore, is a debtor, also having his debtors. For this reason, the just God established the standard for you on how to behave towards your debtor, a standard that he will apply to his own. There are two works of mercy that set us free; the Lord briefly explained them in the Gospel: Forgive and you will be forgiven; give and it will be given to you. Forgive and you will be forgiven, look to forgiveness; Give and it will be given to you refers to rendering a favor. Regarding forgiveness, you not only want your sin forgiven, but you also have someone you can forgive. So it is re-

Hodierna etiam die ad ipsam reni pertinet capitulum quod sequitur, quod moda cum legeretur audimus. Cum enim dixisset hoc Dominus Iesus Petro, subiecit et interrogavit Magistrum, quoties ígnoscetet fratri qui in illum peccasset; et quaesivit utrum sufíiceret septíes (cf. ibid., 21). Respondit illi Dominus: Non solum septies, sed etiam septuagies septies (ib., 22). Deinde narravit simiiitudinem valde terribilem: quia simile est regnutn caelorum homini patrifamilias, qui posuit rationem cum servis suis; in quibus invenit debitorem decem miilium talentrum. Et cum iussisset, ut omnia quae habebat, et omnis eius familia, et ipse vendeetur, et debitum solveretur, advolutus genibus domini sui, rogabat eum dilationem, meruit remissionem. Misertus est enim dominus eius, sicut audivimus, et omne debitum dimisit ilii. At ille debito liber, sed iniquitatis servus, posteaquam egressus est a facie domini sui, invenit etiam ipse debitorem suum, qui debenbat, non decem millia Talentum, quantum ipsius debitum Fuit, sed centum denarii: coepit eum suffocatum trahere, et dicere, Redde quod deben. At ille rogabat conservum, sicut et ipse rogaverat dominum: sed non talem iste invenit conservum, qualem [515] ille dominum. Non solum remitiere illi debitum noluit: sed nec dilationem dedit. Contortum rapiebat ad solutionem, iam debito dominico liber. Displicuit conservis; et renuntiaverunt domino suo quid actum esset: et dominus fecit adesse servum, et dixit ei, Serve nequam, cum

mihi tanta duties, misertus tui, omnia dimisi tibi; nonne ergo et te oportebat misereri conservi tui, sicut et ego tui misertus sum? Et iussit omnia, quae illi dimiserat, exigi (cf. Mt 18:23-34). CAPOT II.—2. Omnis homo debitar Dei est, et debitorem habet fratrem. Misericordiae opera duo. Mendici Dei sumus.—Ergo hanc simiiitudinem ad nostram instructionem proposuit, et admonendo perire nos noluit. Sic, inquit, et vobis faciet Pater vester caelestis, si non remiseritis unusquisque vestrum fratri suo ex cordibus vestris (ib., 35). Ecce, fratres, res in aperto est, admonitio utilis; et valde salubris oboedientia debentur, ut quod iussum est impleatur. Quia omnis homo et debitor est Dei, et debitorem habet fratrem suum. Quis est enim qui non sit debitor Dei, nisi in quo nullum potest inveniri peccatum? Quis est autem qui non habeat debitorem fratrem, nisi in quem nemo peccavit? Putasne, quisquam in genere humano reperiri potest, qui non et ipse aliquo peccato obstrictus sit fratri suo? Debitor est ergo omnis homo, habens tamen et ipse debitorem. Ideo Deus iustus constituit tibi regulam in debitore tuo, quod faciet et ipse cum suo. Duo sunt enim opera misericordiae, quae nos liberant, quae breviter ipse Dominus posit in Gospel: Dimittite, et dimittetur vobis; date, et dabitur vobis (Luke 6,37.38). Dimittite, et dimittetur vobis, ad ignoscendum pertinet. Date, et dabitur vobis, ad praestandum beneficium pertinet. Quod ait de ignoscendo, et tu vis tibi ignosci quod peccas, et habes alium cui tu possis ignoscere.

Fierce when rendering a favor, a beggar asks of you, and you are also a beggar of God. For when we pray, we are all beggars of God; We are standing at the door of the father of the family; Furthermore, we prostrate ourselves and groan in supplication, wanting to receive something, and this something is God himself. What does the beggar ask of you? Bread. And what do you ask of God but of Christ who says: I am the living bread that came down from heaven? Do you want to be forgiven? Forgive: Forgive and you will be forgiven. Do you want to receive? Give and it will be given to you. 3. But listen to something that in this very clear precept can create difficulty. Regarding the remission in which forgiveness is requested and must be granted, it can cause the same difficulty as it did for Peter. How many times, he said, should I forgive? Is seven enough? It is not enough, said the Lord: I do not say to you: Seven, but: Seventy-seven. Now begin to count how many times your brother has sinned against you. If you could reach seventy-eight, that is, go beyond seventy-seven, then plot your revenge now. Is what he says so true? Are things like this, so that if he sins seventy-seven times, you must forgive him; If, on the other hand, he sins seventy-eight, is it permissible for you not to forgive him? I dare to say, yes, I dare, that even if he sins seventy-eight, you must forgive him. I have said that even if he sins seventy-eight times, you must forgive him. And the same if he sinned a hundred times. Why give figures? How many times he sins, absolutely all of those times you have to forgive him. So, have I dared to exceed the measure of the Lord? Rursus quod pertinet ad tribuendum beneficium; petit te mendicus, et tu es Dei mendicus. Omnes enim quando oramus, mendici Dei sumus: ante ianuam magni patrisfamilias stamus, immo etiam prosternimur, supplices ingemiscimus, aliquid volentes accipere; et ipsum aliquid, ipse Deus est. Quid a te petit mendicus? Panem. Et tu quid petis a Deo, nisi Christum, qui dicit, Ego sum pañis vivus, qu de cáelo descended? (lo 6.51). Ignosci vobis vultis? Ignoscite: Remitüte, et remittetur vobis. Accipere vultis? Date, et dabitur vobis (Luke 6,37,38). CAPUT I I I. — 3. Quoties ignoscenium fratri.—Sed quid in hac aperta praeceptione moveré possit, audite. In remissione ubi venia petitur, et ab ignoscente debentur, hoc potest moveré, quod et Petrum movit. Quoties debeno, inquit, ignoscere? Sujjicit usque septies? Non sufficit, ait Dominus: Non dico tibi, septies; thirst, septuagies septies (Mt 18,21,22).

Iam tu enumerates quoties in te peccaverit frater tuus. Si potueris pervenire usque ad septuagesimam et octavem culpam, ut transeas septuagies septies, tune molire vindictam. Itane verum est quod dicit, et veré ita se res habet, ut si peccaverit septuagies septies, ignoscas; si autem [516] peccaverit septuagies octies, iam liceat tibi non ignoscere? Audeo, audeo dicere, ut et si septuagies octies peccaverit, ignoscas. Yes autem peccaverit, ut dixi, septuagies octies ignosce. Et si centies peccaverit, ignosce. Et quid dicam toties et toties? Omnino quoties peccaverit, ignosce. Ergo
Forgiveness of offenses

He set the limit for forgiveness at the number seventy-seven; Will I presume to exceed that number? It isn't true; I have not dared to add anything. I have heard my own Lord speaking through the Apostle, in a place where neither measure nor number is predetermined: Forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another, as God forgave you in Christ. You have seen the model. If Christ forgave your sins seventy-seven times and only up to that number, and denied forgiveness once it was exceeded, you also set a limit, beyond which you do not forgive. If, on the other hand, Christ found thousands of sins in sinners and forgave them all, do not discount mercy; Rather ask that the riddle of that number be solved. It is not in vain that the Lord spoke of seventy-seven, since there is no fault to which you should deny forgiveness. Look at that servant who, although he had a debtor, owed ten thousand talents. I think that ten thousand talents are equivalent, at least, to ten thousand sins. And I don't want to go into whether talent contains all the sins. That his fellow servant, how much did he owe him? One hundred denarii. Isn't this already more than seventy-seven? However, the Lord was angry because they were not forgiven. It is not only the number one hundred that is greater than seventy-seven, since one hundred denarii is perhaps equivalent to a thousand aces. But what is that compared to the ten thousand talents? 4. Therefore, if we want to be forgiven, must we be willing to forgive all the sins that ego ausus sum supergredi modum Domini mei? lile in seventieth and seventh number ignoscendi limitem fixit: hunc ego limitem transilire praesumam? Non est verum, non sum ausus plus aliquid. Ipsum Dominum meum audi loquentem in Apostólo suo, ubi modus et numerus praefixus non est. Ait enim: Donantes vobismetipsis, si quis adversus aliquem habet querelam, sicut Deus in Christo donavit vobis (Col 3:13). Audistis formam. Si septuagies septies peccata tibi donavit Christus, si huc usque ignovit, et ultra negavit; Put et tu limitem, et ulterius noli ignoscere. Puto enim, quia decem millia talentrum, ut parum sit, decem millia peccatorum sunt. Nolo enim dicere unum talentum, quod omnia peccata concludat. Servus autem ille quantum ei debenbat? Centum denarii debenbat. Iam plus non est quam septuagies septies? Et tamen iratus est Dominus, quia ei non dimisit. Non solum enim centum plus sunt quam septuaginta septem; sed centum denarii forte mille asses sunt. Sed quid ad decem millia Talentum? CAPUT IV.—4. Omnia debita dimittenda.-—Ac per hoc omnes culpas, quae in nos cornrnittuntur, paratí simus ignoscere, si nobis desideramus

they commit against us. If we review our sins and count our work commitments, with our eyes, with our ears, with our thoughts and with countless other movements, I don't know if we would sleep without the talent. For this reason, every day in prayer we ask and call on the divine ears, every day we prostrate ourselves and say: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. What debts? All of them, or just a part? You will answer that all. Do the same with your debtor. This is the norm to which you have to adjust, this is the condition you set. By praying and saying: Forgive us as we forgive our debtors, you refer to that covenant and agreement. 5. In conclusion, what does seventy-seven mean? Listen, brothers, a great mystery, an admirable sacrament. When the Lord was baptized, the holy evangelist Luke mentioned his genealogy by the order, succession and branch leading to the generation from which Christ was born. Matthew began with Abraham and, in descending order, reached Joseph; Lucas, on the other hand, began to count in ascending order2. Why one in a downward direction and another in an upward direction? Because Matthew recommended to us the generation of Christ insofar as he descended to us; That is why at the birth of Christ he began to count from top to bottom. Luke, on the other hand, began counting at the baptism of Christ; From this begins its ascending count. He began to count in ascending order until completing seventy-seven generations. From ignosci. Si enim considermus peccata nostra, et numeremus quid facto, quid oculo, quid aure, quid cogitatione, quid innumerabilibus motibus; nescio utrum dormiamus sine talent. Ergo quotidie petimus, quotidie divinas aures praying pulsamus, quotidie nos prosternimus et dicimus: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos iimittimus debitoribus nostris (Mt 6,12). What is your debt? Omnia, an aliquam partem? You answer: Omnia. Sic ergo et tu debitori tuo. Hanc ergo regulam ponis, hanc condicionem loqueris: hoc pact et plácito quando oras, commemoras, ut dicas, Dimitte nobis, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris. 5. Insignis hac de re figura.—Quid sibi ergo vult septuagies septies? (Mt 18,22). Audite, frates, magnum mysterium, admirable sacramentum. Quando Dominus baptizatus est, Luke evangelista sanctus ibi commemoravit generationes eius, quo ordine, qua serie, quo stemmate ad illam generationem ventum fuerit, qua natus est Christus (cf. Lk 3:21-38).

Matthaeus coepit [517] ab Abraham, et venit usque ad Ioseph descending (Mt 1:1-16): Luke autem ascending coepit numerare. Quare ille descending, ille ascending? Quia Matthaeus generationem Christi commendabat, qua descendit ad nos; ideo when natus est Christus, coepit numerare descending. Luke autem quia tune coepit numerare, when baptizatus est Christus; ibi est initium ascensionis: iste ascen1

Forgiveness of offenses

Who did he start telling about? Pay attention to this. The starting point was Christ and the arrival point was Adam, the first to sin, who begot us with the bond of sin. Counting seventy-seven generations he reached Adam; That is to say, from Christ to Adam there are the seventy-seven generations mentioned and as many others, consequently, from Adam to Christ. If, then, no generation was overlooked, no guilt was overlooked either to which forgiveness was not due. Counting seventy-seven generations of the Lord, a number that the Lord recommended when speaking of the forgiveness of sins, has the same meaning as having begun to enumerate them from baptism, in which all are forgiven. 6. Regarding this, receive, brothers, an even greater mystery. The mystery of the forgiveness of sins is contained in the number seventy-seven. All those generations are found from Christ to Adam. Therefore, ask more diligently about the secret contained in that number and investigate its obscurities; Call with greater request so that it will be opened to you. Justice lies in the law of God; It admits no doubt, since the law is contained in the ten commandments. This is the reason why he owed ten thousand talents. It is that memorable decalogue, written with the finger of God and delivered to the people through his servant Moses. That one owed ten thousand talents; In them all sins are signified by their relationship with the number of the law. The other owed one hundred denarii, a figure symbolically no less, since one hundred times one hundred makes ten thousand, dendo numerare coepit, numerando autem complevit generationses septuaginta septem. What was the number? Intendite a quo. Exorsus est numerare a Christo usque ad ipsum Adam, qui primus peccavit, et nos cum peccati obligatione generavit. Pervenit usque ad Adam, et numerantur generations septuaginta septem: hoc est, a Christo usque ad Adam, quas diximus septuaginta septem; et ab Adam usque ad Christum septuaginta septem. Si ergo mile generatio praetermissa est, mile culpa praeteritur, ubi non debeat ignosci. Nam ideo ipsius septuaginta septem generationes enumeravit, quem numerum Dominus in peccatorum remissione commendavit; quoniam a baptism coepit enumerare, ubi omnia peccata solvuntur. CAPUT V.—6. Alia figure from eodem. Decalogus.—Et in hoc, fratres, adhuc accipite sacramentum maius. In seventy-seventh number mysterium est remissionis peccatorum. Tot generations inveniuntur a Christo usque ad Adam.

Deinde paulo diligentius interroga ipsius numeri secretum, latebrasque eius inquire: pulsa diligentius, ut aperiatur tibí. Iustitia lege Dei constat: verum est. Nam lex in decem praeceptis commendatur. Ideo ille debenbat decem milita talentrum. Ipse est ille memo rabilis Decalogus scriptus digito Dei, traditus populo per Moysen famulum Dei. Debebat ergo ille decem millia talentrum: omnia peccata significat, propter numerum legis. Debebat et ille centum denarii: non
