and ten times ten, a hundred. We have not gone outside the number of the law and in both you will find all the sins. Both were debtors and both deplored him and asked for forgiveness; But that bad, ungrateful, evil servant did not want to pay in kind, he did not want to lend what he, unworthy, had been lent. 7. See therefore, brothers; Whoever begins with baptism is free, the ten thousand talents have been forgiven; and upon leaving he must meet his fellow servant, his debtor. Focus your attention on the sin itself, for the number eleventh means transgression of the law. The law is number ten, sin is eleven. The law passes through ten, sin through eleven. Why the sin for eleven? Because to get to the number eleven you have to go past ten. The measure is fixed in the law; the transgression of it is sin. The moment you pass the number ten you come to hit the eleven. Therefore, great is the mystery symbolized when the tabernacle was ordered to be made. There are many things that were said there in the form of a mystery. Among other things, it was ordered that eleven, not ten, curtains be made of goat hair, since goat hair symbolizes the confession of sins. Are you looking for something else? Do you want to convince yourself that in this number of seventy-seven all sins are contained? The number seven is usually taken for the totality, since time develops in the succession of seven days, and, once those seven days are over, we begin again to return to the same thing again and again. It

The same thing happens with the centuries; You never get out of the number seven. When he said seventy-seven he indicated all the sins, because eleven times seven equals seventy-seven. He therefore wanted all sins to be forgiven who signified them in the number seventy-seven. Let no one hold them against him by denying forgiveness, so as not to have him against him when he prays. God says, in effect: Forgive and you will be forgiven. Since I forgave first, you forgive even if it is later. But if you don't forgive, I will turn back and demand from you everything I had forgiven you. The truth does not lie; Christ does not deceive nor is he deceived, who added these words: Thus will your heavenly Father who is in heaven do. You meet the Father, imitate him, for if you refuse to imitate him, you expose yourself to being disinherited: This is what your heavenly Father will do to you if each of you does not forgive your brothers from the heart. But do not just say with your mouth: "I forgive him," deferring forgiveness from the heart. God showed you punishment and threatened you with revenge. God knows how you say it. Man only hears your voice, but God examines your conscience. If you say, "I forgive," forgive. It is better to raise your voice and forgive from the heart than to be soft in speech and cruel in your heart. 8. I am already seeing undisciplined children asking for forgiveness; They don't want to be spanked and, when we want to give them some correction, they put these words in front of us. "I sinned, forgive me." I forgive him and he sins again. "Forgive me". You

minus ab eodem number. Nam et centies centum fit decem miüia; et you say deni, centum. Et ille decem millia talentrum, et ille decies denos. A legitimo enim numero non recessum est, in quo utroque invenies utraque peccata. Uterque debitor, et uterque veniae deplorator et impetrator: sed ille servus malus, servus ingratus, iniquus, noluit rependere quod accepit, noluit praestare quod illi indigno praestitum Fuit. CAPUT VI.—7. Seventy-seventh number peccata omnia esse praesignata. Peccata dimissa replicantur non iimittenti.—Videte ergo, fratres: quisque incipit a Baptismo, liber exit, dimissa sunt illi decem millia talentrum; et cum exierit, invenire habet conservum suum debitorem. Observet ergo ipsum peccatum: quia numerus undenarius transgressio legis est. Lex enim denarius, peccatum undenarium. Lex enim per decem, peccatum per undecim. Quare peccatum per undecim? Quia transgressio denarii est, ut [518] eas ad undenarium. In lege autem modus fixus est: transgressio autem peccatum est. Iam ubi transgrederis denarium, ad undenarium come. Adeo magnum mysterium figuratum est, quando iussum est tabernaculum fabricari. Fine ibi numerous dictates sunt, in magno sacramento. inter cetera vela cilicina iussa sunt fieri, non decem, sed undecim (Ex 26,7): quia per cilicium ostenditur confessio peccatorum. Quid autem amplius quaeris? Vis nosse omnia peccata contineri number isto seventy-seventh? Septuplum solet pro toto compute:

quoniam septem diebus volvitur tempus, et finito septenario, rursus ad caput reditur, ut eadem forma volvatur. Per huiusmodi formae revolutions saecula transeunt: a septenario tamen numero non receditur. Omnia enim peccata dixit, quando septuagies septies dixit: quia illud undecim duc septies, frunt septuagies septies. Omnia ergo dimitti peccata voluit, qui ea seventy-seventh number praesignavit. Nemo contra se teneat non ignoscendo, ne contra illum teneatur, quando orat. Dicit enim Deus, Dimitte, et dimittetur tibi. Be ego prior dimisi: dimitte vel postea. Nam si non dimiseris, I revoke you; et quidquid tibi dimiseram, replicabo tibi. Non enim mentitur Vetitas; non enim fallit, aut fallitur Christus, who subiecit, they say: Sic et vobis jaciet Pater vester, who in caelis est. Invenís Patrem, I will imitate Patrem. Si enim imítari non vis, exheredan disponis, Faciet ergo ita vobis, inquít, Pater vester caelestis si non remiseritis unusquisque fratribus vestris ex cordibus vestris (Mt 18:35). Ne dicas in lingua, Ignosco, et corde differes. Supplicium enim otendit tibi Deus, minando vindictam. Novit Deus ubidicas. Vocem tuam homo audivit: conscientiam tuam Deus inspicit. If you say, Resigned, resign. Melius est cum clamas ore, et dimittis in corde, quam blandus ore, crudelis in corde. CAPUT VII.—8. Ita ignoscendum, ut non neglegatur disciplina.—Iam ergo obsecrant pueri indisciplinati, et nolunt vapulare, qui sic praescribunt nobis, quando volumus daré disciplinam: “Peccavi, ignosce mihi.”

I forgive. Sin for the third time. "Forgive me". For the third time I forgive him. On the fourth time I spank him and he replies: "Have I already bothered you seventy-seven times?" If, relying on this precept, the rigor of discipline is put to sleep, once it is suppressed, unpunished evil rages. What is to be done, then? Let us correct with words and, if necessary, with lashes 3, but let us forgive the crime, let us cast off the guilt from the heart. That is why the Lord added from the heart, so that, if discipline is imposed out of charity, the softness of the heart will not be removed. Is there anything more pious than a doctor with a scalpel? He who is going to be cut cries and is cut, nevertheless; cries the one to whom the fire is going to be applied and it is applied. There is no cruelty whatsoever. Far be it from us to speak of cruelty in the doctor! He is cruel to the wound, so that the man may heal, because if he contemplates the wound, the man perishes. My brothers, this is, therefore, my advice: let us love our brothers who have sinned in any way; Let us not deny them the charity of our hearts and, when necessary, let us apply discipline, lest abandoning it, malice grows and we begin to be accused by God, since it has been read to us: Correct sinners in the presence of all, so that others may feel fear. Therefore, if anyone distinguishes the moments, he resolves the question; That is, everything is true, everything is well said. If the sin is secret, correct it in secret; Ecce ignovi, et iterum peccat. Ignosce: ignovi. Peccat tertio. Ignosce: tertio ignovi. Iam fourth vapulet. Et ille: «Numquid septuagies septies te fatiguevi?» Si hac praescriptione severitas disciplinae dormiat, repressa disciplina saevit impunita nequitia. Quid ergo faciendum est? Corripiamus verbis, et si opus est, et verberibus; sed delictum dimittamus, culpam de corde abiciamus. Ideo enim Dominus subdidit, de cordibus vestris (ib.), ut si per caritatem imponitur disciplina, de corde lenitas non recedat. Quid enim tam pium quam medicus ferens ferramentum? Plorat secandus, et secatur: plorat urendus, et uritur. Non est illa crudelites; absit ut saevitia medid dicatur. Saevit in vulnus, ut homo sanetur: quia si vulnus palpetur, homo perditur.

Sic ergo ista monuerim, fratres mei, ut fratres nostros qui pecca[519Jverint omni moda diligamus, de corde nostro caritatem in eos non dimittamus, et disciplinam, cum opus est, demus: ne per solutionem disciplinae crescat nequitia, et incipiamus propter Deum accusari; quia recitatum est nobis, Peccanles coram omnibus corripe, ut ceteri timorem habeant (1 Tim 5:20). Certe si quis, quod solum verum est, distinguit tempora, et solvit quaestionem, verum est. Despite the bad memories he retained (Confessions I, 9,14), Augustine continues to accept that sometimes whippings are still necessary. In his time the severity must have been less than in times past, against which Quintilian complained (Institution oratory I, 3,14), but the principle that "the letter enters with blood" was still in force. Do not forget that in Latin study is equivalent to manum ferulae subducere (present the hand to the ruler).
If the sin is public and manifest, publicly correct him so that he may amend and others may be afraid.
Topic: The rich young man (Mt 19,17). Place: Carthage. Date: Year 411.

1. The Lord said to a certain young man: If you want to attain life, keep the commandments. He did not say: "If you want to reach eternal life," but: If you want to reach life, simply calling eternal life life. Let us recommend above all the love of that life. Indeed, this life, whatever it may be, is the object of love; Be that as it may, although it is full of tribulations and miseries, men are afraid to end it and are filled with dread. From here you can see and consider how much one must love eternal life, given that the love for this miserable life is such and that it must end sometime. Consider, brothers, how much one must love the life that never ends. You love this life in which you toil so much, run, worry and long; You can hardly count the necessary things in this miserable life: sowing, plowing, replanting, sailing, grinding, cooking, weaving; and after all this you find yourself with a life that is ending. Look how much you have to suffer in this miserable life that you love so much; If peccatum in secreto est, in secreto corripe. Si peccatum publicum est et apertum, publishe corripe: ut ille emendetur, et ceteri timeant.
DE VERBIS EVANGELII MATTHAEI, CAP. 19,17: «If you see VENIRE AD VITAM, SERVA MANDATA»

CAPUT I. — 1. Aeterna vita quantum amanda sil, intettegitur ex amore huius vitae.—Dixit Dominus carem adolescenti: Si vis vinore ad vitam, serva mandata (Mt 19,17). Non dixit, Si vis comere ad vitam aeternam: sed, Si vis comere ad vitam; eam definiens vitam, quae fuerit aeterna vita. Huius ergo vitae amorem nos primitus commendemus. Etenim amatur et qualíscumque vita ¡sta; et ipsam qualemcumque, aerumnosam, miseram, finiré homines timent, et pavescunt. Hinc videndum est, hinc consideradum, quemadmodum amanda sit aeterna vita; quando sic amatur misera ista et quandoque finienda vita. Consider yourself, fratres, quantum amanda sit vita, ubi nunquam finias vitam. You love ergo istam vitam, ubi tantum laboras, curris, satagis, you yearn; et vix enumerantur quae necessaria sunt in misera vita; seminare, arare, novelkre, navigare,

And do you think you have to live forever, never dying? Temples made of stone and marble, reinforced with iron and lead, fall, however; and does man think that he will never die? Learn therefore, brothers, to seek eternal life, in which you will not have to endure these things, but will reign forever with God. For whoever wants life, as the prophet says, loves to see good days. In fact, when the days are bad, death is desired rather than life. Do we not see and hear men who, when they are involved in some tribulations and hardships, battered and sick, and see that they have to fatigue, say nothing else but: "O God, send me death, hasten the end of my days"? But if the disease ever comes, they run, doctors are brought, money and gifts are promised. Then death tells you: «Here I am, as you recently asked the Lord; Why do you want me to leave now? I have seen that you are a fraud and lover of this miserable life. 2. Referring to these days we are talking about, the Apostle says: Rescuing time, because the days are bad. Are not, in fact, evil these days that we spend in the corruption of this flesh, in and under the great weight of the corruptible body, among so many temptations, among so many difficulties; When pleasure is false, no security in joy, fear a torment, greed avid and sadness arid? See how bad the days are'; and yet, no one wants me to grind, coquere, texere: et post haec omnia finiré habes vitam. Ecce quae pateris in misera ista quam diligis vita: et putas te semper victurum, et nunquam moriturum? Templa, saxa, marmora, ferro plumboque consolidata, tamen cadunt: et homo nunquam se putat moriturum? Discite ergo, fratres, quaerere aeternam vitam, ubi ista non tolerabitis, sed in aeternum cum Deo regnabitis. Qui enim vult vitam, sicut dícit propheta, diligit videre dies bonds (Ps 33,13). Nam in diebus malis mors potius optatur, quam vita. Nonne audimus et videmus nomines in aliquibus tribulationibus et angustiis, conflictationibus et aegritudinibus dum sunt constituti, et vident se laborare, nihil aliud dicere nisi, Deus mitte mihi mortem, accelera dies meos? Et aliquando venit aegritudo; curritur, adducuntur medici, solidi et wrist promittuntur. Dicit tibi ipsa mors: Ecce adsum, quam paulo ante a Domino petebas; How can I escape? Inveni te falatorem, et miserae vitae amatorem. 2. Mali sunt dies huius vitae.

Vera ac beata vita, aeterna.—De his autem diebus quos agimus, ait Apostolus, Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt (Eph 5,10)- Non sunt ergo dies mali quos agimus in corruptela huius carnis, in tanta vel sub [520] voluptas, nulla securitas gaudii, timor torquens, avid cupiditas, arid tristitia? Ecce quam bad dies: et nenio vult finiré ipsos bad dies, mul1
Allusion to the fall of Rome.

come to an end and much is what men pray to God to live longer. Living longer, what else is it but tormenting yourself longer? Living longer, what is it if not adding bad days to other bad days? When children grow up, it seems as if days are added to them, but they do not notice that they are diminished; Even the way of counting is false. As they grow, their days become shorter rather than longer. Give, for example, eighty years to any man. What he has experienced, that is subtracted from the whole. And naive men rejoice at the many birthdays, both of their own and those of their children! Oh prudent man, you are sad if the wine in your vat decreases; you lose days and you're glad! 2 These are bad days, and the worse the more they love each other. It flatters the world so much that no one wants to end this eventful life. The truly true and joyful life will take place when we have been resurrected and reign with Christ. For the wicked must also be resurrected, but they will go to the fire. Therefore, there is no life if it is not happy. And there can be no happy life if it is not eternal, in which the days are good; They are not even many, but only one. Only by custom are those of this life called days. That day knows neither beginning nor end. Tomorrow does not succeed that day, since yesterday does not precede it. This day, or these days, and this life, true life, has been promised to us. It is the reward of some work. If, then, we love the reward, let us not fail in the work and we will reign forever with Christ. tumque hinc rogant homines Deum, ut diu vivant. Quid est autem diu vivere, nisi diu torqueri? Quid est aliud diu vivere, quam mal dies malis diebus addere? Et cum crescunt pueri, quasi accessunt illis dies; et nesciunt quia minuuntur: et ipsa est false computatio. Crescentibus enim decedunt dies potius, quam accessunt. Constitue alicui homini nato, verbi gratia, octoginta annos: quidquid vivit, de summa minuit. Et inepti homines gratulantur plurimis natalitiis, tam suis, quam filiorum suorum. O virum prudentem! Si tibi vinum minuatur in utre, tristaris: dies perdis, et gaudes? Mali ergo sunt dies: et eo peiores, quia diliguntur. Sic blanditur hic mundus, ut nemo velit finiré aerunosam vitam. Vera enim vita vel beata haec est, cum resurgemus et cum Christo regnabimus. Nam et impii resurrecturi sunt, sed in ignem ituri. Vita itaque non est, nisi beata.

Et vita beata esse non potest, nisi aeterna, ubi sunt dies boni; nec multi, sed unus. Ex consuetudine huius vitae appellati sunt dies. Dies ille nescit ortum, nescit occasum. lili diei non succedit crastinus; quia non praecedit eum hesternus. Hunc diem, vel hos dies, et hanc vitam, et veram vitam in promissis habemus. Alicuius ergo operis merces est. Si enim mercedem amamus, in opere non deficiamus: et in aeternum cum Christo regnabimus. See Supplementary Note 23: Temporality according to Saint Augustine vol. VII p.751.
SERMON Theme: Call (Mt 19,17-25).
Location: Probably Hippo. Techa: After the year 425.

1. The evangelical reading, brothers, that recently hit our ears, asks, more than an expositor, a listener to put it into practice. What is clearer than this light: If you want to come to life, keep the commandments? What else am I going to say? If you want to come to life, keep the commandments. Who is there who doesn't want life? And yet, who is there who wants to keep the commandments? If you do not want to keep the commandments, why do you seek life? If you are lazy to work, why do you rush to receive the reward? That rich young man said that he had fulfilled the commandments; He heard other greater precepts: If you want to be perfect, you lack only one thing: go, sell everything you have and give it to the poor, and you will not lose it, but you will have treasure in heaven; and come and follow me. In fact, what good would it do you if you don't follow me? As you have heard, he went away sad and crestfallen, because he had many riches. What he heard, we have also heard. The Gospel is the mouth of Christ; He sits in heaven, but he does not stop speaking on earth. SERMO OF
VERBIS EVANGELII MATTHAEI, CAP. 19,17-25: «If you see VENIRE AD VITAM, SERVA MANDATA», ETC.

CAPUT I. — 1. Mandatorum observatio ad promerendam vitam. Evangelium, os Christi.—Evangélica lectio, quae moda personuit in auribus nostris, fratres, auditorem magis atque factorem, quam expositorem desiderat. What does Clarius do, Si vis coming ad vitam, was tnandata useful? Quid ergo dicturus sum? Si vis vinore ad vitam, serva mandata (Mt 19:17). Quis est qui nolit vitam? et also quis est qui velit servare mandata? Si mandata servare non vis, quare vitam quaeris? Si ad opus piger es, quare ad mercedem festinas? Dixit se ille dives adolescens servasse mandata: audivit praecepta maiora, Si vis perfectus es se, unum tibi deest; Vade, vende omnia quae habes, et da pauperibus: nec perdes, sed habebis thesaurum in cáelo; et veni, sequere me (ib., 21). Nam quid tibi prodest, si feceris, et non sequaris me? Abscessit autem tristis ac maestus, sicut audistís: habebat enim fines divitias. Quod audivit ille, audimus et nos. Os Christi, Evangelium est. In cáelo sedet: sed in terra loqui non cessat. Nos non simus surdi: nam ille clamat. We are non simus mortui:
to the rich perfectly

Let us not therefore be deaf, since he cries out. Let us not be killed, for he thunders. If you don't want to do the most, do the least. If the weight of the greater is excessive for you, take the lesser at least. Why are you lazy for one or the other? Why are you opposed to both? The greatest are: Sell everything you have and give to the poor and follow me. The minor ones: You will not kill, you will not commit adultery, you will not seek false testimony, you will not steal, honor your father and mother, you will love your neighbor as yourself. Do this. What's the point of inviting you to sell your things if I can't get you out of stealing other people's things? You heard: You shall not steal, and you snatch them. In the presence of such a great judge I no longer consider you a thief, but rather a kidnapper. Forgive yourself, have compassion for yourself. This life is still a delay for you, do not reject the correction. You were a thief yesterday, don't be one today too. Maybe you were even today; Don't be tomorrow. Put an end to evil once and for all and demand good as a reward. You want to have good things, but you don't want to be good; Your life is the opposite of what you want. If possessing a good villa is a great good, how great an evil it is to have a bad soul! ' 2. The rich man went away saddened, and the Lord said: How difficult it is for one who has riches to enter the kingdom of heaven! And by the comparison he proposed to demonstrate it, he showed that being difficult is equivalent to being completely impossible. Everything that is impossible is difficult, but not everything difficult is impossible. To see how difficult it is, pay attention to the similarity: nam ille tonat. Si maiora non vis faceré, minora fac. Onus maiorum ad te multum est, vel minority prende. Quid ad utraque piger is? quid utrisque adversaris? Maiora sunt, [521] Vende omnia quae habes, et da pauperibus, et sequere me (ib.). Minora sunt, Non homicidium iacias, Non adulteres, Non falsum testimonium quaeras, Non fureris, Honora patrem et matrem, Diliges proximum tuum tanquam te ipsum (ib., 18-19). This fact. Quid ad I cry to you, ut bandages res tuas, cui extorquere non possum ne rapias alienas? Audisti, Non furaberis; you rapis Ante conspectum tanti Iudicis, iam te non furem teneo, sed raptorem. Parce tibi, miserere tui. Adhuc vita is dat tibi dilationem, noli abicere correptionem. Fuisti heri fur; noli et hodie. Iam strong and today you were; you were noli Aliquando fini malum, et pro mercede demands bonum. Bona habere vis, et bonus esse non vis: contrary est vita tua votis tuis.

Si magnum bonum est habere villam bonam, quantum malum est habere animam malam? CAPUT II.—2. Divites difficile salvantur. Pauperes quid cavere oportet.—Discessit dives contristatus, et ait Dominus: Quam difficile est, ut qui divitias habet, intret in regnum caelorum! (ibid., 23). Et quam is set difficult, similarityine purpose, otendit tam esse difficile, ut omnino sit impossible. Omne enim impossibile difficile est: sed non omne difficile impossibile est. Quale difficile est, similidadinem attende: Amen dico
See sermon 56:14.

Truly I tell you, it is easier for a camel to enter the depths of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. A camel entering the hole of a needle! Even if I had said a flea, it would be impossible. Therefore, when the disciples heard this, they were sad and said, If this is so, who can be saved? Who of the rich? Poor people, listen to Christ; I speak to the people of God. There are many poor people; At least you achieve it; but, nevertheless, listen. You who glory in your poverty, avoid pride, lest the humble rich surpass you; avoid impiety, lest the pious rich surpass you; Avoid drunkenness, lest the sober rich conquer you. Do not boast of your poverty, if they should not boast of their riches 2. 3. Let the rich listen, if there be any; listen to the Apostle: Ordain the rich of this world; sign that there are rich people from another world. The rich of the other world are the poor, the apostles, who said: As having nothing, and possessing everything. So that you would know which rich people he was talking about, he added: from this world. Therefore, let the rich of this world listen to the Apostle: He commands, he said, the rich of this world not to behave arrogantly. The first worm of riches is pride3. Like a bad moth, it gnaws everything and reduces it to ashes. Order them, then, not to behave arrogantly nor vobis, facüius est camelum per foramen acus traniré, quam divitem intrate in regnum caelorum (ib., 24). Camelum intrare per foramen acus: si diceret pulicem, impossible esset. Denique hoc audito, contristati sunt discipuli, et dixerunt: Si ita est, quisnam poterit salvus fieri? (ibid., 25). Quis divitum? Pauperes, audite Christum, populo Dei loquor. Plures pauperes, vel vos apprehendite; et also audite. Quicumque de paupertate gloriamini, cávete superbiam, ne vincant vos humiles divites: cávete impietatem, ne vincant vos pii divites: cávete ebrietatem, ne vincant vos sobrii divites. Nolite de paupertate gloriari, si non debent illi de divitiis gloriari. CAPUT I I I. — 3. Divitibus quid praecipi velit Apostolus. Vermis divitiarum, superbia.—Audiant divites, si tamen sunt; audiant Apostolum: Praecipe ditivibus huius mundi: quia sunt divites alterius saeculi. Pauperes sunt divites alterius saeculi, Apostoli sunt divites alterius saeculi, qui dicebant: Tanquam nihil habentes, et omnia possidentes (2 Cor 6,10).

Ut sciatis de quibus loquatur ditivibus, addidit: huius mundi. Audiant ergo Apostolum divites huius mundi: Praecipe, inquit, divitibus huius mundi, non superbe sapere. Primus vermis divitiarum superbia. Mala tinea, totum The association between wealth and pride is constant in Augustine (see Supplementary Note 34: Pride and Riches vol. I p.756), but it is also common for him to warn the poor against it. See Rule 2: The work of monks 25,33. On the other hand, the Saint constantly attests that most of Augustine's listeners were poor: Sermon 107 A (= Lambot 5); Enarration to Psalm 51:14. See Supplementary Note 34: Pride and Riches vol. VII p.756.
Calling the rich to perfection

Put your hope in the uncertainty of riches, lest you go to bed rich and wake up poor. Nor put your hope in the uncertainty of riches - these are the words of the Apostle - but in the living God. The thief takes your gold, but who will take God from you? What does the rich have if he does not have God? What doesn't the poor have if he has God? Therefore, do not put your hope in riches, he says, but in the God who abundantly grants us all things to enjoy, including himself. 4. If, then, you should not put your hope in riches or trust in them, but in the living God, what should you do with them? Listen to what: Be rich in good works. What does this mean? Explain it to us, Apostle. Many do not want to understand it because they do not want to undertake it. Explain it to us, Apostle; Do not give opportunity to evil to act with the darkness of your word. Tell us what you indicated in these words: Be rich in good works. Listen, understand it; they are not allowed to make excuses; rather, begin to accuse each other and say what we recently heard in the psalm: For I recognize my sin. Tell us what it means: Be rich in good works. What does it mean: Give easily? Is this also difficult to understand? Give easily, distribute. You have it and that other doesn't have it, share it so that they can share it with you. Give here and they will give you there. Distribute bread here and they will distribute bread to you there. What bread? The one here: the one you collect with your sweat and fatigue a rodit, et ad cinerem usque perducit. Praecipe ergo non superbe sapere, ñeque sperare in incerto divitiarum: ne forte dives dormías, et pauper surgas. Ñeque sperare in incerto divitiarum (Apostoli verba sunt); thirst in Deo, inquit, alive. Fur tibi tollit aurum, quis tollit tibi Deum? Quid habet dives, si Deum non habet? Quid non habet pauper, si Deum habet? Non ergo sperare in divitiis, ait; thirst in Deo vivo, qui praestat nobis abundantr omnia ad fruendum (1 Tim 6:17); cum quibus omnibus et se ipsum. [522] 4. De divitiis quid praestandum.—Si ergo non debent de divitiis sperare, non in eis fidere, sed in Deo vivo; de divitiis quid facturi sunt? Audi quid: Divites sint in operibus bonis (ib., 18). Quid est hoc? Explain, Apostle. Multi enim quod nolunt faceré, nolunt intellegere. Expone, Apostóle: noli will give occasionem mali operis per obscuritatem sermonis. Dic quid dixeris: Divites sint in operibus bonis.

Audiant, intellegant: non permíttantur se excusare, sed se potius incipiant accusare, et dicere quod audimus modo in Psalm: Quoniam peccatum meum ego agnosco (Ps 50,5). Say your quid est, Divites sint in operibus bonis. CAPUT IV.—Vacile tribuant.—Quid est, Vacile tribuant? Numquid et hoc non íntellegitur? Vacile tribuant, communicent (1 Tim 6:18). Habes tu, non habet alius: communica, ut communicetur tibi. Communica hic, et communicabis ibi. Communica hic panem, et accipies ibi panem. Quem hic panem? Quem colligis cum sweat et labore, former maledicto pri-

consequence of the curse that fell on the first man; the one there: He who said: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Here you are rich, there you will be poor. You have gold, but you still don't have Christ present. Give what you have to receive what you don't have. Be rich in good works, give easily, distribute. 5. So, are they to lose their property? He said: Share, not "Give it all." Reserve for yourself enough or more than enough. Let us give a certain part of this. What part? A tenth? The tithes were given by the scribes and the Pharisees. Let us be ashamed, brothers; The tenth part was given by those for whom Christ had not yet shed his blood. In case you think that you do something great because you break your bread with the poor, which barely means a thousandth of your possibilities, know that the scribes and Pharisees gave the tenth part. Still, I do not rebuke you; do at least that. Such is my thirst, such is my hunger, that I rejoice in these crumbs. But I will not keep quiet about what he said when he was alive who died for us. If your righteousness, he said, is not superior to that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. He does not caress us; As a doctor he goes to the raw part of the wound. If your justice is not superior to that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. The scribes and Pharisees paid tithes. What does this mean? Ask yourself this question. See what you do, how much you count on; what you give and what my hominis. Quem ibi panem? Qui dixit, Ego sum pañis vivus, qui de cáelo descendí (lo 6,51). Dives is hic, sed pauper is ibi. Habes aurum, sed nondum tenes praesentem Christum. Eroga quod habes, ut accipias quod non habes. Divites sint in operibus bonis, facile tribuant, communicent. 5. Quantum in pauperes erogandum.—Ergo perdituri sunt res suas? Communicent, dixit; non, "Totum dent." Teneant sibi quantum sufficit, teneant plus quam sufficit. Dermis inde quamdam partem. What are we parting? Decimam partem. Decimas ibant Scribae et Pharisaei (cf. Lk 18:12). Erubescamus, fratres; tenths dadant, pro quibus Christus nondum sanguinem fuderat. Decimas ibant Scribae et Pharisaei: ne forte aliquid magnum faceré te putes, quia frangís panem pauperi; et vix est millesima ista facultatum tuarum. Et tamen non reprehendo: vel hoc fac. Sic site, sic esurio, ut et ad istas micas gaudeam. Be tamen quid dixerit vivus, qui pro nobis mortuus est, non tacebo.

Nisi abundaverit iustitia vestra, inquit, super Scribarum et Pharisaeorutn, non intrabitis in regnum caelorum (Mt 5,20). Ule nos non palpat: medicus est, usque ad vivum pervenit. Nisi abundaverit iustitia vestra plus quam Scribarum et Pharisaeorum, non intrabitis in regnum caelorum. Scribae et Pharisaei decimas ibant. Who is he? Question yourself ipsos. Videte quid faciatis, de quanto faciatis;
The same argument appeared in sermon 9:19, but there he spoke not of the thousandth, but of the hundredth.
to the rich perfectly

you reserve; what you use in works of mercy and what you leave for lust. Therefore, give easily, distribute, treasure for yourselves a good foundation for the future, to achieve true life. 6. I have advised the rich; listen now you poor people. The first, give; the latter, do not steal. Some give of your wealth; The others curb your desires. Listen to the poor, the Apostle himself: It is a great gain. Profit is the acquisition of some wealth. And there is great gain in piety with enough. You have the world in common with the rich, but not the house. You have heaven and light in common with them 5. Seek what is enough; look for that, nothing more. Other things oppress, not elevate; they burden, they do not honor 6. Great gain piety with enough. Above all, mercy. Piety which is the worship of God. Pity is enough. We brought nothing into this world. Or did you bring something? Not even you rich people brought anything. Here you found everything; you were born naked like the poor. The weakness of the body is common to both, common is crying, a witness to misery. We brought nothing into this world—I speak to the poor—; but we can't get anything out of it either. Having food and shelter, let's be happy, because those who want to get rich... Those who want to get rich, not those who are. Those who are, be it. They heard what quid detis, quid vobis relinquatis; quid misericordiae impendaos, quid luxuriae reservetis. Ergo, Facile tribuant, communicent, thesaurizent sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum, ut apprehendant veram vitam (1 Tim 6, 18-19). CAPUT V.—6. Pauperes tenentur frenere cupiditates. Pietas.—Admonui divites: audite, pauperes. You erogate: you rappere nolite. Vos tribuite facultates: vos rénate cupiditates. Audite, pauperes, eumdem ipsum apostolum: Est autem quaestus magnus. Quaestus est acquisitio lucri. Est autem quaestus magnus, inquit, pietas cum sufficientia (ib., 6). Comtnunem habetis cum divitibus mundum: non communem habetis cum [523] divitibus domum: sed habetis commune caelum, communem luzm. Sufficientiam quaerite, quod sufficit quaerite, plus nolite. Ceteragravant, non sublevant; onerant, non honorant. Quaestus magnus, pietas cum sufficientia. In primis pietas. Pietas est Dei cultus. Pietas cum sufficientia. Nihil enim intulimus in hunc mundum. An attulisti hoc aliquid? Be nec vos, divites, aliquid attulistis. Totum hic invenistis, cum pauperibus nudi nati estis.

Communis est in utroque infirmitas corporis; communis vagitus, miseriarum testis. Nihil enim intulimus in hunc mundum (pauperibus loquitur); sed nec auferre aliquid possumus. Victum et tegumentum habentes, his contenti simus. Nam qui volunt divites fieri The same thought is widely developed by Saint John Chrysostom among others. See the Homily to 1 Tim 12:4. In Latin, a play on words is established between onerant and honorant or, in other cases, onus and honor.

refers to them: be rich in good works, give easily, share. They already heard it. Hear it, you who are not yet. Those who want to become rich fall into temptations and snares and into many harmful desires. Don't you feel afraid? Listen to what follows: They plunge men into perdition and death. Are you not afraid yet? Greed is, in fact, the root of all evil. Greed consists not in being rich, but in wanting to be rich. That's greed. Are you not afraid of plunging into death and perdition? Don't you fear greed, the root of all evil? You pull out the roots of the brambles of your estate, and do you not uproot from your heart the root of all ambitions? You cleanse your field from which you obtain the fruit that satisfies your belly, and do you not purify your heart so that your God may dwell in it? Greed is, in fact, the root of all evil; following which some went astray from the faith and came into much pain. 7. You heard what you should do, what you should fear; You heard how the kingdom of heaven is bought and how it is spent. All agree on the word of God. God made both the rich and the poor. Scripture speaks: The rich and the poor met; The Lord made them both. The rich and the poor met. Where else but in this world? The rich man was born, the poor man was born. You found yourself walking down a path at the same time. You do not oppress; you do not deceive This one needs, that one has. The Lord made them both. through which
He has help for the needy; through those who do not have, prove those who have. We have heard it, we have said it; let us fear, let us take precautions, let us pray, let us arrive.

(ibid., 7-9). Qui volunt fieri; non, Qui sunt. Nam qui sunt, sint. Quod ad illos pertinet audierunt, ut divites sint in operibus bonis, jadíe tribuant, communicent (ib., 18). CAPUT VI.—Audierunt ipsi. Vos qui nondum estis, audite: Qui volunt divites fieri, incidentunt in temptationem et laqueos, et desideria fines et noxia. Non timetis? Audite quod sequitur: Quae mergunt homines in interitum et perditionem. Not times? Radix est enim omnium malorum avaritia. Avaritia est, velle esse divitem, non iam esse divitem. Ipsa is greedy. Mergi non times in interitum et perditionem? Non times radicem omnium malorum avaritiam? De agro tuo exstirpas radicem spinarum, et non exstirpas de corde tuo radicem malarum cupiditatum? Purgas agrum tuum unde fructum capiat venter tuus; et non purgas cor tuum, ubi habitet Deus tuus? Radix est enim omnium malorum avaritia: quam quidam sequentes, a fide pererraverunt, et inseruerunt se doloribus multis (ib., 9-10). 7. Conclusion.—Audistis quid faciatis, audistis quid timeatis, audistis unde ematur regnum caelorum, audistis unde impediatur regnum caelorum. Omnes in verbo Dei concordate. Et divitem et pauperem Deus fecit. Scriptura loquitur: Dives et pauper occurrerunt sibi; fecit autem both Dominus (Prov 22,2). Dives et pauper occurrerunt sibi. In qua via, nisi in ista vita? Natus est dives, natus est pauper. Occurristis vobis pariter ambulantes viam. Your noli premere, your noli fraudare. Iste eget, ille habet. Fecit autem both Dominus. Per eum qui habet, iuvat egentem: per eum qui
Topic: The rich young man (Mt 19:21). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. Today's Gospel reading is an invitation to speak to your charity about the treasure in heaven. Well, contrary to what the greedy infidels think, God did not want us to lose our things. If we understand well, believe piously, and devoutly accept what we have been commanded to do, we were not ordered to lose them, but were told where to place them. No one can avoid thinking about his treasure and following his riches along a certain path of the heart. If they are buried, the heart goes downwards; If, however, they are kept in heaven, the heart will be above. If, then, Christians want to do what they know they also profess...—and not all those who hear it know it, and I hope those who know it do not know it in vain! Therefore, whoever wants to have his heart up, put there, there, what he loves; and although bodily he is on earth, he dwells with Christ in his heart; as non habet, probat habentem. Audivimus, diximus: timeamus, caveamus, oremus, perveniamus. SERMO
DE VERBIS EVANGELII MATTHAEI, CAP. 19.21: «VADE, SELL OMNIA QUAE HABES, ET DA PAUPERIBUS», ETC.

CAPUT I.—1. Thesaurus in cáelo reponendus. Sursum cor.—Evangelium nos admonuit lectione praesenti, de thesauro caelesti loqui Caritati vestrae. Ñeque enim, sicut infideles avari putant, [524] Deus noster will lose us voluit res nostras: si bene intellegatur, et pie credatur, et devotee accipiatur quod praeceptum est nobis; non nobis praecepit ut seguiremus, sed locum otendit ubiponeremus. Nemo enim potest nisi cogitare de thesauro suo, et quodam cordis itinere divitias suas sequi. Si ergo in terra obruuntur, ima petit cor: si autem in cáelo reservantur, sursum erit cor. Si ergo volunt faceré Christiani quod norunt se etiam profiteri: ñeque enim hoc omnes qui audiunt noverunt; atque utinam non frustra noverint, qui noverunt: qui ergo vult cor sursum habere, ibi, ibi ponat quod amat; et in terra positus carne, eum Christo habitet

The Church was preceded by its head, so the Christian must be preceded by his heart. As the members must go to the place where the head preceded them, Christ, in the same way when resurrected must go again to the place where the heart of man has now preceded him. Let us, then, leave here with the part in which it is possible for us; Our entire being will follow wherever any of our parts have gone. The earthly house is in ruins; The celestial house is eternal. Where we have proposed to go, let us emigrate in advance. 2. We heard that a certain rich man asked the good teacher for advice on how to obtain eternal life. It was a great thing that he loved and a vile thing that he did not want to despise. In this way, listening with a perverse heart to him whom he had called a good teacher, out of a love greater than what was vile, he lost possession of charity. If I had not wanted to achieve eternal life I would not have asked for advice on how to achieve it. How do you explain, brothers, that he rejected the words of him whom he himself had called a good teacher, words taken from his faithful doctrine? Are you a good teacher before you teach and a bad teacher after you have done so? He was called good before teaching. He did not hear what he wanted, but what he should hear; He came full of desires, but he left sad. What would have happened if he had been told: "Lose what you have", when he left sad because he was told: "Keep well what you have"? Go, he said, sell what you have and give it to the poor. Are you afraid of losing it? Listen to what follows: And you will have a

treasure in heaven. Perhaps you would manage to have a servant as guardian of your treasures; guardian of your gold will be your God. Whoever gave it on earth, he himself keeps it in heaven. Perhaps he would not have hesitated to entrust to Christ what he had and was saddened because he was told: Give it to the poor, as if thinking in his heart: «If you had said to me: Give it to me and I will keep it for you in heaven, I would not have hesitated to entrust it to my good lord and teacher; but now you have said: Give it to the poor. 3. No one is afraid to give to the poor; Let no one think that the one who receives is the one whose hand he sees. The one who receives is the one who ordered you to give. And we do not say this because it seems so to us by human conjecture; Listen to him who advises you and gives you security in the Scripture: I was hungry, he said, and you gave me food. And when he answered him after enumerating the services: When did we see you hungry?, he replied: When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me. The poor beg, but the rich receive; You give to the one who will consume it and the one who will return it receives. And he must not return what he received; He wanted to borrow at interest, he promised to return more than you gave him. Now put your greed into motion, consider yourself a usurer. If you truly were, you would be recriminated by the Church, condemned by the word of God, all your brothers would execrate you like a cruel usurer who wishes to exploit the tears of others. Be a usurer, no one forbids you. You want to give to a poor person who will cry when it comes time to give back; He gives to the right person, that is, to the one who even exhorts you to receive what he promised.

corde: et sicut Ecclesiam praecessit caput eius, sic christianum praecedat cor eius. Quomodo membra itura sunt quo praecesserit caput Christus, sic iterum resurgens iturus est quo nunc praecesserit cor hominis. Eamus ergo hinc, ex qua parte possumus: sequetur totum nostrum quo praecesserit aliquid nostrum. Domus terrena ruinosa est: domus caelestis aeterna est. Quo comere disponimus, ante migremus. CAPUT II.—2. Conúlium salutis petens, nec lubenter audiens. Deus ipse servat quod pauperi datar.—Audivímus divitem quemdam a bono magistro quaerentem consilium adipíscendae vitae aeternae. Magnum erat quod amarat, et vile erat quod contemnere nolebat. Itaque perverso corde audiens quem iam dixerat magistrum bonum, maiore amore vilitatis, possessionem perdidit caritatis. Nisi vitam aeternam consequi vellet, consilium de habenda vita aeterna non requireret. Quid ergo est, fratres, ut verba eius quem magistrum bonum ipse dixerat, de fideli doctrina sibi deprompta respueret? Magister ille bonus est antequamdocat; cum docuerit, malus? Antequam doceret, dictus est bonus. Non audivit quod voluít, sed audivit quod debuit: desiderans venerat, sed tristis abscessit. What if he says: "Perde quod habes"? quando tristis abscessit, quia dictum est: "Bene serva quod habes." Vade, inquit, vende omrita quae habes, et da pauperibus. Forte times ne perdas? Vide quid sequitur: Et habebis thesaurum in cáelo (Mt 19,21). Custodem tibi thesaurorum

tuorum forte servulum aliquem posuisses: custos auri tui erit Deus tuus. Qui dedit in terra, ipse servat in cáelo. Fortassis non dubitasset ille Christo commendare quod habebat, et ideo contristatus est, quia dictum est ei, Va pauperibus: tanquam in corde suo dice: «Yes, say: 'Da mihi, ego tibi in cáelo servabo'; “non dubitarem daré Domino meo, magister bonus”; nunc autem dixisti: Da pauperibus. CAPUT I I I. — 3. Deus in paupere accipit. Fenus pium et fenus iniquum.—Nemo timeat erogare pauperibus; nemo putet eum accipere cuius manum videt. Ule accipit qui iussit ut dares. Ñeque hoc ex nostro corde aut humano coniectura dicimus: ipsum audi et te monentem, et tibi securitatem scribentem. Esurivi, inquit, et dedistis mihi manducare. Et cum enumeratis officiis eorum respondissent: Quando te vidimus esurientem? ille responded: Cum uni ex minimis [525] meis fecistis, mihi fecistis (Mt 25,35.37.40). Mendicat pauper, sed accipit dives: das ei qui consummate, accipit ille qui reddat. Ñeque hoc redditurus quod accipit: fenerari se voluit, plus promittit quam dederis. Exsere nunc avaritiam tuam, te puta feneratorem. Certe si esses, obiurgareris ab Ecclesia, confutareris verbo Dei, exsecrarentur te omnes fratres tui, tanquam crudelem feneratorem, de lacrimis alienis acquirere cupientem. This fenerator, nemo prohibit you. Pauperi vis daré, qui quando reddiderit planget: da idealo, qui etiam hortatur ut recipias quod promittit,

4. Give to God and call him to judgment. Furthermore, give to God and you will be called to judgment to receive. No doubt you were searching the earth for your debtor; He was also looking for a place to hide from your presence. You appeared before the judge to say: "Order that a certain debtor of mine appear in court." After hearing this, he leaves and does not even want to greet you, you who perhaps, when he was in need, with your loan you were his salvation. So you have someone to give to. Give to Christ; He takes you to court so that you may receive, you who are surprised that he has received something from your hands. In fact, to those on his right he will gladly say: Come, you who are blessed by my father. Where to? Come, receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you since the beginning of the world. Why this? I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink; I was naked and you clothed me; I was a pilgrim and you took me home; sick and in prison and you visited me. I did not receive directly, but through mine. What you gave them reached me; Be sure, you have not lost it. On earth you set your eyes on the ideal ones; You have the truly ideal one in heaven. Certe in terra quaerebas debitorem tuum: quaerebat et ille, sed ubi se absconderet a facie tua. Adieras iudicem et dixeras: Iube illum debitorem meum conveniri. lile audito hoc, discedit, et nec salutare te quaerit: cui forte genti salutem commodando praestiteras. Habes ergo cui eroges. Da Christo; ipse te convenit ultro, ut recipias, et mirantem quia aliquid accepit te accepit. Ñam illis ad dexteram positis ultro ipse dicet: Venite, benedicti Patris mei. What? Come, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab origine mundi. Pro qua re? Esurivi, et dedistis mihi manducare; sitivi, et dedistis mihi potum; nudus eram, et vestistis me; hospes, et adduxistis; aeger et in prison, et visitatis (ib., 34-36). Et illi: Domine, quando te vidimus? (ibid., 37). Quid est hoc? Convenit debitor, et creditores excusant. Non vult eos fidelis debitor failedi. Recipere doubts? Accepi, et ignoratis? Et respondert quemadmodum accepit: Cum uní ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis (ib., 40). Non accepi per me: accepi per meos. Quod illis datum est, ad me pervenit: securi estote, non perdidistis. you gave food, and everything else. I received earth, I will return heaven; I received temporal things, I will restore eternal things; I received bread, I will give back life. Furthermore, I received bread and I will return bread; I received drink and I will give drink; I received hospitality and I will give a house; being sick I was visited and I will give health; I was seen in prison and I will return freedom. The bread that you gave to my poor was consumed; The bread that I will give nourishes and does not run out. Give us, then, that bread, the bread that came down from heaven. By giving the bread, he will give himself. What did you want when you lent at interest? Give coins and also receive coins; but give few and receive more than given. “I,” says God, “will transform everything you gave me into something better.” What would not be your joy if, by giving a pound of silver, you received one of gold? Examine yourself and question greed: "I gave a pound of silver and I receive a pound of gold." How are silver and gold similar? Furthermore, how are the earth and the sky alike? Both the gold and the silver would have to be left here; You, on the other hand, will not remain here forever. I will give you something else, I will give it to you in greater quantity, I will give it to you better and I will give it to you forever. This is how our greed is calmed, brothers, so that the other one, which is holy, can be ignited. The one who forbids you from doing good in any way speaks to you in a perverse way; you want to serve a bad lady and not recognize the good Lord. And sometimes there are two ladies who take over the heart and tear into various parts the bad servant, worthy of serving them. inquit, et dedistis mihi manducare, et cetera. Terram accepi, caelum dabo: temporalia accepi, aeterna restituam: panem accepi, vitam dabo. Immo etiam hoc dicamus: "Panem accepi, panem dabo: potum accepi, potum dabo: hospitium accepi, domum dabo: aeger visitatus sum, salutem dabo: in carcere visus sum, libertatem dabo." Pañis quem dedistis pauperibus meis, consumptus est: pañis quem ego dabo, et reficit et non deficit. Det ergo nobis panem, pañis ille qui de cáelo descendit. Cum panem dabit, se ipsum dabit. CAPUT V.—Quid enim volleys, when you fenerabas? Nummos daré, et nummos accipere: sed pauciores daré, plures accipere. Ego tibí, inquit Deus, omnia quae dedisti, in melius commutabo. Si enim dares libram argenti et reciperes libram auri, quanto capereris gaudio? Inspice, et interroga avaritiam: «Libram argenti dedi, libram auri recipio». Quid [526] simile argentum et aurum? Magis ergo, quid simile terra et caelum?

6. Sometimes two opposite ladies take over a man, greed and lust. Greed says: "Guard"; lust: «Spend» \ Subjected to two ladies who command and demand different things, what are you going to do? Both have their own ways of speaking. When you start not wanting to obey and regain your freedom, since they cannot command, they flatter. And his flattery is more to be feared than his commands. What does greed say? «Save for yourself, save for your children. If you feel needy, no one will give you. Don't live from day to day; look for your future. On the contrary, lust says: “Live while you are alive; Treat your soul well. You have to die and you don't know when. You don't know who you should leave it to or if they should own it. You deprive yourself and take it away from your gluttony; When you have died, perhaps he will not put a chalice on your grave 2, or if he does, he will get drunk and not a drop will reach you. Therefore, treat your soul well when and as long as you can. One thing greed commanded: «Keep for yourself; look for your future. Lust is different: «Spend; Treat your soul well. 7. Get fed up, oh free man called to freedom! Get tired of the servitude of such ladies. Recognize your redeemer, your manurnisor. Serve him; send easier things, not contrary things. I dare say more. Note the prosopopoeia. It refers to the custom of celebrating banquets next to the tombs, especially of martyrs; It was customary to bring meals that were sometimes distributed among the poor, but they were almost always consumed by those who carried them. See The City of God VIII, 27. The custom was African (Confessions VI, 2,2) and Augustine tried to banish it from his people despite how deeply rooted it was. Read Letter 29 in this regard. Also Against Fausto XX, 21.

Let your Lord appear saying the same things and your Redeemer not saying the opposite. If you don't want to, there is no need in your house who serves reluctantly. Pay attention to your Redeemer, pay attention to your price. He came to redeem you; spilled the blood. He who bought you at such a high price valued you highly. You recognize who has bought from you; Consider what He redeemed you with. I overlook the remaining vices that superbly dominated you; In fact, you were the servant of innumerable and perverse ladies. The words that were directed to you, that ordered contrary things, those same ones you hear from the mouth of your Lord, who, on the other hand, does not command anything contrary to each other. It does not eliminate their words, but it takes away their power. What was greed telling you? «Keep for yourself; look for your future. The word does not change, the man changes. If you like, compare the counselors now. On the one hand, greed; on the other, justice. 8. Examine those contrary things. “Keep for yourself,” says greed. Suppose you want to obey; Ask him where you have to keep it. She will show you a protected place, a walled enclosure, an iron ark. Since you keep a lot, whoever thinks of stealing it from you also thinks of killing you. Finally, even if you protect your treasure and your clothes against thieves with any type of defense, protect them against rust and moths! What do you have to do? The one who takes it away is not the external enemy, but rather the one who consumes it within. 9. In conclusion, the advice given by greed is not good. In effect, he ordered you to keep it without giving you a place where you could do it. Also say the second part: “Look to the future.” Why future? For a few, uncertain days. To a man who may not even live tomorrow, he says: "Look to the future." But suppose he lives as long as avarice judges; not how much he shows, how much he teaches, how much he trusts; May he live, grow old and end his days, as greed judges. A bent old man, leaning on his cane, still seeks profit and listens to greed, which tells him: "Look to the future." Why future? If he speaks to him when he is already expiring, he tells him: "Look out for your children." If only those old people who have no children were not miserly! Even to them, even to those who have no reason to excuse their iniquity, he never ceases to say: "Look to the future." But perhaps they suddenly blush; Let us consider those who have children and see if they are certain that they will possess what they are left with. While you are alive, pay attention to the children of others, of whom some lost through the evils of others what they had possessed and others consumed through their own evil what they had had; in both cases

The children of the rich become poor. Avoid being born servants of greed. "But," they say, "my children will possess this." It is an uncertain thing. I do not say: "It is false"; but whatever you do, it is uncertain. Finally, suppose it is true: what do you want to leave them? What you acquired for yourself. Certainly what you acquired was not left to you, and yet you possess it. If you could have something that you did not inherit, they can also have it even if you don't let them have it. 10. The counsels of greed have been refuted; Let the Lord now say the same things, let justice speak now. The words will be the same, but the meaning will be different. Your Lord tells you: "Keep for yourself, look to your future." Ask him too; "In what place should I keep?" You will have a treasure in heaven, where no thief will break in and no moth will destroy it. With a view to what future will you keep it? Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you since the beginning of the world. The duration of this kingdom is shown by the end of the sentence. Non est foris hostis auferens, sed est intus absumens. CAPUT VIII.—9. Aliud stolidum consilium.—Non ergo bonum consilium dedit avaritia. Ecce iussit ut serves, et non invenit daré locum ubi serves. Dicat etiam consequentia: «Consulate in posterum». In quantum posterum? In dies paucos et incertos. It says: "Consule in posterum, homini fortassis victuro nec in crastinum." Sed ecce vivat quantum putat avaritia, non quantum ostendit, non quantum docet, non quantum fidit: sed quantum putat vixerit, senuerit, finierit; adhuc senex incurvus, baculus innixus, lucrum quaerit, et audit avaritiam dicentem: "Consule in posterum." In quod posterum? Iam exspirans loquitur: "Propter filios tuos", inquit. Utinam vel illos senes non avaros haberemus, qui filios non habent. Etiam ipsis, etiam talibus, etiam iniquitatem suam nulla pietatis imagine excusantibus non cessat dicere: Consule in posterum. Sed forte ipsi cyto erubescunt: illos videamus qui filios habent, utrum certi sint filios suos possessuros esse quae reliquerint. Intendant cum vivunt, filios aliorum, alios alienis improbitatibus quod habuerant amittentes, alios propria nequitia quod possederant consumants: et remanent inopes filii divitum.

Parcite nasci servi avaritiae. "Sed possidebunt hoc, inquit, filii mei." Incertum est: non díco: «Falsum est»; sed quod feceris, incertum est. Postremo, fac certum: quid eis vis relinquere? Quod acquisisti tibi. Certe quod acquisisti relictum non erat, et habes. Si tu habere potuisti quod tibi relictum non est, poterunt ergo habere et illi quod tu non reliqueris. CAPUT IX.—10. Consilium Dei id iubentis quod avaritia.—Refutata sunt consilia avaritiae: sed Dominus eadem dicat, iustitia iam loquatur: ipsa erunt verba, non ipsa sententia. Serva tibi, ait Dominus tuus, consult in posterum. Et hunc interroga: Ubi servabo? Habebis thesaurum in cáelo (Mt 19,21): ubi fur non accesot, ñeque tinea corrumpet (cf. Mt 6,20). In quantum posterum servabis? Venile, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab origine mundi. Hoc regnum quantorum dierum est, ostendit finis ipse sententiae. Cum de sinistris diceret: Sic ibunt illi in ambustionem aeternam; ait de dexteris: Iusti autem in vitam aeternam (Mt 25,34.46). Hoc est consu[528]lere in posterum. Posterum, quod posteriora non habeat. Dies illi sine fine, dicti sunt dies, et dictus est dies. Ait enim quidam, Ut habitem in domo Domini in longitudinem dierum (Ps 22,6), cum de illis diebus diceret. Et dies dictus est, Ego hodie genui te (Ps 2,7). Et illi dies unus dies; quia iam nec tempus: dies Ule nec ab hesterno praeceditur, nec crastino exeluditur,

Others were the words that greed told you and, at the same time, greed itself was overthrown in them. 11. All you have to do is say: "And what do I do with my children?" Listen there also to the advice of your Lord 3. If your Lord were to say to you: "I who created them know better than you who begat them," perhaps you would find nothing to answer. But you have to keep your eyes on that rich man who walked away sad and who was rebuked in the Gospel; Perhaps you say to yourself: “That rich man did wrong in not selling all his possessions and giving them to the poor, since he had no children; I, however, have them; "I have someone to save them for." Also in this weakness your Lord supports you. I will dare to speak for his mercy; I will dare to say something, not the result of my presumption, but of His mercy. “Save for your children too,” but hear me out. If, as happens in human things, someone loses one of their children...—understand, brothers, understand that greed has no excuses either here or in the future world. We are faced with human things; It is not that we desire them, but that we use them as examples. One who was a Christian was lost, that is, you lost a Christian son, and, therefore, you did not lose him, but sent him ahead. Not even he abandoned you, he simply preceded you. Ask your faith; surely you too must go where he preceded you. I say something simple, to which I believe no one has a reply. "Is your son alive?" Ask your faith. If, then, he lives, why do his brothers take possession Ergo in ipsum postemm consulamus: et non diverse sunt verba, quae tibi dicebat avaritia; et eversa est avaritia. 11. Avarorum false pietas in filios. Filio mortuo sua pars est transmittenda.—Restat utdicas: Et quid ago de filiis meis? Audi et inde consilium Domini tui. Si tibi dicat Dominus tuus: «Melius ego cogito qui creavi, quam tu qui generasti»: forte quod dicas non habebis. Sed divitem illum aspecturus es qui tristis abscessit, et in Gospel reprehensus est; et dices tibi forte: lile dives ideo male fecit non venderé omnia, et daré pauperibus, quia filios non habebat: ego autem habeo filios; habeo quibus servem. Et in hac infirmitate consisted tibi Dominus tuus. CAPUT Serva et filiis tuis: sed audi me.

from his side? But you will say, "Should he take possession of it again?" Then send him to where he preceded us; If he cannot come to where his goods are, his goods can go to where he is. Notice who you are in. If your son resided in the palace, became a friend of the emperor, and said to you: "Sell the share I have there and send it to me," would you find a way to answer him? Now your son is with the emperor of all emperors and with the king of all kings and with the lord of all lords; send it to him. I don't tell you: "He has what it takes." The Lord in whose house your son is feels need on earth. He wants to receive here what he gives in heaven. Make the journey, as some misers usually do: give the pilgrims what you will receive in your homeland, 12. Finally, I am no longer talking about you, I am talking about your son. You hesitate to give what is yours, you also hesitate to return what belongs to others: it is clear proof that you did not save it for your children. Warn that you do not give it to your children, because you take it away from themselves. You certainly take it away from that one. Why is he unworthy to receive just because he lives with a more worthy person? You would be right if the one with whom you live did not want to receive, already rich in your house, but in the divine one. Far be it from me to tell you: "Give what you have"; What I tell you is: "Return what you owe." "But his brothers will have it," you say. Oh perverse doctrine, by which you teach your children to wish death on their brothers! If with the assets of their dead brother they become richer, iturus es, quo ille antecessit. Rem briefly medical, cui puto quod nemo responderat. Vivit filius tuus? Interrogate fidem tuam. Si ergo vivit, quare invaditur pars eius a fratribus eius? Are you saying: Numquid rediturus est, et possessurus? Mittatur ergo illi quo praecessit ille: ad rem suam vinore non potest, res eius ad eum iré potest. Vide cum quo sit. Si in palatio militaret filius tuus, et amicus Imperatoris ieront, et diceret tibi: «Vende ibi partem meam, et mitte mihi»: numquid invenires quid responderes? Modo cum Imperatore omnium imperatorum, et cum Rege omnium regum, et cum Domino omnium dominorum est filius tuus: mitte illi. Non dico: "Necessarium habet ipse"; Dominus ipsius, apud quem est filius tuus, eget in terra. Hic vult accipere quod dat in cáelo. Quod faceré nonnulli avari solent, fac traiectitium: da in peregrinos, quod recipias in patria tua. CAPUT XI.—12. Mortuo debentur, quod vivo servabatur.—Postremo iam de te nihil; of filio tuo loquor.

Dubitas date tuum, dubitas et reddere alienum: certe convincingris, quia non filiis tuis servabas. Ecce non das filiis tuis, quia tolles filiis tuis. Huic certe tolles. See how they look in your home. What will you do then? Do you divide the patrimony and teach patricide? 13. But I do not want to talk about a lost son, so that I do not seem to threaten human adversities. Let's talk about something somehow better and more desirable. I'm not saying now that you have one less child; think you have one more. Reserve a place for Christ among your children, add your Lord to your family; Let your creator join the offspring, let your brother be counted among your children. With such a difference, he deigned to also be a brother. And being the only son of the Father, he wanted to have co-heirs. How great is his largesse! Why are you so sterile? You have two children; count him as the third; you have three, count it as the fourth; If you have five, let him be the sixth; If you have ten, let him be the eleventh. I don't want to continue; reserve for your Lord the place of one of your sons. What you give to your Lord will benefit you and your children; What you keep in a bad way for your children will harm you and them. Give him a portion, which you judged would correspond to a son. Act as if you yourself had fathered one more. 14. What is so great about this, my brothers? I give some advice: do I put a noose around the throat? As the Apostle says: I say this for your benefit, not to trap you. I think, brothers, that it is something easy and simple for a father to get used to the idea that he has one more child and buy possessions such that both he and his children will possess forever. Greed has nothing to answer for. You have acclaimed these paerunt, vide quemadmodum se attendant in domo tua. Quid ergo facies? Patrimonium divides, et parricidia twelves? 13. Christus filiis annumerandus in patrimonii divisione.—Sed nolo dicere de uno amisso, ne casus humano vidar minari. Melius quodam moda prosperiusque loquamur. Non dico, unum minus habebis, computa quia unum plus habes. Fac locum Christo cum filiis tuis, accessat familiae tuae Dominus tuus, accessat ad prolem Creator tuus, accessat ad numerum filiorum tuorum frater tuus. Cum enim tantum intersit, et frater esse dignitus est. Et cum sit Patri Unicus. voluit habere coheirs. Ecce ille quam largiter! your quate tam steriliter? Duos filios habes, tertium illum computa: tres habes, quartus numeretur: quintum habes, sextus dicatur: decem habes, undecimus sit. Nolo amplius dicere: unius filii tui serva locum Domino tuo.

Quod enim dabis Domino tuo, et tibi proderit et filiis tuis: quod autem male servas filiis tuis, et tibi oberit et filiis. Dabis autem portionem unam, quam unius filii deputasti. Deputa te unum amplius genuisse. CAPUT XII.—14. Avaritiae excusatio sublata.—Quid magnum, fratres mei? Consilium do, numquid guttur ligo? Sicut ait Apostolus: Haec ad utilitalem vestram dico, non ut laqueum vobis initiation (1 Cor 7:35). Puto, fratres, quia parva et facilis cogitatio est, putare patrem filiorum habere unum filium amplius, et comparare cultura praedia quae possideas in aeternum, et ipse et filii tui. Topic: The workers of the eleventh hour (Mt 20, 1-16). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. In the holy Gospel you have heard a parable that is appropriate to current times regarding the workers in the vineyard. It is now the time of the bodily harvest; There is, however, another spiritual harvest in which God enjoys the fruit of his vineyard. We worship (colimus) God, and God cultivates (colit) us.' But if we worship God, it is not to make him better; we do it with worship, not with the plow. He, on the other hand, cultivates us like a farmer cultivates his field. By cultivating ourselves it makes us better, because the farmer also makes his field better with his cultivation. And he looks for the fruit in us so that we worship him. We are His field of cultivation, since He never ceases to remove the bad seed from our hearts with His word; to open our hearts with its arbitrator, sermonem de faciendis eleemosynis. Vox ista vestra laudantium, tune accepta est Domino, si videat et manus operantium.

"I want to sleep." "But it will cause your death." He, for the love of sleep, answers: "I want to die." But charity adds: "I don't want it." This same loving affection is frequently expressed by the son towards his elderly father who will die a few days later, having already finished the days of his life. If he sees him lethargic and notices from the doctor that his father suffers from that illness, he says to himself: “Wake up your father; If you want him to live, don't let him fall asleep. He behaves like a child with the old man: he hits him, pinches him, pokes him, causes him discomfort out of pity and does not allow someone who must die soon due to his old age to die immediately; and if he lives, the son is glad to live a few more days with him who is to die and to whom he is to succeed. Topic: The two blind men of Jericho (Mt 20:30-34). Location: Unknown. Date: Around the year 400.

1. Your holiness knows as I do that Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, is the doctor who seeks our eternal salvation, and who took upon himself the illness of our nature so that our illness would not be eternal. He assumed a mortal body in which to put death to death. And although he was crucified in what he took from our weakness, as the Apostle says, he nevertheless lives by the power of God. From the same Apostle are these words: And since he no longer dies, death will no longer have power over him. All this is well known by your faith. From which it also follows that we know that all the miracles he performed on bodies serve as a warning so that, from here on, we perceive what will never pass or have an end. He restored to the blind the eyes that death would surely once close; He resurrected Lazarus, who was going to die again. Everything he did for the benefit of the health of bodies was not done so that they would be eternal; although, nevertheless, even to the same body it must ultimately give eternal health. SERMO

(CHAP. 20,30-34) CAPUT I. — 1. Medicus noster, Christus. Miraculis corporalibus aedificabat fidem.—Bene nobiscum novit Sanctitas vestra, Dominum nostrum et salvatorem lesum Christum medicum esse nostrae salutis aeternae; et ad hoc eum suscepisse infirmitatem naturae nostrae, ne sempiterna esset infirmitas nostra. Assumpsit enim cotpus mortale, in quo occideret mortem. Et quamvis crucifixus est ex infirmitate nostra, sicut ait Apostolus; sed vivit ex virtute Dei (2 Cor 13:4). Eiusdem Apostoli verba sunt: ​​Et quia iam non moritur, et mors ei ultra non dominabitur (Rom 6,9). Haec ergo bene note sunt fidei vestrae. Simul et hoc consequens est, ut noverimus omnia miracula, quae corporaliter fecit, valere ad admonitionem nostram, ut percipiamus ab eo quod non est transiturum, ñeque finem habiturum. Oculos reddidit caecis, quos erat utique mors aliquando clausura: resuscitavit Lazarum, iterum moriturum. Et quaecumque ad salutem corporum fecit, non ad hoc fecit, ut sempiterna essent: cum tamen daturus sit etiam ipsi corpori in fine sempiternam salutem.
See note 15 to sermon 51.

But since what was not perceived by the eyes was not believed, through these temporal things that were seen, faith was built in those that were not seen 2. 2. Let no one, therefore, say, brothers, that our Lord Jesus Christ does not now do these same things and, therefore, put the early times of the Church before the present. For in a certain place the Lord himself puts those who do not see and believe before those who see and therefore believe. In fact, even in those same times the weakness of his disciples fluctuated so that, in order to believe that the one they saw had been resurrected, they thought they had to touch him. It was not enough for the eyes to see, unless the hands also went to the limbs and touched the scars of recent wounds. So that disciple who doubted, after having touched and recognized the scars, exclaimed: My Lord and my God! The scars manifested the one who had healed all the wounds in others. Couldn't the Lord have been resurrected without the scars? (Yes), but he knew the wounds existing in the hearts of his disciples, and to heal these he had kept those in his body. And what did the Lord say to the one who had confessed and said My Lord and my God? Because you have seen me, you have believed; Blessed are those who do not see and believe. Who was he referring to, brothers, if not us? Not because we were going to be the only ones, but because we were going to come behind. After a short period of time, after

who moved away from mortal eyes to strengthen faith in the hearts, as many as believed, believed without seeing, and their faith had great merit. To acquire that faith they only put in motion a pious heart, not a hand ready to touch. 3. The Lord did all this to invite faith. This faith is now boiling in the Church, spread throughout the world. He also now performs major healings, thinking of which he did not disdain to perform minor ones. For as the soul is better than the body, so the health of the soul is also better than that of the body. Now blind flesh does not open its eyes through a miracle of the Lord, but its heart does open through his word. A mortal corpse is not resurrected now; Instead, he resurrects the soul that lay dead in a living corpse. The deaf ears of the body are not opened now, but how many are those who have the ears of the heart closed, which, however, open when the word of God penetrates, so that those who did not believe believe and those who lived badly live well and those who did not obey obey! We say: "That one is a believer," and we are surprised when we hear it referred to people whose hardness we knew. Why are you surprised that he now believes, is innocent and serves God, if not because you realize that he who you knew was blind sees; that the one you knew was dead lives; What does the one you knew who was deaf listen to? See, then, another type of dead, to which the Lord was referring when he said to a certain person who delayed following him because he wanted to bury his father: Let the dead bury their dead, Certainly, the gravediggers

The dead are not dead in the body, because, if that were the case, they would not be able to bury dead bodies. However, he calls them dead; Where are they except internally, in the soul? In the same way that in the realm of the visible it often happens that in a house that is intact and in good condition the owner of it lies dead, so also in a healthy body many have a dead soul internally. The Apostle awakens them with these words: Arise, you who sleep, and come out from the dead and Christ will illuminate you. It is the same one who gives light to heaven and who resurrects the dead. With his voice, through the Apostle, he shouts to the dead: Get up, you who sleep. The blind man will be illuminated by the light, once he has risen. How many were the deaf that the Lord had before his eyes when he said: Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear! Who was in his presence without bodily hearing? What other ears was he looking for, then, but those of the inner man? 4. Likewise, what eyes did he require when speaking to those who certainly saw, but with the eyes of the flesh? In fact, when Philip said to him: Lord, show us the Father and it is enough for us, he well understood that it could be enough to show us the Father; But how could the Father be enough for someone who was not equal to the Father? Why wasn't it enough for him? Because I didn't see him. Why didn't I see him? Because the eye with which to see him was not yet healthy. What was visible to these eyes in the flesh of the Lord was seen not only by the disciples who honored him, but also by the Jews who crucified him. Therefore, whoever wanted to be seen from another

way, required different eyes. And, consequently, to him who said: Show us the Father, he answered: Have I been with you so long and you have not yet known me? Felipe, who sees me, also sees the Father. And in order to heal the eyes of faith in the meantime, he is first admonished according to faith, so that he can come to reality. And so that Philip would not think that God should be thought of as he saw the Lord Jesus Christ in his body, he immediately added: Don't you believe that I am the Father and the Father is in me? He had already said before: He who sees me sees the Father. But Philip did not yet have a healthy eye with which to see the Father and, therefore, with which to see the Son himself as equal to the Father. So, then, he set out to heal and strengthen with the medicine and soothing of faith the gaze of the still dirty mind, incapable of seeing so much light, and he said to it: Don't you believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me? Therefore, he who cannot yet see what the Lord is about to show, must not seek to see before he believes, but rather believe first that he may heal the eye with which he must see. To these servile eyes only the form of a servant was manifested, because if he who did not consider being equal to God an object of plunder, could already be seen as equal to God by those whom he wanted to heal, he would not have needed to annihilate himself and take the form of a servant. And since there was no possibility of seeing him as God but as man, the one who was God became man so that what was seen would heal the cause of what was not seen. Ad hoc sacrosancta mysteria celebrantur; ad hoc sermo Dei praedicatur; ad hoc exhortatione Ecclesiae morals, id est, Augustine's statement is resounding: our only task in this life is to heal the eye of the heart to be able to see God, the goal and destiny of man. There are many diseases that prevent your vision: anger, greed, cupiditas, libido, iniquity, secular concupiscence (n.6). This work of healing is not easy and the multiple activity of the Church is directed towards it.

What are those two blind men by the road if not the two towns that Jesus came to heal? Let us show them in the sacred scriptures. In the Gospel it is written: I have other sheep that are not of this fold; It is fitting that these also be drawn to him so that there may be one flock and one shepherd. What, then, are these two towns? One the Jew and the other the Gentile. I was not sent, he says, but to the sheep that perished of the house of Israel. To whom did he say these words? To the disciples when that Canaanite woman screamed and admitted that she was a dog to deserve the crumbs from the lords' table. And since he deserved them, the two peoples to whom he had come are already revealed: that is, the Jew, to whom these words refer: I have not been sent except to the sheep that perished of the house of Israel, and the Gentile, to whom this woman anticipated in figure, whom he had at first rejected by saying: It is not right to throw the children's bread to the dogs, and to whom, having answered: That's right, Lord, but dogs also eat the crumbs that fall from the table. of his lords, he answered: O woman, great is your faith; let it be done according to your will.
