Thus, even before his passion and glorification, the Lord pointed out the two peoples; He had come to one to keep the promises made to the patriarchs and to the other because in his mercy he did not reject him, so that what was promised to Abraham would be fulfilled: In your lineage all people will be blessed. This is the reason why the Apostle also, after the resurrection and ascension of the Lord, after having been despised by the Jews, turned to the Gentiles. But he did not remain silent either before the churches formed by believing Jews: He was, he said, unknown to the Jewish churches, which live in Christ. They had only heard that he who previously persecuted us now announces the faith that once swept us; and in me they glorified God. For this reason, for having made the two peoples one, Christ is called the cornerstone. The angle, in effect, joins two walls with different directions. Is there anything more diverse than circumcision and the foreskin? Here is a wall that comes from Judea and another that comes from the Gentiles; but they join together in the cornerstone: The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. In a building there is no angle except when two walls coming from different directions meet at a point and join in a certain unit. The two blind men who cried out before the Lord were, in figure, these two people. 11. Pay attention now, dearly beloved. The Lord passed by, Quia ille dixerat: Non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum; sed tantum dic verb, et sanabitur puer meus (ib., 8,10.8). Ita ergo Dominus ante passionem et clarificationem suam duos iam populos designabat: unum, ad quem venerat propter promissa Patrum; et alterum, quem propter misericordion non repellebat: ut impleretur quod promissum erat Abrahae, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes (Gen 22,18). Propterea et Apostolus iam post resurrectionem Domini et ascensionem, ubi contemptus est a Iudaeis, perrexit ad Gentes. Nec tamen Ecclesiis quae de Iudaeis crediderant, tacuit: Eram, inquit, ignotus facie Ecclesiis ludaeae, quae sunt in Christo. Tantum autem audiebant quia qui aliquando nos persequebatur, nunc evangelizat fidem quam aliquando vastabat: et in me, inquit, magnificabant Deum (Gal 1,22-24). Sic et angularis lapis dicitur Christus, qui fecit utraque unum (Eph 2,20.14). Angulus enim duos parietes copulate from different sources.

Quid tam diversum, quam circumcisio et praeputium, habens unum parietem of Iudaea, alterum parietem of Gentibus? Sed angulari lapide copulantur. Lapidem enim quem reprobaverunt aedificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli (Ps 117,22). Angulus in aedificio non est, nisi cum duo parietes former diverse venientes in unum conveniunt, et quadam unitate iunguntur. Isti ergo duo parietes secundum typum, duo caeci erant clamantes ad Dominum. CAPUT XII.—11. Transiens Iesus interpellatur, et sanat.—Attendite

the blind people screamed. What does it mean to pass? Do temporary works, as we already said. Our faith is built on conformity to these transitory works. We believe, in fact, in the Son of God, but not only insofar as he is the Word through whom all things were made; For if he had always remained in the form of God in which he is equal to God, he would not have annihilated himself by taking the form of a servant; Nor would the blind have sensed him to be able to shout at him. But as he performed temporary works, that is, as he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death and death on a cross, the two blind men cried out: Have mercy on us, son of David. The very fact that David's lord and creator wanted to also be his son, he realized in time, he did it in passing. 12. What is it, brothers, to cry out to Christ but to conform to the grace of Christ with good works? I say this, brothers, lest we raise our voices too much, but let our customs remain silent. Who is the one who cried out to Christ to expel his inner blindness as he passed by, that is, by dispensing to us the temporal sacraments with which we are invited to acquire the eternal ones? Who is the one who shouts for Christ? He who despises the pleasures of the world cries out to Christ; who says, not with his tongue, but with his life: The world is crucified for me and I for the world, he is the one who cries out to Christ. Shout out to Christ who distributes and gives to the poor so that his justice remains forever and ever. rare bags that do not age, an unfailing treasure in heaven: as if hearing the sound of the footsteps of Christ passing by, the blind man shouts for these things, that is, make them come true. say? I don't know how to say it, but I don't know how to shut up either. This is what I say and I say it openly: I fear Jesus in all that passes and in all that remains, and that is why I cannot remain silent. Good Christians, those truly enthusiastic and eager to fulfill God's precepts written in the Gospel, feel hindered by bad and lukewarm Christians. The very multitude of those who are with the Lord forbids them to cry out, that is, forbids them to do good, lest by their perseverance they be healed. Let them cry out, do not get tired or allow yourself to be carried away by the authority of the masses; Do not even imitate those who, being Christians from ancient times, live badly and are envious of good works. Do not say: "Let us live as such a great multitude lives." Why not as the Gospel commands? Why do you want to live according to the rebuke of the mob that prevents it from shouting and not according to the footsteps of Christ who passes by? They will insult you, they will revile you, they will call you to turn back; You scream until your scream reaches the ears of Jesus. For those who persevere in doing what Christ commanded, ignoring the crowd that forbids it, and do not overestimate themselves because they seem to follow Jesus, that is, because they call themselves Christians, but have greater love for the light that Christ will restore to them than fear of the noise of those who forbid it, will in no way be separated; Christ will stop and heal them. 14. He receives his healing when he understands that Christ is God. Let your charity understand this; Pay attention to the great mystery that I am going to tell. Everything done over time by our Lord Jesus Christ instills faith in us. We believe in the Son of God; not only in the Word by whom all things were made, but also in the Word made flesh to dwell among us, born of Mary the Virgin and the other things contained in faith 8, which have been made manifest to us so that Christ might pass by and so that the blind, hearing the noise of his steps, would shout with their works, manifesting with their lives the profession of their faith. Jesus stops now to heal those who scream. In fact, he who says: And if we had known Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him. To the extent that is possible in this life, he saw the divinity of Christ. There is the divinity of Christ and there is his humanity. Divinity stops, humanity passes. What does it mean that divinity stops? It does not change, it is not destroyed, it does not regress. His coming to us did not mean separating himself from the Father; nor his ascension to move locally. Having taken the meat, he changed places; God, on the other hand, does not even change his place when he takes the flesh, because he does not reside in any place. Let us be touched by Christ who stops and heals our eyes. Whose eyes? Those of those who cry out when he passes, that is, those of those who do good through that faith that has been given to us in time to instruct us, still infants. incommutable aeternitate. Ibi enim sanatur oculus, quando intellegitur Christi divinitas. Percipiat hoc Caritas vestra: attendite quod dicam grande sacramentum. Omnia temporaliter gesta a Domino nostro Iesu Christo, fidem nobis inserunt. Credimus in Filium Dei, non solum in Verbum per quod facta sunt omnia; sed in ipsum Verbum factum carnem, ut habitaret in nobis, natum of the virgin Mary, et cetera quae fides habet, quae nobis exhibita sunt, ut Christus transiret, et ut caeci vestigia transeuntis audientes, clamarent operibus, vita professionem fidei commemorantes. He who lacks that one thing that makes everything else useful possesses everything he possesses in vain. Let us therefore embrace charity, striving to maintain the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. Universa inutilite habet, qui unum illud, quo universis utatur, non habet. CAPUT XIX.—Amplectamur itaque caritatem, studentes servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis (Eph 4,3). It is often the case that a man is accused and, once accused, defends himself; When the accused has defended himself rationally and correctly, those who hear him say: "He got out of there." Where did it come from? Without moving from his place, he left there. How did he get out of there? After having justified and defended himself with all justice. This is what the saints did when they shook the dust from their feet against those who did not receive the peace they announced to them. From there came that watchman to whom it was said: I have set you as a watchman over the house of Israel. To him it is said: If you warn the wicked and he does not turn from his iniquity and evil way, he will die in his iniquity and you will save your soul. If he does this, he leaves there, not because of bodily separation, but because of the justification of his actions. He did what had to be done, even if the other did not obey what he should have obeyed. All you have to do is get out of there. 24. Thus cried Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Let's see if they did this, if they abandoned the people of God and went to other towns. How frequently and how vehemently did Jeremiah rebuke the sinners and criminals of his people! However, he lived among them, with them he entered the only temple, he celebrated the same mysteries. He lived in the same assembly of evil men, but he left there crying out. This is getting out of there, this is not touching what is unclean: not consenting with the will and not forgiving with the mouth. abandon the good ones mixed in that town, in which they too could have existed? Brothers, while Moses himself was receiving the law on the mountain, the people were making an idol below. It is certainly already clear to your prudence how such testimonies of the Scriptures are to be understood. The prophet rightly said clearly: Depart and leave there and do not touch the unclean thing. To understand what he said, I pay attention to what he did. With what he did he explains to me what he said. He said: Depart. Who did he say it to? Certainly to the righteous. Who did he tell you to separate from? Without a doubt of the sinners and wicked. I ask now if he himself separated from such. The answer is negative. Then he wanted to say something else, since he would certainly be the first to do what he ordered. would have had it at the right time, that is, in their time, it would have no guilt, since a tree without knowledge lacks guilt. Add to this that, as read in another evangelist who also narrates this scene, It was not the time for those fruits. It was the time when the fig tree sprouts the tender leaves that we see appear before the fruits; The proof of this is that the day of the Lord's passion was approaching, which we know when it falls; Even disregarding this, we should believe the evangelist, who says: It was not the time of the figs. Theme: Parable of the banquet and wedding dress (Mt 22:1-14). Place: Restitutía Basilica of Cartago. Date: Between the year 411 and 416.

1. All the baptized know which is the wedding of the king's son and which is his banquet. The Lord's table is ready for everyone who wants to participate in it. No one is prohibited from approaching, but the important thing is the way you do it. The Holy Scriptures teach us that there are two banquets of the Lord: one to which the good and bad come, and another to which the bad do not have access. To the extent that this passionate love resides in us, to that same extent we are not without sin. Charity grows, passionate love decreases. For charity to ever reach its perfection, other love must be extinguished. Put on your wedding dress. I am addressing you, those who do not yet have it. Jesus, son and Lord of David
Theme: Jesus, son and Lord of David. The hypocrisy of scribes and Pharisees (Mt 22,42-25,12). Location: Unknown. Date: After the year 400.

1. As we have heard in the Gospel that has just been read, the Jews were asked how Jesus Christ, our Lord, was the son of David, if David himself considers him his Lord. Question they couldn't answer. They knew about the Lord only what they saw. He appeared to them, in fact, as the son of man; hiddenly, however, he was also the Son of God. Hence comes the fact that they believed they could defeat him and that they insulted him, when he was hanging from the cross, with these words: If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross and we will believe in him. They saw something and something was hidden from them. If they had known him, they would never have crucified the king of glory. They knew, however, that Christ would be the son of David, for even now they await his coming. Their arrival is hidden from them, but because they want to. If they did not recognize him when he was hanging from the cross, that does not mean that they should not have recognized him as reigning. In what name have all peoples been summoned and blessed if not in that of him whom they do not recognize as Christ? He is, in fact, the son of David; certainly of the

descendant of David, according to the flesh, and son of Abraham. If it was said to Abraham^: In your race all people will be blessed, and they are seeing that the promise is reality in our Christ, why do they still wait for him who has already come and do not fear his second coming? Jesus Christ himself, our Lord, using prophetic testimony to affirm his person, said that he was stone. But such a stone that if someone stumbles against it, it will smash, and if it falls on someone, it will crush him. He stumbles against it when he lies in the humility of the flesh; In this humility he makes the one who stumbles crash; When he comes in glory he will crush the proud. God is patient and day by day invites you to believe. 2. The Jews, therefore, did not know how to answer the question that the Lord proposed to them regarding the filiation of Christ, the Messiah. In fact, when they answered that he was the son of David, he continued asking: How then does David, inspired, call him Lord, saying: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right until I put your enemies under my feet? If, then, David, inspired, calls him Lord, how is he his son? He did not say, "He is not your son," but rather, "How is he your son?" When you say "how?", you ask, you don't deny. It is as if he were saying to them: “You rightly say that Christ is the son of David, but why does David call him Lord? If you call him your Lord, how is he your son? The Jews would know this if they were instructed in the Christian faith that we profecentur omnes gentes (Gen 22:17), et vident iam in Christo nostro benedici omnes gentes; Quid expectant quod iam venit, et non timent quod venturum est? Lapidem enim se dixit ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus, prophetico ad se assertendum utens testimony. Lapidem autem talem, ut si quis in eum offenderit, conquassetur; super quem autem lapis ille venerit, conterat eum (cf. Lk 20,17,18). Quando enim in eum offendentem, humilis iacet: iacendo humilis quassat offendentem, veniendo excelsus conterit superbientem. Iam ergo Iudaei illa offensione quassati sunt: ​​restat ut eius praeclaro adventu etiam conterantur, nisi forte cum vivunt, agnoverínt, ne moriantur. Patiens enim est Deus, et illos quotidie invitation ad fidem.

But, not knowing this, they fell silent and, keeping their mouths closed, they were not able to open their ears, to know, indoctrinated, the answer to the question to which they did not know how to answer. 3. It is a great mystery to know how he is both Lord and son of David, how a person is man and God; how in the human form he is less than the Father and in the divine form equal to him; how to combine these two statements of his: The Father is greater than me and I and the Father are one thing. It is a great mystery and, therefore, in order to understand it, customs must be accommodated. The mystery is closed to the unworthy and opens to those who deserve it. We do not knock on the Lord's door with stones, or with doorknobs, or with our fists, or with kicks. It is life that calls; It is to life that it opens. It is asked, it is sought, it is called with the heart; the heart opens. Heart that must be pious so that your request, your search and your call are appropriate. The first condition is to love God freely; This is true piety: not to seek any other reward outside of him, even if we expect it from him. There is nothing better than him. Indignis enim clausum est, promerentibus aperitur. Nec lapides, nec vectes, nec pugni, nec calces sunt quibus pulsamus ad Dominum. Vita pulsat, vitae aperitur. Can he ask of God for whom God is a vile thing? He gives you a piece of land and you rejoice, as a land lover, made of land. If you rejoice when you are given land, how much more should you rejoice when you are given the same one who made heaven and earth! God, therefore, must be loved freely. In fact, the devil, unaware of the interior of holy Job, accuses him of a great crime, saying: Does Job worship God disinterestedly? 4. Therefore, if the adversary reproaches him for this, we must fear that he will reproach us. We have to deal with those who are skilled in slander. If he tries to pretend what does not exist, how much more will he blame us for what really exists! Let us rejoice, however, that the judge is such that he cannot be deceived by our accuser. Well, if we had a man as judge, the enemy would make him believe whatever he wanted. No one more clever than the devil to pretend! Even now it is he who invents the false crimes attributed to the saints 2. Since he cannot assert his accusations before God, he spreads them among men. And what profit does he derive from it, the Apostle saying: Our glory is the testimony of our conscience? Or do you think that he invents the crimes without any malice? He knows very well the evil it causes if it is not resisted with the vigilance of faith. That is why he spreads slander referring to the good, to exspectet ex illo. Illo enim melius est nihil. Et quid carum petit a Deo, cui Deus ipse vilis est? Terram dat, et gaudes, amator terrae, et factus terra. Si gaudes, quando dat terram; how much amplius gaudere you must, cum se ipsum tibi dat, qui fecit caelum et terram? Free ergo amandus est Deus. Parable of the ten virgins
Topic: Parable of the ten virgins (Mt 25,1-13). Location: Carthage? Date: In the year 410 or 411.

1. Those of you who were present yesterday, remember our promise.' A promise that, with God's help, I must fulfill today, not only for you, but also for the crowd that has gathered. It is not easy to find out who are the ten virgins, and who are the five wise ones, and who are the five foolish ones. Judging by the content of the reading that I wanted to be read today to your charity 2, as the Lord gives me to understand, it does not seem to me that this parable or similarity refers only to those who, due to their particular and more excellent holiness, receive in the Church the name of virgins, whom, with a more frequent term, we have become accustomed to calling sanctimonials3. On the contrary, if I am not mistaken, it applies to the entire Church. And even if we refer it to the sanctimonial calls, why do we talk about ten? In no way can such a great multitude of virgins be reduced to such a meager number! Someone may say: "What if, although there are many in name, in reality they are so few that they are barely found?"

Every soul that lives in a body is associated with the number five, because it uses five senses. Qui autem ambulat ad testimonium alienum, oleum non portat secum. Si ideo abstines ab illicitis, et facis bona opera, ut ab hominibus lauderis, non est intus oleum. Denique cum coeperint nomines non laudare, deficiunt lampades. Intendat itaque Caritas vestra. Antequam dorment illae virgines, non est dictum quia exstinguebantur lampades illarum. Sapientium lamps burn with internal oil, with conscientiae securitate, with interiore gloria, with intimate caritate. Ardebant tamen et illarum fatuarum. Quarc tune ardebant? Quia non deerant laudes hominum. Postea vero quam surrexerunt, id est, in resurrectione a mortuis, coeperunt aptare lampades suas, id est praeparare Deo operum suorum reddere rationem.

Et quia tune nemo est qui laudet, omnis homo causae suae vacat, nemo est tune qui non de se cogitet: non ergo erant qui oleum vendeent; coeperunt deficere lampades, et converterunt se fatuae ad quinqué prudentes: Date nobis de oleo vestro, quia lampades nostrae extinguuntur (Mt 25.8). Hoc quaerebant quod consueve[578]rant, id est, alieno oleo luzre, ad alienas laudes ambulare. Da/e nobis de oleo vestro, quia lampades nostrae extinguuntur. 11. Fatuae Virgines irridentur a sapientibus.—At illae: Ne forte, inquiunt, non sufficiat nobis et pobis, ite potius ad pendentes, et emit
Parable of the ten virgins

mockery. Why who is he mocking? Because they were prudent and wisdom resided in them. Their wisdom did not come from themselves, but there lived in them the wisdom spoken of in a certain book, which, when the evils with which it has threatened them come, will say to those who have despised it: And I will laugh at your misfortune. What is so strange that the wise laugh at the foolish? What is laughing? 12. Go to those who sell it and buy it yourselves, for you were not used to living well except because the men who sold you the oil praised you. What does it mean: they sold you the oil? They sold you praise. Who but flatterers sell praise? How much better it would have been for you not to have condescended to them, to have carried oil within yourself and to have done all good works with a right conscience! Then you would say: The righteous will rebuke me and rebuke me with mercy, but the oil of the sinner will not anoint my head. It is better, he says, for the righteous to rebuke me, for him to argue with me, for him to slap me and correct me before the sinner's oil anoints my head. What is the oil of the sinner, but the caresses of the flatterer? 13. Go therefore to those who sell it; That's what you used to do. We don't give it to you. Because? Lest it not be enough for us and you. What is it: not enough? This statement does not come from despair, but from sober and pious humility. Well, even if a good person has the convobis (ib., 9). Non consulentium, sed irridentium est ista responsio. Quare irridentium? Quia sapientes weret, quia sapientia erat in illis. Non enitn sapientes de suo erat: sed illa in illis erat sapientia, de qua scriptum est in quodam libro, quae dicit contemptoribus suis, cum venerint ad mala, quae illis minata est: Et ego ves brings perditioni superridebo (Prov 1,26). Quid mirum est, quia sapientes irrident fatuas? Quid est irridere? CAPUT IX.—12. Oleum ementes et pendentes.—Ite ad pendentes, et emit vobis (ib.): quae non solebatis bene vivere, nisi quia vos homines laudabant, qui vobis oleum vendebant. Quid est, oleum vendebant? Laudes vendebant. Qui vendunt laudes, nisi flatterers? Quanto magis non acquiesceretis adulatoribus, et intus oleum portaretis, et propter bonam conscientiam omnia bona opera faceretis: tune dicetetis, Emendabit me tustús in misericordia, et arguet me; oleum autem peccatoris non impingttabit caput meum (Ps 140.5).

Melius, inquit, emendet me iustus, arguat me iustus, colaphizet me iustus, corrigat me iustus, quam impiguet caput meum oleum peccatoris. Quid est oleum peccatoris, nisi blandimenta adulatoris? 13. Prudentium virginum humilitas.—Ite ergo ad pendentes; hoc faceré consuestis. We autem non vobis damus. Quare? Ne forte non sufficiat nobis et vobis. Quid est, non sufficiat? Non desperatione dictum est, sed sobria et pia humilitate. Quamvis enim bonus habeat bonara

quiet science, how can you know what will be the judgment of him whom no one deceives? He has a clear conscience, he has no scruples about crimes committed in his heart, but thinking about certain daily sins of human life, although his conscience is clear, he nevertheless says to God: Forgive us our debts, because he fulfilled what follows: As we also forgive our debtors. From the heart he broke his bread with the hungry, from the heart he clothed the naked; With the inner oil he did his good works and, nevertheless, that clear conscience trembles before the day of judgment. 14. Now see what it means: Give us oil. In response they heard: Go rather to those who sell it. Because you have become accustomed to living righteously through human praise, you do not bring oil with you; We, however, are not going to give it to you, lest it not be enough for us and you. We can barely pass judgment on ourselves, how much less can we judge you! What does it mean: We can barely pass judgment on ourselves? When the righteous king sits on his throne, who will boast of having a chaste heart? Perhaps you will not find anything in your conscience, but you will find the one who sees better, the one whose divine gaze penetrates the most secret. Maybe I'll see something, maybe I'll find something. How much better it will be for you to say to him: Do not enter into judgment with your servant! How much better it will be for you to also say: Forgive us our debts! Because it is also said to you, with reference to those torches, those lamps: "I was hungry and you gave me food." What conscientiam; unde scit quemadmodum iudicet ille quia a nemine fallitur? Habet bonam conscientiam, non illum titillant crimina in corde concepta; sed propter quotidiana quaedam vitae humanoe peccata, licet bona conscientia sit, tamen dicit Deo, Dimitte nobis debita nostra: quia fecit quod sequitur: Sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris (Mt 6,12). Fregit panem esurienti ex corde, vestivit nudum ex corde: de oleo interiore fecit opera bona, et tamen in illo iudicio trepidat ipsa bona conscientia. 14. Pulsantibus ostium cur non aperitur.—Vide quid est, Date nobis oleum. Audierunt, Ite potius ad vendentes. Quia laudibus humanis bene vivere consuestis, vobiscum oleum non portatis: non autem nos damus; ne forte non sufficiat nobis et vobis. Vix enim de nobis iudicamus, quanto minus possumus iudicare de vobis? Quid est: Vix de nobis iudicamus?

Quia cum rex iustus sederit in throne, quis gloriabitur castum se habere cor? (Prov 20,8.9). Forte tu non invenís aliquid in conscientia tua; et invenit ille qui melius videt, cuius acies divina penetrat altiora: videt forte aliquid, invenit forte aliquid. Quanto melius illi [579] say, Ne intres in iudicium cum servo tuo? (Ps 142,2) Etiam quanto melius dicis, Dimitte nobis debita nostra? Quia et dicitur tibi propter illas faces, propter illas lampades: Esurivi, et dedisti mihi manducare (cf. Mt 25,
Parable of the ten virgins

say? Didn't they do it too? They didn't do it before him. How did they do it then? In the way that the Lord prohibits when he says: Try not to do your justice in the presence of men to be seen by them; Otherwise you will not have the reward of your Father who is in heaven. Do not be like the hypocrites when you pray. They love to stand in the squares and pray to be seen by men. Truly I tell you, they have already received their reward. They bought the oil, they paid the price; They bought it, they were not deceived in human praise; They searched for them and obtained them. But these praises will not help them on the day of judgment. Those others, however, how did they do them? Let your good works shine before men so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. He did not say, "And they glorify you." The oil you have is not from yourself. Boast 7 saying: "I have oil, but received from him." What do you have that you haven't received? Therefore, some acted in one way and the others in another. 15. It is not surprising that when they go to buy, when they look for those who praise them, they do not find; When they look for those to console them, they do not find. The door is open, the husband and wife come, the Church already glorified with Christ, to unite each member to itself. And they went with him to the wedding and the door was closed. Then the foolish ones also arrived; Did they perhaps buy oil or did they find someone to sell it to them? For this 35). Quid ergo? et illae non illud fecerunt? Non fecerunt ante illum. Sed quomodo fecerunt? Quomodo prohibet Dominus, qui dixit: Cávete faceré iustitiam vestram coram hominibus, ut videamini ab eis: alioquin non habebitis mercedem apud Patrem vestrum qui in caelis est. Et nolite similes esse hypocritis, quando oratis. Amant enim stare in plateis et orare, ut videoantur ab hominibus. Amen dico vobis, perceperunt mercedem suam (Mt 6,1.5). Emerunt oleum, pretium dederunt: emerunt, non sunt fraudan laudibus humanis; quaesierunt human laudes, habuerunt. Istae laudes humanoe in die iudicii non eos adiuvant. Illae autem quomodo fecerunt? Luceant opera vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in caelis est (ib., 5, 16). Non ait: You. Non enim de tuo habes oleum. Iacta te, et dic: Habeo: sed ab eo. Quid enim habes, quod non accepisti? (cf. 1 Cor 4:7). Ergo illae sic fecerunt, illae sic.

15. idem tractatur argumentum.—Non est autem mirandum, cum eunt emere, cum quaerunt a quibus laudentur, et non inveniunt; cum quaerunt a quibus consolentur, et non inveniunt; aperta est ianua, come sponsus et sponsa, tune glorificata cum Christo Ecclesia, ut singular membra ad totum se colligant. Et intraverunt cum eo ad nuptias, et clausum est ostium (Mt 25:10). Et illae fatuae venerunt: sed numquid oleum ' Apostille against the Pelagians.
The servant who hides his talent

They found the doors closed. They started calling, but it was late. 16. We were told, truthfully and without any deceit: Knock and it will be opened to you. But now, while the time of mercy lasts, not when it is the time of judgment. We must not confuse these times, since the Church sings the mercy and judgment of the Lord. This is the time of mercy: do penance. Do you have it in your power to do it at the time of judgment? You will find yourself among those virgins to whom the door was closed. Lord, Lord, open to us. Did they not do penance by not taking oil with them? But what did their late penance profit them, when true wisdom laughed at them? Therefore, the door was closed to them. Who knows everything, didn't he know them? What does it mean, therefore, I do not know you? I disapprove of you, I reprove you. I don't know you in my art; my art ignores vices. This is a great thing: he is unaware of vices and yet he judges them. He doesn't know them because he doesn't make them; He judges them when he fails them. So, I don't know you. 17. The five wise virgins went and entered. How many you are, my brothers, in the name of Christ! Let the five prudent virgins be found among you, that is, those who belong to this prudence signified in the number five. The hour will indeed come; It will come and at a time we do not know. He will come at midnight, stay awake. This is how the Gospel story concludes: Watch, because you know neither the day nor the emerunt, aut a quibus emerent invenerunt? Ideo ianuas clauses invenerunt: pulsare coeperunt, sed sero. CAPUT X.—16. Quomodo prudentes quinqué virgines imitandae.— Dictum est, verum est, non fallaciter dictum est, Púlsate et aperietur vobis (Mt 7,7): sed moda quando tempus est misericordiae, non quando tempus est iudicii. Non enim possunt confundí ista tempora, cum misericordiam et iudicium Domino suo cantet Ecclesia (cf. Ps 100,1). Tempus est Misericordiae; age paenitentiam. Tempore iudicii illam habes agere? Eris in virginibus illis, contra quas clausum est ostium. Domine, Domine, aperi nobis (Mt 25:11). Numquid non paenitentiam egerunt, quia secum oleum non portaverunt? Et quid illis profuit sera paenitentia, quando eas irridebat vera sapientia? Clausum est ergo ostium. Et quid illis dicturn est? Non novi vos (ib., 12). Non illas novit, qui omnia novit? Quid ergo est, Non novi vos? I reproach you, I reproach you.

In arte mea non vos agnosco; ars mea nescit vitia: hoc est autem magnum, et nescit vitia, et iudicat vitia. Nescit fazando, judicat arguendo. Sic ergo non novi vos. 17. idem tractatur argumentum.—Ierunt, intraverunt quinqué prudentes. Quam multi estis, fratres mei, in [580] nomine Christi; sint in vobis quinqué prudentes, sed noüte quinqué nomines. Sint in vobis quinqué prudentes, ad istam prudentiam quinarii numeri pertinent. Veniet enim hora, et quando nescimus, veniet. Midnight come, watch yourself. Sic clausit Evangelium: Vigilate, quia nescitis diem ñeque horam (ib., 13).

hour. If, then, we must sleep, how will we be awake? Watch with your heart, with faith, with hope, with charity, with works. And once you have fallen asleep in the body, it will be time to get up. When you have risen, prepare the lamps. May they not go out then, may they burn with the inner oil of conscience; then that husband will embrace you with disembodied hugs, then he will introduce you to the house where you will never sleep, where your lamp can never go out. Today, however, we grow weary and our lamps fluctuate amid the winds and temptations of this world. But let our flame burn vigorously so that the wind of temptation rather increases the fire than extinguishes it.
Theme: The servant who hides his talent (Mt 25, 24-30). Location: Hippo. Date: After the year 425.

The brothers, gentlemen and bishops like me have deigned to visit us and rejoice us with their presence; but I don't know why Si ergo dormituri sumus, quomodo vigilamus? Corde vigilance, fide vigilance, spe vigilance, caritate vigilance, operibus vigilance: et quando corpore dormiveris, veniet tempus ut surgas. Cum autem surrexeris, praepara lampades. Tune non exstinguantur, tune interiore conscientiae oleo vegetentur: tune sponsus ille incorporáis nexibus amplectatur, tune te introducat in domum, ubi nunquam dormías, ubi nunquam tua lampas possit exstingui. Hodie vero laboramus, et lampades nostrae Inter ventos saeculi huius tentationesque fluctuant: sed ardeat in robore flamma nostra, ut ventus tentationis augeat ignem potius, quam extinguat.
DE VERBIS EVANGELII MATTHAEI, UBI SERVUS PIGER, QUI TALENTUM ACCEPTUM NOI.UIT EROGARE, DAMNATUR: CHAP. 25, 24-30.
unde dictus. Episcopalus officium impositum

Domini fratres et coepiscopi mei praesentia quidem sua nos visitare et exhilatare dignified sunt: sed nescio quare nolunt me fessum adiuvare. Vominus (lord) had already become the usual term for a bishop (see Sermons 111,2; 179,2; etc.).
The martyrdom of Saint John the Baptist

They don't want to help me with my tiredness. I have said to exalt your charity in their presence, so that your audience may intercede in a certain way on my behalf before them, so that, when I ask them, they too may preach. Give what you have received; Deign to work before looking for excuses. You will gladly receive the few things I tell you, because I am tired and can barely speak. We also have the story of the benefits granted by God through his martyr 3; Let us listen to it together with pleasure. What is it about? What am I going to tell you? You have heard in the Gospel the reward for good servants and the punishment for bad ones. The only sin of that reprobate and harshly condemned servant was not wanting to give. He kept in full what he had received; but the Lord sought the benefits obtained from it. God is greedy for our salvation4. If those who did not give it are condemned in this way, what should those who lose it expect? We, then, are administrators; we give, you receive. We look for the benefits: live well. Such is the benefit obtained from our expenditure. But do not think that giving is not also your thing. You cannot give from this higher place, but it is possible for you wherever you are. Where Christ is reproached, defend him; respond to those who murmur about him; correct those who blaspheme; stay away from their company. If you win over some, Hoc ideo Caritati vestrae dixi ipsis audientibus, ut quodammo audientia vestra intercedat pro me apud illos, ut quando eos rogo faciant et ipsi sermonem. Erogent quod acceperunt, operari magis quam excusare dignentur. A me autem fatigueto et vix loquente, pauca libenter acápite. Habemus enim et libellum de beneficiis Dei per sanctum Martyrem datis, pariter libentius audiamus. Who is it? quid dicam vobis? Audistis in Gospel et bonorum servorum meritum, et poenam malorum. Et malitia tota serví illius reprobati graviterque damnati ista fuet, quia noluit erogare. Servavit integrum quod accepit: sed Dominus eius lucra quaerebat. Avarus est Deus ad salutem nostram. Si sic damnatur qui non erogavit, quid debent exspectare qui perdunt? Nos ergo dispensatores sumus, nos erogamus, vos accipitis. Lucra quaerimus: bene vivite. Lucra enim erogationis nostrae ista sunt. Sed etiam ad vos nolite existimare non pertinere erogationem. Non potestis erogare de isto loco superiore, sed potestis ubicumque estis.
Ubi reprehenditur Christus, defendite: murmuratoribus answer yourself, blasphematores corripite, ab eorum vos societate alienate yourself. Sic erogatís, si alíquos lucramini. Shake vícem nostram

That is your giving. Do our times in your house. The bishop (episcopus) receives this name because he observes from above, because he is concerned with monitoring5. To each one, then, in his house, if he is the head of it, must correspond the office of the episcopate, that is, to monitor what the faith of his people is, lest any of them fall into heresy, be it the wife, or the son, or the daughter, or even the servant who was bought at such a dear price. Apostolic discipline put the lord in front of the servant and subjected the servant to the lord. Christ, however, paid the same price for both. Do not despise the least of your people; Seek with all care the salvation of those in your household. If you do this, you are giving; you will not be lazy servants and you will not fear such despicable condemnation.

Topic: The martyrdom of Saint John the Baptist (Mark 6, 17-29). Location: Outside Hippo. Date: After the year 396. 1. After reading the present chapter of the holy Gospel that the Lord wanted to place before our eyes, to the Church, amadísi in domibus vestris. Episcopus inde appellatus est, quia superintendit, quia intendendo curat. Unusquisque [581] ergo in domo sua, si caput est domui suae, debent ad eum pertinere episcopatus officium, quomodo sui credant, ne aliqui ipsorum in haeresim incurrant, ne uxor, ne filius, ne filia, ne ipse servus, quia tanti est emptus. Apostolic discipline praeposuit dominum servo, et servum subdidit domino (Eph 6,5; Tit 2,9): Christus tamen pro ambobus unum pretium dedit. Minimum vestros nolite contemnere, domesticorum vestrorum salutem omni vigilantia procúrate. Haec si facitis, erogatis: pigri serví non eritis, damnationem tam detestandam non timebitis.
(Caillau-Saínt-Yves 2,6) (MA

Beautiful text that denotes the preeminence of Augustine over the rest of the African bishops of that time, who never chose to speak in his presence, always leaving this burden to him even if he was tired. Speaking was sometimes a torment for the Saint who often repeats that he likes learning more than teaching, listening than speaking. See Letters 116,4,9; 167,6,21: Eight issues of Dulcido 111,6; V, 4, etc. It refers to the martyr Saint Stephen. See note 1 to sermon 79. This is a favorite thought of the Saint. He repeats it several times. See sermon 359:2 and Commentary on Psalm 99:10.
Former GOSPEL. OF MARTYRIO IOHANNIS BAPTISTAE (Mark 6,14-29). ET DE PERSECUTIONE QUAE ETIAM TEMPORE PACIS SUSTINENDA ES T CHRISTIANIS

De praesenti capitulo, fratres dilectissimi, sancti evangelii, quod nos dominus docere voluit, certe ecclesia Christi non ambigit quod martyr Indeed, the Greek word episcopos is composed of epi (on) and scopéo (to look).

Our brothers, there is no doubt in your mind that Jíian is a martyr. Already before the passion of the Lord he merited martyrdom, before he was born and before he suffered, but not as the author of salvation, but as the precursor of the judge. He went before the Lord, accepting him as a humble gift, granting the greatest height to the celestial master. Where do we deduce that John was a martyr? Was he captured by the persecutors of Christians, taken to court by them, interrogated, confessing Christ and suffering death? The martyrs after the passion of Christ can say this. Where, then, does the condition of martyr come from? From the fact that his throat was slit? It is not the penalty, but the cause that makes a martyr 1. Who offended a powerful woman? How did he offend her? For what reason? For telling the truth to the king who had become her husband, that is, that it was not lawful for him to have his brother's wife. The truth conquered hatred and as a result it reached passion and obtained the crown. These are the fruits of the future century. Lust is given over to the dance and innocence is condemned; condemned by men, but crowned by omnipotent God. 2. Let no one say: "I cannot be a martyr because the persecution of Christians is over." You have just heard that John suffered martyrdom; and if you consider it carefully, he died for Christ. "How, you say, did he die for Christ if he was not questioned about it or forced to deny it?" Listen to Christ himself who says: I am the way, the truth and the life. If Christ is the truth, for Christ it suffers and is legitimate, says Iohannes. Et ante passionem domini martyrium meruit: ante natus, ante passus; non tamen salutís auctor, sed iudicis praecursor. Praeibat enim ante dominum, sumens ipse obsequium humile, dans altitudinem caelesti magistto. Unde dicimus martyrem esse Iohanem? Numquid a persecutoribus Christianorum comprehensus, adductus, interrogatus, Christum confessus, et passus est? Hoc enim ceteri martyres post Christi passionem possunt dici. Is this ergo unde martyr? Who is decollatus? Non enim facit martyrem poena, sed causa. Who offended potently mulierem? Unde offended? qua de re offended? Saying verum regi, marito eius facto, quia non liceret ei habere uxorem fratris sui (cf. Mark 6, 18). Veritas odium meruit, et odium merendó ad passionem coronamque pervenit. Hi sunt fructus futuri saeculi. Saltat denique luxuria, et damnatur innocentia; sed ab hominibus damnatur, a deo omnipotent coronatur. 2.

Nenio ergo dicat, Non possum esse martyr, quia persecutio non est Chrístianis. Audis quia Iohannes martyrium tulit; et, si verum consideres, pro Christo mortuus est. Quomodo, inquis, pro Christo, qui non est interrogatus de Christo, nec coactus deniale Christum? Audi ipsum Christum [425] dicentem: ego sum via, et veritas, et vita (lo 14,6). This is a refrain continually repeated in the amidonatist polemic and in the sermons on the martyrs.

crowned mind who is condemned for defending the truth. Let no one look for excuses; all times are open for martyrdom. And let no one say that Christians do not suffer persecution. It is not possible to empty the apostle Paul's sentence of content, since it is true; through him Christ spoke; He didn't lie, then. It goes like this: All who desire to live godly in Christ will suffer persecution. It speaks about everyone, without excluding or separating anyone. If you want to prove the truth of what he said, start living godly in Christ. You will see how true it is. Perhaps because the persecution by the earthly kings ceased, the devil no longer attacks? That ancient enemy is always alert against us; Let's not sleep, then. Suggests pleasures; he gets into snares, bad thoughts; to incite a more damaging fall, puts gains ahead, threatens damage. The precise moment is reached and it is difficult to reject the bad suggestion and willingly accept the present death. Understand, brothers. If someone, for example a noble person, who has your life in his power, forces you to bear false testimony, without saying to you: "Deny Christ", what do you think you would do: choose falsehood or die for the truth? And yet, nothing more than "Deny Christ" is what that persecutor tells you. If, as we have already said, Christ is the truth, he who denies the truth effectively denies Christ. Everyone who tells a lie denies the truth. Why do you give false testimony? Because he fears, certainly. Don't all Christians who fight for the truth suffer persecution? Currently toSi Christus est veritas, pro Christo patitur, quisquis pro veritate damnatur, et legitime coronatur. Nemo ergo se excuse!: omnia tempora patent martyribus. Nec aliquis dicat, persecutionem non fieri Christia(253)nis. Sententia Pauü apostoli vacuari non potest, quia vera est; Christus per eum est locutus, non est mentus. Ait enim: omnes qui pie volunt will live in Christo lesu, persecutionem patientur (2 Tim 3,12). Omnes, ait: neminem exclusit, neminem separavit. Si verum vis provere quod dixit, incipe pie vivere in Christo, et videbis verum esse quod dicit. Numquid, quia persecutio a terrenis regibus conquievit, ideo diabolus non saevit? lile hostis antiquus semper contra nos vigilat: non dormiamus. Illecebras suggerit, insidias, cogitationes bad immittit; ut deterioration lapse provocet, profit ponit, damna minatur.

Venitur ad articulum eius, et cum labore malum suggestionis respuitur, ut praesens mors libenter suscipiatur. Intelligite, brothers. Si quis te cogat, verbi gratia nobilis quidam, et habens in potestate sanguinem tuum, cogat te falsum dicere testimonium, et non tibi dicat, Nega Christum, quid putas, will choose falsum, an mori pro vero? Et tamen nihil tibi aliud dicit persecutor quam, Nega Christum. Si enim Christus est veritas, ut iam diximus, proferto Christum negat, qui veritatem negat. Omnis autem negat verum, qui mendacium loquitur. Ipse qui dicit falsum testimonium, unde? Quia timet, certe.

Two are put to the test and each one suffers temptation in his concrete life. / 3. What would someone who threatens you with death do to you, the bloodthirsty, swollen with power, elevated like smoke; What was your enemy going to do to you that would impel you to perjury and false testimony? What was I going to do to you? Weakness responds: "It would kill me." "I wouldn't kill you." "I know well that it would kill me." If so, I too will answer you: "You, brother, you who bear false witness are the ones who put yourself to death." That one would bring death, but to your body; what would it do to your soul? The house would be torn down, but the one who lived in it would be crowned. Look what your enemy would have done to you if you had stood by the truth and had not borne false witness: He would certainly have brought about death for you, but of the body, not of the soul. Topic: The multiplication of the loaves and the wedding garment (Mark 8:1-9; Mt 22:11-14). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. In exposing the Holy Scripture to you, I act as if I were breaking bread for you. You hungry people, receive it and belch your fill with the praise of your heart. And those of you who have rich people's banquets, do not be weak in good works and actions. What I serve to you is not mine. From what you eat, from that I eat; from what you live, from that I live. In heaven we have our common pantry: from there comes the word of God. 2. The seven loaves signify the septiform operation of the Holy Spirit'; the four thousand men, the Church constituted on the four gospels; the seven baskets of remains, the perfection of the Church. Perfection is very frequently symbolized by this number. Why was it said: I will praise you seven times a day? Does the man who praises the Lord most often err? What does it mean, then, I will praise you seven times, but: I will never cease to praise you? Whoever says seven times means all the time. Therefore, the story takes place in SERMO

Sed non est durum nec grave quod ille imperat, qui adiuvat ut fiat quod imperat. Nam et illum verum est quod ei dicitur in Psalm: Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras (Ps 16,4). Et illud verum est quod ipse dixit: lugum meum lene est, et onus meum leve est (Mt 11:30). Quidquid enim durum est in praeceptis, ut sit lene,

Hoc est enim amare se, velie do voluntatem suam. Praspone his voluntatem Dei: disce amare te, non amarando te. Nam ut sciatis vitium esse se amare, sic Apostolus dicit: Erunt enim homines se ipsos lovers. Et numquid qui amat se, fidit in se? Incrpit enim deserto Deo amare se, et ad ea diligenda quas

loving what is outside oneself, comes out of oneself; to such an extent that, having said the Apostle: There will be men who love themselves, he immediately added: lovers of money. You already see that you are outside. You began to love yourself; If you can, stay within yourself. Why are you going outside? Have you become rich with money, you lover of money? You began to love what is outside of you and you went astray. Therefore, when man's love from himself is set in motion towards the things that are outside, he begins to become as vain as the things with which he walks and, in a certain way, to waste his strength as if he were a prodigal son. He becomes empty, he becomes empty, he becomes impoverished, he feeds swine. And while he labors in shepherding them, it happens to him that sometimes he remembers and says: How many of my father's mercenaries eat bread while here I perish from hunger! But when he says this, what is written about the son who spent his assets with prostitutes, who wanted to have in his possession everything his father kept just for him? He wanted to dispose of it as he pleased, he squandered it and found himself in need. What is said about him? And returning inside. If he came back inside, it means he had gone out of himself. He who had fallen outside of himself and had gone away from himself, first of all returns to himself to return to where he had fallen outside of himself. In the same way that, falling out of himself, he remained in himself, so coming back to himself, he must not remain in himself so as not to come out of himself again. What did he say when he came to himself so as not to remain in consciousness? I will get up and go to my father. Behold, having fallen outside of himself was equivalent to having fallen outside of his father; sunt extra se, pellitur a se: usque adeo ut cum dixisset idem Apostolus: Erunt homines seipsos lovers, continuo subiceret, amatores pecuniee (2 Tim 3,2). Iam vides quia foris es. Amare te ccepisti: sta in te, si potes. What are you saying? Numquid pecunia dives factus es, amator pecunia;? Ccepisti diligere quod est extra te, perdidisti te. Cum ergo pergit amor hominis etiam a se ipso ad ea quae foris sunt, incipit cum vanis evanescere, et vires suas quodam moda prodigus erogare. In case of persecution, should not everything be despised for the sake of Christ? You love the world, but put first the one by whom the world was made. Great is the world, but greater is he by whom the world was made. Beautiful is the world, but more beautiful is he by whom the world was made. Soft is the world, but softer is he by whom the world was made. The world is evil, but he by whom the world was made is good. How can I justify and explain what I just said? God help me. What have I said? What have you applauded? 'That is the question, but the truth is that you have already applauded. How is it that the world is bad when he who made the world is good? Did not God make all things and they were all good? Does not the Scripture testify that God made every thing good by saying: And God saw that it was good? And encompassing everything, in conclusion, thus it is said that God made all things: Behold, they were extremely good. 5. How then is the world evil and he who made the world good? As? For the world was made by him and the world did not know him. By him the world was made, that is, heaven and earth and everything in them. Therefore, the world is bad because those who prefer to cumbere are bad. Videntur his verbis Domini exhortata martyria. Si persecutio est, nonne pro Christo debent cuneta contemni? the Son of man to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him. 9. But in this world holy, good, reconciled, saved; better, in need of salvation, although now he is saved in hope—in hope we are saved—; In this world, then, that is, in the Church, which follows Christ in its fullness, it has been said to all: Whoever wants to follow me, let him deny himself. It is not something that only virgins should hear and not married ones; or only widows and not wives; or only the monks and not the married; or only the clergy and not the laity; but it is the entire Church, the totality of the body, all the members with their own and distinct functions, that must follow Christ. Let the one Church in its entirety follow her, follow her the dove, the bride, the redeemed one and the one who received the blood of Christ as a dowry. There virginal integrity finds its place; there the widow's own continence; there marital chastity; Adultery and illicit lewdness worthy of punishment do not take place there. Let these members who have their place there follow Christ, each one in his own kind, in his position, in his own way; deny, that is, do not boast of yourselves; Take up your cross, that is, while you are in the world, tolerate for Christ whatever suffering the world brings you. Amen to the only one who does not disappoint, the only one who does not suffer deception, the only one who does not deceive. Love him because what he promises is true. But since it is not given instantly, faith wavers. Resist, persevere, endure, endure procrastination: all that is carrying the cross.

10. Let the virgin not say: "There I will be alone." Not only will Mary be there, but the widow Anna will also be there. The married woman should not say: "The widow will be there, not me." It is not true that Ana is there and Susana is not. However, those who are to be there examine themselves so that those who have an inferior position here do not envy, but rather love, the better position in others. So that you realize, I am going to give you an example: one chose married life and another the life of continence; If the one who chose married life desired adultery, he looked back: he desired what is illicit. Whoever, on the other hand, from the life of continence, wants to return to marriage later, looked back: he chose a lawful thing but he looked back. Should marriage be condemned, then? No; marriage should not be condemned. He notices where the one who chose him had entered. I had already gone before. When he lived lasciviously in adolescence, he had marriage before his eyes, he tended towards it; On the other hand, once he chose the life of continence, marriage is behind him. Remember, says the Lord, Lot's wife. Lot's wife stood motionless as she looked back. Let each one, therefore, be afraid to look back from the place where he could have arrived, and go along the path, follow Christ. Forgetting what is behind, reaching forward, in your interior intention pursue the palm of God's vocation in Christ Jesus. Those who are married put themselves before those who are not married; confess that these are better; love in them what you do not personally possess and in them love Christ.

Omnibus iussum est ut se abnegent.—Sed in hoc mundo sancto, bono, reconciliato, salvato; immo salvando, nunc autem spe salvato, Spe enim salvi facti sumus (Rom 8,24): in hoc ergo mundo, hoc est Ecclesia, quae tota sequitur Christum, universaliter dixit: Qui vult me ​​sequi, abneget semetipsum (Mt 16,24). Non enim hoc virgines debent audire, et maritatae non debent; aut viduae debent, et nuptae non debent: aut monachi debent, et coniugati non debent; aut clerici debent, et laici non debent: sed universa Ecclesia, universum corpus, cuneta membra per officia propria distincta et distributa, sequantur Christum. All sequatur ipsa unique, sequatur columba, sequatur sponsa, sequatur redempta et dotata sanguine sponsi. Habet ibi locum suum integritas virginalis: habet ibi locum suum continentia vidualis; habet ibi locum suum pudicitia coniugalis: non ibi habet locum suum adulterium; non ibi habet locum suum illicita et punienda lascivia. Ista autem membra quae habent ibi locum suum in genere suo, et in loco suo, et in suo moda, sequantur Christum; abnegent se, id est non praesumant de se; tollant cruze suam, id est, tolerant in world pro Christo quidquid intulerit mundus. Ament eum qui solus non decipit, qui solus non fallitur, solus non fallit: ament eum, quia verum est quod promittit. Sed quia non modat, titubat fides. Last, persevere, tolerate, porta dilationem, et tulisti cruzem.

CAPUT VIII.—10. Varii gradus sequentium Christum, quidve in Mis sit retro respicere.—Non dicat virgo: Sola ibi ero. Non enim sola ibi erit Maria, sed erit ibi et Anna vidua. Non dicat nupta: Vidua ibi erit, non ego. Non enim erit ibi Anna, et non ibi erit Susanna. Sed plane inde se probent qui ibi futuri sunt, ut qui habent hinc inferiorem locum, non invideant, sed diligant in alus meliorem locum. Etenim, verbi gratia, fratres mei, ut advertatis: coniugalem vitam quisque elegit, continentm vitam quisque elegit; si ille qui elegit vitam coniugalem, concupiverit adulteria, retro respexit (cf. Lk 9:62); illud concupivit quod illicitum est. [589] I will see a continentia ad nuptias postea rediré voluerit, retro respexit: licitum elegit, et retro respexit. Ergo damnandae sunt nuptiae? No. Non sunt damnandae nuptiae: sed ille qui eas elegit, quo accesserat vide. Iam ante ierat. Quando vivebat lascive adolescens, nuptiae ante illum erant; ad eas se tendebat: eum vero elegit continentiam, nuptiae post illum sunt. Memores estote, ait Dominus, uxoris Lot (Luke 17:32). Uxor Lot retro respiciendo remansit (cf. Gen 19:26). Quisque ergo quo potuit pervenire, inde timeat retro respicere: et ambulet in via, sequatur Christum: quae retro oblitus, in ea quae ante sunt extentus, secundum intentionem intus sequatur ad palmam vocationis Dei in Christo Iesu (Phil 3,13.14). Coniugati praeponant sibi innuptos; fateantur eos esse meliores: in eis diligant quod ipsi non habent; et in illis Christum ament.

1. You have heard, brothers, the Scripture that exhorts and invites us to be vigilant in view of the last day. Let each one think about his or her own, lest by giving an opinion or judging that the day of the end of the world is far away, you fall asleep regarding yours. You have heard what he said about him: that both the angels and the Son do not know him and only the Father knows him. This poses a big problem, namely, that guided by the flesh we judge that there is something that the Father knows and the Son does not know. With all certainty, when he said "the Father knows him," he said it because the Son also knows him, although in the Father. What is there in that day that has not been made in the Word by whom the day was made? "Let no one, he said, look for the last day, that is, when it will arrive." But let us all be vigilant through a righteous life so that our last particular day does not catch us off guard, because the way each one has left his last day, so he will find himself on the last day in the world. Nothing you haven't done here will help you then. It will be the works themselves that elevate or oppress each one. SERMO

You only pay attention to the fact that you are mortal, and you are arrogant as the devil. seriously and, what is worse, without knowing when? The sorrow is certain and the hour uncertain; and, of human things, only of this punishment do we have absolute certainty. 3. Everything else we possess, whether good or bad, is uncertain. Only death is certain. What am I saying? A child has been conceived: it may be born, it may be aborted. That's how uncertain it is. Maybe it will grow, maybe it won't; It is possible that he will grow old, it is possible that he will not; maybe he is rich, maybe poor; he may achieve honors, he may be despised; maybe he will have children, maybe not; You may get married and you may not. Anything else you can name among the goods is the same. Look now at the evils: you may get sick, you may not; maybe a snake bites him, maybe not; It may be devoured by a beast or it may not be. Review all evils. The “maybe yes, maybe no” will always be present. On the other hand, can you say: "Maybe he will die, maybe he won't"? Why do doctors, after having examined the disease and seeing that it is fatal, say: “He will die; will not escape death"? Already from the moment of man's birth it must be said: "He will not escape death." To be born is to begin to get sick; With death the disease comes to an end, but it is unknown whether it leads to something worse. That rich man had ended up with a delicious illness and came to another tortuous one. That poor man, on the other hand, put an end to the disease and became healthy. But he chose here what he was going to have later; What he harvested there, he had sown here. when nescimus? Poena certa est, hora incerta: et de ista poena sola certi sumus in rebus humanis. 3. Therefore, we must stay awake while our lives last and choose what we will have in the future. 4. Let us not love the world; He oppresses his lovers, he does not lead them to good. Why then does the Lord Himself say: Rejoice because I have overcome the world? Let us answer him, if it seems good to you: «Rejoice. If you won, rejoice. Why should we do it? Christ love you. Christ loves sinners as a doctor loves the sick: with a view to eliminating the fever and healing him. It is not his desire that he be always sick, so that he always has someone to visit; What he wants is to heal him. Therefore, the Lord did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to justify the wicked. He made a faithful man from an idolater, a sober man from a drunkard, and a parsimonious man from a lustful man; He made a miser generous, not towards hunters, condescending to the devil, but towards the poor. In this way he will be crowned by Christ and acquires for himself what cannot pass away. Will he not give the reward to the righteous? More difficult was what the Lord already did: convert a wicked person into a righteous person. Pay attention, my brothers: what is more incredible, making a wicked man a righteous man, or making a righteous man an angel? Being just and being impious are opposite things; Not so being just and being an angel. Will not the one who transformed you into the opposite of what you were take you to angelic plenitude from the close human condition? Therefore, when you begin to be just, you begin to imitate the angelic life, since when you were impious you were far from their life. Present faith, you become righteous and submit to God, you who blasphemed him; and, although you were turned towards the creatures, you already desire the Creator. 2. Observe what he has given you. Impius et pius contra sunt sibi: pius et angelus non sunt contra. Ex vicino te non implebit, qui ex contrario te commutavit? Iam enim cum pius esse coeperis, imitari incipis vitam angelicam: cum autem impius esses, remotus eras [a vita] angelorum.

Alio autem die, ubi opportunius erat, commemoiavimus eos huius miserrimae He is referring to the Donatists, who placed the validity of baptism and, more generally, of all the sacraments in the sanctity of the minister. Augustine's contrary thesis is expressed in the famous phrase: «Does Peter baptize? It is Christ who baptizes. Does Judas baptize? It is Christ who baptizes. See the Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 5. It refers to the conference between Donatists and Catholics that, with a view to achieving the union of the two churches, took place in Carthage in the year 411 under the presidency of the cognitor (judge) Marcellinus. The abbreviated minutes were left to us by Augustine in the three books of his work Brief relation of the conference held with the Donatists. The cognitor (judge) of whom Augustine speaks in this text was the tribune Marcellinus.

He had been sent to Africa by the Emperor Honorius to try to resolve the conflict that divided the Church. He presided and acted as judge in the famous conference of 411, giving victory to the Catholics and proscribing the Donatists for which they accused him of having allowed himself to be corrupted by them (Letter 141,1,12). He himself was in charge of putting into practice the decrees of the Conference, being harsh especially towards the circumcelions, who had to suffer his torture (Letter 133,2; 134,2). He was executed two years later, after having been condemned by the tribune Marinus, count of Africa, who was trying to suppress the revolt of a certain Heracleano. Apparently, it was the Donatists who persuaded Marinus that he was in conspiracy with the rioters. He was a faithful and devout Christian, a student of Scripture, and a personal friend of Augustine. He sent her several of his books, wrote her several letters; In turn, he proposed several questions to him, kept him up to date with events and served as a link with other characters. The bishop of Hippo dedicated his great work The City of God to him.

and he excuses himself? Look, you urge him and he doesn't come, you beg him and he doesn't follow you, well, what does he say? I will go first to bury my father. He showed the Lord the faith of his heart, but pity withheld him. When our Lord Jesus Christ destines men to the Gospel, he does not want any excuse of carnal and temporal piety to come between them. Certainly, the law commands this pious action, and the Lord Himself accused the Jews of overthrowing this command of God. Saint Paul also says in his letter: This is the first commandment of the promise. Which? Honor your father and mother. There is no doubt that it is God's command. This young man wanted, therefore, to obey God by burying his father. But there are places, times and issues appropriate to this matter and this place. The father must be honored, but God must be obeyed; You have to love your parent, but you have to put yourself before the Creator. I, says Jesus, call you to the Gospel; I am calling you for another work more important than the one you want to do. Let the dead bury their dead. Your father has died. There are other dead people who can bury the dead. Who are the dead that bury the dead? Can a dead person be buried by other dead people? How will they shroud him if they are dead? How will they transport the body if they are dead? How will they mourn him if they are dead? They shroud him, take him to bury and cry for him despite being dead, because here we are dealing with the infidels. Here the Lord commanded us what is written in the Song of Songs when the Church says: Ordain charity in me.

Even if you imitate the saints, always attribute everything to grace, because the fact that you are part of that rest is due to the grace of God, not to your own merit. The prophet Isaiah already said, remembering that remnant: If the Lord Sabaot had not left us a remnant of our lineage, we would have been like Sodom and would have been like Gomorrah. And thus says the Apostle: Likewise at this time a remnant was saved by free election; and if it is by grace, it is no longer by works. That is to say, don't boast about any pauci anymore. Nam septem millia ibi habeo. Et adiunxit: Sic ergo et in hoc tempore. Crediderunt enim aliqui Iudaei, et multi fuerunt reprobati: sicut et ille qui vulpium foveas gestabat in animo. Sic ergo, inquit, et in hoc tempore, relice per electionem gratiae salvae factae sunt (Rom 11, 2-5): id est, idem Christus est qui tune, et moda, qui et illi tune Eliae dixit, Reliqui mihi. What is it, Reliqui mihi? Ego illos elegi, quia vidi mentes illorum de me praesumentes, non de se, nec de Baal. Non sunt mutati, sic sunt ut a me facti sunt. Et tu qui loqueris, nisi de me praesumeres, ubi esses? Nisi gratia mea plenus esses, nonne ante Baal etiam ipse genu flecteres? Gratia autem mea plenus es; Quia nihil of tua virtute, sed totum of mea gratia praesumpsisti.

Noli ergo in hoc gloriari, ut putes te in servitio tuo non habere conservos: sunt quos elegi, sicut et te, de me scilicet praesumentes: sicut ait Apostolus, Et nunc relice per electionem gratiae salvae factae sunt. Then he added to the twelve disciples, whom he called apostles, another seventy-two and sent them all, as appears from his words, to the already seasoned harvest. What was that harvest? Since the harvest is not found in the Gentiles where it had not been sown, it only remains to understand that it was found in the Jewish people. To this harvest came the owner of it, To this harvest he sent the reapers. To the Gentiles, however, he sent not reapers, but sowers. It seems to us, then, that the harvest was gathered in the Jewish people. The apostles themselves were chosen from it. There it was already ripe for harvesting, since the prophets had planted it. It delights to contemplate God's agriculture, to enjoy his gifts and to work in his field. He worked there who said: I worked harder than all of them. But didn't the Lord of the harvest give him the strength to do so? For this reason he adds: But not I, but the grace of God with me. That he was well established in the profession of agriculture is sufficiently demonstrated by saying: I planted, Apollo watered. This apostle, from Saul converted into Paul, that is, from pride in the least - Saul, in fact, derives from Saul and Paul from paulo (little) l -, interpreting in a certain way his name, says: I am the least of all the apostles. This Paul, that is, this little one, this minimum, was sent to the Gentiles. He himself says that he was sent first to the Gentiles. He writes it, fine, operanii autem pauci. Rogate dominum messis ut mittat operarios in messem suam (Luke 10:2). Tune adiecit disciples duodecim quos et apostólos nominauit, alios septuaginta et duos, et misit omnes, sicut ex uerbis eius apparet, ad paratam messem. What was Messi's era? Non enim illa messis in his gentibus erat ubi nihil erat seminatum. Restat ergo ut intellegamus istam messem fuesse in populo iudaeorum. Ad illam messem uenit dominus messis. Ad illam messem misit messores; ad gentes autem non messores, sed seminatores. Intellegimus ergo messem factam in populo iudaeorum. Ex illa enim messe apostoli ipsi electi sunt. Ibi iam quod meteretur maturum erat, quia ibi prophetae seminauerunt. Delectat inspicere agriculturem dei et oblectari donis eius et operari in agro eius. In hac enim agri[45]culture operabatur qui dicebat: Plus ómnibus Mis laborauit. Sed uires ei non ibantur ad operandum a domino messis? Ideo subiecit: Non ego autem, sed gratia dei mecum (1 Cor 15,10).

Nam se in agriculture uersari satis otendit, ubi ait: Ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit (1 Cor 3,6). Hic autem apostolus de Saul Paulus, hoc est de superbo minimus—Saulus autem a Saule denominatur, Paulus a modico nominatur; paulum enim modicum est, unde nomen suum quodam moda interpretatum ait: Ego enim sum minimus inter omnes apostólos (1 Cor 15:9)—iste ergo Paulus, id est modkus et minimus, missus est ad gentes. Praecipue ad gentes se missum ipse dicit. Augustine's interpretation is placed within his system of seeing meaning everywhere. In reality, here it is nothing more than abandoning the Semitic form of the name to take the Latin one.

He states in his letter to the Galatians that, after the call of the Lord Jesus, he came to Jerusalem and compared his Gospel with that of the other apostles, and that they shook hands as a sign of concord and harmony, because in no way did he disagree with what they had learned from Jesus. Next he says that he and they agreed to go, he to the Gentiles and they to the circumcision, he as a sower and they as reapers. No wonder the Athenians, although without knowing it, gave him that name, for, hearing him speak, they said: Who is this sower of words? 2. Pay attention, then. Rejoice in contemplating with me two kinds of harvest: one in season and the other in perspective. It matures in the Jewish people, and the one that is budding, in the Gentile. Let's try it. How, but with the Scripture of the owner of the harvest? We have what is written in this chapter: The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Pray to the owner of the harvest to send workers to the harvest. And since in that harvest they were going to meet Jews who were going to contradict them and persecute them, he added: See that I am sending you like lambs in the midst of wolves. Such is the harvest; Let's talk a little more about it to demonstrate it more. Next to the well where, according to the Gospel of Saint John, the weary Lord sat, great mysteries were worked out that the brevity of time prevents us from commenting on in their entirety. However, listen carefully to what can be said. We set out to demonstrate that the harvest was in the town in

that the prophets preached. In effect, they were the sowers so that the apostles could later be the reapers. As the Lord Jesus conversed with the Samatitana woman, when he told her, among other things, how he should be worshiped, she answered: We know that the Messiah called the Christ is coming and that he will teach us all things. To which Christ replied: It is I who is speaking to you. Believe what you hear, what you see. It's me, the one who's talking to you. What had she said? We know that the Messiah will come, whom Moses and the prophets announced, who is called Christ. The harvest was already loaded. It had received the virtue of germination thanks to the sowing of Moses and the prophets and, now mature, it awaited the apostles for the harvest. As soon as he heard those words, he believed and, leaving the jar, he ran quickly and began to announce the Lord. Meanwhile, the disciples had gone to buy food. Upon their return, they were amazed to see the Lord talking to the Samaritan woman, but they did not dare to ask her: What or why are you talking to her? Although surprised, they suppressed their curiosity. The name of Christ was not new to this Samaritan woman; I was already waiting for his advent; I had faith that it would come. How would this be possible, if no one had planted? Hear this same thing in clearer words. The Lord says to his disciples: You say that summer is still far away; Lift up your eyes and see the fields white for harvest. And he added: Others worked and you were associated with their tasks. He is sent to the Gentiles and does not remain silent when remembering the grace received primarily and especially for this function. He says in his writings that he was sent to preach the Gospel where Christ had not yet been announced. But since that other harvest has already taken place and the Jews that remained were chaff, let us pay attention to the harvest that we are. The apostles and prophets sowed. The Lord himself sowed; He was, in fact, in the apostles, since he also reaped; They did nothing without him; He is perfect without them, and to them he says: Without me you can do nothing. What does Christ say, sowing among the Gentiles? See the sower went out to sow. There reapers are sent to harvest; Here the non-lazy sower goes out to sow. But what did the fact that some fell on the road, some on stony ground, some among the thorns have to do with this? If I had feared those bad lands, I would not have come to the good land either. As for us, what do we care? Why are we interested in talking about the Jews, about the straw? The only thing that concerns us is not to be a path, not to be stones, not to be thorns, but good earth—oh God! my heart is prepared—to give thirty, sixty, a hundred, a thousand times one. Be it more, be it less, but it is always wheat. Let it not be a path where the enemy, like a bird, snatches the seed stepped on by passers-by; nor stony where

scarcity makes the earth germinate quickly that which later cannot withstand the heat of the sun; nor thorns that are the earthly ambitions and cares of a vicious and dissolute life. And what is worse than the fact that concern for life does not allow us to achieve life? What is more miserable than losing your life for worrying about life? Is there anything more unfortunate than, through fear of fate, falling into death itself? Remove the thorns, prepare the field, sow the seed, harvest time arrives, long to reach the granary and the fear of fire disappear. 4. Ad nos itaque pertinet, quos qualescumque dominus in agro suo constituit operarios, dicere ista uobis: seminare, plantare, rigare, aliquibus etiam arboribus circumfodere et confinum stercoris adhibere. Pertinet ad nos haec fideliter agere, ad uos fideliter capere; ad dominum adiuuare nos operants, uos credentes, omnes laborantes, sed mundum in illo uincentes. Quod ergo ad uos pertinet dixi; quid ad pertineat uolo dicere. Forte alicui uidetur ex uobis, moda quia haec dixi, superfluum Augustine speaks very frequently of the duties of pastors. This phrase, which he places in the heart of a listener, was to be more than a literary device. Although there were many who listened with pleasure to his sermons, no matter how long, for others the minutes seemed endless. They were the occasional attendees, those who would not have hesitated to go to the amphitheater in the event of a coincidence of functions. In order not to burden them, on the days when he saw many of these people, Augustine either spoke briefly or deferred the sermon to another occasion when only those interested attended. See sermon 51,1.

Si est illic filius pacis, With this thought, Augustine places himself on the same level as his listeners.

Everyone receives everything from God. There is not one food for Augustine and another for his listeners. He expresses it beautifully in sermon 339,4: «I feed you the same as I eat; I am a servant like you, not a father of a family; I put on your table the same thing on which I live, that is, what I extract from the treasure of the Lord, from the banquet of that father of the family who, being rich, became poor for us so that with his poverty we could become rich. See also sermon 112 A,7 ( = Caillau II, 11). Agustín's view is broad: it encompasses the past and the future. He had been bishop for one or at most two years.
