there is, it will return to you. Let's analyze everything briefly. Don't carry any bags. What do we do? Indeed, when we go on a trip we carry a bag; We carry bags for the road. No saddlebag. We may not take it. No shoes. What is it about? Are we commanded to walk with bare feet? See that we also walk with shoes. We do not hide our feet when we speak: we are shod before your eyes. Furthermore, if someone greeted us on the road and we did not return the greeting, we would be branded as arrogant. We incur the same disobedience to the Lord. We greet, in effect, whoever we meet along the way. The other thing is easier: saying Peace to this house when we enter someone's. But how do we overcome the obstacle of the bag and the shoes? Let us direct our gaze to the Lord in case he consoles us and grants us the understanding of those words, since even in what we said was simple, saying: Peace to this house when entering it, there is nothing easier than which, if, like what follows, we take it in a carnal way, there too a danger is presented to us. What does it say? Say: Peace to this house. Nothing could be simpler. But how does it continue? If there is a son of peace in it, your peace will rest on him; If there is not, it will return to you. What is it about? How can peace return to me? Does it mean that I will only have it if it comes back, while if it rests on him I will lose it? Far from the minds of the healthy such an idea! Consequently, neither that thing should be taken in a carnal way and, therefore, perhaps, neither the coat, nor the shoes, nor the bag; nor this thing about not greeting anyone on the way, which is required in eo pax uestra; si quo minus, ad uos reuertetur (Luke 10:4-6). Breuiter percurrenda sunt omnia. Nolite, inquit, portare sacculum. Quid agimus? Portamus sacculum, fatemur, quando iter agimus: sumpticulos in uia portamus. Ñeque peram. Forte non portamus peram. Calciamenta ñeque. Crux? Nudo pede ambulare nos iussit? Videtis et uos: calciati ambulamus. Non enim uerba proferimus et pedes abscondimus; before our eyes calciati ambulamus. Iam uero, si quis nos in uia salutauerit et non eum salutauerimus, superbi iudícabimur; in blasphemiam domini blasphemamur. Salutamus ergo et in uia homines. Let us prove that he is our help: Without me you can do nothing. Let us also prove that he is our example: Christ suffered for us, says Saint Peter, leaving us an example so that we can follow in his footsteps. Well, even the Lord himself had a purse on the way of his pilgrimage, a purse that he entrusted to Judas. Although he was a thief, he put up with him by his side. But I, with the forgiveness of my Lord, desiring to learn, say to him: «Lord, you endured Judas the thief, how come you had what he could steal from you? You forbid me, a miserable and powerless man, to even carry a purse. You carried it and it was in it that you had to endure the thief. If you had not taken it, he would not have found what to steal. What's left but for him to tell me: "Understand what you hear: Don't carry a bag"? What does it mean don't carry a bag? Do not be wise to yourselves alone. Receive the Spirit. In you there must be a source, never a reservoir; from where something can be given, not where it accumulates. Say the same about the saddlebag. 7. And what are shoes? What are the ones we use made of? Made of dead animal leather. We cover our feet with the skins of dead animals. What are we ordered? Renounce the works of death. We were warned of this figuratively in Moses, when the Lord said to him: Take off your shoes, for the place in which acceperimus, superbia uidetur imposita, ne quemquam in uia salutemus. 6. Adtendamus dominum nostrum, exemplum uetum et adiutorium. Iste dominus noster loculos habuit in uia, ipsos loculos Iudae commendauerat. Patiebatur quidem furem. Sed ego, cum pace [50] domini mei, discere cupiens, dico domino meo: Domine, patiebaris furem Iudam; unde habebas quod tibi tollendum esset? Me hominem miserum infirmum monuisti nec sacculum portare. Your portasti loculos, et erat ubi furem patereris. If you don't wear it, you need to inueniret quod auferret. Quid restat nisi ut dicat mihi: Intellege quod audis: Noli portare sacculum. Quid est sacculus? Pecunia conclusa: occulta sapientia. Quid est: Nolite portare sacculum? Nolite fieri sapientes penises uosmetipsos. Accipe spiritum: fons in te deben esse, non sacculus; unde erogetur, non ubi includatur. Hoc est et pera quod sacculus. 7.

This is sacred ground. Is there any land holier than the Church of God? Since we are in it, let us take off our shoes, let us renounce the works of death. Regarding the footwear that we wear in our walk, the Lord himself offers me comfort, because if he had not been footed, the Baptist would not have said of him: I am not worthy to untie the strap of his shoes. Let us obey, then, and let inveterate pride not infiltrate our hearts. "I," someone will say, "fulfill the Gospel, because I walk barefoot." Well, you can, I can't. Let us keep what we have each received; Let us be inflamed in charity, let us love one another, and in this way I love your strength and you endure my weakness. 8. What do you think that you do not want to understand in what sense these words were said and, therefore, you are forced to censure the Lord for being inconsistent for having brought a bag and shoes? What do you think? Do you like it that on the way, when we meet one of our loved ones, we do not greet those who are our superiors or return the greeting to those who are our inferiors? Do you fulfill the Gospel when, when greeted, you remain silent? If you did so, you would be similar not to the traveler who goes on a journey, but to the milestone stone that marks the path. Let us, then, abandon our stupidity, understand the words of the Lord and greet no one on the road; Otherwise, we will say that he did not want us to do what he ordered. What does it mean, then, greet no one on the road? It can simply be taken as if he ordered us to do with presenim quo stas terra sánela est (Ex 3,5). Quid tam terra sancta quam dei ecclesia? In illa ergo stantes, calciamenta soluamus, mortuis operibus renuntiemus. Nam de his calciamentis quibus calciati ambulamus consolatur me idem ipse domi(609)nus meus. Si calciatus non esset, non de illo Iohannes says: Non sum dignus corrigiam calciamenti soluere (Luke 3,16). Spectet ergo intellegens oboedientia; non subrepat superba duritia. Ego, inquit, euangelium impleo, quia nudo pede atribulo. Your pots. Ego non possum. Quod simul accepimus custodymus. Caritate flagremus: inuicem diligamus. Ac sic fiet ut ego amem fortitudinem tuam et tu portes infirmatem meam. 8. Itane placet ut iter agents oceurramus caris nostris et eos non salutemus maiores, non resalutemus minores?

Ideone euangelium imples quia salutaris et taces? Hic ueto non uiatori iter agenti, sed miliario similis eris iter ostendenti. acclamations from those who understood; but I also see the silence of the many who still demand an explanation. Since we are talking about the path, let us behave as if we were on the path: the quickest ones, wait for the slowest ones and walk together. What did I say? Whoever greets on the road greets occasionally, because the opportunity presented itself, since he was not exactly going to greet the one he actually greets. He had one thing on his hands, but another came up. He was busy with a task and another task crossed his mind. What is it, therefore, to say hello occasionally? Announcing salvation out of opportunism. And what else is it to announce salvation but to announce the Gospel? Therefore if you preach, do it out of love, not out of opportunism. There are men who preach the Gospel looking for something else. Of them the Apostle says lamentingly: They all seek their own interest, not that of Jesus Christ. These also greeted, that is, they announced health, they preached the Gospel, but they were looking for something else, and that is called greeting out of opportunism. And what is this? If you are such, whoever you are, you do it; Furthermore, you who do it, if you are such, do not do it, but it is done in you. In fact, you are not that person, whoever you are, but perhaps that person is someone else. 10. The Apostle also tolerated these; but he did not command them to be so. They also do something and are instruments of good. They seek their own, but they proclaim Christ. Don't worry about what the preacher is looking for; what it advertises, that's it. Don't look, or be interested in what he intends. Listen to the uideo in silentio requestantes. Sed quia de uia loquimur, tamquam in [52] uia ambulemus. Veloces, tardos exspectate et pariter atribuíate— Quid ergo dixi? Who in uia salutat per occasionem salutat, not ad eum ibat quem salutat. Aliud agebat, aliud oceurrit. Aliud petebat, aliud de (610) transuerso quod ageret inuenit. Quid est ergo per occasionem salutare? Per occasionem salutem adnuntiare. Quid est autem aliud salutem adnuntiare, quam euangelium praedicare? Si ergo praedicas, hoc age per dilectionem, non per occasionem. Sunt enim homines qui, quaerentes aliud, euangelium adnuntiant: de quibus apostolus gemens dicit: Omnes enim sua quaerunt, non quae Iesu Christi (Phil 2,21). Et hi salutabant, hoc est salutem adnuntiabant, euangelium praedicabant, sed aliud requirebant, et ideo per occasionem salutabant. Et quid est hoc?

"He who despises you, despises me"
Theme: "Whoever despises you despises me" (Luke 10:16). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. What Jesus Christ our Lord spoke at that time was recorded in writing so that it could also be heard by us. We have heard, then, his words. What would be the point of having seen him, if we had not listened to him? On the contrary, nothing harms us if we do not see it, if we listen to it. He says: He who despises you, despises me. If he said these words only to the apostles, despise us. But if his word reached us, he called us and put us in their place, be careful not to despise us, lest the injury you do to us reach him. If you do not fear us, fear him who said: He who despises you despises me. What moves us to speak to those of us who do not want to be despised by you, but the desire to rejoice in your good customs? Let your good works be a consolation for our dangers. Live well so as not to die badly. 2. When saying: "Live well so as not to die badly," you must not think of those who perhaps lived badly and died in their beds, had pompous funerals and were deposited
FROM VERBIS EVANGELII LUCAE: «QUI vos SPERNIT, ME SPERNIT». CHAP. 10.16

CAPUT I.—1. Pastoribus debita reverentia Pastorum solada.-—Dominus noster Iesu Christus quod discipulis suis loquebatur illo tempere scribebatur, et nobis ad audiendum parabatur. Audivimus ergo verba eius. Quid enim nobis prodesset, si videretur, et non auditetur? Nec modo aliquid obest, quia non videtur, et tamen auditur. Dicit ergo: Qui vos spernit, me spernit (Luke 10:16). Si solis Apostolis say: Qui vos spernit, me spernit, spernite nos. Si autem sermo eius pervenit ad nos, et vocavit nos, et in eorum loco constituit nos; videte ne spernatis nos, ne ad illum perveniat iniuria quam nobis feceritis. Si enim nos non timetis, illum tímete qui dixit: Qui vos spernit, me spernit. Quid autem nos loquimur vobis, qui sperni nolumus a vobis, nisi ut de vestris bonis moribus gaudeamus? Periculorum nostrorum sint solatia, vestra bona opera. Vivite bene, ne moriamini male. 2. Mors quaenam veré bona vel mala sit.—Nec in his verbis quae dixi: Vivite bene, ne moriamini male, attendatis eos qui forte male

ted in sarcophagi of great value and in tombs carved with extraordinary work and care 1. Don't even judge that I meant a banality with that of living well so as not to die badly; It is possible that some of you think to yourself: "I would like to die like that other person." The opposite may be the case: when faced with a man who lived well and, according to the opinion of men, died badly because he died in a landslide or because he perished in a shipwreck or was devoured by wild beasts, that carnal man says: "Why live well? See that so-and-so lived well and died badly. Turn within yourself, and if you are faithful, there you will find Christ 2. It is he who speaks to you there. I scream, but he teaches more with his silence than I do by speaking. I speak through the sound of my word; he speaks inwardly instilling thoughts of fear. Let him engrave within you the words that I dared to say to you: "Live well so as not to die badly." Since there is faith in your heart and, consequently, Christ dwells in it, he will teach you what I wish to proclaim. 3. Remember that rich man and that poor man about whom we are told in the Gospel. The rich man dressed in purple and linen and ate sumptuously every day; The poor man, on the other hand, lay, riddled with ulcers that the dogs licked, hungry and begging for a few crumbs, at the rich man's door. You remember it; vixerunt, et in lectulis suis mortui sunt; et acta est pompa fuñáis eorum, et positi sunt in pretiosis sarcophagis, in sepulcris pulcherrime et operosissime fabricatis: et quia forte dicit sibi unusquisque vestrum: Vellem sic mori, putetis me rem vanam dicere voluisse; quoniam dixi velle me ut bene vívatis, ne male moriamini. CAPUT II.—Contra forte oceurrit aliquis, qui et bene vixit, et secundum opinionem hominum male est mortuus: forte a ruina est mortuus, a naufragio mortuus est, a bestiis mortuus est; et dicit unusquisque catnalis in corde suo: Quid est bene vivere? Ecce ille sic vixit, et sic est mortuus. Redite ergo ad cor: et si fideles estis, invenietis ibi Christum; ipse vobis loquitur ibi. Ego enim clamo:' ille vero in silentio plus docet. Ergo loquor per sonum sermonis: ille intus loquitur per timorem cogitationis. Ergo ipse inserted in corde vestro verbum meum: quoniam dicere ausus sum: Bene vivite, ne male moriamini. Ecce quoniam fides est in cordibus vestris, et ibi est Christus, et ipse habet docere quod ego cupio personare. 3.

But why do you remember it, if not because Christ dwells in your hearts? Tell me, then, what did you ask him in there and what did he answer you? The Gospel continues with these words: It came to pass that the poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell; and in the midst of the torments he lifted up his eyes and saw Lazarus resting in Abraham's bosom. Then he cried out, saying: Father Abraham, have pity on me and send Lazarus to dip his finger in water and drip a drop on my tongue, for I am consumed with pain in these flames. He who was proud in time is a beggar in hell. The poor man managed to get the desired crumb, the rich man did not get a drop of water. Thinking about these two, tell me: "Who died well and who died badly?" Do not ask the carnal eyes, enter the heart. If you ask the eyes, they will answer you falsely, because the rich man's funeral was exceedingly splendid and brilliant in the eyes of the world. But of what use were the armies of male and female servants who mourned him? Of what the flock of sycophants? Of what the splendor of funerals? Of what the valuable tomb? I'm seeing him covered in perfumes. What shall we say, then, brothers; This one died well or badly? If you ask the eyes of the world, he died optimally; If you ask the inner teacher, very badly.

from whom did they steal other people's? No wonder I said: "Live well so you don't die badly," so you don't die like that rich man. Only the time after death tells the truth about it. Look now at the poor man, but not with carnal eyes, for you will be deceived; look at the faith, look at the heart. Put him before your eyes, lying ulcerated on the ground, surrounded by dogs that come to lick his wounds. Just imagining it like that, you instantly spit, turn your face away, cover your nose. Look at him with the eyes of the heart. He died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's bosom. While the rich man's family was seen crying, the angels were not seen rejoicing. What did Abraham respond to the rich man? Remember, son, that you received goods in life. During your life you considered nothing good except what you had in it. You received it, but days passed, you lost everything and you were left alone to be tormented in hell. 5. It is useful for you, brothers, that I tell you these things. Look for the poor, for the handicapped and for those who can walk. Take care of the poor; do good works. Those of you who are used to doing them, do them; and those of you who are not used to it, do them too. Increase the number of benefactors, since the number of faithful has increased. You still do not see how great the good you do is, nor does the farmer see the harvest when he sows, but he trusts in the earth 3. Why don't you trust in God? The day of our harvest will come. Theme: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38-42). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. The words of our Lord Jesus Christ that were read to us in the Gospel warn us that there is something unique to which we must strive as we work involved in the concerns of this world. We tend because we are still walkers who have not reached rest; because we are still on the road, not in the homeland; We tend with desire, not with joy. However, let us strive and do it without ceasing and without laziness so that we can arrive one day. 2. Martha and Mary were two sisters not only in the flesh, but also in devotion. Both united to the Lord, both served Him in unity of heart when He lived in the flesh in this world. Marta welcomed him into her house as pilgrims are usually welcomed. The servant receives the Lord, the sick receives the Savior, the creature receives the Creator. He received him to feed him in the quia moda laborantes agimus, laborantes operamur recepturi, sicut scriptum est: Euntes ibat et flebant, lactantes semina sua; venientes autem venient cum exsultatione, bearers manipulos suos (Ps 125,6). Tendimus autem adhuc peregrinantes, nondum manentes; adhuc in via, nondum in patria; adhuc desiderano, nondum fruendo. These two lives are the ones that I have described to you as far as possible; Now you reflect on them without haste. Reflect and pause more calmly than I did, on the content of this life—and I am not referring to the bad, perverse, lustful or impious one, but to the laborious one, full of unpleasantness, full of fears and agitated by temptations, the same innocent life that Martha led. The disordered life was far from that house; It was not found in Martha or Mary and, if ever Non ergo dominus opus reprehendit, sed munus distinxit. Circa fines is, inquit, occupata: porro unum est necessarium. Iam hoc sibi María elect: transit labor multitudinis, et remanet caritas unitatis. Ergo quod elegit, non auferetur ab ea; a te autem, quod elegisti—utique hoc sequitur, utique hoc subintellegitur—a te, quod elegisti, auferetur. Sed bonus tuo auferetur, ut quod melius est detur. Aufere, tur enim a te labor, ut requies detur. Tu nauigas, illa iam in pottu est. 4. Videtis ergo, carissimi, et quantum arbitror iam intellegitis, in his duabus mulieribus, quae ambae fuerant domino gratae, ambae amabiles, ambae discipulae; uidetis ergo, et magnum aliquid intellegitis, quicumque intellegitis, quod audire et scite debentis, etiam qui non intellegitis: in his duabus mulieribus duas uitas esse figuratas, praesentem etfuturam, laboriosam et quietam, aerumnosam et beatam, temporalem et aeternam.

Duae sunt uitae, quas descripsi breuiter ut potui: iam de illis uos (618) copiosius cogitate. Quid habeat haec uita—non dico malam, non iniquam, non nefariam, non luxuriosam, non impiam; sed laboriosam, aerumnis pienam, timoribus punishtam, temptationibus sollicitam: hanc ipsam innocentem uitam dico, qualem decebat habere Martham—hanc ergo, quantum

existed, it was driven away with the arrival of the Lord. Therefore, there remained in that house where the Lord stayed two lives represented in the two women: both innocent, both worthy of praise; one industrious, one idle, none sinful, none lazy. I repeat: both innocent, both worthy of praise; However, as I indicated, one was industrious and the other was idle. Neither of them is sinful (the industrious woman must guard against this), neither is lazy (the idle woman must guard against this). In that house these two lives and the source of life itself coexisted. Marta was an image of present realities; Maria, of the future ones. We are now in Martha's chores; We await Maria's occupation. Let's do this right now, to achieve the fullness of what is there. But do we have anything from there here? In what proportion do we have it? What do we have from there? In fact, we do something here that belongs there. Away from human affairs, family cares abandoned, you have gathered here, you stand 4, you listen; By doing this, you become like Mary. You play the role of Mary more easily than I play the role of Christ. If I tell you something that belongs to Christ, it feeds you because it belongs to Christ, the common bread on which I also live, if I live at all. For now we live, brothers, if you stand firm in the Lord; not in you, but in the Lord. Since neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, because the one who gives the increase is God. 5. And now that you have heard and understood this, how much is potestis, inspicite, et de hac, ut dixi, copiosius quam loquimur cogitate. Vita uero iniqua deerat ab illa domo, nec cum Martha at, nec cum María; et si aliquando fuet, domino intrante fugit. Remanserunt ergo in illa domo, quae susceperat dominum, in duabus feminis duae uitae: ambae innocentes, ambae laudabiles: una laboriosa, altera otiosa: nulla facinerosa, nulla desidiosa. Ambae innocentes, ambae, inquam, laudabiles: sed una laboriosa, ut dixi, altera otiosa: nulla facinerosa, quam cauere debent laboriosa: nulla desidiosa, quam cauere debent otiosa. Erant ergo in [57] illa domo istae duae uitae, et ipse fons uitae (Ps 35,10). In Martha erat imago praesentium, in Maria Futurum. Quod agebat Martha, ibi sumus; quod agebat Maria, hoc speramus: hoc agamus bene, ut illud habeamus plene. Nam quid inde habemus, in quantum habemus, quamdiu hic sumus? Quantum est, quod inde habemus? Quid est, quod inde habemus? Name and mode inde aliquid agitur.

Remoti a negotiis, sepositis familiaribus curis, conuenistis, statis, auditis: in quantum hoc agitis, Mariae similes estis. Et facilius uos quod agit Maria, quam ego quod Christus. Si quid tamen dico Christi, ideo uos pascit, quia Christi est, quia pañis communis, unde et ego uiuo, si uiuo. Nunc autem uiuimus, si uos statis in domino (1 Thes 3,8): non in nobis, sed in domino; quia ñeque qui plantat est aliquid, ñeque qui rigat, sed qui incrementum dat deus (1 Cor 3:7). 5. Quantum tamen est, quod de illa uita audiendo et intellegendo
As has already been indicated, the faithful used to listen to the homily standing.

in you of that life of which Mary was the image? Spend this night of the century. At dawn I will stand in your presence and contemplate you. You will grant joy and gladness to my ears and humiliated bones will rejoice. Humiliated bones, as if they were limbs of a cripple. This is what Mary did: she humbled herself and the Lord filled her. I was sitting. What then did it mean when I said: At dawn I will stand in your presence and contemplate you? If the dawn symbolizes the future century, how is she sitting and is she similar to someone who is standing? After the night of the present century, I will stand before you, he says, and I will see; I will stand and contemplate. He didn't say, "I'll sit down." How is Mary, sitting, the image of such a great thing, if I will stand in your presence and contemplate you? Do not be disturbed by this; It is due to the poverty of the flesh, since the body cannot be required to sit and stand at the same time. If he is sitting, he is not standing, and if he is standing, he is not sitting; Both things at the same time are not possible for the body. But if I prove that it is possible for the soul, will there be reason to doubt? If man can do something similar now, he will be able to do it much more easily once all difficulties have disappeared. Here is an example. Saint Paul himself says: Now we live if you stand firm in the Lord. The great Apostle, better yet, Christ through him, orders us to be firm, to stand. How can we understand what the same Apostle, or rather, Christ through him, also says: However, let us walk in that to which we have come? Here we have standing and walking; and it is still a short walk, so he adds: Run in such a way

so that you reach the prize. Pay attention, then, beloved, and understand. He commands us to walk and stand, not so that when we stand we stop walking, or that when we walk we stop standing, but that we do both at the same time: walk and stand. What does it mean to stand and run? That we must remain and progress. Show me, Lord, your ways. Once we know the ways of the Lord, what is asked of us but to walk in them? Guide me, Lord, on your path. What do we want but to walk? In another text, on the contrary, as if wanting us to remain motionless, he says: Do not allow my feet to move. And in another place, congratulating and giving thanks to someone: And he did not allow my feet to move. If it were said to the psalmist: How have you longed to be shown the ways of the Lord, to guide you along His path, and you do not want your feet to move and, even more, you give thanks because they did not move? How then did you walk without moving your feet? His answer would be this: "I walked because I acted at the same time, and I remained motionless because I did not move away." Do not be surprised, brothers; See that what the body cannot do, the soul can do. As far as the body is concerned, when you walk, you are not motionless, and when you remain motionless, you do not walk. But according to the soul, according to the faith, according to the attention of the mind, be still and walk, remain and progress, for now we live, if you abide in the Lord, and run so that you obtain the prize. Therefore, dearly beloved, you will sit and you will stand. We will be sitting because we will humbly contemplate the Lord, and we will be standing because we will remain eternally in him.

Auditui meo dabis gaudium et laetitiam, et exultabunt ossa humiliata (Ps 50,10). Humiliata ossa, tamquam haerentis membra. Hoc agebat Maria: humiliabatur, et implebatur. Sedebat: quid est ergo quod dixi: Mane adstabo et contemplabor? Quomodo adstanti similis sedet, si mane significat futurum saeculum? Praesentis saeculi nocte transacta: Adstabo, inquit, et uidebo, adstabo et contemplabor. Non dixit: sedebo. Quomodo huius tantae rei imaginem Maria sedens gerit, si adstabo et contemplabor?^ Ne uos ista conturbent, carnalis inopia est: non potest utrumque exigí de corpore, ut simul uno tempore et stet et sedeat. If enim sedet_, non stat; si stat, non sedet: simul utrumque non potest corpus. Sed si probauero quia potest animus, numquíd erit unde dubitemus? Quia si moda aliquid tale potest, multo facilius tune poterit homo, omni dífficultate finita. Ecce unde capiatis exemplum. Ipse ait Paulus: Nunc uiuimus, si uos statis in domino. Tantus apostolus, immo per apostolum Christus, stare nos iussit. Quomodo item ipse apostolus, immo ipse per apostolum Christus, dicit nobis: Verumtamen in quod peruenimus, in eo ambulemus? (Phil 3:16). Hic stare, hic ambulare: parum est ambulare, siecurrite ut comprehendatis (1 Cor 9:24). Attendíte ¡taque, carissimi, et in[58]tellegite; et ambulare nos iubet, et stare nos iubet; non ut, quando stamus,

ambulare desinamus, aut, quando ambulamus, stare cessemus; sed simul utrumque, et stemus, et curramus. Quid est, et stemus, et curramus? Et permaneamus, et proficiamus. Vias tuas, domine, notes fac mihi (Ps 24,4). Vtique per uias domini notes factas quid iubemur, nisi ambulare? "Deduc me, domine, in uia tua (Ps 85,11): quid optmus, nisi ambulare? Et rursus quasi figi uno loco: Ne des ad mouendum pedes meos (Ps 120,3). Et gratulans alio agensque gratias: Et non dedit in motum pedes meos (Ps 65,9). Si ei diceretur: Quomodo uias domini optati notes fieri tibi, quomodo te ab illo in uia eius deduci uoluisti, et optas non moueri pedes tuos, gratiasque agis non data in motum pedes tuos? Quomodo ambulasti, qui pedes non mouisti: Et ambulaui, quia feci, quia non recessi. fratres: ecce, quod non potest corpus, potest Secundum corpus, quando ambulas, non stas: quando stas, non ambulas; ergo, carissimi, et sedebitis, et stabitis, quia humiliter creatorem conspiciemus;

6. And I add more. We will lie down, which is neither sitting nor standing. We will lie down. I would not dare to affirm it if the Lord's promise did not exist: He will make them lie down. As if promising his servants a great reward, he tells them: He will make them sit down and pass by and serve them. This is the life that is promised to us: it will make us lie down and in passing it will serve us. It is the same thing that he said when he admired and praised the faith of the centurion: Truly I say to you, many will come from the East and from the West, and will recline at table with Ahrahán, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. Magnificent promise, happy fulfillment. Let us work to deserve it; May the Lord help us so that we can get to where, lying down, he will serve us. What does it mean to lie down, if not to rest? And what does it mean to serve, if not to feed? What food is that? What drink will that be? Without a doubt, the same truth. That food restores and does not diminish; feeds and feeding gives fullness. Nor is it transformed into the one whom it feeds, but by remaining whole it gives fullness. Don't you think that God can feed your eye in the same way that it is now fed by this material light? Your eye feeds on light. Whether many or few see it, its greatness is the same; The eyes are fed with it and yet it does not suffer any loss. The eye receives it without it diminishing; He collects it, but not a single part. Can the light do this in the eyes, and cannot the Lord do it with the transformed man? It can, there is no doubt that it can. Why haven't you taken it over yet? Because you are busy with many cares, the work absorbs you, or rather, absorbs all of us.

of Martha. Who is free to exercise this service? Who breathes free from these cares? Let us do it holily, let us do it with charity, for the time will come when, as we lie down, he will pass by and serve us. He would not be our servant if he had not passed from here to the Father. Here he was when he made the promise. And so that we would not think that he had to appear in the form of a servant, he says: Passing by it will serve them. Also referring to this transit, the evangelist says: The time had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father. And also: Have I been with you for so long and you still haven't met me? If Felipe had understood what he had just heard, he would have responded: "I haven't known because you haven't passed yet." For this reason it is also said to Mary after the resurrection: Do not touch me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father. 7. Therefore, dearly beloved, I beseech you, I exhort you, I advise you, I command you, I beseech you that we may all together desire that life and run towards it living together, so that, persevering in it, we may find rest. The moment will come, a moment that will have no end, when the Lord will make us sit down at the table and he will serve us. What will he serve us but himself? Why are you worried about what you will eat? You have the same Lord. What should be our delicacy if not in the beginning the Word existed and the Word was God? What will lying down be but resting? What will it be to feed ourselves but to delight ineffably with its contemplation. In your right is delight. One thing I asked of the Lord, that I will seek; not the crowd in

6. Nam plus addo: et discubituri sumus, quod utique nec sedere nec stare est. Discumbemus. Non audetem dicere, nisi promitteret dominus: Faciet eos discumbere. Promittens magnum praemium seruis suis: Faciet eos discumbere, inquit, et transiens ministrabit eos (Luke 13:37). Haec nobis uita promittitur, quia faciet nos discumbere dominus, et transiens ministrabit nobis. Hoc etiam dictum est, cum esset illius centurionis fides mirata atque laudata: Amen dico uobis, quia multi ab oriente et occidente uenient, et recumbent cum Abraham, Isaac et lacob in regno caelorum (Mt 8,11). Magna promissio, felix redditio. Agamus ut mereamur, adiuuemur ut uleamus illo peruenire, ubi nobis discumbentibus dominus ministrabit. Quid enim erit discumbere, nisi requiescere? Et quid erit ministrare, nisi pascere? Quis ille cibus est? Quis ille potus est? Nimirum ipsa ueritas. Ille cibus reficit, nec deficit: pascit, et pascendo Integros facit; nec consumitur in eum quem pascit, sed manens integer integrat. Non credis quoniam sic potest pascere deus, cum moda ab isto lumine sic pascatur oculus tuus? Oculus tuus pascitur luz. Multi uideant, tanta est [59] illa: pauci videant, tanta est illa; et illi reficiuntur oculi, et ipsa non deficit. Sumit inde, nec minuit: carpit, nec praecidit. Haec lux potest oculo: et deus non potest homini commutato? Potest, plane potest: quare nondum capitis? Quia circa fines oceupati estís: negotium Marthae uos

occupauit, immo omnes nos. Quis enim ab hoc ministry subueniendi uacat? Quis ab hac cura respirat? Innocenter hoc agamus, caritate agamus: ueniet etiam illud, ut discumbamus, et transiet, et ministrabit nobis. Non enim tune nobis ministraret, nisi hinc ad patrem transiret: hic enim erat, quando promittebat. Et ne tale aliquid nos exhibiturum arbitraremur, qualem formam serui contemplabamur, transiens, inquit, ministrabit eis. Et euangelista de hoc transitu: Cum autem uenisset hora, ut lesus transiret de hoc mundo ad patrem (lo 13,1). Tanto tempore, ait, uobiscum sum, et non cognouisti me? (14.9). Si sciret quid audiret, responderet: Non cognoui, quia nondum transisti. Vnde et Mariae dicitur post resurrectionem: Noli me tangere, nondum enim ascendí ad patrem (lo 20,17). 7. Ergo, carissimi, obsecro uos, hortor uos, moneo, praeccipio, rogo, illam uitam simul desideremus, ad eam simul ueniendo curramus, ut in ea perseuerando sistamus. Come time, et sine fine erit illa hora, quando dominus faciat nos discumbere, et ministret nobis. Quid, I don't even know? Quid quaeritis quid manducetis? Ipsum dominum habetis. Quid enim erit unde pascamur, quid, nisi, In principle erat uerbum, et uerbum erat apud deum, et deus erat uerbum? (1,1). Quid erit discumbere, nisi requiescere? Quid erit pasci, nisi illius contemplatione ineffabiliter delectari? Delectatio in dextera tua (Ps 15,11). Vnam petii a domino, hanc requiram: non

which I am busy, but I asked the Lord for one thing, this will I seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to contemplate the delight of the Lord. You will not enjoy this happiness while working. Vacate and see. That? That I am the Lord. Excellent vision, happy contemplation. What else, then, is "lie down and eat," but rest and see. Therefore let us not take it carnally, nor think, so to speak, of licentious banquets. The present will pass; It must be tolerated, but not loved. If you want to carry out the office of Martha, there is moderation, there is mercy. Moderation in bearing, mercy in giving. Work will pass and rest will come; but rest is not reached except through work. The ship passes and arrives at the homeland, but the homeland cannot be reached unless it is with the ship. If we consider the waves and storms of this world, our life is a sea voyage. And I do not doubt that we do not sink because we are carried by the wood of the cross 5. plana, circa quae sum occupatus: sed unam petii a domino, hanc requiram, ut inhabitem in domo domini per omnes dies uitae meae, ut contempler delectationem domini (Ps 26,4). Non est ist beatitudo laborantium. Vacate et uidete: quid? quoniam ego sum dominus (Ps 45:11). Magna uisio, felix contemplated. Quid est autem aliud, Discumbite et mandúcate, nisi, Vacate et uidete? Non ergo carnaliter sapiamus, nec uenerales, ut ita dicam, epulas cogitemus. Transibunt ista: toleranda sunt, non amanda. Si uis in eis implere officium Marthae, adsit modestia, adsit mercy: modestia in temperando, mercy in erogando. Transit labor, et ueniet requies; sed [60] ad requiem non nisi per laborem. Transit nauis, et uenit in patriam; sed ad patriam non nisi per nauem. Nauigamus enim, si adtendamus fluctus tempestatesque huius saeculi. Nec dubito quod ideo non mergimur, quia crucis ligno portamur. This idea is frequent in Augustinian texts. See, among others, sermon 75,2; Enarration to Psalm 103,4,3; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 2,2.

Theme: The inopportune friend (Luke 11:5-13). Place: Carthage. Date: Year 410 or 411. 1. We have heard the exhortation of our Lord, celestial teacher and most faithful counselor, exhorter that we ask and giver when we ask. We have heard him in the Gospel exhorting us to ask insistently and to call until we seem impertinent. He proposed an example in this direction. «If any of you had a friend, from whom he asked for three loaves at night because another friend who came from a trip had shown up at home and found himself with nothing to offer him, if he answered that he was already resting and his servants with him and, therefore, do not bother him; If, however, he insists and perseveres calling, without being cowed by indelicacy; On the contrary, forced to do so by necessity, the other will rise up, if not because of friendship, at least because of his stubbornness and will give him as many loaves as he wants. How many did you want? Only three. To the parable the Lord added an exhortation, in which he ardently encouraged us to ask, seek and knock until we obtain what we ask for, what we seek and what we call for, using an example by contrast: That of the judge who, despite SERMO

Ad petendum a Deo, similarityinibus Christus hortatur.—Audivimus nos exhortantem Dominum nostrum, caelestem magistrum, et fidelissimum consiliarium, eumdem hortatorem, ut petamus, et datorem cum petimus. Audivimus eum in Gospel hortantem nos eum petere instantor, et pulsare usque ad similarityinem improbitatis. Proposuit enim nobis, exempli gratia: Si quis vestrum haberet amicum, a quo nocte peteret tres panes, cum illi amicus de via venisset, et quod ei aponeret non haberet: si autem ille responderat iam se requiescere, et servos suos secum, nec debenré illius precibus inquietad, He autem pulsando instet et perseveret, nec pudere territus abscedat, sed necessitate coactus immineat: surrecturum illum, etsi non propter amicitiam, certe propter illius improbitatem, et daturum ei quantos voluerit. How many autem voluit? Nihil plus ille voluit quam tres. In hac ergo similarityine adiunxit hortationem Dominus, et omnino stimulavit [619] nos petere, quaerere, pulsare, doñee accipiamus quod petimus, quod quaerimus, quod pulsamus, usus exemplo a contrari: sicut de illo iudice qui nec Deum timebat, nec
of not fearing God or feeling any respect for men,

Because of the simplicity of your faith, you ignore; You do not have, therefore, with which to repair the strength of the hungry and his demand served as a wake-up call to you to know your indigence. And for this reason, by wanting to teach you are forced to learn, and the confusion that someone who did not find in you what they were looking for puts you in, forces you to search in order to deserve to find. 3. And where will you look? Where but in the books of the Lord? Maybe what he asked you is in the book, but it is obscure. Perhaps the Apostle said it in one of his letters, but in such a way that you can read it, although not understand it; You are not allowed to pass, therefore, forward. But whoever asks you continues to urge; You, however, are not allowed to ask Paul or Peter or any prophet directly. This family rests with their Lord; The ignorance of this century is strong, that is, it is midnight and the hungry friend urges. Maybe a simple faith was enough for you, but not for him. Should we abandon it? Should it be thrown out of the house? Call with your prayer to the Lord himself with whom his family rests, ask, insist. He does not need to be overcome by importunity, like that friend, to get up and give you. He wants to give. If by calling you have not yet received anything, keep calling, because you want to give. Defer giving what you want to give so that by deferring it you will desire it more ardently, lest, granting it to you, it will later seem a vile thing to you.' 4. When you have obtained the three loaves, that is, the

At the daily insistence of a certain widow, overcome by fatigue, he gruntingly gave her what he did not know how to grant as a favor. Our Lord Jesus Christ, who asks with us and gives with the Father, would not exhort us so insistently to ask if he did not want to give. Let human apathy be ashamed: he is more willing to give than we are to receive; He wants to show us mercy more than we want to see ourselves free from our miseries. And let it be very clear: if we are not freed from it, we will remain miserable; If he exhorts us, he does it for our good. 2. Let us be vigilant and give faith to those who exhort us; Let us fulfill those who promise and rejoice with those who give. Maybe we also had a friend who came on a trip and we didn't have anything to give him; In our need, we receive for him and for ourselves. It is almost impossible that one has not come across a friend who asks him something to which he does not know how to answer; The need to give showed him his lack. You are presented with a friend who is going on a journey, that is, on a journey through this life, through which we all pass as pilgrims, since no one remains in it as master, but to every man it is said: Repair your strength, continue, set out on your way and leave your place to the one who comes behind. Or perhaps it is another friend of yours, who comes from a bad trip, that is, from a bad life, tired for not having found the truth, heard and known which leads to happiness, and tired and exhausted in the midst of all the lust and scarcity of the world, who comes to you and says: "Give me the reason for your faith; make me a Christian. Perhaps he asks you what, homines reverebatur, et tamen cum eum quaedam vidua interpellaret quotidie, taedio victus dedit quod benefit non potuit invitus (Luke 18:1-8). Dominus autem noster Iesus Christus inter nos petitor, cum Patre dator, non utique nos tantum hortatetur ut peteremus, nisi daré vellet. Erubescat humano pigrítia: plus vult ille daré, quam nos accipere: plus vult ule misereri, quam nos a miseria liberari: et utique si non liberati fuerimus, nos miseri remanebimus. Nam ille quod nos hortatur, propter nos hortatur. CAPUT II.—2. Amicus de via veniens reficiendus.—Evigilemus, et hortanti credamus, promittenti obsequamur, et ad dantem gaudeamus. Fortassis enim et nobis aliquando venit amicus de via, et non ínvenimus quod ei apponeremus; et necessítatem passi sumus, et accepimus et nobis et illi.

Fieri enim non potest, nisi ut aliquis passus fuerit amicum aliquid interrogantem, quod respondé non possit: et tune se invenit non habere, quando coactus est daré. Venit tibi amicus de via, id est, de vita huius saeculi, in qua omnes velut peregrini transeunt, nec ullus quasi possessor manet; sed omni homini dícitur: Refectus es, transí; age iter, da venturo locum (Eccli 29,33). Aut forte de via mala, hoc est, de vita mala, fatiguetus nescio quis amicus tuus, non inveniens veritatem, qua audita et percepta beatus fiat, sed lassatus in omni cupiditate et egestate saeculi, come ad te,

tanquam ad christianum, et dicit: Redde mihi rationem, fac me Christianum. And interrogat quod forte tu per simplicitatem fidei nesciebas: et non est unde reficias esurientem, et te admonitus invenís indigentem; et cum vis Porquere, cogeris discere: et dum erubescis eum qui interrogavit, quod quaerebat non in te inveniens, compelleris quaerere, ut merearis invenire. 3. Amicus alius media nocte interpellatus ut det tres panes.—Et ubi quaeras? Ubi, nisi in dominicis Libris? Fortassis quod ille interrogavit, in libro positum est, sed obscurum est. Forte dixit hoc Apostolus in Epístola sua. Sic dixit, ut legere possis, intellegere non possis: traniré non permitteris. Urget enim interrogator: ipsum Paulum, aut Petrum, aut aliquem prophetam interrogare non sineris. Iam enim requiescit familia ista cum Domino suo, et saeculi huius ignorantia valida est, hoc est, nox media, et urget amicus esuriens. Tibi forte sufficiebat simplex fides, illi non sufficit. Numquid deserendus est? numquid of domo proiciendus est? CAPUT III.—Ergo ad ipsum Dominum, ad ipsum cum quo familia requiescit, pulsa orando, pete, urge. Non quomodo amicus ille in similarityine positus, taedio victus ariset et dabit. I will give vult: tu pulsans nondum accepisti: pulsate, I will give vult. Et quod daré vult, differt, ut amplius desideres dilatum, ne vilescat cyto datum. [620] 4. Tres panes dati.—Cum autem perveneris ad tres panes, This is his constant thought. food that is the knowledge of the Trinity, you will have something to live with and something to feed others with. Do not be afraid that a pilgrim will come on a journey; On the contrary, make him a member of your family by welcoming him. Don't be afraid that your supplies will run out either. That bread is not finished; but rather he will put an end to your poverty. It is bread, and it is bread, and it is bread: God the Father, God the Son and God the Holy Spirit. The Father is eternal, the Son is co-eternal, and the Holy Spirit is co-eternal. The Father is immutable, the Son immutable and the Holy Spirit immutable. Creator both the Father and the Son, as well as the Holy Spirit. Pastor and giver of life both the Father and the Son, as well as the Holy Spirit. Food and eternal bread the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Learn this yourself and teach it. You live on it and feed the other. God, who is the giver, cannot give you anything better than himself. Miser! What else do you want? If you ask for something more, what will be enough for you, if God is not enough for you? 2. 5. But in order for what is given to you to be sweet, it is necessary that you possess charity, that you have faith, that you have hope. These things are also three: faith, hope and charity. Nec peregrinum venientem de via reformides, sed excipiendo civem domesticum facías: nec timeas ne finias. Non pañis ille finietur, sed indigentiam tuam finiet. Aut si aliud petas, quid tibi sufficit, cui Deus non sufficit? CAPUT IV.—5. Fides, spes, caritas, Dei dona.—Sed opus est ut habeas caritatem, habeas fidem, habeas spem: ut possit tibi dulce esse quod datur.

Et haec ipsa tria sunt, fides, spes, caritas, Et haec ipsa dona Dei sunt. Nam fidem ab ipso accepimus: Sicut Deus, inquit, unicuique par ti tus est mensuram fidei (Rom 12,3). Et spem ab ipso accepimus, cui dicitur: In quo spem dedisti mihi (Ps 118,49). that has been given to us. Although they are somewhat diverse, they are all gifts from God. Now all three remain: faith, hope and charity, but the greatest of them is charity. Of those loaves it was not said that one was greater than the other, but simply that three loaves were asked for and obtained. 6. Here are three more things. Which of you, if his son asks for bread, gives him a stone? Or which of you who asks for a fish gives him a snake? Or whoever asks for an egg gets a scorpion? If, then, you, being evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father, who is in heaven, give good things to those who ask him! Let us examine, then, these three things, in case those other three are contained in them: faith, hope and charity, the greatest of which is charity. Consider these three things: the bread, the fish, and the egg, the greatest of which is the bread. We can precisely put bread as a symbol of charity. The stone was opposed to the bread, because hardness is contrary to charity. The fish symbolizes faith. A saint said—and I like to repeat it—: “Pious faith is like a good fish. "He lives among the waves, without being torn apart or turned over." Godly faith lives among the temptations and storms of this world; The world rages, but she remains unbreakable. Now notice how the snake represents the opposite of faith. Thanks to her faith, she was taken as a wife to whom it is said in the Song of Songs: Come from Lebanon, my wife, come sanctum, qui datus est nobis (Rom 5,5). Sed haec itidem tria aliquantulum sunt diverse; sed omnia Dei dona. Maneat enim tria haec, fides, spes, caritas: maior autem borum caritas (1 Cor 13:13). In illis panibus non est dictus aliquis pañis maior allus: sed simpliciter petiti, et dati tres panes. 6. Tria eadem rursus means it. Pañis, faces. Pisces, fides.—Ecce alia tria: Quis est vestrum, a quo petit filius suus panem, numquid lapidem porrigat ei? Aut quis est vestrum, a quo petit piscem, numquid serpentem porriget ei? Aut a quo petit ovum, numquid porriget ei scorpionem? Si ergo vos, cum sitis mali, nostis bona data I will give filiis vestris; quanto magis Pater vester qui in caelis est, dabit bona petentibus se? (Luke 11:11-13). Tria ergo rursum ista consideramus, ne forte ibi sint illa tria, fides, spes, caritas: maior autem horum caritas. It puts ergo tria, panem, piscem, ovum: maior horum pañis. Ideo bene panem intellegimus in his tribes caritatem.

Propterea pañi lapidem opposuit, quia duritia contra est caritati. Piscem fidem intellegimus. Dixit quidam sanctus, et nos dicere delectat. Pisces bonus, pia est fides. Vivit Inter fluctus, nec frangitur aut solvitur fluctibus. Vivit inter temptationes tempestatesque huius saeculi, pia fides: saevit mundus, et integra est. Tantum contrarium fidei serpentem illum observa. In fide enim desponsata est illa, cui dicitur in Canticis canticorum: Come from Lebanon, sponsa mea, veniens et pertransiens ab initio fidei (Cant 4,8). Ideo et desponsata, quia desponsationis initium fides est.

and come out of the faith that was your beginning. She is betrothed because faith is the beginning of a betrothal, since the husband makes a promise and is bound by the promised faith. And I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve with his cunning, so your minds will be corrupted by departing from the chastity that is due to faith in Christ. And in another place: May Christ dwell in your hearts through faith. So let the devil not corrupt your faith, let him not devour the fish. 7. It remains to examine hope, which in my view can be compared to the egg. Hope has not yet reached its object, and the egg, although it is already something, is not yet the chicken. Quadrupeds give birth to children; birds, hope for children 3. Hope induces us to despise present things and hope for future things, to forget what is behind and to tend, with the Apostle, to what is ahead. It goes like this: One thing I do: forgetting what is behind and tending to what is ahead, I continue running, setting my eyes on the goal, towards the palm of the supreme calling of God in Christ Jesus. There is nothing so opposite to hope as looking back, that is, putting trust in things that slide and pass. Therefore, it must be put into what has not yet been given to us, but which must be given to us at some point and will never pass away. However, when temptations fall on the world like a rain of sulfur on Sodom, the experience of the woman of

Lot. She looked back and in that same place she was turned into salt to season the prudent with her example. This is how the apostle Saint Paul speaks of hope: In hope we have been saved. The hope that is seen is not hope. Well, what you see, how do you expect it? But if we wait for what we do not see, we wait patiently for it. What you see, how do you expect it? Here we have the egg. It is, yes, an egg, but it is not yet a chicken. It is wrapped in the shell; He cannot be seen because he is covered. Wait for him, therefore, with patience. Give it heat so that life can sprout. Pay attention; tend towards what is ahead, forget about what is behind; what is seen is temporary. Let us not look, he says, at what is seen, but at what is not seen. Things seen are temporary and things unseen are eternal. So extend hope to what is not seen, wait, endure. Don't look back. Protect your egg against the scorpion. He notices that he hurts with the tail behind him. Let the scorpion not destroy your egg, that is, let this world not kill your hope with its poison, which is more harmful the further back it is. How many things the world doesn't tell you! How much there is an uproar behind your back so that you look back, that is, so that you put your hope in the present - although I should not have used this word because what is never present is not present 4 -, turn your mind away from what Christ promised and has not yet given, but will give because he is faithful, and try to find rest in a world that must perish!

Promittitur enim ab sponso aliquid, et promissa fide detinetur. Opposuit autem Dominus serpentem pisci, diabolum fidei. Pro[621]pterea desponsatae huic dicit Apostolus: Desponsavi vos uni viro, virginem castam exhibitere Christo: et: Timaeus ne sicut serpens Evam seduxit astutia sua, sic et vestri sensus corrumpantur a castitate quae est in Christo (2 Cor 11, 2.3); id est, quae est in fide Christi. Habitare enim, inquit, Christum per fidem in Cordibus vestris (Ephes 3,17). Diabolus ergo non corruptat fidem, non devoret piscem. CAPUT V.—7. Ovum, spes.—Restat spes, quae, quantum mihi videtur, ovo comparatur. Spes enim nondum pervenit ad rem: et ovum est aliquid, sed nondum est pullus. Quadrupedes ergo filios pariunt, birds autem spem filiorum. Spes ergo ad hoc nos hortatur, ut praesentia contemnamus,futura exspectemus: ea quae retro sunt obliviscentes, cum Apostólo in anteriora extendamur. Sic enim dicit: Unum autem, quae retro oblitus, in ea quae ante sunt extentus, secundum intentionem sequor ad palmam supernae vocationis Dei in Christo lesu (Phil 3,13.14). Nihil ergo tam inimicum est spei, quam retro respicere, id est, in eis rebus, quae praeterlabuntur et transeunt, spem will put: sed in his quae nondum datae sunt, sed dandae quandoque nunquam transibunt. Quando autem scatet tentationibus mundus, velut pluvia Sodomae sulfúrea, metuendum est exemplum uxoris

Loth. Retro enim respexit; et ubi respexit, ibi remansit. In salem conversa est (Gen 19,26), ut prudentes condiret example. Apostolus Paulus de hac spe ita loquitur: Spe enim salvi facti sumus. Spes autem quae videtur, non est spes: quod enim videt quis, quid sperat? Si autem quod non videmus speramus, per patientiam exspectamus (Rom 8,24,25). Quod enim videt quis, quid sperat? ovum est. Est ovum, et pullus nondum est. Et testudine tectum est: non videtur, quia operitur: cum patientia exspectetur; fervescat, ut viviscat. Intend, extende in anteriora, obliviscere praeterita. Quae enim videntur, temporalia sunt. Non respicientes, inquit, quae videntur, sed quae non videntur. Quae enim videntur, temporalia sunt; quae autem non videntur, aeterna (2 Cor 4:18). In illa ergo quae non videntur, extende spem: exspecta, sustine. Noli retro respicere. Ovo tuo scorpium time. Vide quia de cauda percutit, quam retro habet. Non ergo scorpius perimat ovum tuum, mundus iste spem tuam, ut ita dicam, poison eo contrary, quo retrario. Quanta tibi loquitur mundus, quanta post dorsum strepit, ut retro respicias: id est, ut in rebus praesentibus (nec praesentibus; non enim diceda sunt praesentia nunquam stantia) spem tuam ponas; et ab eo quod promisit Christus et nondum dedit, sed quia fidelis est dabit, averías animum tuum, et velis requiescere in mundo pereunte.

8. This is why God mixes well-being and earthly happiness with bitterness: so that another happiness may be sought whose sweetness is not deceptive. The world relies on these bitternesses to try to separate you from what, having it before you, you tend, and to make you look back. Because of these bitterness and tribulations you murmur and say: "See that nothing remains standing in Christian times." Why are you fussing? It is not the promise of God or of Christ that these things will not perish. He, who is eternal, promised me eternal things; If I believe it, from mortal I will become eternal. Why do you cry, oh filthy world? Why are you shouting? Why are you trying to take me away from him? You want to hold me down by being perishable. What wouldn't you do if you lasted forever? Who would you not deceive if you were sweet, if you do it by being bitter, falsifying delicacies? If I keep hope, if I retain it, my egg has not been broken by the scorpion. I will bless the Lord at all times; His praise is always in my mouth. Whether the world is happy or it falls apart, 'I will bless the Lord who made the world. I will bless him, without a doubt. Whether it goes well according to the flesh, or whether it goes badly, I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise is always in my mouth. Because if I bless when things go well for me, and I curse when things go badly for me, I have already received the sting of the scorpion, already wounded I looked back. Far be it from us to act that way. The Lord gave it to me, the Lord took it from me; As it pleased the Lord, so it was done; blessed be the name of the Lord.

9. The city that begat us according to the flesh still stands 6. Thank God! May she also be engendered spiritually and pass with us into eternity! But if the city that gave birth to us according to the flesh perishes, the city that gave birth to us spiritually endures. The Lord built Jerusalem. Did he lose his building because he was asleep or because the enemy entered it and found it defenseless? If the Lord does not guard the city, the watchman watches in vain. But what city? He who guards Israel does not sleep nor will he sleep. And who is Israel but the offspring of Abraham? And who is the offspring of Abraham but Christ? Now your seed, he said, is Christ. What does it say to us? You are Christ's, therefore you are Abraham's offspring, heirs by virtue of the promise. And in your Seed, he says, all peoples will be blessed. The holy city, the believing city, the pilgrim city is founded in heaven. Oh faithful!, do not corrupt hope, do not lose charity; Gird up your loins, go up, set your torches before you, wait for the Lord when he comes from the wedding. Why do you tremble because the earthly kingdoms perish? The heavenly one was promised to you so that you would not perish along with the earthly ones. Because its ruin was predicted and in a way that leaves no doubt. We cannot deny that prediction. The Lord whom you wait for told you: Nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom. Earthly kingdoms change, but he of whom it was said: And his kingdom will have no end will come.

Clades et vastationes quomodo Christianis useful.— Ideo enim Deus felicitatibus terrenis amaritudines miscet, ut alia quaeratur felicitas, cuius dulcedo non est fallax: et de ipsis amaritudinibus conatur mundus avertere ab eo quod intendis in anteriora, et retro convertere. Non hoc promisit mihi Deus, quod ista non peribunt: non hoc mihi promisit Christus. Aeterna promisit aeternus: si credidero, ex mortali fiam aeternus. Quid strepis, or munde immunde? quid strepis? Félix Sít mundus, evertatur mundus: Benedicam Dominum, qui fecit mundum. Benedicam prorsus. Secundum carnem bene sit, secundum carnem male sit: Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore; semper laus eius in ore meo. Nam si benedico when bene est, et blasphemo when male est: suscepi scorpionis aculeum, compunctus retro respexi; quod absit a nobis. Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit; sicut Domino placuit, ita factum est: sit nomen Domini benedictum (Iob 1,21).

CAPUT VII.—9. Civitas et regnum in caelis aeternum eos manent.— Manet civitas quae nos carnaliter genuit. Deo gratias. Utinam et spiritualiter generetur, et nobiscum transeat ad aeternitatem. Si non manet civitas quae nos carnaliter genuit, manet quae nos spiritualiter genuit. Aedificans lemsalem Dominus (Ps 146,2). Numquid dozing aedificium suum perdidit, aut non custodíendo hostes admisit? Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, in vanum vigilat qui custodit eam (Ps 126,1). Et quam civitatem? Non dormit, ñeque dormitabit, qui custodit Israel (Ps 120,4). Who is Israel, nisi semen Abrahae? Quid est semen Abrahae, nisi Christus? Et semini tuo, inquit, quod est Christus. Et nobis quid? Vos autem Christi: ergo semen Abrahae estis, secundum promissionem heredes (Gal 3,16.29). In semine tuo, inquit, benedicentur omnes gentes (Gen 22:18). Civitas sancta, civitas fidelis, civitas in terra peregrina, in cáelo fundata est. O fidelis, noli corrumpere spem, noli amittere caritatem, accinge lumbos tuos, ascende, praetende luzernas tuas, exspecta Dominum, quando veniat a nuptiis (Luke 12,35.36). Quid expavescis, quia pereunt regna terrena? Ideo tibi caeleste promissum est, ne cum terrenis perires. Nam ista peritura praedícta sunt, praedícta omnino. Non enim deniale possumus quod piaedictum est. Dominus tuus quem exspectas, dixit tibi: Exsurget gens super gentem, et regnum super regnum (Mark 13,8). Habent

10. Those who promised eternity to earthly kingdoms did not do so out of truth, but rather lied to flatter. One of his poets introduces Jupiter, who addresses the Romans with these words: «I did not establish spatial terms nor temporal limits for them; I gave them an eternal empire» 7. In no way does it respond to the truth. The eternal kingdom that you gave them, oh you who gave nothing!, is it on earth or in heaven? Without a doubt, on earth. And even if it were in heaven, Heaven and earth will pass away. Even the things that God himself made will pass away; how much more quickly those that Romulus did! If we wanted to call Virgil to account and reproach him for having said such things, perhaps he would take us to a corner and say: "I know this too, but to sell my words to the Romans, what was I going to do but flatterarily promise them what was false? 8 Keep in mind that when I said 'I gave them an eternal empire' I acted with caution, since I put it in the mouth of Jupiter. Personally I did not say any falsehood; I left the role of liar to Jupiter. Do you want to check that I already knew that? In another place where I was speaking in my own name, without already introducing the stone Jupiter, I said: 'Neither the affairs of Rome themselves, nor the kingdoms themselves destined to perish' 9. See that I said that the kingdoms must perish. I said it; I did not remain silent

that kingdoms must perish. 'They must perish': speaking in truth I did not keep silent about it; 'they must always survive': it is a promise born of flattery» 10. 11. Let us not lose heart, therefore, brothers. All earthly kingdoms will come to an end. If the present moment represents the end, God knows. Perhaps it has not arrived yet and we wish that it does not arrive due to a certain weakness or compassion or misery of ours. But is it not for this reason that it must come? Strengthen your hope in God, long for the eternal, hope for the eternal. You are Christians; My brothers, we are Christians. Christ did not descend into the flesh to seek pleasure. More than loving, let us tolerate present things. In view we have the evil and ruin of adverse things and the false flattery of prosperous things. Fear the sea, even when it is calm. Let us not hear the words in vain: “Uplift your heart.” Why do we put our hearts on the earth, when we see the earth collapsing? I cannot but urge you to accumulate reasons with which you respond in defense of your faith to those who mock and blaspheme the Christian name. May no person with their murmuring separate you from the hope of the future. All those who blaspheme our Christ based on present difficulties are the tail of a scorpion. We put our

Augustine is using the highest Roman "authority" to confront the accusations against Christianity that came daily from pagan mouths. He denies the interpretation they used to give him. Without a doubt, what was announced as happening in Rome meant for many Christians the advent of the end of the world. The shock that it caused in the men of that time can be deduced from the words of Augustine. Saint Jerome, already ready to write his great commentary to the prophet Ezekiel, gave up the undertaking upon learning of the fact. Augustine admits the possibility that the end of the world is near, but advises not to rush to judgment. See Supplementary Note 22: The Ages of the World Vol. VII p.751.
