CAPUT I.—1. Praeceptum de cavenda omni avaritia.—Qui Deum timetis, non dubito quin verbum eius cum timore audiatis, et cum hilaritate faciatis; ut quod promisit, moda speietis, post accipiatis. Dominum moda audivimus praecipientem nobis, Christum Iesum filium Dei. Praecepit nobis Veritas, quae nec falliit, nec fallitur: audiamus, timeamus, caveamus. Quid ergo praecepit? Dico, inquit, vobis, abstinete ab omni avaritia (Luke 12:15). Quid est, ab omni avaritia? What is it, ab omni? Quare addidit, ab omni? Posset enim sic dicere, Cávete ab avaritia. Pertinuit ad eum, ut [628J adderet, ab omni; et diceret, Cávete ab omni avaritia. 2. Qua occasione datum a Christo.—Quare hoc dixerit, velut occasio ipsa unde natus est sermo, apparet nobis in sancto Evangelio. Interpel-

He fought the Lord against a brother of his who had fled with all the assets and refused to give him the part that corresponded to him. You realize how just their cause was. He did not intend to take away what was not his; He only asked for the goods that his parents had left him. He asked for nothing else when he turned to the Lord as to a judge. He had an evil brother, but against that unjust brother he had found a just judge. Should I waste this opportunity in such a good cause? On the other hand, who would say to his brother: "Give your brother his share," if Christ did not do it? Was another judge going to say it, whom the kidnapper and richer brother might have corrupted with gifts? This man, miserable and deprived of his paternal property, having found such a good judge, approaches him, questions him, pleads with him and explains his case in a few words. What need did he have for words when he spoke to someone who could also see the heart? Lord, he says, tell my brother to share the inheritance with me. The Lord does not answer "Let your brother come"; nor did he send him to tell him to appear, nor in his presence did he say to the one who had questioned him: "Prove what you have said." He asked for half of the inheritance; He requested half, but on earth, and the Lord offered it all to him in heaven. The Lord gave him more than he asked for. 3. Tell my brother to share the inheritance with me. The cause is just and its presentation brief. But let's listen to the judge and teacher. Man, he tells him; man, you who consider this inheritance great, what are you but a man? Do it something more than lavit enim eum quidam contra fratrem suum, qui totum patrimonium abstulerat, et fratri suo partem suam non reddebat. Quam bonam ergo causam habuerit iste interpellator, advertitis. Non enim rapere quaerebat aliena, sed sua a parentibus sibi relicta quaerebat: ipsa Domino interpellato et iudicante poscebat. Habebat iniquum fratrem: sed iustum iudicem invenerat contra iniquum fratrem. Should I lose in tam bona causa istam occasionem? Aut quis diceret fratri eius: Redde partem suam fratri tuo, si Christus non diceret? Ule iudex hoc dicturus erat, quem forte frater ditior et raptor praemio corrumpebat? Miser ergo et paternis opibus destitutus tali ac tanta iudice invento accessit, interpellat, rogat, causam suam brevissime exponit. Utquid enim opus erat causam perorare, quando ei loquebatur, qui cor poterat et videre? Domine, inquit, dic fratri meo, ut dividet mecum hereditatem (ib., 13). Non ei dixit Dominus: Veniat frater tuus.

Sed nec misit, ut adesset, aut cum adfuisset, interpellatori dixit: Proba quod dicebas. Petebat dimidiam hereditatem, petebat in terra dimidiam: in cáelo Dominus offerebat totam. Plus Dominus ibat, quam Ule postulabat. CAPOT II.—3. Divider hereditath Christus esse nolens quid doceat. Donatistae notantur.—Dic fratri meo, ut dividat mecum hereditatem. Just cause, brevis cause. Sed audiamus et iudicantem et docentem. Homo, ait, Homo: qui enim pro magno habes istam hereditatem, quid es nisi homo? Volebat íllum faceré alíquid plus quam est homo. Crux
The detachment of riches

man: here is what the Lord desired. What did he intend to do more to those who wanted to keep him from greed? What else did you want to do to him? I will tell you: I said, you are gods and all children of the Most High. This is what I wanted it to be: to count among the gods those who do not have greed. Man, who has made me a divider among you? Nor did Saint Paul, a servant of Christ, desire this office for himself, when he said: I beseech you, brothers, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you. And those who, under the protection of his name, divided Christ, said: Each one of you says: I am of Paul, I of Apollo, I of Cephas, I of Christ. Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or was your baptism in the name of Paul? See, then, how perverse are the men who want those who did not want to be a divider to exist divided. Who, he says, has made me a divider between you? 4. You asked for a favor, now listen to the advice: I tell you: beware of all greed. Perhaps you call someone who goes in search of someone else's things as avaricious and greedy; I tell you more: "Do not covetously or greedily desire even your own goods." This is the meaning of everything. Beware of all greed, he says. This is a great weight! If perhaps it is weak people on whom it is imposed, ask that whoever imposes it deigns to grant the strength. Should it not be considered a light thing, my brothers, that our Lord, Redeemer and Savior, who died for us, who gave his blood as the price of our ransom, who is our lawyer and judge, plus illum volebat faceré, cui volebat avaritiam tollere? Quid eum plus volebat faceré? Say vobis: Ego dixi, dii estis, et filii Altissimi omnes (Ps 81,6). Ecce quod eum volebat faceré, inter déos numerare qui avaritiam non habet. Homo, quis me constituit divisorem inter vos? (Luke 12:14). Et Paulus apostolus servus ipsius, quando dicebat, Obsecro vos, fratres, ut idipsum dicatis omnes, et non sint in vobis schismata, nolebat esse divisor. Denique monuit eos qui ad ipsius nomen currebant, et Christum dividebant: Unusquisque vestrum dicit, Ego sum Pauli, ego Apollo, ego Cephae, ego Christi. Divisus est Christus? Numquid Paulus pro vobis crucifixus est? aut in nomine Pauli baptizati estis? (1 Cor 1,10-13). Videte ergo, quam malí sint homines, qui volunt esse divísum, qui noluít esse divisor. Quis me, inquit, constituit divisorem inter vos? CAPUT III.—4.

Avaritiae damnatur qui vel sua cupide servat.— Petisti beneficium: audi consilium. Ego dico vobis, cávete ab omni cupiditate (ib., 15). Forte, inquit, tu avarum et cupidum díceres, si quaereret aliena: ego autem dico, cupide et avare non appetas nec tua. Hoc est, ab omni. Cávete, inquit, ab omni avaritia. Magnum pondus. Si forte hoc pondus infirmis imponitur; rogetur ut qui imponit, vires daré dignetur. [629] Non enim leviter habendum est, fratres mei, quando Dominus noster, Redemptor noster, Salvator noster, qui mortuus est pro nobis, qui

say: Beware. It is not a light thing. He knows what immense evil it is; We who do not know, let us believe him, Beware, he says. Because? About what? Of all greed. "I keep what is mine, I do not steal what belongs to others." Beware of all greed. Not only is he miserly who steals what is not his, but also he who keeps what is his greedily. If in this way he who keeps his own things with greed is accused, what will be the sentence of the one who steals what belongs to others? Beware, he says, of all greed, because man's life does not consist in having an abundance of the things he possesses in this world. He who stores a lot, how much does he take to live? Taking and in a sense mentally separating what you need to live, consider for whom you leave the rest, lest, perhaps by saving so that you have something to live with, you accumulate something to die with. Pay attention to Christ, pay attention to Truth, pay attention to severity. Beware, says the Truth. Beware, says severity. If you do not love the truth, at least fear severity. Man's life does not consist in the abundance of the things he has. Believe Christ, who does not deceive you. Do you say the opposite? "Man's life consists of what he has." You deceive yourself; He doesn't cheat on you. 5. The fact that the questioner had asked for his share, without wishing to touch the other's share, arose from the fact that in this phrase the Lord not only said: "Beware of greed," but added: From all greed. Even this was little. He proposed an example taken from a certain rich man whose fields had produced a great harvest. There was a rich man to whom his fields sanguinem suum pretium dedit, ut redeemeret nos, advocatus et iudex noster; It is not slight, when it says: Cávete. Novit ille quantum mali sit: nos non novimus; illi credamus. Dig yourself, restless. Crux? where? Ab omni avaritia. Non solum avarus est qui rapit aliena; sed et ille avarus est qui cupide servat sua. Sed si sic culpatur qui cupide servat sua; quomodo damnatur who rapit aliena? Cávete, inquit, ab omi cupiditate: quia non in abundantia hominis est vita eius ex bis quae ibi habet (ib.). Fine who recondit, how much inde tollit ut vivat? Cum tulerit inde, et quodam moda cogitatione separaverit quod sufficiat unde vivat, videat cetera cui remaneant: ne forte cum servas unde vivas, colligas unde moriaris. Ecce Christus, ecce veritas, ecce severitas. Cávete, dicit veritas: Cávete, dicit severitas. If you don't love veritatem, time severitatem. Non in abundantia hominis est vita eius ex bis quae habet. Crede illi, non te fallit. Against you say?

Immo in abundantia hominis est vita eius ex his quae habet. Ille te non fallit: you fail yourself. CAPUT IV.—5. Vives imprudens qui reservare proponit, non erogave.—Ex hac ergo occasione, quia interpellatore ille partem suam quaerebat, non alienam invadere cupiebat, nata est ista sententia Domini, ut non diceret: Cávete ab avaritia, sed adderet, ab omni avaritia. Parum Fuit: dat alterum exemplum de quodam divite, cui successerat regio. Erat, inquit, homo
The detachment of riches

had provided success. What does it mean: They had brought you success? That the farm he owned produced an extraordinary harvest. Of what magnitude? So abundant that I had nowhere to put it. Because of his abundance he quickly became narrow, having already been miserly. How many years had passed and yet his barns had been enough for him! But he had harvested so much wheat that the granaries that had previously been sufficient were not enough. And the wretch pondered not how to distribute what he had collected in excess, but how to keep it. By force of thinking he found a solution, which made him consider himself wise. How prudent he was to think about it and how wise to discover it! But what did he think was wise? I will tear down the old barns and make new, larger ones and fill them, and I will say to my soul, What will you say to your soul? My soul, you have many goods stored for many years, rest, eat, drink and feast. This is what the wise inventor of this solution said to his soul. 6. And God, who does not disdain to speak with fools, said to him... Perhaps some of you will say: "How did God speak with a fool?" Oh brothers, how many fools do you not talk to now when you read the Gospel! Aren't those who listen to it when it is read and do not act accordingly? What does the Lord say? He called the miser who had considered himself wise because of the invention of such a project a Fool. Fool, who considers himself wise; Fool, you who said to your soul: You have an abundance of goods stored up for many years. Today your soul will be required of you. Today the soul to which you said: You have many blessings, cui succeserat regio will be claimed from you. Quid est, successerat? Magnos fructus attulerat regio quam possidebat. Quam magnos fructus? Ut non inveniret ubiponeret: factus est súbito per abundantiam angustus, avarus antiquus. Quot enim anni iam transient, et tamen horrea illa suffecerant? Tantum ergo natum est, ut loca non sufficerent quae solebant. Et quaerebat consilium miser, non quomodo erogaret quod plus natum erat, sed quomodo reservaet: et cogitando invenit consilium. Quasi sapiens sibi visus est, inventing consilium. Prudenter cogitavit, sapienter vidit. Quid vidit sapienter? Destruam, inquit, horrea vetera, et faciam nova amplificara, et implebo ea: et dico animae meae. What do you say animae tuae? Anima, habes fines bona in annos purimos reposita, requiesce, manduca, bibe, epulare (ib., 16-19). Hoc dixit sapiens inventor consilii animae suae. CAPUT V.—6.

Animae consulendum non ut habeat bona, sed ut ipsa sit bona.—Et Deus ad illum: qui nec cum stultis loqui dedignatur. Aliquis vestrum forte dicat: Et quomodo Deus cum stulto locutus est? O fratres mei, cum quantis stultis hic loquitur, quando Evangelium recitatur? Quando lectum est, qui audiunt et non faciunt, stulti non sunt? Quid ergo ait Dominus? Quia ille sibi iterum in inveniendo consilio sapiens videbatur: Stulte, inquit; Stulte, qui tibi sapiens videris: Stulte, qui dixisti anitoae tuae, Habes biena bona reposita in annos purimos:

nes; and he will be left without any good. Be good at disdaining these assets so that when they call you, you come out safely. Is there anyone more stupid than the man who wants to have many things and does not want to be good? You are unworthy of having it, you who do not want to be what you want to have. Do you want to have a bad farm? No, certainly; you want it good. Or do you want to have a bad wife? No, you want it good. Or, to conclude, do you want to own a bad little house or bad shoes? Why then do you only want to have a bad soul? On this occasion he did not tell that fool that he dreamed of vanities, that he built granaries, blind to see the poor man's stomach; He did not say: "Today your soul will be thrown into hell"; He did not say any of this to him, but: It will be required of you. I don't say where your soul will go; The only certain thing is that, whether you like it or not, he will leave this place where so many things are reserved for him. Oh fool! You thought of filling new and larger warehouses, as if there was nothing more to do with the riches. 7. Maybe that one was not yet a Christian. Let us hear it, brothers, we, to whom, because we are believers, the Gospel is read to us, who worship the one who told us these things and we carry his sign in our hearts and on our foreheads. It is extremely interesting to know where a man carries the sign of Christ, whether only on his forehead or on his forehead and his heart. You heard what the holy prophet Ezekiel said today; how God, before sending the exterminator of the evil people, sent before him the one who was to seal saying: hodie repetitur a te anima tua (ib., 20). Cui dixisti, Habes fines bona; hodie repetitur, et nullum habet bonum. Contemnat haec [630] bona, et sit ipsa bona; ut quando repetitur, exeat secura. Quid enim est iniquius nomine, qui fines bona habere vult, et bonus ipse esse non vult? Indignus is qui habeas, qui non vis esse quod vis habere. Numquid enim vis habere villam malam? Don't utique, be bonam. Numquid uxorem malam? No, sed bonam. Numquid denique casulam malam? Numquid vel caligam malam? Quare animam solam malam? Non hic dixit stulto huic vana cogitanti, horrea aedificanti, et ventres pauperum non videnti; non illi ait: Hodie anima tua rapietur ad gehennam: nihi] horum dixit; thirst: repeat tea. Non tibidico anima tua quo sit itura: hinc tamen ubi illi tanta servas, velis nolis, est migratura. Ecce, stulte, cogitasti implere horrea nova maiora, quasi non sit quid inde fiat. CAPUT VI.—7. Signum Christi in fronte intus portantes securi sunt inter malas.—Sed fortasse ille nondum Fuit Christianus.

Nos audiamus, fratres, quibus credentibus Evangelium recitatur, a quibus qui illa dixit adoratur, cuius signum a nobís in fronte portatur, et in corde habetur. Interest enim plurimum ubi habeat homo signum Christi, utrum in fronte, an ct in fronte et in corde. Audistis quid hodie Ezechíel sanctus With this Augustine alludes both to the signatio on the forehead of the catechumens (Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 10,3), a rite prior to baptism; as well as the custom of crossing oneself, especially in times of trouble (see Comments on Psalm 50:1, where the saint criticizes inconsistency).
The detachment of riches

Go and point to the foreheads of those who groan and grieve for the sins of my people that are committed in their midst. He did not say that they are committed outside of them, but in their midst2. But they moan and hurt and that is why they are marked on the forehead, on the forehead of the inner man, not on the outside. Well, there is one forehead on the face and another on the conscience. Sometimes, when the inner forehead is touched, the outer one blushes, turning red with modesty or turning pale with fear. Therefore man has an inner forehead; In it the chosen ones were sealed to avoid extermination, because although they did not correct the sins that were committed among them, they were hurt and that same pain separated them from the guilty. They were separated in the eyes of God and mixed in those of men. They are secretly marked so as not to be openly damaged. Then the exterminator is sent and told: Go, exterminate, spare neither small nor great, neither female nor male; but do not approach those who have the sign on their forehead. How great security has been given, my brothers, to you who groan in this people and grieve for the iniquities that are committed among you, without committing them yourself! 8. To avoid perpetrating these iniquities, beware of all greed. I'll tell you even more. What does all greed mean? He is avaricious when it comes to sensuality for whom his wife is not enough. Even idolatry was called avarice, because he is avaricious, as far as divinity is concerned, to whom propheta loquebatur, quemadmodum antequam mitteret Deus exterminatorem populi iniquí, misit primitus signatorem, et ait illi: Vade, et da signum in frontibus eorum qui gemunt et maerent de peccatis populi mei, quae fiunt in medio eorum. Non dixit, quae fiunt extra ipsos; thirst, in medio eorum. Gemunt tamen et maerent: et ideo signedati sunt in fronte; in fronte interioris hominis, non exterioris. Est enim frons in facie, est frons in conscientia. Denique aliquando quando interior frons pulsatur, exterior obrubescit: aut modesty obrubescit, aut timore pallescit. Est ergo frons hominis interioris. Ibi signedati sunt illi, ne vastarentur: quia etsi peccata quae fiebant in medio eorum, non corrigebant; tamen dolebant, et ipso se dolore separabant; et separati Deo, oculis hominum mixti erant. Signantur occulte, non laeduntur aperte.

Mittitur postea vastator, et dicítur ei: Vade, vasta, non parcas minoribus, maioribus, masculis, feminis: sed ad eos qui habent in fronte signum, non appropinques (Ez 9,4-6). Quanta securitas vobis data est, fratres mei, qui estis in hoc populo gementes, et maerentes iniquitates quae fiunt in medio vestrum, et non facientes? CAPUT VIL—8. Omnis avaritia, ne peccetur, praecidenda.—Ut autem iniquitates non faciatis, Cávete ab omni avaritia. I say vobis latius, quid est ab omni avaritia. In libidine avarus est, cui uxor non sufficit sua. Et ipsa idololatria dicta est avaritia: quia et in ipsa divinitate avarus est,
Against the Donatists.

The only true God is not enough for him. For who seeks many gods but the greedy soul? And who makes false martyrs but also the greedy soul? Beware of all greed. You love your things and you boast because you don't go after other people's things. Warn the evil you do by not listening to Christ who says: Beware of all covetousness. You love your possessions; you do not usurp what belongs to others; They are the fruit of your work; you possess them with justice; you turned out to be an heir; Someone gave it to you because you deserved it. You sailed, you faced dangers, you did not defraud anyone, you did not swear falsely, you acquired what God wanted and you guard it eagerly, apparently with a good conscience because you did not acquire it through bad ways and you are not concerned about other people's property. But listen to how many evils you can do because of your possessions if you do not obey him who said: Beware of all covetousness. Suppose, for example, that you become a judge. Since you do not seek what is foreign, you do not allow yourself to be corrupted. No one will give you a gift while saying to you: "Judge against my enemy." “I won’t,” would be your response. How could you be convinced to do so, you, a man who does not seek what is outside yourselves? But warn of the evil you could commit in defense of your property. Whoever asks you to judge badly and to rule in his favor and against his enemy is perhaps a powerful man and with his slander he can cause you to lose your property. You behold its power and influence; You think about it and also about your belongings that you keep and love; not precisely in those you possessed, but in those who took possession of your heart. You pay attention to this bondage of yours by which the wings of virtue are not free and you say in your cui non sufficit Deus unus et verus. Quae sibi facit multos déos, nisi avara anima? Quae sibi facit false martyres, nisi avara anima? Cávete ab omni avaritia. Ecce amas tua, et áctas te, quia non quaeris aliena: vide quid mali facías non [631] audiendo Christum dicentem: Cávete ab omni avaritia. Ecce amas tua, non tollis aliena: de labore habes, de iustitia habes: heres relictas es, donavit tibi quem promeruisti: navigasti, periclitatus es, fraudm non fecisti, mendacium non iurasti, quod Deus voluit acquisisti: et servas cupide tanquam in bona conscientia, quia non habes de malo, et non quaeris aliena. Si non audieris illum qui dixit: Cávete ab omni avaritia, audi quanta mala facturus es propter tua. Ecce contigit, verbi gratia, ut fiers iudex.

Non corrumperis, quia non quaeris aliena: nemo tibi dat praemium, et dicit: Iudica contra adversarium meum. absit; homo qui non quaeris aliena, quando tibi hoc persuaden potest? Vide quid mali facturus sis propter tua. lile qui vult ut male iudices, et pro ipso feras sententiam contra adversarium ipsius, forte potens homo est, et potest tibi calumniam faceré, ut perdas tua. Attendis potentiam ipsius, cogitas illam, cogitas tua quae servas, quae amas: non quae possedisti, sed quibus male inhaesisti. Attendis víscum tuum, propter quod liberas virtutis non habes pennas: et dicis apud te ipsum: Offendo hominem istum, multum potest ad tempus; suggeret de me mala, et pros-
The detachment of riches

interior: "If I offend this man who is so powerful in this world, he will raise a slander against me, I will be banished and I will lose everything I have." Then you will judge badly, not to seek what is someone else's, but to preserve what is yours. 9. Present to me a man who heard Christ, present to me a man who heard with fear: Beware of all covetousness. And don't tell me: "I am a poor, plebeian, mediocre, vulgar man, when can I expect to become a judge?" "I am not concerned about that temptation whose danger you have placed before my eyes." You see that I also tell the poor what they should fear. The rich and almighty calls you to bear false testimony in his favor. 3. What should you do in such a circumstance? Tell me. You have some good savings; you worked, you acquired them and you have kept them. He urges you: "Bear a false testimony on my behalf and I will give you as much and as much." You who do not seek what is foreign say: “Far from me such a thing; I do not seek what God did not want to give me, I do not receive it, depart from me. «Don't you want to receive what I give you? "I deprive you of what you have." Now try yourself, examine yourself. What are you looking at me? Go inside yourself, look inside yourself, examine yourself internally 4. Sit next to yourself, put yourself in your presence and spread yourself on the rack of the precept of God, torment yourself with fear and do not flatter yourself. Answer yourself. What will you do if someone threatens you like that? "I will take from you what you acquired with so much work if you do not bear false testimony in my favor." Give him this testimony: Beware of cribor, et perdo quod habeo. Iudicaturus is male, non cum quaeris aliena, sed cum servas tua. CAPUT VIII.—9. Rursus de periculo avari vel sua cupide servantis.— Da mihi hominem qui audivit Christum, da mihi hominem qui cum timore audivit: Cávete ab omni cupiditate; et non mihi dicat: Ego homo pauper sum, plebeius, mediocris, gregalis; When do I judge myself futurum? Non timeo istam tentatkínem, cuius periculum ante oculos posuisti. Ecce dico et pauperi quid timere debeat. Vocat te dives et potens, ut pro illo indicas falsum testimonium. Quid facturus is mode? Dec mihi. Habes bonum peculium: laborasti, acquisisti, servasti. Exigit ille: Dec pro me falsum testimonium, et tantum et tantum dono tibi. Tu qui non quaeris aliena: Absit a me, inquis: non quaero quod mihi noluit Deus daré, non accipio; come back to me Non vis accipere quod do? quod habes tollo. Ecce moda tests you, moda interrogates you. Can you help me?

Intus takes care of you, intus sees you, intus examines you; See ad te, et constitue te ante te, et in equuleum praecepti Dei extende te, et timore torque te, et noli te palpare: respond tibi. Ecce si hoc quisquam minetur, quid facies? Tollo tibi quod cum tanta labore acquisisti, nisi pro The frequency with which it appears in Augustinian sermons must be evident proof of the frequency in real life. all greed. «O my servant, whom I redeemed and set free, the Lord will say to you; whom I adopted as a brother as a servant, whom I grafted as a member into my body, listen to me: 'May I take from you what you acquired; will not deprive you of me'! Do you save your goods so as not to perish? Did I not tell you: Beware of all covetousness? 10. I see that you are disturbed, that you doubt. Your heart, like a ship, is buffeted by storms. Christ sleeps; wake up the sleeper and you will not suffer the raging storm 5. Wake up the one who wanted nothing here and you will have in his entirety the one who went to the cross for you and whose bones were counted by the mockers when, naked, he hung from the tree, and beware of all greed. It is little to guard against the greed of money; Beware of the greed of life. Dreadful and fearful greed! Sometimes a man despises what he has and says, "I will not bear false witness." «Do you dare to tell me that you won't say it? I will take from you what you have. "Take away what I have, but you will not deprive me of what I carry inside." In fact, he who said: The Lord gave it to me, the Lord took it away from me, had not been impoverished. As it pleased God, so it was done; Therefore, blessed be the name of the Lord. Naked I came out of my mother's womb, naked I will return to the earth. Naked on the outside, clothed on the inside. Naked on the outside of clothes that rot, but clothed on the inside. With what? Let your priests clothe themselves with justice. But, once you have despised what you possess, what would you do if I told you: "I will kill you." If you have listened to Christ, answer him: «Kill me? The two brothers who dispute an inheritance

Theme: The two brothers who dispute an inheritance (Luke 12:13-21). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown. Jesus Christ, our Lord, who grants love, rebukes greed. He wants to uproot the bad tree and plant the good one. No good fruit springs from worldly love, no bad fruit from divine love. These are the two trees of which the Lord said: The good tree does not produce bad fruit; On the other hand, the bad one bears bad fruit. Our word, when it comes from God, the Lord, is the sure one placed at the root of the evil tree. The same word of the holy Gospel that was read wounded the bad trees; but it prunes, it does not cut. Know that what the one who created you does not want you to have is not good for you. 1. The Lord does not want worldly greed to exist in us. No one, therefore, should say: "I seek what is mine, not what belongs to others." Beware of all greed. Do not love too much your possessions that can perish, for you will undoubtedly lose those that cannot perish. "I, you say, do not want to lose what is mine or appropriate what belongs to others." This excuse or pretext is a sign of a certain greed, not the glory of love. Of love it was said: SERMO

The criterion that God uses to grant or deny what we ask of Him is the usefulness it brings us, a usefulness that we are not always able to see, but that we must believe.

He does not look for the things that are his, but rather what interests others. He does not seek his own comfort, but rather the salvation of his brothers. Well, if you paid attention and realized, also the one who requested support from the Lord was seeking his own interest, not someone else's. His brother had taken all his assets, leaving him without the part that corresponded to him. He saw the Lord as righteous—he could not have found a better judge—and asked for his help, saying: Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. If, on the other hand, they lived in harmony, they would always have the entire inheritance, since what is divided is diminished. If they lived together in their house, as when their father was alive, each one would possess everything. If they had two properties, for example, both would belong to both of them and anyone who asked about them would respond that they were theirs. If you asked one of them: "Whose property is this?", they would answer: "Ours." And if you continued asking: "Whose is the other?", I would respond in the same way: "Ours." You did not acquire one, but you lost another, because you divided the inheritance. The soul has its own riches, as does the flesh its own. He then presents a certain rich man for our consideration as an example so that we avoid all greed. What does "all" mean? Even of the goods you call yours. Do you possess eternal life? This is a great possession! And how little it costs! Do you want to know how little it costs? Oh fool, who makes calculations on earth and meanwhile loses heaven! That possession is eternal life. When you reach it, it will be such that you will no longer be able to emigrate from there, but you will possess it always and without end. You see how big it is. Consider how little it costs. It only costs what your warehouses cannot contain, what does not fit within its walls, what is excess and for which reason you want to expand the dimensions. What then is this? What is the price of ownership? If only it were given to the poor, who are the luggage carriers! 2 You know and see that those you give walk on the earth; but what you give they take to heaven and, after having transported it there, you do not receive what you give. For for earthly goods you must receive heavenly goods; for the expired the immortal, for the temporal the eternal. If you gave them at interest and for an amount of silver you received the same amount of gold, for example, for a pound of silver, a pound of gold, what would be more profitable for you? Would you be overjoyed if you had been allowed to earn so much interest? What profit is given in our case? Consider what you give and what you receive. You give what you have to melt here and you receive what you have never to lose. Therefore, give what is superfluous in your life to receive what makes you live always. Therefore, if you noticed, in the same reading of the Gospel the Lord says: Man's life does not consist in the abundance of the things one possesses. The riches of the flesh are gold, silver, bread, possessio est! Quam uili ualet! Vultis nosse quam uili ualet? Talis possessio est, talis possessio est uita aeterna, ad quam cum ueneris,—o stulte qui in terra computas et caelum perdes!—talis est illa possessio quo cum ueneris, migrare inde non poteris, sed etiam perpetuo et sine fine aliquo possidebis. Quam magna est uides. Quam uili ualet attende. Valet quantum non capiunt apothecae tuae, quod non possunt capere, quod redundant, propter quod uis faceré amplificares. Quid est autem? Quantum est pretium possessionis? Si daretur pauperibus laturariis? Nosti enim et uides quia quibus das in terra ambulant. Quod das in caelum portant, et cum portauerint ad caelum, non quod das hoc recipis. Pro terrenis enim caelestia accepturus es, pro mortalibus immortalia, pro temporalibus sempiterna.

I will love if you are my house. Recognize and love the one who gave you, not from any good of his, but from Himself. You will have God. You will be full of God. These are the sublime riches of the soul. The riches of the body are superfluous because our body needs little to get through life. The riches of the soul are not superfluous. How much God gives you, how much mercy God grants you, how much charity God grants you, how much justice and chastity He provides you, how much He gives you of Himself, cannot be superfluous. Your inner riches are great. What name do they receive? God. Oh poor name! Having God, have you nothing? Oh rich man, if you lack God, do you really have anything? Returning again to the words of the Lord, let us guard against all covetousness. "Everything" did you say? If it's something of mine! The Lord says "everything." Were you told not to own property? Own them, but without greed. This way you will truly own them. If you covet them instead of possessing them, you will be the one possessed. If you want to have money, don't love it. If you don't love it, you will have it. If you love him, he will own your money. You will not be lord of money, but as a servant and slave you will go wherever it drags you. Are you not a slave when you are carried away by its greed? Doesn't your love for him keep you up at night? If you were a man's slave, perhaps he would allow you to sleep. If you don't have money and you are greedy, driven by your greed you spend the night awake to get it. If you have it, be careful not to lose it. Furthermore, you fear that you too will perish because of him. I think that when you had little, you slept more peacefully.

Beware of all greed. May your being poor be of benefit to you. You don't want to be rich. God is enough for you, he will not abandon you. He thought of you before you existed, and will he not think so that you may live? You believed in him, you praised him and you hoped in him, and are we going to lack what he knows we need? What he gives to strangers, will he deny to his children? Should he deny to those who praise him what he gives to those who blaspheme him? Think that when you have him, you have all things. Your Father knows, says the Lord himself in the Gospel, what is necessary for you before you ask him. Regarding the things of the body, he also spoke in this way: Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all things will be given to you as added. But do not be surprised if ever the righteous suffer hunger while the wicked belch indigestible. The first is proven, the second condemned. He who praises God in poverty is tried, and he who offends Him in abundance is condemned. The Scripture says: The rich and the poor met; the Lord made one and another. Where were they found? On a certain path. What is that path? The present life. Here the rich and the poor met, because the rich is born and the poor is born. They found each other. They saw each other on the road. Both are on the same path, one loaded, the other lightened. But the lightened one is hungry; The burdened one groans under the weight. Lighten the load. Give something of what you carry on your shoulders to the one you found, and thus neither one will groan nor the other will be hungry, and both will reach the end. Topic: The signs of the times (Luke 12:56-59). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. We have heard the Gospel and in it the Lord who rebukes those who know how to judge the appearance of heaven and do not know how to discover the time of faith in the kingdom of heaven that is approaching. The Lord was addressing the Jews, but his words also extend to us. Jesus Christ himself, our Lord, began the preaching of his Gospel like this: Do penance, for moda irasceris alteri, quando de te male loquitur: sic irascere tibi, quando de altero male loqueris. Labia tua ne loquantur dolum. Quod est intus in corde tuo, hoc dicatur foris. Non aliud pectus tegat, et aliud lingua proferat. Declines to bad, et fac bonum. Nam quomodo dicturus sum ei: Vesti nudum, qui adhuc vult spoliare vestitum? Nam qui premit civem suum, quo[636]modo habet suscipere peregrinum? Ergo per ordinem, prius declines to bad, et fac bonum: prius accinge lumbos tuos, et tune accende luzmam. Et cum hoc feceris, securus exspecta vitam et dies bonds. Quaere pacem, et sequere eam: et tune bona fronte dice Domino: Feci quod iussisti, redde quod promisisti.

CAPUT I. — 1. Tempore misericordiae utendum ad paenitentiam. Vitro fragiliores sumus.—Evangelium audimus, et in eo Dominum eos arguentem, qui faciem caeli norunt provere, et tempus fidei regni caelorum appropinquantis nesciunt invenire. Iudaeis autem hoc dicebat: sed etiam ad nos sermo pervenit. Dominus autem ipse Iesus Christus Evangelii

The kingdom of heaven is approaching. His precursor John the Baptist began with identical words: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Now the Lord rebukes those who refuse to do penance as the kingdom of heaven approaches. The kingdom of heaven, as he said, will not come with ostentation. And in another place: The kingdom of heaven is within you. Therefore, let each one receive the preceptor's admonitions with prudence so as not to waste the time of the Savior's mercy that is granted in this time of forgiveness for the human race. Man is forgiven so that he converts and there is no one to condemn. God will see when the end of the world will come; Now, for now, is the time of faith. I don't know if the end of the world will find any of us here. Maybe not. But the end of time is near for each of us, since we are mortal. We walk in the midst of falls. If we were made of glass, we would fear these falls less. What is more fragile than a glass glass? However, it is preserved and lasts for centuries. Although you fear falling in a glass glass, you don't fear old age or fever in it. We are weaker and more fragile and, because of this our fragility, at every moment we fear the accidents with which human life is full.' And although these misfortunes do not appear, time is ticking. Man can avoid a blow, but can he avoid death? He avoids what threatens him externally, but will he be able to throw away what threatens him?

emanates internally from him? Now worms appear in your intestine, now some illness suddenly attacks you. And finally, no matter how much man guards against these setbacks, when old age arrives there is no way to defer death. 2. Let us therefore say to the Lord and do what he commands us. Let us see who is the adversary with whom he frightened us by saying: If you go with your adversary to the magistrate, make every effort on the way to free yourself from him, lest he hand you over to the judge, the judge to the bailiff, and he puts you in prison, from where you will not come out until you have paid the last cent. Who is this adversary? If it is the devil, we are already freed from him. With what price? The Apostle speaks of him referring to our redemption: That he brought us out of the power of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of the Son of his love. We have already been rescued, we have renounced the devil; How is it that we should strive to free ourselves from him so that he does not make us captive to sin again? But this is not the adversary that the Lord warns us about. In another place, another evangelist said it in such a way that, if we put together the texts of both and compare the words of both, we will instantly see who the adversary is. Here is what he said: As you go with your adversary to the magistrate, do your best to get rid of him. Before sin they were a reason for glory, after it they became an occasion for shame. In fact, they were naked and were not ashamed, since they had nothing before they had committed the sin. They could not be ashamed of the works of their creator either, because no evil coming from their works had yet contaminated the good works of the Creator. Hence, the human race was born: man from man, the guilty from the debtor, the mortal from the mortal, and the sinner from the sinner. This tree symbolizes those who always refused to bear fruit. The security threatened the roots of such a tree. The settler intercedes, the punishment is postponed, offering help instead. The settler who intercedes is every saint who within the Church prays for those outside it. And what does it mean: Lord, forgive him also for this year? That is, in this time of grace forgive sinners, forgive the unfaithful, forgive the barren, forgive the unfruitful. I'll dig around it, I'll put a basket of compost in it; and if it bears fruit, good; If not, you will come and cut it off. You will come, but when? At the trial. You will come, but when? Then he will come to judge the living and the dead. At halftime forgiveness is granted. What is the meaning of digging a hole around it, if not to teach humility and penitence? The hole is ground below. You have to understand the compost basket in a good way. It is dung, but it produces fruit. The farmer's dung is the sinner's pain. Those who do penance understand it well and do it truly, they do it in the dung. Thus, to this tree it is said: Do penance; the kingdom of heaven has arrived.

Theme: The barren fig tree (Luke 13:6-13). Location: Unknown. Date: Between the year 410 and 412. 1. The fig tree is the human race. The three years are the three times: one before the law, another during the law and the third under grace. It is not wrong to understand the human race as symbolic of the fig tree, since the first man, upon sinning, covered his shame with fig leaves, thus hiding the members from which we were born. Themembersque inquam, ut eant. Non enim veniunt, ut stent nobiscum: sed cum transeunt per nos, terunt nos, et minus minusque valere nos faciunt. Talis est via, ín ​​qua venimus. DE ARBORE FICI IN QUA DOMINUS FOLIA TANTUM INVENIT. ET DE MULIERE CURVA DECEM ET OCTO ANNOS HABENTE IN INFIRMITATE (LE 13, 6-17)

1. Arbor ficulnea, génus humanum est; triennium autem, tria tempora: unum [690] ante legem, alterum sub lege, tertium sub gratia. Non est autem inportunum, ut arbor ficulnea intellegatur genus humanum. (641) Primus enim homo, quando peccavit, foliis ficulneis pudenda velavit: haec velavit, unde nati sumus; membra, quae ante peccatum fuerant glorianda, post peccatum pudenda sunt facta. Denique nudi werent, et non

conjundebantur (Gen 2,25): non erat unde erubescerent, quando peccatum non praecesserat; nec poterant de sui creatoris operibus erubescere, quia operibus creatoris sui bonis nullum malum opus suum miscuerant. Natum est ergo inde genus humanum: homo de homine, obnoxius de debitore, mortalis de mortale, peccator de peccatore. Hos ergo appellat in hac arbore, qui per omne tempus fructum will give noluerunt; et inminebat securis radicibus arboris infructuosae. Intercedit colonus: differtur supplicium, ut adhibeatur auxilium. Quod autem intercedit colonus, omnis sanctus intra ecclesiam orat pro eis qui sunt extra ecclesiam. Et quid hoc, dominate, resign illi et hoc anno? Id est, tempore isto sub gratia part peccatoribus, part infidelibus, part sterilibus, part infructuosis. Circumfodio ei, et adhibeo cophinum stercoris: si fecerit fructum, bene; si minus, veniens amputabis eam (Luke 13:8-9). Come, when? In iudicium. Come, when? Inde venturus est indicare vivos et mortuos. Interim mode parcitur. Quid est autem, fossam circumfodere, nisi humilitatem, paenitentiam docere? Fossa enim humilis terra est. Cophinum stercoris in bono intellege. Sordes sunt, sed fructum dant. Sordes cultris, dolor est peccatoris: qui agunt paenitentiam, in sordibus agunt, si tamen intellegant, et veraciter agant. Huic ergo arbori dicitur: agite paenitentiam, adpropinquavit enim regnum caelorum (Mt 3,2).

2. What does the woman who had been ill for eighteen years symbolize? Remember. God completed his work in six days. Three times six make eighteen. Topic: Guests who refuse to attend (Luke 14, 16-24). Place: Carthage, Restituta basilica. Date: Between the year 411 and 420. L. These holy readings have been proposed to us so that you can listen to them and so that we, with the help of the Lord, can say something about them. In the Apostle's reading, thanks are given to the Lord for the faith of the Gentiles, precisely because it is his work. In the psalm we said: God of virtues, convert us to you, show us your face and we will be saved. In the Gospel we have been invited to a dinner; rather, others were called, we were not called, but led. Not only led, but also coerced. So we have heard that a certain man prepared a great dinner. Who is that man if not the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus? He had sent people to bring the guests; for them to come, since it was time. Who are the guests if not those called by the prophets, who had been sent previously? How long has it been since the prophets were sent and invited to Christ's supper? Wouldn't it have been enough to say "I bought oxen"? Without a doubt there is something here whose darkness incites us to investigate and understand it, and since it is as if closed, it invites us to knock. The five yoke of oxen are the bodily senses. It is known to all that the senses of the flesh are five. If some have not realized it, when it is explained to them they later recognize it. Therefore, there are five senses in the body: sight in the eyes; the ear in the ears; the smell in the nostrils; the taste on the palate and the touch in all the members. With sight we perceive white, black, any kind of color, light, dark. With our ears we perceive noise, both strident and harmonious. With smell we perceive what smells soft or strong. With taste the bitter and the sweet. With touch we feel hard and soft, soft and rough, hot and cold, heavy and light. There are five senses and they are even. This is easily seen in the first three, since there are two eyes, two ears, and two nostrils. There are three yoke. In the jaws, that is, in the sense of taste, there is a certain duplication, because nothing is perceived by taste if the tongue and the palate do not touch it. Hence, although vision belongs to the eyes, nevertheless, we are used to saying that we see through the other senses. As? First of all, with regard to the eyes themselves, you usually say: 'See how white this is; look and see how white. This belongs to the eyes. However, what is specific to each one of them does not apply to the others. «Look and see how white it is; listen and see how sonorous; smell and see how soft it is; taste and see how sweet it is; touch and see how morbid. Although he was still preparing to speak to his father, saying within himself: I will get up and go and tell him, his father, knowing from afar his thoughts, went out to meet him. What does it mean to go out to meet him if not to anticipate him with his mercy? While he was still far away, he says, his father came out to meet him, moved by mercy. Why was he moved with mercy? Because the son had already confessed his misery. And running towards him he fell on his neck. That is, he put his arm around his son's neck. The arm of the Father is the Son; He gave him, therefore, to carry Christ, a burden that does not weigh, but rather relieves. My yoke is easy, he said, and my burden is light. He leaned on the upright one and leaning on it did not allow him to fall again. So light is the burden of Christ, that not only does it not oppress, but it relieves. And not like the loads that are called light: although they are certainly less heavy, they still have their weight. It is one thing to carry a heavy load, another to carry it light, and another to carry no load at all. He who carries a heavy burden is seen to be oppressed; He who wears a light one feels less oppressed, but always oppressed; He who, on the other hand, does not carry any burden, is seen to walk with his shoulders unencumbered. The burden of Christ is not of this style. It is advisable that you wear it, to feel lightened; If you get rid of it you will find yourself oppressed. Those who do not play in unison, dissent; those who agree, play at the same time. Who does not delight in this holy symphony, that is, the voices going in agreement, not each one on its own, without anything inappropriate or out of tune that could offend the ear of a connoisseur? Concord belongs to the essence of the choir. In the choir what pleases is the only voice that is the result of many others, which, coming from all of them, maintains unity, without dissonances or discordant tonalities. 1. The admonition that is given to us must be passed on to others. The recent evangelical reading invited us to become friends with the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive those who make them into eternal tabernacles. Who are those who are to possess the eternal tabernacles, but the saints of God? And who are those who are to be received by them in such tabernacles, but those who relieve their need and joyfully supply what they need? Let us remember, then, that in the last judgment God has to say to those who are on his right: I was hungry and you gave me food and the other things that you know. When asked when they offered him such services, he will respond: When you did it to one of my little ones, you did it to me. These little ones are those who receive in the eternal tabernacles. He said that to those on the right, who had done it, and he said the same thing to those on the left, who had not done it. But what did those on the right who did it receive or, better yet, what will they receive? Come, he said, receive the kingdom prepared for you since the creation of the world. But what does it mean that they make friends with the mammon of iniquity? What is the mammon of iniquity? First of all, what is mammona? It is not a Latin word. It belongs to the Hebrew language, a relative of the Punic language 2. These languages ​​are related to each other due to a certain similarity in meaning. What the Punics call mammon, the Latins call profit. What the Hebrews call mammona, in Latin is called riches. To express it in our language, this is what our Lord Jesus Christ says: Make friends with the riches of iniquity. Some, misunderstanding this sentence, steal what belongs to others and distribute what is stolen to the poor, thinking that in this way they fulfill what is commanded. They say, then: the mammon of iniquity consists in stealing other people's things; giving some of it especially to the needy saints is equivalent to making friends with the mammon of iniquity. This way of understanding the text must be manducare. Quando uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis (Mt 25, 4540). Hi sunt minimi. Quare minimi? Quia humiles, quia non elati, non superbi. Appende minima istos, et serious pondus invenies. CAPOT II.—2. Mammona iniquitatis. See how he runs who is quick to make friends with the mammon of iniquity. And so as not to find himself guilty for any other chapter, he says: If I take anything from anyone, I will return fourfold. Ut accipiat veniam, de se ipso exigit poenam; et recte dicit Deo: Averte oculos tuos a peccatis meis, quoniam peccatum meum ego agnosco (Ps 5, 11.5). Si tu agnoscis, et ille ignoscit. Qui faciebatis, nolite faceré: non licet. CAPUT III.—3. Zacchaeus imitandus.—Sed iam si fecistis, et pecunias such habetis, et inde sacedlos implestis, inde thesaurizabatis: de malo est quod habetis, iam nolite malum addere, et facite vobis amicos de mammona iniquitatis. Numquid Zacchaeus de bonus habebat? Legite et videte. Maior erat publicanorum, id est, cui vectigalia publica conferebantur: inde habebat divitias. Multos praesserat, multis abstulerat, fines congesserat. Intravit domum eius Christus, et venit salus super domum eius: sic enim ait ipse Dominus, Hodie salus domui huic jacta est. Sed ipsam salutem videte.

Primo desiderabat Dominum videre, quia statura parvus erat: sed turba impediente ascendit in arborem sycomori, et vidit transeuntem. Ule autem aspexit eum, et ait: Zacchaee, descend; I gave you an opportunity to help me. You hang, sed I don't suspend you, hoc est, I don't differentiate you. Volebas videre transeuntem, hodie me apud te invenies inhabitantem. Ingressus is ad eum Dominus: repletus ille gaudio ait: Dimidium rerum mearum do pauperibus. Ecce quomodo currit, qui currit facete amicos de [650] mammona iniquitatis. Et ne reus aliunde teneretur: Si cui aliquid tuli, ait, quadruplum reddam (Luke 19,2.9). Inflixit sibi con-

condemnation to avoid incurring condemnation. Therefore, with what you have that comes from evil, do good. It can also be understood in another way. I won't shut her up. The mammon of iniquity is the riches of the world, wherever they come from. In whatever way they are accumulated, they are riches of iniquity. What does “they are riches of iniquity” mean? It is money that iniquity calls by the name of riches. If you are looking for true riches, there are others. Job abounded in them even though he was naked, when his heart was full of God and, having lost everything, he uttered praises to God, like precious stones. Of what treasure if he possessed nothing? Those are the true riches. Only iniquity calls the others that way. If you have them, I don't blame you: an inheritance came, your father was rich and he bequeathed them to you. You acquired them honestly. You have your house full as the fruit of your sweat; I don't blame you. However, do not call them riches, because if you do so, you will love them, and if you love them, you will perish with them. Lose them, so as not to perish; donate them, to acquire them; sow them, to reap them. Do not call them riches, because they are not true. They are full of poverty and always subject to misfortunes. How can we call wealth what makes you fear the thief, makes you feel

fear of your servant, fear that I will kill you, take them and flee? If they were true riches, they would give you security. 5. Therefore, true riches are those that, once possessed, we cannot lose. And so as not to fear the thief because of them, let them be where no one takes them. Listen to the Lord: Store up your treasures in heaven, where the thief has no access. Then they will be real riches: when you change their place. While they are on earth, they are not riches. But the world, iniquity, calls them riches. That is why God calls them mammon of iniquity, because it is iniquity that calls them riches. Listen to the psalm: Lord, deliver me from the hand of the children of strangers, whose mouth speaks vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. His children are like vines planted in their youth; his daughters adorned, adorned in the likeness of the temple. Their barns are full, overflowing from one to another. His oxen are fat, his sheep are fruitful, multiplying in their travels. There is no ruin on its wall, no access, nor clamor in its squares. You have seen the happiness that the psalm describes; but listen to what it is and to whom he proposed as children of iniquity. His mouth speaks vanity and his right hand is the right hand of iniquity. Of these he spoke, and his happiness, as he presents it, is only earthly. But what did he add? They declared the man who has these things blessed. Who said this? The strange children, the aliens and those who did not belong to the seed of Abraham; These declared the people who have these things blessed. Who

demnationem, ne incuretet damnationem. Ergo qui habetis de malo, facite inde bonum. Qui non habetis de malo, nolite acquirere de malo. This bonus tu qui bonum facis de malo: et cum coepetis aliquid boni faceré de malo, noli remanete tu malus. Nummi tui convettuntur in bonum, et tu remanes malus? CAPUT IV.—4. Mammona iniquitatis cui dictae divitiae.—Est quidem et alius intellectus; nec ipsum tacebo. Mammona iniquitatis, divitiae sunt saeculi omnes, undecumque sint. Undecumque enim congregentur, mammona iniquitatis est, id est, divitiae sunt iniquitatis. Quid est, divitiae sunt iniquitatis? Pecunia est, quam nomine divitiarum appellat iniquitas. Si enim veras divinas quaeris, aliae sunt. Talibus Iob nudus abundabat, quando in Deum cor plenum habebat, et laudes Deo perditis omnibus rebus tanquam gemmas pretiosissimas proferebat (Iob 1,21). De quo thesauro, si nihil habebat? Ipsae sunt verae divitiae. Istae autem ab iniquitate appellantur divitiae. Habes illas, non reprehendo: hereditas venit, pater tuus dives Fuit, et dimisit tibi. Honeste acquisisti: de iustis laboribus plenam domum habes, non reprehendo. Tamen etiam sic noli illas dicere divitias. Nam si dicis illas divitias, amabis illas: et si amaveris illas, peribis cum illis. Perde, ne pereas: dona, ut acquiras: semina, ut goals. You have divided noli appellare; quia verae non sunt. times, propter quas times servum tuum, ne te occiso auferat, et fugiat? Si verae divitiae essent, securitatem tibi darent. CAPUT V.—5. Divitiae quae verae et quae false.—Ergo íllae sunt verae divitiae, quas cum habuerimus, will lose non possumus. Et ne forte propter illas furem timeas, ibi erunt ubi nullus auferat. Audi Dominum tuum: Thesaurizate vobis thesauros in cáelo, quo fur non accesoat (Mt 6,20). Tune erunt divitiae, quando eas migraveris. Quamdiu in terra sunt, divitiae non sunt. Be divitias vocas illas mundus, iniquitas vocat. Deus ideo mammona iniquitatis, quia divitias illas vocat iniquitas. Audi Psalmum: Domine, liberate me from manu filiorum alienorum, quorum os locutum est vanitatem; et dextera eorum dextera iniquitatis. Quorum jilii sicut novellae constabilitae a iuventute sua. Filiae eorum compositae, circumornatae sicut similarity templi. Cellaria eorum plena, eructuantia ex hoc in illud. Boves eorum crassi, oves eorum fecundae, multiplicatae in itineribus suis. Non est ruina maceriae, ñeque transitus, ñeque clamor in plateis eorum. Vidisti Psalmum, qualem felicitatem descripsit: sed audi quid sit, quos proposuit filios iniquitatis. Quorum os locutum est vanitatem, et dextera eorum dextera [651] iniquitatis. Ipsos proposuit, et dixit congratulatem eorum tantum super terram. Et quid adiunxit? Beatum dixerunt populum cui haec sunt. Sed qui dixerunt? Filii alieni, alienigenae, et non pertinent ad semen Abrahae: ipsi dixerunt populum beatum cui

did they say it? Those whose mouth spoke vanity. Therefore, it is vanity to say that those who possess these things are blessed. Those strange children, those whose voice spoke vanity, proclaimed blessed the people who have these things; what do you say? Those riches are false, give me the real ones. You disapprove of these, show me that which you praise. You want me to despise this, tell me what I should prefer. Say it the same psalm. He who said "Blessed are the people who have these things," he himself gives us the answer, as if we had said to him, that is, to the psalm: "This you have taken from us; what have you given us? Look, we despise this and that, what do we live with? What will we achieve happiness with? Those who spoke will receive it from their same things. They said that men who possessed wealth were happy. You, what do you say? As if he had been questioned in that way, he answers and says: “Those proclaim the rich blessed; But I say: Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord. You have just heard what true riches are; make friends with the mammon of iniquity and you will be the happy people whose God is the Lord. Sometimes we pass by a road, we see lush and fertile farms and we ask who owns that farm. It is said of its owner and we also say: "Blessed is that man." We are talking vanity. Blessed is the owner of that house, of that farm, of that livestock; blessed is the master of haec sunt. Who said? Quorum os locutum est vanitatem. Ergo vanum est, dicere beatos esse eos quibus haec sunt. Et tamen dicitur ab eis quorum os locutum est vanitatem. Ab ipsis dicuntur istae divitiae, quae vocantur mammona iniquitatis. 6. Verae divitiae. Colimus nos Deum, et colit nos Deus.—Tu autem quid dicis? Quia illi fílii alieni, quia illi quorum os locutum est vanitatem, dixerunt beatum esse populum cui haec sunt; what do you say? Falsae sunt istae divitiae, da mihi veras. Reprehendis ista, ostende quod laudas. Vis ut contemnam hoc, ostende quod praeferam. Dicat ipse Psalmus. Qui enim dixit, Beatum dixerunt populum cui haec sunt; tale nobis dat responsum, quasi diceremus illi, id est, ipsi Psalmo, Ecce hoc nobis tulisti, et nihil nobis dedisti: ecce ista, ecce ista contemnimus, unde vivimus? where beati erimus? Quia qui locuti sunt, ipsi de se ipsis container.

Homines enim divitias habentes beatos esse dixerunt. What do you say? CAPUT VI.—Respondet quasi sic interogatus, et dicit, lili dicunt divites beatos: ego dico, Beatus populus cuius est Dominus Deus ipsius (Ps 143, 11-15). Audisti veras divitias, fac amicos de mammona iniquitatis, et eris beatus populus, cuius est Dominus Deus ipsius. Aliquando transimus viam, et videmus amoenissimos et uberes fundos, et dicimus: Cuius est

that servant, blessed is he who has that family. Eliminate vanity if you want to hear the truth. Blessed is he whose God is Lord. It is not the one who owns this property, but the one who owns God. But to clearly proclaim the happiness that things produce, you say that that farm made you happy. Because? Because you live off what she gives you. When you want to highly praise your farm, you say: "I feed on it, I bring my sustenance from it." Look where you bring your livelihood from. You bring it from him to whom you say: In you is the source of life. Blessed are the people whose God is the Lord. Oh Lord, my God! oh Lord, our God! so that we can reach you, make us happy with your happiness. We do not want that which comes from gold, or silver, or farms; We do not want that which comes from these earthly things, very vain and fleeting, typical of this expired life. Let our mouth not speak vanity. Make us happy not to lose you. If we possess you, we neither lose you nor perish. Make us happy with the happiness that comes from you, because happy is the people whose God is the Lord. Nor will he be angry if we say that he is our property, our possession. We read that God is part of my inheritance. Sublime thing, brothers; We are his inheritance and it is our inheritance, because we worship him and he cultivates us 4. It means no affront to him to cultivate us, because if we worship him as our God, he cultivates us as his field. And so that you know that he ille us fundus? Asseritur illius: et nos dicimus: Beatus homo: vanitatem loquimur. Beatus cuius est illa domus, beatus cuius est ille fundus, beatus cuius est illud pecus, beatus cuius est ille servus, beatus cuius est illa familia. Tolle vanitatem, si vis audire veritatem. Beatus est, cuius est Dominus Deus ipsius. Non enim cuius est fundus iste, beatus est: sed cuius est ille Deus. Sed ut apertissime beatitudem rerum annunties, dicis quod beatum te fecit fundus tuus. Quare? Quia inde vivis. Nam quando laudas pro magno fundum tuum, hoc dicis: Ipse me pascit, inde vivo. He attends unde vivas. Ule est unde vivis, cui say: Apud te est fons vitae (Ps 35,10). Beatus populus cuius est Dominus Deus ipsius. O Domine Deus meus, o Domine Deus noster, ut veniamus ad te, fac nos beatos déte. Nolumus de auro, ñeque de argento, nec de fundís: nolumus de terrenis istis, et vanissimis, et caducae vitae transitoriis. Non loquatur os nostrum vanitatem.

Fac us beatos de te, quia non perdemus te. Cum tenuerimus te, nec te perdemus, nec nos peribimus. Fac nos beatos de te, quia Beatus populus, cuius est Dominus Deus ipsius. Nec irascitur si dixerimus de Deo, Fundus noster. Legimus enim quoniam Dominus pars hereditatis meae (Ps 15:5). Magna res, fratres, et hereditas ipsius sumus, et hereditas nostra est: quia et colimus eum, et colit nos. Nulla est iniuria illi quia colit nos. seemed incredible to men, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ came to convince them of it. He, being the Son of God, born of the Father in an invisible and ineffable way, coeternal and equal to the Father, and with the only Father God, since he is the Word of God by which all things were made and the Council of the Father by which all things are governed, by taking flesh and appearing to the eyes of men, he deposits on earth all his greatness and incomprehensible majesty and power that could not be known by men. Because God, that is, divinity himself, was not seen in Christ, his visible flesh was despised. He, however, proved the invisible divinity with miracles. And when he seemed such that he could be looked upon with disdain by human eyes, he acted in such a way that by his very works he manifested that he was the Son of God. Although he did wonderful things, taught useful things, corrected and amended vices, taught virtues and performed healings over time to heal the minds of non-believers, the people in which he was born and nurtured and where he did such great things, in anger, killed him. He, who had come to be born, had undoubtedly also come to die; But he did not want the death of the flesh that he had taken to give a demonstrative example of the resurrection to be fruitless, but rather he allowed it to happen by the hands of the wicked so that, since they did not want to do what he commanded, what he wanted would be manifested. It happened like this. Christ was killed, buried; He rose again as we know, as the Gospel attests, as he already announced to the entire world. You also see how the Jews still

1. Christianotum fides, quae ab impiis et infidelibus irridetur, haec est, quia nos dicimus esse aliam vitam post istam vitam, et esse a mortuis resurrectionem, et esse post transactum saeculum in fine iudicium. Hoc cum in rebus humanis non crederetur, praedicaretur autem, et antiuntiaretur a prophetis servís dei, et a lege quae per Moysen data est.

et adhuc incredibile hominibus videretur, venit dominus et salvator noster Iesus Christus, qui hoc hominibus persuaderet. Qui cum sit Filius dei, natus de Patre invisibiliter et ineffabiliter, coaeternus Patri, [142] et aequalis Patri, et cum Patre unus deus, cum sit Verbum Patris, per quod facta sunt omnia, et consilium Patris, per quod reguntur universa, tantam magnitudeinem suam, et incomprehensibilem maiestatem ac potestatem, quae non poterat cognosci ab hominibus, deposuit ad terras, accipiiendo carnem, et apparendo oculis hominum. Cum ergo deus, id est ipsa divinitas, in Christo non videretur, caro visa contemnebatur; ille autem interiorem suam divinitatem miraculis approbabat; et cum talis videretur, qui humanis oculis posset sperni, tantum faciebat, ut in ipsis operibus appareret Filius dei. Cum ergo magna faceret, utilia praeciperet, corrigeret vitia, punishret, virtutes doceret, sanitates etiam corporum operanetur, ut sanaret mentes infidelium, iratus populus, ubi est natus et nutritus et tanta ista fecit, occidit eum. Ille autem, qui nasci venerat, utique et mori venerat; nec mortem carnis suae, quam propter exemplum demonstrandae resurrectionis acceperat, voluit esse infructuosam, sed permisit (922) eam magis manibus impiorum, ut, cum illi nollent faceré quod íubebat, pateretur ille quod volebat. They do not want to believe in Christ, even after he rose from the dead and, glorified in the eyes of his disciples, ascended to heaven; when the announcements of the prophets are already fulfilled throughout the earth. But there is more; The same prophets who announced that Christ would be born, die, resurrect and ascend to heaven, all also announced his future Church spread throughout the earth. The Jews, since they did not see Christ resurrected and ascended to heaven, could at least see the Church established throughout the world. When this came true, what was previously said by the prophets was fulfilled. 2. What happens to them is what we have just heard in the Gospel: they do not listen to Christ risen from the dead, because they did not listen to him when he was on earth. This is what Abraham said to that rich man who, tormented in hell, wanted someone to be sent to those who still lived on earth to announce to their brothers what was in hell and, before having to reach that place of torment, they would live justly, doing penance for their sins, so that they would deserve to go to Abraham's bosom and not to those torments to which the rich man ended up. While the rich man, belatedly merciful, said this, who had despised the poor man who lay at the door of his house and for which perhaps he felt arrogant in front of him, his own tongue burned and he longed for a drop of water. When he lived on earth he did not do what he should have done to avoid getting there and, when he began to be merciful to others as well, it was too late. What does Abraham say? If not escutoto orb ptaedicavit; et adhuc Iudaei videtis quia tiolunt ctedere in Christum, iam postea quam resurrexit a mortuis, et glorificatus in oculis discipulorum suorum ascendit in caelum, cum íam impleantur per totum orbem temrum ptaeconia prophetarum. Etenim omnes prophetae, qui praenuntiaverunt Christum nasciturum, et moriturum, et resurrecturum, et in caelum ascensurum, praenuntiaverunt etiam ecclesiam eius per omnes gentes futurem. Iudaei autem, si non víderunt Christum resurgentem, et ad caelum euntem, viderent saltem ecclesiam toto orbe diffusam, quod utique cum impleretur, praedicta prophetarum dicta implerentur. 2. Fit in illis quod moda audivimus ex gospel: ideo enim non audiunt Christum, qui a mortuis resurrexit, quia Christum in terra positum non audierunt.

Hoc enim dixit Abraham illi diviti, qui apud inferos torquebatur, et volebat aliquem mitti ad superos, ut fratribus eius nuntiaret quid agitur apud inferos, et ante quam vendeent ad loca illa tormentorum, viverent bene, agents paenitentiam de peccatis suis, ut mererentur iré potius in sinum Abraham, non ad illa storm quo dives ille pervenit. Cum ergo hoc ageret ille dives sero miserkors, qui pauperem iacentem ante ianuam suam contempserat, et propterea forte superbus in illum erat, ipsa lingua ardebat, et ibi stillam aquae [143] desiderabat. Cum ergo non egisset apud superos quod agendum illi erat ne illuc vinoet, sero coepit esse et pro alus misericors. be quid

chan to Moses and the prophets, not even if one were raised from the dead would convince them. It is totally true, brothers; Today the Jews are not convinced to believe in him who rose from the dead, because they did not listen to Moses or the prophets; Because if they wanted to listen to them, there they would find that what has now been fulfilled has been predicted and they do not want to believe. What we have said about the Jews, let us apply it to ourselves, lest while we focus our attention on others, we also fall into the same impiety. The Jews, dear brothers, do not read the Gospel; but they do read Moses and the prophets, whom they do not want to listen to, because, if they wanted to, they would believe in Christ, since Moses and the prophets predicted that Christ would come. Let us not, therefore, when we read the Gospel, be like them when they read the prophets. As I said, among them the Gospel is not read in public, but among us. 3. You have heard, then, in the Gospel that there are two lives: one present, one future. We possess the present one; In the future we believe. We meet in the present; We have not yet reached the future. While we live in the present, let us make merits to acquire the future, since we have not yet died. Is the Gospel read in hell? If in fact it were so, the rich man would listen to him in vain, because there could no longer be fruitful penance. We are read here and here we hear it where, while we live, we can be corrected, so as not to reach those torments. Do we believe or not believe in what Abraham told us? si Moysen et prophetas non audiunt, ñeque, si quis a mortuis resurrexerit, persuadebit eos (Luke 16:31). Omnino verum est, fratres, ideo Iudaei hodie non persuadentur ut credant in eum qui resurrexit a mortuis, quia Moysen et prophetas non audierunt: nam si illos audire vellent, ibi invenírent praedictum esse, quod moda inpletum, est, et nolunt adhuc credere. Quod ergo de ludaeis diximus, de nobis agamus, ne, cum ad alios attendimus, et nos in ipsam impietatem incidamus. Evangelium, carissimi, ludaeis non legitur, Moyses et prophetae leguntur, quos nolunt audire; quod si audire vellent, crederent in Christum, quia Moyses et prophetae Christum venturum praedicaverunt. Non ergo nos tales simus, quando nobis legitur evangelium, quales sunt illi, quando illis leguntur prophetae; apud ipsos enim, ut dixi, evangelium non recitatur, apud nos recitatur. 3.

Ecce audistis moda ex gospel duas vitas, unam praesentem, alteramfuturam: praesentem habemus,futuram credimus: in praesenti sumus, adfuturam nondum pervenimus.
