Quod utique si recitaretur, frustra illud dives audiret, quia iam fructuosa paenitentia esse non poterat. Nobis ibi legitur, et ibi a nobis auditur, ubi dum vivimus corrigi possumus, ne ad illa storm veniamus. Credimus quod legitur, an non
The rich sucker and the poor Lazarus

read? Far be it from me to think that your charity does not believe it: you are Christians and in no way would you be if you did not believe in the Gospel of God. Thus, since you are Christians, it is manifest that you believe in the Gospel. We have just heard, as it was now read aloud to us, that there was a rich man, undoubtedly arrogant, undoubtedly proud of his riches, who dressed in purple and linen and feasted splendidly every day. At his door, however, lay a poor ulcer patient named Lazarus, whose wounds even the dogs licked; He wanted to be satisfied with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table and he couldn't. Here is the great sin of the rich man: the one whom he should have shared in his benevolence wanted to be satisfied with the crumbs and could not. So, if that rich man had taken pity on the poor man who was lying at his door and had wanted to be merciful with the help of his wealth, he too would have come to the place where the poor man came. It was not poverty that brought Lazarus to the resting place, but humility; Nor was it riches that kept that rich man from such great rest, but rather pride and unbelief. So that you can see, brothers, that this rich man was an unbeliever when he lived on earth, let's prove it with the same words that he spoke in hell. Pay attention. He wanted someone from among the dead to go and announce to his brothers what was in hell; When it was not granted, Abraham said: You have Moses and the prophets, listen to them, with their answer: No, father Abraham, because if it were someone from here I would convince you, let us demonstrate.

He also did not believe Moses and the prophets when he lived on earth, but he wanted someone to rise from the dead to convince himself. Focus your attention now on such and see where they will be. The example of this rich man is a warning to us, assuming there is faith. How many are there who now say: “Let us see to it that everything goes well for us while we live; Let us eat and drink and enjoy these pleasures. What is it that we are told will happen next? Who has come from there? Who has risen and come here? 1 They say the same thing that that rich man said who, once dead, experienced what he did not believe when he was alive. It is better to be fruitfully corrected while alive than to be fruitlessly tormented once dead. 4. Now let's change the words, if there is anyone among us who usually says that. God does not manifest now what he commands us to believe; and does not manifest it to be a reward for faith. If I told you, what merit would you have in believing it? It wouldn't be about believing, but about seeing. God does not show it to you for this main reason: so that you believe. He commands you to believe and postpones you seeing; but if you do not believe when he orders you to believe, he does not reserve for you the reality of what you believe in; On the contrary, it reserves for you what the rich man was tormented with. And when our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ comes, of whom it is proclaimed that, although he already came, he will return again, he will come with the reward for believers and unbelievers: to the believers he will give rewards; to the unbelievers he must

credimus? Absit ut hoc opinemur de caritate vestra, quia non creditis: christiani enim estis, nec christiani ullo moda essetis, si gospel dei non crederetis; quia ergo christiani estis, manifestum est vos gospel credere. Audivimus, moda recitatum est: Erat dives, utique superbus, utique extollens se in divitiis, qui induebatur purpura et bysso, et epulabatur cotidie splendide (ib,, 19). Iacebat autem ad ianuam eius ulcerosus pauper quidam nomine Lazarus, cuius etiam ulcera canes lingebant; et cupiebat saturan de micis quae cadebant de mensa divitis (ib., 21), et non poterat. Ecce crime divitis, quia utique de micis saturan cupiebat, et non poterat, cui partícipanda humanitas erat. Ule ergo dives, si compateretur pauperi ante ianuam suam iacenti, et vellet [144] esse de divitiis illis misericors, illuc comeret et ipse, quo venit et ille pauper. Non enim illum Lazarum paupertas duxit ad requiem, et non humilitas; aut vero illum divitem ab illa tanta requie divitiae retraxerunt, et non superbia et infidelitas. Nam ut noveritis, fratres, quia apud superos dives iste infidelis Fuit, de verbis ipsius approbemus, quae dixit apud inferos. Intend it. Voluit aliquem a mortuis iré, ut nuntiaret fratribus ipsius quid agitur apud inferos; et cum illi hoc non concederetur, dicente Abraham habent Moysen et prophetas, audiant tilos; non, pater Abraham, inquiens, sed, si quis hinc ab injerís ierit, persuadebuntur (Luke 16,29.30), ostendit, quia et ipse, cum esset apud superos, non credebat Moysi et prophetis,

sed aliquem arisere sibi a mortuis cupiebat. Attendite such way, et videte ubi erunt: exemplo huius divitis admonemur, si fidem habetis. Quanti sunt qui moda dicunt, Bene nobis sit, cum vivimus: manducemus et bibamus, et deliciis istis perfruamur. Quid est quod nobis dicitur quia erit postea? quis huc inde rediit? quis huc inde surrexit? Dicuntur haec; hoc dicebat dives ille, et, quod non credebat vivus, expertus est mortuus. Melius vivus fructuose corrigeretur, quam mortuus infructuose torqueretur. 4. Nunc ergo mutemus verba ipsa, si quis forte in nobis est, qui haec solet dicere. Non enim ostendet deus moda, quod nos iubet credere; ideo illud non ostendit, ut merces sit fidei. Si enim ostendat tibi, quod meritum habes quia credis? non est iam credere, sed videre: magis tibi hoc non ostendit deus, ut credas. Imperat tibi quod credas, servat tibi quod videas. Be si non credas, cum imperat fidem, speciem suam non tibi servat; sed illud tibi servatur, unde dives ille apud inferos torquebatur. Et cum venerit dominus noster et salvator Iesus Christus, qui sic annuntiatur moda venisse, ut speretur etiam esse venturos, veníet cum retributionibus fidelium (924) et infidelium: fidelibus praemia daturus, infideles in ignem aeternum missurus. Et dixit hoc in gospel The same way of reasoning appears in sermon 41.4 and 299 E,4 (= Guelf, 30).
The rich sucker and the poor Lazarus

send to eternal fire. He also said in the Gospel how this final judgment is to be carried out: he must place some on the right, others on the left; He will separate all nations, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats: the righteous will be on the right, the wicked on the left. To the righteous he will say: Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the beginning of the world; to the wicked and unbelievers: Go to the eternal game that is prepared for the devil and his angels. How else could the judge be more useful to you than by telling you the final sentence, so that you can not incur it? Brothers, anyone who threatens does not want to hurt, because if he wanted to hurt, he would seek surprise. Whoever says "pay attention" does not want to find someone who can hurt. Men calculate the harm that may befall them, they compare the punishments; They are the same ones who do not want to believe God who continually admonishes saying: "Pay attention." And what is the punishment here for the one who errs? It is perhaps some annoyance and some whipping, either to amend, or to test 2. Either one receives amends for his sins, lest by not amending he incur greater punishments; Or else the faith of each one is put to the test to see with what tolerance or how much patience he endures the father's whipping, without complaining about him when he punishes, rejoicing when he caresses, but rejoicing, yes, when he caresses, but in such a way that he also shows gratitude to the one who punishes, because he whips every child he receives. How many things the martyrs suffered and how many toquomodo sit in fine iudicatutus: positurum se alios ad dexteram, alios ad sinistram, et discreturum omnes gentes, sicut pastor separat oves ab haedis; iustos ad dexteram future, impios ad sinistram; lustis se dicturum, come benedicti patris mei, percipite regnum, quod vobis paratum est ab initio mundi; impiis autem et infidelibus, ite in ignem aetemum, qui paratus est diabolo et angelis eius (Mt 25,34.41). Quid [145] tibí amplius potuit prodesse iudex, quam ut definitivem sententiam suam tibi diceret, ne in illam possis incurrere? Fratres, omnis qui minatur, non vult ferire; nam, si subitaret, et feríret. Qui dicit, Observa, non vult invenire quem fairat. Homines sibi pestas conciliant, nomines sibi poenas comparant, qui tandiu diceti deo, Obsérvate, nolunt credere. Et quidem errantis poena quae hic est? Forte aliqua afflictio, et aliquod flagellum aut emendatorium aut probatorium est.

Aut enim emendatur quisque pro peccatis suis, ne incidat in maiores poenas non emendatus; aut probatur uniuscuiusque fides, qua tolerantia aut qua patientia sub flagello patris permaneat, non murmurans de patre punishante, et gaudens ad blandientem, sed ita gaudens ad blandientem, ut gratias agat et punishnti: quia flagellat omnem filium quem recipit (Hebr 12,6). Quanta martyres The Latin term etnendatorius is an Augustinian neologism that appears repeatedly in his writings: Free will III, 25,76; Letter 211.11; Commentary on Psalm 37:3, etc.

they read! How many chains, how many harshnesses, prisons, torments, flames, beasts; how many kinds of death! They trampled everything. They certainly saw something with the spirit so that they did not worry about what they saw with the body. They had the eye of faith and, directed towards future things, they despised present things. He whose eye is closed to the future is filled with dread of the present and does not reach the future. 5. There is, then, a faith that must be built in us. At present, whoever does not want to believe that Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, that he suffered, was crucified, believes, relying on the Jews, that he existed and was taken to death; He believes, relying on the Gospel, that he was born of a virgin and that he was resurrected. There are, without a doubt, reasons to believe. Not even the Jewish enemies dare say: "There was no such Christ in our race," or "There was no man whom I do not know and whom Christians worship." "He existed, they say, and our parents killed him, and he died as the man he was." If we find that the things that followed his death were predicted by the prophets, namely: that the whole world was to follow his name, that all the peoples and all the countries of the nations were to worship him, that all the kings were also going to be subjected to his yoke, and we see that after the death of Christ all those things that had been predicted before his birth have been fulfilled, how can we fall into the deception of not wanting to believe what remains, having seen that many other things were fulfilled? have they already fulfilled between us? Ourselves, brothers, not only those of us who are passi sunt, quanta toleraverunt! quas catenas, quos squalores, quos carceres, quos cruciatus, quas flammas, quas bestias, quae genera mortís! Calcaverunt omnia. Videbant enim aliquid spiritu, ut quod videbant corpore non curarent: erat in illis oculus fidei, tendebatur oculus infutura, contemnebant praesentia. Cuius autem oculus de futuris extinctus est, expavescit ad praesentia, et non pervenit adfutura. 5. Est ergo fides, quae aedificatur in nobis. Modo quicumque non vult credere quia natus est Christus de Maria virgine, quia passus est, quia crucifixus est, credat Iudaeis quia Fuit et occisus est, credat gospel quia de virgine natus est et resurrexit: est enim unde credat. Et inimici Iudaei non audent dicere, Non Fuit Christus in gente nostra; aut, Non fuet iste homo nescio quis, quem colunt christiani. Fuit, dicunt, et parentes nostri occiderunt illum, et mortuus est ut homo.

Si ea quae consecuta sunt mortem ipsius invenimus dicta a prophetis, quia in nomen eius cursurus erat totus mundus, quia adoraturae illum erant omnes gentes et omnes patriae gentium (cf. 21,28), quia omnes etiam reges sub íugum ipsius mittendi erat, et videmus impleta post mortem Christi quae praedicta erant ante nativitatem Christi, quomodo nos fallimus, si cetera credere nolumus, cum videamus tumba in nobis impleta? Nos enim ipsi, fratres, non soli nos qui hic sumus christiani, (923), nos totus [146] mundus sumus moda. Ante paucos annos non eramus; et mirum est S.Ag. 10

Christians in this city, we, Christians, are the whole world. A few years ago we were not and it is wonderful how it has happened that those who for centuries were not Christians are now. We read it in the prophets; lest we judge that it occurred by chance, we find that it had been predicted. In this way our faith increases, is edified and strengthened. There is no one to say: "It happened suddenly." As? Look at this thing that never existed on earth. In Scripture God sometimes becomes a debtor to the Jews, but in due time he had to pay his debt. Where did God contract his debt? Had he received a loan from someone, the one who also gives everything to everyone, the one who made the things he gives? There were not even men to whom I could give something. Someone may say: "God granted me these goods because of my merits." Think a little: he granted you those goods for your merits. That you existed, to whom was it granted? What did he give you that didn't exist? That you exist is a free gift; Before you existed you didn't deserve it. Trust him who deigned to give you the other things free of charge as well. We have, therefore, the grace of God and the whole world had in a certain way God as its debtor; Better yet, he didn't have it because he didn't know the deposit he had posted. He became a debtor with his promise, not because he received any loan 3. For there are two ways one addresses a debtor: "Return what you received or what you promised." Since, with reference to what God promised, one cannot say "Return"—he received nothing from the man who gave him everything—it only remains that he is a debtor because he deigned to promise. quomodo factum sit, ut quod per tot saecula noneront moda sint. Legimus illud in prophetis: ne putemus casu evenisse, invenimus praedictum esse. Hinc enim augetur fides nostra, hinc aedificatur, hinc comfortatur. Nemo est qui dicat, Súbito accidit. Where? Ecce hoc quod numquam Fuit in terra. Nonnunquam in scripturis debitor ín illis deus tenebatur, sed tempore suo debitum redditurus. Unde autem debenbat deus? an ab aliquo mutuum acceperat, qui omnibus omnia insuper donat, qui fecit quibus donaret? Non enim vel ipsi nomines, quibus aliqua donarentur, erant. Potest aliquis dicere, Meritis meis deus con^ cessit haec bona? Puta, concessit meritis tuis bona ista. Ut esses, cui concessit? Who weren't you, quid tibi donavit? Ut esses gratis: non enim Dromerueras illud, ante quam esses. Crede ei, quia et cetera gratis tibi donare dignitus est.

Habemus ergo gratiam dei, et tenebat deum quodam moda debitorem mundus totus; immo non tenebat, quia cautionem quam fecerat nesciebat. Promittendo se fecit debitorem, non mutuum accipiendo. Nam duobus modis dicitur debitor: Redde quod accepísti, aut quod promisisti. Quia quod promisit deus, non potest dici, Redde—nihil enim ab homine accepit, qui totum homini dedit—restat ut debitor non sit, nisi quia polliceri dignitatus est.
See the note to sermon 110,4.
The rich sucker and the poor Lazarus

6. This promise was recorded in the Scriptures, Scriptures that were possessed only by the Jewish people who God wanted to be born from the flesh of his servant, of his faithful servant, of the one who believed in him. How did that town emerge? Of the old Abraham and the barren Sarah. That she gave birth, that the same Isaac from whom the Jewish people came was born, was a miracle. The old man did not expect anything from his members, nor did he dare to expect anything from the sterility of his spouse. God offered him something he did not count on and he trusted the God who offered it to him, who had not dared to expect it from him (God). After having believed, when the child had been born to him, from whom—as he expected—an immense offspring was going to emerge, God asked him to sacrifice the son. Abraham's faith was so great that he did not hesitate to sacrifice his only son on whom the promise was based. Did he doubt? Did he perhaps say to God: “Lord, it was a great gift from you to have granted me a son in my old age; Unexpectedly, satisfying my great desires, with great joy a son was born to me, and now you demand that I put him to death? Wouldn't it have been better if you hadn't given it to me, rather than taking it away after it was granted? He didn't say this; On the contrary, he believed in the usefulness of everything he saw wanted by God. This is faith, brothers. Without a doubt, that poor man was elevated to the bosom of Abraham, and that rich man was taken to the torments of hell. So that you may realize that sin was not in riches, consider that Abraham, in whose bosom Lazarus rested, was rich. As Scripture teaches, he was rich here on earth: he possessed much gold, much silver, many heads of cattle, numerous 6. Haec pollicitatio in scripturis erat: hae scripturae in una gente Iudaea, quam elegit nasci de carne servi sui, fidelis sui, qui in illum credidit. Et quomodo gens illa nata est? De Abraham sene, et de Sarra sterili: ut parturiretur, ut nasceretur ipse Isaac, unde venit gens Iudaeorum, miraculum fit. Nihil de membris suis senex sperabat, nihil de sterelitate coniugis suae opte audebat; quod omnino non computabat, deus illi obtulit, et offerenti deo credidit, qui a deo optere non ausus est. Et cum credidisset, et natus ei esset filius, de quo credidit nascituram innumeram prolem, petiit deus ipsum filium immolari sibi. Tantae autem fidei Fuit Abraham, ut non dubitaret immolare unicum, de quo acceperat promissum.

Numquid haesitavit et dixit deo: Domine, pro magno mihi concessisti filium in senectute; pro magnis votis, pro magna laetitia, insperato mihi natus est filius: hunc exigís ut occidam? nonne melius erat ut non dares, quam ut datum auferres? Non haec dixit, sed credidit useful esse, quicquid deum videbat velle. Haec est fides, fratres. Certe pauper ille in sinum Abrahae sublatus [147] est, et dives ule ad storm inferorum. Ut sciatis non in culpa esse divitias, Abraham dives erat, in cuius sinu Lazarus requiescebat. Dives hic erat in terra, sicut habemus docentum scripturam: habebat multum auri, argenti, pecorum, familiae; dives erat, sed superbus non erat. Ut noveritis quia in divite

family. He was rich, but he was not arrogant. This shows that in the rich man only pride was tormented, only vices. They, not the goods that come from God, had deserved the punishment; These are good, whoever receives them; But whoever uses them well receives a reward and whoever uses them poorly is rewarded with punishment. Pay attention to how Abraham possessed wealth. Did he save them, perhaps, for his children? What would be his contempt for them, if he offered his own son to God who ordered it! 7. Therefore, this Scripture to which God had made himself a debtor with his promise remained hidden from the Jews. Our Lord Jesus Christ came. He was born in accordance with the same Scripture, because in accordance with it the promise was fulfilled; He suffered according to the Scripture because in it he was announced as one who would suffer; He was resurrected according to the Scripture because in it he was announced as the one who would be resurrected; according to the same Scripture, he ascended into heaven, because in it he was announced in this way. After his ascension, ignored by the Jews, he began to send his apostles to the towns and in a certain way awaken the sleepers, saying: "Rise, collect the debt that was once promised to you." Who is the one who wakes up his creditor and returns what he owes him? It was not the people who rose up on their own initiative, relying on the fact that they had God as their debtor; They were called, they began to put their eyes on the Scripture and found in it that what they were receiving had been prosola torquebatur superbia, sola torquebantur vitia. Ipsa meruerant poenam, non substantia dei: substantiada enim dei bona, cuicumque datura fuerit; sed bene utenti merces acquiritur, male utenti poena retribuitur. Attendite autem, quomodo habebat Abraham divitias. Numquid filiis suis servabat? Si ipsum filium iubente deo obtulit, divitias quomodo contempsit? 7. Ergo haec scriptura, ubi se deus promittendo fecerat debitorem, latebat apud ludaeos. Venit dominus noster lesus Christus, secundum ipsam scripturam natus, quia secundum ipsam redditus; secundum ipsam scripturam passus, quia in ipsa praenuntiatus passurus: secundum ipsam scripturam resurgens, quia in ipsa praenuntiatus resurrecturus: secundum ipsam scripturam ascendens in caelum, quia in ipsa praenuntiatus ascensurus.

Postea quam ascendit ignoratus a Iudaeis, coepit mittere apostólos, suos ad gentes, et quodam moda excitare dormientes, et dicere: Surgite, recipite debitum quod olim vobis promissum est. Quis est qui excitat creditorem suum, et offert illi quod deben? Non enim gentes, quia debitorem habebant deum, surrexerunt: vocatae sunt, in scripturam intendere coeperunt, et ibi invenire quia quod accipiebant iam olim ipsis promissum erat. Acceperunt Christum promissum, et exhibitum; acceperunt gratiam dei, Spiritum sanctum promissum, et exhibitum; acceperunt ipsam ecclesiam per omnes gentes dispersa, promissam et exhibitam.
The rich sucker and the poor Lazarus

already inserted previously. They received Christ who had been promised to them and was now manifesting himself to them; They received the same Church extended to all peoples, promised and manifested. God had promised the destruction of the idols that the people worshiped. This is how it is read in Scripture and you can find it there. Now you see how God has accomplished in our times 4 what he had promised so many thousands of years before. Men had turned from him by whom they had been made to that which they themselves had made. Since he who does a thing is always better than the thing done, for that very reason God is better; better not only than the man whom he made, but also better than all the angels, virtues, powers, seats, thrones 5 and dominions, because he created them all, just as anything he does is inferior to man. Men had reached the point of madness of worshiping an idol, they who should be condemned even if they worshiped the one who made the idol. It is indisputable, brothers, that the craftsman is better than the idol he made; However, even though men who worship the craftsman are abominable, they worship the same idol made by the craftsman. They would be abominable if they worshiped the craftsman, but they would be better than those who worship the idol. If, then, the best are condemned, how many will my tears be for the worst! If I said that he who worships the craftsman must be condemned, what must be the condemnation of he who abandons the craftsman and worships the idol, who certainly abandons the best and turns to the inferior! Who is the Idola, quae colebant gentes, promiserat deus se eversurum; legitur in scripturis, ibi illud invenís. Videtis quemadmodum hoc temporibus nostris fecit deus, quod ante tot milia annorum promisit. Etenim converterant se homines, ab eo a quo facti erant, ad illud quod ipsi fecerant: et cum sit semper melior qui facit quam illud quod facit, ideo melior est deus, non solum homine quem fecit, sed ómnibus angelis, virtutibus, potestatibus, sedibus, thronis, dominatio[148]nibus, quia omnia ipse condidit; ut sit inferius quicquid facit homo, quam est ipse homo. Ad tantam dementiam ducti weret homines, ut adorarent idolum; qui damnari debenrent si adorarent fabrum, qui fecerat idolum. Manifestujn est, fratres, quia faber melior quam idolum quod fecit; et, cum detestandi essent homines, si fabrum adorarent, ipsum idolum adorant, quod factum est a fabro.

Detestandi essent adoring fabrum; sed meliores essent, quam qui adorant idolum. If ergo damnantur meliores, how do I plan worse? Si vero adorantem fabrum damnandum esse dixi, qui dimittit fabrum et adorat idolum, qui utique meliorem dimisit et ad inferiorem se contulit, quomodo damnandus est? Sed quem meliorem cousin resign? Deum, a quo ipse factus est. Imaginem dei quaerit? In se habet: non It is alluding to the laws against idols of the year 399.
Note that Augustine separates the Sees from the Thrones. On imperfect Augustinian angelology, see Enquiridion 58.

better who he first abandoned? God, by whom it was created. Do you seek the image of God? He has it in himself; The craftsman could not make the image of God, but God could make an image of himself. He did not make anything other than yourself, but made you in his image. Therefore, by worshiping the image of man that the craftsman made, you break the image of God, which God impressed on yourself. Therefore, when he calls you to return, he wants to give you back that image that you, rubbing it in a certain way with earthly ambition, lost and obscured. 8. This is where it comes from, brothers, that God seeks his image in us. This was what he remembered to those Jews who presented him with a coin. When they said to him: "Sir, is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?", his first intention was to tempt him; If he said "it is lawful," he would be accused of wanting Israel to live under a curse, wanting it to be subject to tribute, to be under the yoke of another king and pay taxes. If, on the other hand, he said "it is not lawful to pay tribute," they would accuse him of ordering something against Caesar and of being the cause of them not paying the taxes due as a subject people. He knew that they were tempting him; He knew, so to speak, the truth from the falsehood and with a few words he exposed the lie coming from the mouths of liars. He did not pronounce the sentence against them through his mouth, but let them themselves pass it against him, according to what is written: By your words you will be declared righteous and by them you will be declared innocent. Why do you tempt me, you hypocrites?, he said to them. Show me the coin. enim potuit faceré faber imaginem dei, sed deus potuit faceré imagine sibi. Non fecit autem aliud tibi, sed te ipsum fecit ad imaginem suam. Adoring autem imaginem hominis, quam fecit ía(927)ber, conteris imaginem dei, quam tibi inpressit deus. Ideo, cum te vocat ut redeas, reddere tibi vult illam imaginem, quam tu ipse cupiditate terrena quodam moda confricando perdidisti et obsoletasti. 8. Inde est, fratres, quod imaginem suam a nobis quaerit deus; hoc commemorat Iudaeos illos, quando illi obtulerunt nummum. Primo enim temptare illum voluerunt, cum dicerent, Domine, licet tributum will I give caesari? (Mt 22:17) ut, si diceret lile, Licet, calumniarentur illi, quia in maledicto voluit esse Israhel, quem voluit esse tributarium, ut subiugatus esset regi, ut daret tributa.

Si autem diceret, Non licet reddere tributa, calumniarentur illi, quia contra Caesarem praecepit, et auctor Fuit ut non redderent tributum suum quod debenbant, quia subiugati erant. Vidit temptantes, tanquam -veritas falsitatem, et convicit breviter mendacium ex ore mentientium. Non enim dixít in illos sententiam ex ore suo, sed fecit ut illi in se dicerent sententiam, quia scriptum est: Ex ore tuo iustificaberis, et ex ore ttio damnaberis (Mt 12,37). Quid me, inquit, temptatis, hypocritae? Osteniite mihi nummum. Ostenderunt. Cuius, ait, babet imaginem et inscriptionem? Replyunt: Caesaris. Et Ule: Red-
The rich sucker and the poor Lazarus

They showed it to him. Whose image and inscription, he said, is it? They answered: Bel Caesar. And he: Give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. As Caesar seeks his image on his coin, so God seeks his in your soul. Give to Caesar, he says, what is Caesar's. What does Caesar ask of you? Your image. What does God ask of you? Your image. But Caesar's is in the coin, God's is in you. If you ever lose a coin, you cry because you lost the image of Caesar; And don't you cry when you worship an idol, knowing that you are insulting the image of God that resides in you? 9. Therefore, brothers, do not forget the promises of the Lord our God and count how many of the number of them he has fulfilled. Before Christ was born, it was promised in Scripture. He kept his promise: he was born. He had not yet suffered, he had not yet been resurrected; Also on this point he fulfilled it: he suffered, he was crucified, he rose again. Your passion is our reward; His blood, our redemption. He ascended to heaven as he had promised; He was also compliant in this. He sent the Gospel throughout all the lands; For this reason he wanted there to be four gospels: to mean in the number four the entire globe of the earth, from east to west and from north to south 6; For this reason he wanted the apostles to be twelve: so that in a certain way they would appear as if distributed in four groups of three, because the world has been called in the Trinity of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Also on this point he fulfilled by sending díte ergo caesari quod caesaris est, [149] et deo quod dei est (Mt 22, 18-21). Sicut Caesar quaerit imaginem suam in nummo tuo, sic quaerit deus imaginem suam in animo tuo. Redde Caesari, ait, quae Caesaris sunt. Quid a te quaerit Caesar? imagine suam. Quid a te quaerit deus? Imagine suam. Sed Caesaris in nummo est, dei imago in te est. Si quando nummum perdis, plangis, quia imaginem Caesaris perdidisti; When you worship idolum, non plangis, quia iniuriam facis in te imagini dei? 9. Tenete ergo, fratres, pollicitationem domini dei nostri, et number iam ex illo numero pollicitationum suarum quanta reddidit. Christus nondum erat natus, in scriptura erat promissus: reddidit illum, natus est. Nondum erat passus, nondum resurrexerat: et hoc reddidit; passus, crucifixus, resurrection. Theme: The rich epulon and the poor Lazarus (Luke 16, 19-31). Location: Unknown. Date: In the year 399 or before.

1. If holy reading fills us with salutary terror in this life, no one will frighten us after it. The fruit of fear is correction. I didn't just say "if divine reading fills us with terror," but "if it fills us with healthy terror." There are many who know how to fear and do not know how to convert. What is more sterile than fruitless fear? How all our hearts were frightened and trembled when we heard that that proud rich man, despising the poor who lay at his door, was tormented in hell, so that not even prayers of supplication could avail him anything, and when he was answered, not with cruelty, but with justice, that no one could come to his aid! At the time when the mercy of God would have come to his aid if he had converted, he neglected himself under the protection of impunity and deserved torment. He was forgiven when he was arrogant and enjoyed boasting about his riches, without thinking about the future torments in which that pride prevented him from believing and which he did not fear either. We must pass this hay to him; That is to say, all dignity of the flesh passes with the world, all this fragility ages. The hay had passed through that rich man; The flower had also passed, but if in the time of his hay and in that of the flower of the hay he had understood the Word of the Lord that remains forever, and having laid down and leveled the heights of pride he had prostrated himself before God and, in the event that he did not want to throw away his riches, he had at least given some of them to the poor who lay at his door, he would have been helped after the time of this hay. Therefore, my brothers, when I heard that voice when the Gospel was read: Father Abraham, send Lazarus to dip his finger in water and drip it on my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame, how we were all shaken in our hearts in case something similar should happen to us after this life and our supplications were in vain! When this life has passed, there will be no room for correction. This life is like a stadium; Either we win in it or we are defeated. Does someone who has been defeated in the stadium seek to fight outside of it, aspiring to the crown they lost? What to do then? If we have felt fear, or terror, if our viscera shook, let's change while there is time. This is the most fruitful fear. No one can change, brothers, without fear, without tribulation, without trembling. We beat our chest when the conscience of our sins stings us. What we hit is something that is inside, some bad thought; come out in omnis dignitas carnis cum saeculo praeterit, omnis ista fragilitas veterescit. Transierat in illo divite faenum, transierat et flos faeni; sed si tempore faeni sui, et tempore floris faeni sui intellegeret Verbum domini quod manet in aeternum, et depositis ómnibus toris superbiae et conplanatis substerneret se deo, et, si nollet proicere divitias, tamen aliquid de ipsis pauperibus íacentibus daret, (290) refrigeraretur illi post tempus huius faeni: non sine causa peteret misericordiam, qvii cum posset non exhibituit misericordionm. 3. Ergo, fratres mei, cum legeretur, et audiremus vocem in gospel pater Abraham, mitte Lazarum, intinguat digitum suum in aqua, et stillet in linguam meam, quoniam crucior in hac flamma (Luke 16,24), quomodo percussi sumus omnes corde, ne aliquid post hanc vitam tale nobis contingat, et frustration deprecemur!

Non enim est locus correctionis, cum ista vita transierit. Ista vita sic est quomodo stadium; aut vincimus hic, aut vincimur. Quid ergo? si timuimus, si exhorruimus, si contremuerunt viscera [448] nostra, mutemus nos, cum tempus est; ipse est fructuosus timor. confession and perhaps there will be nothing that hurts us. Let all sins come out in confession. But since he was arrogant then, that humor had caused a tumor, not a rash. Poor Lazarus, on the other hand, lay at the door full of ulcers. Let no one, brothers, be ashamed to confess their sins. Once the tribulation of recognizing oneself as sinners has passed, the rest of merits comes: the angels will come, take this ulcer patient and place him in Abraham's bosom, that is, in everlasting rest, in the secret place of the Father. The one wanted to be satisfied with the crumbs that fell from the other's table; He, who fed his ulcers to the dogs, was not fed by the rich man. Consider, brothers, that this is a poor person who feels need. Blessed, he said, is he who cares for the needy and the poor. Pay attention to him and do not despise him like the ulcer patient who lay at the door. Give to the poor, because the one who receives is the one who wanted to feel need on earth and enrich from heaven. Iacebat ergo ad ianuam iste ulceribus plenus, dives autem contemnebat eum: cupiebat saturari de micis quae cadebant de mensa eius; ulceribus suis canes ipse pascebat, et a divite non pascebatur. Adtendite, fratres, quia eget pauper: beatus, inquit, qui intellegit super egenum et pauperem (Ps 40,2); adtendite, et nolite contemnere tamquam ulcerosum iacentem ad ianuam. or guest? And he: When you did it to one of my little ones, you did it to me. Mercifully he wanted his person to be in a certain way in the little ones who are weary on earth, coming from heaven to their aid. So you give to Christ when you give to someone in need. Or do you fear that either such a guardian will lose something, or such a rich man will not reward? Omnipotent is God, omnipotent is Christ; you can lose nothing. Entrust it to him and you will lose nothing. When do you trust him? When you give it to a poor person. Such riches will not pass away, even though the flesh has passed away like hay and the nobility of man like hay flower. Therefore, brothers, if we have unanimously felt ourselves filled with terror, let us correct ourselves now, while there is time, so as not to suffer after this life the pains and torments of the burning flame, such as those suffered by the proud and merciless rich man; then it will not be the time to come to help, because it is not the time for correction. They come to someone's aid the moment they are corrected. This life is that of correction, this life is that of help and succor. Returned to the Lord... aut hospitem? Et ille: cum uni ex minimis meis jecistis, mihi jecistis (Mt 25,35-40). In minimis suis laborantibus in terra quodammodo personam suam misericorditer esse voluit, subveniens de cáelo omnibus qui laborant. Christo ergo das, cum das genti: ati times, ne aut talis custos aliquid perdat, aut talis dives non retribuat? Omnipotens est deus, omnipotens est Christus: I will lose nihil potes: commenda illi, et nihil amittis. When do you commend? when you are paupers. Such divitiae non transeunt, cum transierit caro ut faenum, et claritas hominis ut flos faeni. Theme: Forgiveness of offenses (Luke 17:3-4). Place: Cartago, in the San Cipriano mensa. Date: Not before the year 423. 1. The holy Gospel, as we heard it when it was read, gives us a warning regarding the forgiveness of sins. Our exhortation will, therefore, have the same object. We are servants of the word, not of our own, but of that of God and our Lord, whom no one serves without it bringing glory and no one despises without punishment accompanying it. The same Jesus Christ, our Lord, who made us when he remained with the Father and who remade us by accepting to be made himself for our benefit; Our Lord God himself tells us, as we have just heard: If your brother sins against you, correct him; and if he does penance, forgive him. And even if he sins against you seven times a day and comes to you and says, "I repent," forgive him. By saying "seven times a day" he wanted it to be understood as "how many times"; lest he sin eight times and you are not willing to forgive him. So what does seven times mean? Always, as many times as you sin and repent. Likewise, the phrase I will praise you seven times a day is equivalent to this one from another psalm: His praise is always in my mouth. The reason

Whoever you are who has your mind set on Christ and desires to achieve what he promised, do not be lazy in fulfilling what he commanded. What did he promise? Eternal life. And what did you order? "Grant forgiveness to your brother." As if I were saying to you: "You, man, grant forgiveness to another man, so that I, God, may also come to You." But let us omit or, better yet, overlook those other, more sublime divine promises, according to which our Creator will make us equal to his angels so that we may live eternally in him, with him and of him; Let us leave all this aside for the moment; Don't you want to receive from your God the same thing that you are ordered to give to your brother? Do you not want to receive, I say, from the Lord your God, the same thing that you are commanded to give to your brother? Tell me you don't want it, and don't give it to him. What does this mean if not that you forgive those who ask you, if you yourself ask to be forgiven? Or also, I dare say, if you have nothing that should be forgiven, do not forgive. Although I admit that I shouldn't have said this. Even if you have nothing to be forgiven, you must forgive, because God also forgives, for nothing has to be forgiven. 3. You will say: "But I am not God, I am a sinful man." Thank the Lord, that you confess to have sins! Forgive, then, so that you may be forgiven. Our own God exhorts us to imitate him. First of all, Christ himself, of whom he said "septies" pro eo quod est semper ponatur, certissima ratio est: septem quippe diebus uenientibus et redeuntibus totum uoluitur tempus. 2. Quisquís ergo Christum cogitas, et cupis accipere quod promisit, noli esse piger faceré quod praecepit. Quid enim promisit? Vitam aeternam. Et quid praecepit? "Da fratri tuo ueniam." you have sin", but: If we say that we do not have sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth does not exist in us. He associated himself in guilt, to also find himself associated in forgiveness. Forgive us our debts. You came to the words I was thinking about: Forgive us, he says, our debts. Do, therefore, what follows. Forgive us our debts. With what right? Why pact? Under what agreement? What autograph do you present? Just as we forgive our debtors. As if the fact of not forgiving were not enough, you are still lying to God. The condition has been established; It is a fixed determination. "Forgive me, as I forgive." Consequently, he does not forgive you if you do not forgive. Forgive me, as I forgive. You want forgiveness to be granted when you ask for it, grant it when it is asked for. These supplications have been dictated by the celestial jurist. He doesn't fool you. Ask in accordance with celestial law; say: Forgive us, as we forgive. And do what you say. Whoever lies in supplications will lack the benefit. Whoever lies in their supplications, in addition to losing their own cause, will find a punishment. And if someone lies to the emperor, when he is present he will be found guilty of lying. When you lie in prayer, with your very prayer you declare yourself guilty. God does not need witnesses at your side to convince you of this. Whoever wrote your pleas, that is your lawyer; If you lie, he is your witness; If you do not correct yourself, he will be your judge. Therefore, say it and do it; because if you don't say it, you don't get anything by asking in a way contrary to what the law establishes; If you say it and don't do it, you will also be guilty of having told a lie. There is no way to save this request except by fulfilling what is said. Can we eliminate this verse from our prayer? Or do you want the first to remain:

Forgive us our debts, and may the second part be erased: Just as we forgive our debtors? You will not erase it, lest you yourself be erased first. In prayer you say, then: "Give"; You say: "Forgive", to receive what you do not have, so that you are forgiven for what you sinned. Do you want to receive? Da. Do you want to be forgiven? Sorry. having done it once, that we must forgive as many times as he has sinned, if he asks for forgiveness. It goes like this: If he sins against you seven times a day and turns to you the same number of times a day saying "I repent," forgive him. If you understand seven days well, you will understand that it is equivalent to saying "how many times." The number seven is usually put to mean universality. From this we understand that the righteous man will fall seven times and rise again; That is, as many times as he is humiliated by any tribulation, he is not abandoned, but delivered from all those tribulations. According to that meaning, the phrase is also understood: Seven times a day I will praise you; Saying seven times a day is equivalent to saying always. This seven times a day is equivalent to what is said elsewhere, namely: His praise is always in my mouth. For we do not personally express the praises of the Lord only with the tongue, so that when we are silent we do not praise, but in all our thoughts, in all our actions and good habits we praise him from whom we have joyfully received such things. We see, in fact, that the apostles also ask that their faith be increased. Did they give themselves the firstfruits of faith and ask the Lord to increase it? No way. What they asked was that he who began the work would himself bring it to completion, according to what was said by the Apostle: He who began a good work in you will himself carry it to the end. fecisse, sed quotienscumque peccaverit dímittendum esse, si veniam postulabit. Non enim laudes domini lingua tantummodo personamus, et quando tacemus non laudamus: plan in ómnibus bonis cogitationibus nostris, in ómnibus actibus et bonis moribus nostris illum laudamus, a quo haec nos accepisse gaudemus. Videmus enim etiam apostólos petere, ut augeatur eis fides (cf. Lk 17:5).

Numquid primitias fidei ipsi sibi dedemnt, et augmenta a domino petiverunt? absit. Hoc ergo petierunt, ut qui inchoavit [233] ipse perficiat, secundum apostolum dicentem: Quoniam qui in vobis opus bonum coepit, perficiet Here the Saint seems to be fighting those who would later receive the name of semi-Pelagians, a heretical group that among other points sought to find a compromise between grace and the free will of man. In this regard, his thought was the following: in the Christian life everything is a work of grace except for the beginning of faith; Believing or not believing is not a gift from God, but the work of man alone. This position is vigorously rejected by Augustine. Read, for example, Letter 217.

Without a doubt, if you give here you will receive there, and you will receive from the one to whom you give. Do not think now of any ragged beggar, but think of: When you did it to one of my little ones, you did it to me. He who made the poor receives in the person of the poor. Receive from the person of the rich man who made the rich man. He receives what he himself gave. You give to Christ what is his, not what is yours. Why do you boast that you found many goods here? Remember how you came. You found all the goods here and, if you misuse them, you have become puffed up with pride. Did you not come out naked from your mother's womb? Give, then, give so that you do not lose what you have. If you give, you have to find it there; If you don't give, you have to leave it here; However, whether you give or not, you must emigrate. But, sometimes, greed has its excuses, although frivolous, condemnable and worthy of being rejected by the ears of the faithful, for not giving the poor what they abound in. He says to himself: "If I give, I will be left without it; Giving abundantly, I will find myself in need and then I will have to beg to receive. I must live in abundance, not only to have food and clothing for my house and my family, but also thinking about unforeseen situations: to have something to pay for slander, to

Don't be afraid, it won't fool you. «But this way, you will say, there will be no correction; Any sin will always remain unpunished. Why do you judge that you return evil for evil when you correct someone who sins? Don't think this way; You return good for evil, and you would not do good if you did not give it. Of course, from time to time correction is softened by meekness,

but the correction is made. It is one thing to eliminate it through negligence and another to soften it with meekness. Discipline be vigilant: forgive and punish. See and hear the Lord in person, think to whom we say every day the words of a beggar: Forgive us our debts. And you, do you feel bored when a brother continually tells you "forgive me, I am sorry"? How many times do you say that to God? Do you dispense with this supplication every time you say the prayer? Do you want God to tell you: "Look, yesterday I forgave you, the day before yesterday I forgave you, for many days I forgave you, how many times must I still forgive you?" You don't want me to tell you: "You always come with the same words, you always say: Forgive us our debts, you always beat your chest, and like hard iron you don't straighten yourself." But since we were talking about correction, does the Lord our God not forgive us when we say in faith, Forgive us our debts? And yet, even if he forgives us, what has been said about him? What is written about him? God corrects the one he loves. But with just words, perhaps? He whips every child he receives. So that the sinful son would not be upset by being corrected with stripes, he also, the only Son without sin, wanted to be whipped. Therefore, apply the corrective, but abandon the anger of the heart. The Lord himself, referring to that debtor from whom he demanded the entire debt again for having been merciless towards his fellow servant, says this: Your heavenly Father will act in the same way with you if each one does not forgive his brother from his heart. Forgive where God sees. Don't lose your charity there; practice a healthy severity. Love and punish, love

and whips. Sometimes you caress and by acting like this you show yourself to be cruel. How come you caress and are cruel? Because you do not recriminate sins and those sins must put to death the one you love perversely by forgiving him. Pay attention to the effect of your word, sometimes harsh, sometimes harsh and bound to hurt. Sin ignores the heart, demolishes the interior, suffocates the soul and makes it perish. Take pity, punish. 6. To better understand what I am saying, put two men before your eyes, dearly beloved. 4. 1. Reading the holy Gospel encourages us to pray and believe and not to boast about ourselves, but about the Lord. What better exhortation to prayer than this parable about the wicked judge? An iniquitous judge, who neither feared God nor respected man, nevertheless listened to a widow who pestered him, overcome by boredom, not moved roboratur: ad trabem perventura est ista fescue. Inveterata ira odium erit; iam ubi odium, homicidium erit: qui odit fratrem suum, homicidal est, inquit. Et aliquando nomines habentes in corde odium reprehendunt irascentes. Odium tenes, irascentem reprehendis? Festucam in oculo fratris tui vides, trabem in tuo non vides (cf. Mt 7,3). Sermo concludatur. CAPUT I. — 1. Fides fons orationis.—Lectio sancti Evangelii aedificat nos ad orandum et credendum, et non de nobis, sed de Domino praesumendum. Quae ad orandum maior hortatio, quam ut nobis de iudice iniquo proposeretur similarity? Iudex enim iniquus, nec Deum timens nec hominem reverens, audivit tamen viduam interpellantem se, victus

for mercy. If, then, he listened who could not bear to be supplicated, how will he listen who exhorts us to pray? After the Lord had persuaded us by this comparison, with an argument by contrast, that it is advisable to always pray and not lose heart, he added the following: However, do you believe that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith on the earth? If faith falters, prayer perishes. Who is there to pray if he does not believe? For this reason, the blessed Apostle, exhorting us to pray, said: Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. And to show that faith is the source of prayer and that the river cannot flow when the spring of water dries up, he added: How are they going to call on Him in whom they did not believe? We create, therefore, to be able to pray. And so that the faith by which we pray may not fail, let us pray. Prayer flows from faith; and the prayer that flows begs firmness for the same faith. So that faith would not fail in the midst of temptations, the Lord said: Watch and pray so that you do not enter into temptation. Watch, he said, and pray that you do not enter into temptation. What is entering into temptation but leaving faith? As temptation advances as faith wanes. As temptation declines as faith advances. But so that your charity may see more clearly that the Lord said: Watch and pray that you do not enter into temptation, referring to faith, so that it does not decline or perish, the Gospel says in the same place: This night Satan asked to crush you like wheat; taedio, non pietate inclinatus. Si ergo exaudivit qui oderat quod rogabatur, quomodo exaudit qui ut rogemus hortatur? Cum ergo nobis ista e contra comparisone Dominus suaderet: Quia oportet semper orare, et non deficere (Luke 18,1); adiecit et ait: V erumtamen cum venerit Filius bominis, whores inveniet fidem in terra? (ibid., 8). Si fides deficit, oratio perit. Quis enim orat quod non credit? Unde et Apostolus beatus, cum ad orandum exhortaretur, ait: Omnis quicumque invokeverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Et ut ostenderet fidem fontem esse orationis, nec posse iré rivum, ubi caput aquae siccatur, adiunxit atque ait: Quomodo autem invokebunt in quem non crediderunt (Rom 10,13.14). Ergo ut oremus, credamus; et ut ipsa non deficiat fides qua oramus, oremus. Fides fundit orationem, fusa oratio fidei impetrat firmitatem. [1] The Manichaeans and Scripture.—The Manichaeans rejected and despised the entire Old Testament as a whole, considering it the work of Satan and in contradiction to the New. To refute this doctrine Augustine wrote his work Against Adeimantus, a disciple of Manes (Retractat. I 22). On the other hand, his position towards the New Testament was radically different. They accepted it as divine Scripture and even used it in their anti-Catholic polemic, but interpreting it in their own way and after having purged it of everything, according to them, that had traces of Judaism. The enemy had also dropped the bad seed in him during the night (Against Faust 17,3). The original writings were corrupted by forgers (Letter 82,2,6). Their attitude in this regard was identical to that of Marcion and other Gnostic sects. On the other hand, they admitted a broader canon. From the same Contra Faustus it is clear that the Manichaeans included the Acts of Peter, Andrew, Thomas and John in the scriptural canon and reproach the Catholics for having excluded them (30,4). Due to the controversy with Felix (2,6) the Acts of Leucius are also known to us. They rejected, however, the Acts of the Apostles because they affirm the coming of the Paraclete (Against Adeimantus 17), contradicting their point of view that he arrived in the person of the founder, Manes. Augustine will reproach them for not preserving from the New Testament texts more than what is in accordance with their doctrinal system, eliminating without problems what they could not twist and accommodate to it (Letter 82,2,6; Against Faust 24,2). [2] Saint Augustine and miracles.—In the present sermon he refers to Saint Stephen, whose miracles were read publicly in liturgical celebrations. He will allude to the same fact in sermon 79. One of the changes that Augustine must note when writing the Revisions (I 13,7) has as its object miracles. In the first years following his baptism, Augustine believed that they were something already past, typical of the apostolic era, and that they did not occur today. And they were not given because they were not necessary to spread the faith, since the world already believed for the most part, this being a greater miracle than any of the others. At the same time, the absence of miracles is a guarantee of a purer faith that depends less on the sensible.

At that time, for Augustine the only miracles that existed, and in abundance, were spiritual ones: God continues to work in the spirits the miracles that in his earthly existence he worked in the bodies (Sermon 88,2,3). But in the year 415 something unexpected happens. The relics of the martyr Saint Stephen arrive in Africa and with them an endless number of wonders. The cures become very numerous. Augustine participates in the enthusiasm of the people and regrets his previous skepticism regarding miracles. Convinced by the facts of its existence, he orders that all these wonderful facts be written down and filed away to be read in the church at the appropriate time. "I made this decision when I saw that miracles similar to those of old are common in our days and that they should not go unnoticed," he says in The City of God (XXII 8,20). Such miracles will serve as an apologetic instrument in the last book

of this great work. You can read about this F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine Shepherd of Souls. Barcelona 1965, 670ff. [ 3 ] The grace of Jesus.—To properly assess what Augustine is stating here, one must place oneself within the Pelagian controversy. For Pelagius and his followers, how much good exists in man depends on his own merits. In this context, Augustine looks for an example that disqualifies, without leaving any doubt, this position. He is going to look for it in the human nature of Jesus, in the man who is Jesus. This human nature, from the first moment of its being, is united to the Word, this being the greatest gift that anyone has ever received. Now, is this the fruit of the merits of the man Jesus? In no way, because this would require a prior existence, which in this case does not exist. We find ourselves, then, before the example of an absolute (tota), unique (singularis) and perfect grace. This union of the Word with the human nature of Jesus is, therefore, "a sufficiently clear and precise document of divine grace" (Letter 187,13,40). Without that grace prior to the possibility of merit, as the man that Jesus is, he would be in no way distinguished from other men. The thought is repeatedly expressed by the saint: Commentary on Psalm 108:23; The Trinity X I I 17,22; Enchyridion 11.36; Correction and grace 11:30; The predestination of the saints 15,30; Unfinished work against Julian I 138; IV 84. See T. VAN BAVEL, Recherches sur la Christologie de saint Augustin, Freiburg 1954, 37ff. [4] Saint Augustine and Mt 16,18.—Clearly and explicitly here Augustine refers to Jesus Christ the famous text of Mt 16,18: On this rock I will build my Church. The text is not unique. Others, from different periods, repeat the same interpretation: Sermon 147,3; 270.6; 295.2; Commentary on Psalm 60:3; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint Luke 124,5. But in other texts, contemporary with the previous ones, he presents the traditional Catholic interpretation: the stone is not Jesus Christ, but Peter: Letter 53,2; Baptism against the Donatists V I I 43,85; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 11,5; Commentaries on Psalms 103 I I s.3.2; 30 I I s.2,5; 39.25; 55.15; 63.4. Finally, in the Revisions (I 21,1) he mentions these two opinions without leaning towards one over the other and leaving the reader to choose the one that seems most correct.

From what has been said, it follows, therefore, that the two interpretations are not successive, in the sense that he first had one and then abandoned it in favor of the other. And, what's more, one interpretation does not exclude the other. The fact that Jesus is the rock, the stone, does not exclude Peter from being one as well. Furthermore, Peter is a stone to the extent that he participates in the firmness of the rock that is Christ. On the other hand, the primacy of Peter seems to be deduced with sufficient clarity also from other Augustinian texts. In the present sermon (n.3) he speaks clearly of his principality among the apostles, an idea that is repeated in Baptism against the Donatists I I 1,2, and Against Julian I 4,13. The very see of Peter, Rome, is a guarantee of the apostolicity and truth of the Church of Christ (Against the fundamental letter of the Manichaeans 4,5; Letter 53,2; 43,3,7). His authority is definitive (Sermon 131,10). On all this see A. TRAPE, La Sedes Vetri in S. Agostino, in Miscellanea A. Piolanti I I, Lateranum, Nova Series, an. XXX (Rome 1964). [5] Deep meaning of the acts of Jesus.—Augustine always considers the acts of Jesus on two levels. One literal or historical and the other spiritual. Like all biblical events, those of Jesus have also been made to mean something deeper than what is perceived at first glance.

first sight. In the same way that we express content through words, God expresses it through actions (Letter 102,6,33). But there is a second aspect. An idea is always present in Augustine's mind that bases his entire subsequent argument: Jesus Christ is the Word of God. Through Him—her—God speaks to us. Jesus Christ is for us the revelation of God, and he is in the fullness of his being and his actions. He reveals him to us not only with his words, but also with his actions. A fact of the Word is a word for man (Treaties on the Gospel of Saint John 24,2). It is obvious, therefore, that each fact points to something (ibid., 8,3). This becomes more evident when it comes to miracles; In them Augustine sees the instruments that Jesus uses to, along with his words, speak to men and present to them the revelation of God (Sermon 130,1). If speaking is carried out through words; If Christ speaks to men through his actions, it can be said that his actions are words. The Bishop repeats it over and over again. They are in that they serve as means of expression and communication for us. The idea remaining unchanged, the ways it is used to express it are varied: compared to the simple facta-verb equation (Sermon 95,3) we find others that specify more: facts are visible words (Sermon 11,1), kinds of locutions (Treaties...25,5), words indicating sacraments (Sermon 136 A, 1), etc. The relationship between fact and meaning is established^ based on constant lines. We can talk about the chronological relationship that consists of updating everything: what Jesus did then, he continues to do now. But it is above all the corporal-spiritual relationship that occupies the greatest space and is most repeatedly applied: what Jesus did in the bodies was a symbol of his action in the souls. His visible actions hid his invisible actions; What he did externally was a symbol of what he did internally. There is, furthermore, the superior-inferior relationship: everything the Lord does—superior—on man or other beings—inferior—is a symbol of what the upper part—mind—must do in man on the lower part—body. In another order of things is the head-member relationship: what Christ—head—performed manifests what Christians—his members—do, should do or will do.

Normally these lines of action are not found in their pure state, but rather intersect with each other. [6] Martha and Mary.—Both in the present sermon and in the following one we find the theme of the two forms of life commonly called active and contemplative; the first dominated by "business" and the second by "leisure"; one that is a duty of charity and another that is characterized by love for the truth; one that is occupation coming from necessity and another that is softness that pro. gives of charity. Two types of life represented in the two sisters, Martha and Mary, respectively. Both ways of life are perfectly Christian and enable man to achieve his perfection. But for Augustine there is no doubt that the contemplative life is better than the active one; which is the best part, the only necessary thing that will not be taken away, as Jesus said to Martha (Luke 10:42). In effect, the contemplative life^ is a certain anticipation of what eternal life will be, the life beyond in the company of God. But although the contemplative life is better, -Augustine does not forget that the active life is often a necessity, and a need for charity. Therefore, while this life lasts, the norm will be to maintain a certain

balance between the two. If he who dedicates himself to the contemplative life can be forced to come down from the mountain due to the demands of charity (Sermon 78,3), he who is involved in action must necessarily resort to contemplation. "Only he who has fire within himself can set others on fire" (Commentary on Psalm 103,11,4). The pastor, before preaching, must pray (Christian Doctrine IV 15,32). The same must be said of the monks. Ultimately, every Christian and therefore every monk must be both active and contemplative. If he cannot do it directly, he can do it through his brothers. See Letter 48,2. And more generally The city, of God X I Those who think that it is a term of Greek origin (paschein = suffer) put the emphasis on the passion and death of the Lord; who, on the contrary, and according to truth, consider it a term of Hebrew origin meaning "passage", "transit", insist on the fact of the resurrection. These are not two contradictory conceptions, or even opposites, but rather a simple accentuation of one aspect over another. In Augustine's thought, although he openly rejects the first etymology (Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 55,1), the Easter festival contains within itself the entire mystery of the passion, death and resurrection of the Lord. All the elements of Pascua-passio and Pasma-transitus are present in their fullness. For the first, you can see Sermon 221 (= Guelf. 5) and 211,6. For the second, also the 221.1 mentioned and 231.5; 232.4; 258.2. It must be said, however, that the Saint develops the second conception much more. Easter-transitus is referred to Christ as the passage from the shame of the cross to the glory of sitting at the right hand of the Father. The word transit does not usually appear, but the thought is present. However, this idea is not the one that occupies the central place. Augustine reserves it for the "transit" of the Christian, founded on the Passover of Christ. Transit that is understood from darkness to light and, above all, from death to life. New life that has a beginning on this earth, but that will reach its fullness only after the resurrection of our bodies, if the Christian who has received that germ with faith has resembled Christ in his death.

The death of the Lord constitutes the guarantee of the future fullness of our life. Therefore, in Augustine the two great traditions about Easter come together. The Asian tradition, which, faithful to the thought of the apostle John, by considering Christ as the true sacrificed Paschal lamb, defended above all Easter as a celebration of the death of the Lord, and the Alexandrian tradition, with its conception of Easter-transit, to be understood above all in a moral sense referring to Christians and with great eschatological tension. At the same time, it is worth adding that if Augustine means the synthesis of the past, it is he himself who lays the foundations for the future conception of the Easter Vigil that commemorates not only the passion, death and resurrection of Christ, but his resurrection alone, leaving the other aspect for the two previous days that together with the Holy Night will form the Holy Triduum. The insistence of the Saint in affirming that the night of the vigil belongs to the day of Easter itself and the radiance with which that night is dressed in Augustinian preaching, already make us foresee the subsequent change.
